weeks the presidency has had regular contacts at the highest level with the leadership in both israel and palestine. a recurring theme in these presidency contacts has been the union's willingness to assist the parties in the way they wish. these contacts have always taken place in close cooperation with the hr and the un secretary-general. i would also like to stress the importance of the fact that the high representative for the common foreign and security policy, mr solana, is part of the international commission headed by senator mitchell which is investigating the current violence in the palestinian territories and which will hopefully eventually come forward with proposals to prevent a recurrence of this violence. the protracted crisis has put the palestinian population in a difficult economic and humanitarian situation. the palestinian authority is also facing major budgetary problems since the israeli government stopped the transfer of tax funds to which it is obliged under the so-called paris protocol. the general affairs council, in a statement of 22 january, called on israel to resume these transfers. the union has also, on the initiative of commissioner patten, made funds available to the palestinian authority on a temporary basis by means of additional appropriations. the human rights situation continues to be a cause for concern. the union has marched on the palestinian authority in response to the recent executions. the union has also marched in israel against the extrajudicial executions of palestinians, which have been confirmed by military means. thank you. the union will continue to do everything possible, in dialogue with the parties and also in close cooperation with the new us administration, to bring the peace process to a successful conclusion in all its stages.

likely situation for the rest of this year. as our resources are limited, we need to examine carefully how to proceed further. if we continue drawing monthly payments from the special cash facility in order to meet the current administrative needs of the palestinian authority, including payment of civil servants’ salaries, education, health and other public services, funds will very soon run out. the palestinian authority is now facing an ongoing fall in revenue and a rising deficit. they will need to adjust their policies. instead of just baling out month-to-month we need to look at how to have also worked together to develop creative solutions to the problems that separate them: jerusalem, the final delineation of the borders, refugees and the settlements to which mr solana referred. a solution to the conflict based on the peaceful settlement of differences, tolerance, respect for human rights and peace building.
mr president, in this long middle east peace process, we feel like we are on a kind of rollercoaster. again and again, slowly and painfully, we climb a slope and, when it seems that we are about to touch the sky, we plummet vertiginously to ground zero. that is - and it is also a bit the myth of sisyphus - an endless, hellish ups and downs, which threatens to wear out the strength and even the hope of almost everyone. at the moment - and despite the optimism we have heard - one has the impression that we are once again at one of the lowest points of the curve, with an oslo process that many have renounced, with the confrontation on the ground in a dead end and with elections in israel that offer particularly unfavourable prospects for peace. however, it is at such times that we must recharge our batteries of confidence and redouble our efforts. today, all this must be summed up in two statements: firstly, we must not lose sight of our essential objective, which is peace in the region, a peace which must be established and consolidated on the basis of acceptance by all of the rules of international law and the decisions of the un security council; and secondly, europe must at once assume, in the settlement of this conflict, a responsibility commensurate with our political weight, our values and our interests. it is neither dignified nor consistent to continue to renounce the leading role that should belong to us, limiting ourselves to being, not interlocutors, but mere accomplices of what the united states does or does not do. unfortunately, we've been stuck too long in the old dynamic of paying but not playing. the performance of ambassador moratinos is magnificent, but to be effective it would need political backing, which unfortunately does not exist. i believe that the union must not be delayed any longer in playing a leading role, which, moreover, should not be proclaimed merely, but should be defined precisely and be full of substance with firm commitments in political and economic terms.
mr president, tragedy is often referred to as a natural disaster, an earthquake for example. the use of the term 'tragedy' for situations such as the spread of mad cow disease - which is certainly on its way to disastrous proportions - or for the situation in palestine is, in my view, inappropriate because, in both cases, there are specific perpetrators. the terrible seismic accident that has struck el salvador or india is not comparable to the situation of frustration and humiliation in which the palestinian people live today. this situation was absurdly aggravated by people with specific names and surnames on the esplanade of the mosques in jerusalem on 29 september last. i am a friend of palestine and i am not an enemy of israel. i think that the provocation by ariel sharon last september, with the consent of those who could have prevented it, and the hundreds of palestinian deaths since then have created a climate in palestinian society which makes it difficult for president arafat to accept delayed - though perhaps reasonable - peace proposals which, had they been put forward earlier, in my view could have led to an agreement. the palestinian authority could have presented a thorny issue such as the right of return of the palestinian refugees to its own constituency as a delicate matter to be dealt with by the israeli government, provided, of course, that the latter had accepted in time more acceptable palestinian demands. it remains to be seen whether the new us administration will be more internationally isolationist than its predecessor. however, i think that clinton's withdrawal has made us diplomacy in the region less active for now. with all due respect and consideration for our american friend, i believe that this is an additional reason for the european union to make even greater efforts now to really boost its role in the area. finally, i would like to say a couple of things. firstly, i hope that the high representative, mr solana, is right in predicting that an agreement may be reached before 6 february - insha'allah - but let us not forget that sharon's shadow still hangs over the country. secondly, i have just returned from a trip by the european parliament delegation to palestine and i would like to encourage all those who can to go to palestine, to go to gaza and the west bank, to go, to meet, to look into the eyes, to listen. maybe they'll understand better.
the council. mr president, i would like to thank you for your reply. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. let me begin by thanking mr miranda for giving us the opportunity to discuss the important question of how the european union can best contribute to peace and harmony in colombia by putting his question to the council. let me also say at the outset that the swedish presidency had the opportunity last week to discuss directly with president pastrana, during his visit to stockholm, the situation in colombia and what the union can do in that context. the union is aware of the serious, multifaceted and interdependent problems facing colombia. we believe that an integrated approach is absolutely necessary to solve these problems. the union has on several occasions reaffirmed its intention to support, to the greatest possible extent and in the most appropriate manner, the efforts to establish a peace process in colombia based on respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. in its statement of 19 january this year, the union expressed its deep concern at the worsening of the armed conflict in colombia and the increasing suffering of the civilian population. the union is convinced that the conflict can only be resolved by a negotiated agreement and therefore calls for the resumption of peace talks. since president pastrana asked the european union for help in his 'plan for peace, prosperity and strengthening the state' in october 1999 here in the european parliament, the council, in response to several questions from the honourable members, has had the opportunity to reiterate the main lines of the union's position on colombia and to inform the european parliament of the progress of work on this important matter. at its meeting on 9 october last year, the council reaffirmed its political support for the efforts to achieve peace made by the democratically elected bodies in colombia and its desire to actively follow, together with the international community, the process of negotiations - a process which, in the context of consultation with civil society and with the consent of all the parties involved, should lead to a peace based on human rights, humanitarian law and fundamental freedoms. the council also announced its intention, as part of the continuation of the efforts under way, to establish a concrete and independent european programme of socioeconomic and institutional support for the peace process in colombia, aimed at promoting and safeguarding respect for human rights, humanitarian law and fundamental freedoms, improving the living conditions of the local population, encouraging alternative crops and protecting biodiversity and supporting the programme with structural reforms in all areas which are fuelling the armed conflict. at the second meeting of the support group for the peace process in colombia, held in bogotá on 24 october last year, the commission announced that the amount of community support for president pastrana's peace efforts would amount to eur 105 million over the period 2000-2006. the funds are allocated to approximately eur 40 million for economic and social development and the fight against poverty, to approximately eur 30 million for so-called alternative development and to eur 25 million to support judicial reform and support for the promotion of human rights. the commission also announced that it will increase the additional support granted to disaster relief projects through echo. the member states are still studying how much to allocate to a european aid package for colombia, but most have already announced their intentions in this matter. the commission has undertaken to coordinate its efforts to establish this package of aid. as regards the fight against drugs, this is mentioned in paragraph 8 of the parliament's resolution of 7 september last year to which the honourable member refers the union has also underlined the crucial importance of combating this scourge which directly affects all european states and their citizens. the union has established a cooperation mechanism on drugs between the union and the countries of latin america and the caribbean a mechanism whose action plan was approved in april 1999 and received substantial political support from the heads of state or government at the 1999 rio de janeiro summit between the european union and the countries of latin america and the caribbean. to facilitate the transition to other export products, colombia also benefits from the generalised system of preferences (gsp) and, since 1990, from the temporary additional preferences system. an agreement on chemical precursors was signed in 1995 between the union and the andean countries and has now entered into force. the council did not express an opinion on the contribution of the united states to the colombia plan, a substantial part of which is intended to be used to combat drug trafficking, as this is a matter of bilateral relations between colombia and the united states. finally, i would remind the honourable member of the guidelines for enhanced operational coordination between the community, represented by the commission, and the member states in the field of external aid, adopted as part of the orientation debate at the general affairs council meeting on 22 and 23 january this year. this will hopefully give us better opportunities in the future to deal in a united way with situations such as that in colombia.
commission. – the eu has offered both political and financial support to the peace initiative of president pastrana of colombia. we are well aware of the concerns that the military component of plan colombia has created especially among representatives of civil society both in colombia and in europe. the eu reservations about some aspects of plan colombia are well known to president pastrana and to his government. the commission does not intend to take part in any initiative with a military dimension. in terms of the fight against drugs we will continue to subscribe to the global and balanced approach endorsed by the united nations general assembly special session on drugs of june 1998. thus in bogota last october the eu stressed the need not to put alternative development projects at risk by non-selective operation of illicit crop eradication. within this context we continue to focus on positive measures such as demand reduction, promoting new crops, offering market opportunities in europe and strengthening the rule of law. as honourable members may know, the eu decided last october to establish a european support package for the peace process in colombia whose overall amounts should be decided at the next donors’ meeting. this package of european support covers contributions both from eu member states and the eu itself. all eu member states indicated their willingness to provide financial contributions to this package and the majority of them have already put forward their pledges. as the swedish presidency just announced, eur 105 million of programmable aid will be made available by the commission over the period 2000-2006. these funds will be dedicated to modernising administration, strengthening democracy and the rule of law, respect for human rights, protecting the environment and developing alternative crops. emphasis will also be put on tackling a series of structural problems in the country and, in particular, political, social and economic reforms. the commission will also continue to provide humanitarian aid to assist the all too many displaced people in colombia. this non-programmable aid has amounted to eur 24 million since 1997. this year it is envisaged that about eur 10 million will be made available for these kinds of interventions. these areas of cooperation are also priority areas for the government. the eu intends to make its contribution effective as soon as possible. for this reason a mission including experts supplied by the commission and the member states is at this moment in colombia in order to identify a project in an area called the magdalena medio, for which the commission could earmark around eur 20 million. in this region, violence is at its highest level and the eu initiative will target the promotion of dialogue between the parties in conflict. this will constitute effective implementation of the concept of a peace laboratory. the conclusions of these experts’ mission should be available by the end of february. apart from our financial commitment, europe is also increasing its political role in the conflict. i shall mention the presence of several member states in the group of friends which secured the meeting area with the national liberation army agreed on 26 january as well as the meeting promoted by the presidency with the revolutionary armed forces of colombia in paris on 15 december. one last word about the risk of an extension of the colombian conflict to neighbouring countries. many have raised their concerns, notably ecuador and brazil. there has been, indeed, an increased flow of refugees crossing the border in the affected areas. for this reason the eu emphasised the need for a regional approach to the drug problem and more specifically to the colombian conflict. this will be one of the major topics of the next eu-andean community meeting on drugs scheduled for the second quarter of this year. the objective will be to put more emphasis on an overall strategy in order to counter the phenomenon of the transfer of illicit crops from one country to another. summing up, we very much welcome this debate and we very much support the line expressed by mr miranda.
mr president, it is clear that the conflict in colombia, which has been going on for more than thirty years, cannot be resolved by military means. we agree, commissioner, that violence can only lead to more violence. the ppe group therefore, beyond what is strictly the plan colombia to end the production and trafficking of drugs, positively values the concerted efforts of president pastrana to dialogue with the guerrillas and the strategy he proposes to go to the root of the problem and attack the causes that provoke it. because the objectives of this strategy are the development of alternatives that will enable colombia to recover economically and socially, to resolve the armed conflict with the guerrillas, to strengthen democratic institutions, to promote social development and, ultimately, to combat drug trafficking. if violence is not stopped through dialogue, if the peasants are not offered alternatives that will enable them to lead a dignified life, if the serious problem of the displaced is not solved, if human rights are not respected, if the foundations on which the rule of law is based are not strengthened and impunity is not ended, if drug trafficking is not stopped, peace for colombia will be nothing more than a hoax. we therefore consider it essential - and we welcome this - that the european union supports president pastrana's peace efforts in line with what the president-in-office of the council has just announced to us and also in line with what the commission, through commissioners nielson and patten, had announced at the time and which we have just now reiterated to us. this aid contributes to resolving social injustices and improving the living conditions of the local population, as well as to strengthening democratic institutions. we also think it is essential that the farc return to the dialogue table and that the zone of détente be extended beyond the weekend just proposed by president pastrana, so that peace talks can continue and be concluded successfully. but it is also because of our commitment to peace and the well-being of the colombian people that we ask president pastrana to intensify his fight against the paramilitaries and against the armed groups who violate human rights and sow pain and death among the civilian population, and that we also ask him to implement the united nations resolutions on human rights, because only in this way, with the concerted efforts of all, with a really intense and determined struggle for peace, will it be possible for hope to be reborn for the colombian people.
mr president, the violence in colombia is a matter of great concern to this parliament, which has already adopted a number of resolutions in support of the peace process in recent years. a real peace process, that is to say, based on concertation between the different parties to the conflict and civil society, both ngos and farmers' organisations and local authorities, and not a plan consisting of funding spraying, which may exclude dialogue with the key actors of peace. europe has been successful in its external action in latin america when it has pursued an autonomous policy, promoted mr president, if latin america suffers from inequalities that end up generating violence, it is in colombia that this tragic dynamic is expressed with all its crude and dramatic character, to the point that i, who am a doctor and a professor of medicine, have to say that in colombia a branch of epidemiology has been created called the 'epidemiology of violence'. the european union has made conflict prevention and the peaceful and negotiated settlement of conflicts a basic principle of its international role. the plan colombia, drawn up between the united states and president pastrana, without the participation of his country's parliament, is going in precisely the opposite direction. that is why i came yesterday from the world social forum in porto alegre with a concrete commitment, which i am defending here, which is the commitment adopted by a group of parliamentarians from latin america, europe and other parts of the world, to make it clear that we must say no to plan colombia and yes to a negotiated and peaceful solution to the conflict. this is where the european union can clearly differentiate itself from other types of intervention. it can be said that the best way to combat drug trafficking is to dismantle the international distribution networks and money laundering networks. against violence, the best solution is to deepen the peaceful conquest of democracy, negotiating and dismantling the networks of paramilitary gangs linked to the army and the state apparatus. against poverty and inequality, the best solution is to advance social reform so that everyone can have rights. so the opportunity is clear to us.
mr president, there is some confusion about the dramatic situation in colombia, and it may be appropriate to recall that just a few days after his electoral victory - by the way, the biggest and most important of any colombian president in recent years - president pastrana met with the leadership of the farc, the largest and oldest guerrilla group on the american continent. it was the first time in thirty years of conflict that an elected president met on colombian soil with the leaders of a guerrilla movement. three weeks after his inauguration, the leadership of the country's second largest guerrilla group, the eln, and representatives of civil society reached an agreement in the german city of mainz. negotiating tables were opened and a demilitarized zone was created with an area equal to that of switzerland and under the control of the guerrillas. however, unfortunately, this whole period has been marked by a marked absence of peace. moreover, violence, murder, extortion, kidnapping and sabotage by armed groups of both left and right have become more widespread than ever. this situation and the widespread violence in the country give rise to great scepticism about the resolution of this conflict. what can the european union do in this situation? as the commission and the council have said, there is no other solution than to support a specific response by the european union aimed at promoting institutional strengthening, respect for human rights, alternative development, humanitarian aid and social development. i ask you, mr commissioner, mr president of the council, whether you think that colombia, in these difficult times it is living, can afford to do without the aid, the resources, that international solidarity is mobilizing. it is clear that an effort must be made and it is also clear, mr president, that moderation becomes a vice when you refuse to commit yourself. the european union cannot and must not have any other commitment than the commitment to support peace with determination. and for peace to be possible, three conditions are required: the cessation of criminal violence, the return of the guerrillas to the negotiating table - in this sense, president pastrana has made an appeal that we hope will be heard - and the firm commitment of the government to associate the actors - all the actors - of the peace process and civil society with the dividends that this peace can bring. and i think that, mr president, with generosity, with realism, with imaginative and bold proposals and, above all, with goodwill, the problem of colombia can find a solution to which the european union must give its solidarity response, as the representatives of the council and the commission have announced to us.

mr president, commissioner, if we really want to improve the environment and to relieve the overloaded european roads by rail, i think we must pursue three objectives: first, absolute separation and independence between the infrastructure managers, who must ensure the proper use of the infrastructure, and the users and service operators; second, the complementarity of the railways with other means to achieve a true door-to-door service; and third, just as there are toll-free motorways, there must be toll-free railways. the cost of transport per tonne of goods must not be a deterrent and, in any case, must be favourable to rail if we really want to change the present situation, to free up our roads and to achieve a real improvement in the environment.
the commission mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i should like to express my satisfaction - as all or almost all the speakers have done - with the final result of the conciliation. let monopoly in the member states of the union does not work. in the current situation of national rail networks, compartmentalised and divided, this does not work. and what is at stake is precisely to the commission is aware of the difficulties facing the judiciary in the member states, and it is aware of the difficulties facing the judiciary in the member states. in essence, the commission broadly mechanisms have been created in the meantime, such as the mutual evaluation mechanism, which has shown in concrete terms the need for a paradigm shift and in some cases has even led the member states commission. – mr president, may i first of all thank all the members who made such valuable contributions to this debate, all of which have been very carefully noted. i would like to say by way of a preliminary reply to what has been said, that those who spoke on the question of consumer confidence are putting their finger on an issue that is of particular importance, in addition to the issues that we are addressing today relating to public health. may i draw your attention to one particular aspect of public confidence that a number of you, in particular mr whitehead, referred to. sometimes it depends to a very large extent on where member states are in the cycle of bse as to the effect on public confidence. public health issues are crucially important but i want to address the consumer confidence aspect for a moment before i go on to the public health aspects. mr whitehead rightly observed that in the uk the level of consumer confidence is high. the consumption of beef in the uk is higher than it was before 1996. why is that the case? what lessons can we draw for consumer confidence from that? i believe it is because people see that the incidence of bse in the uk is falling despite the fact that the number of cases is still the highest in the european union by some considerable distance. so why are consumers relaxed about it to the extent that they are now consuming beef more than they were before 1996? i believe it is because they realise that the scientific advice had been correct; that the lawmakers have responded correctly and put safety measures in place and that the public authorities in the uk properly implemented that legislation and the consequence is that we have a falling incidence of bse. so consumers have concluded from that: somebody is in charge, they are doing something about it, they appear to know what they are doing because the incidence is falling. therefore their confidence rises and they consume beef. that feeling has to be achieved in the rest of europe, but it will take time because consumers do not have that sequence of events in their minds in the rest of the european union and we all know why: because a number of member states who declared themselves to be free of bse within a very short space of time after making the declaration had to then admit that there was bse in that member state. that quite obviously provoked an immediate reaction in consumer confidence because it says to consumers: the people in charge do not know what they are talking about and are not protecting me. we do not want to make microbiologists out of consumers, but they must have the feeling that there is someone in charge, who knows what they are doing and that what they are doing is effective in ensuring the protection of the consumer. let me now deal with some of the issues that you raised surrounding public health and the procedures that are needed. a number of you mentioned the question of testing. this was discussed in the council last monday. testing at 30 months remains the norm, but will be kept under review. a huge number of tests under way will provide invaluable information within a very short period of time. we do not yet have enough tests and have not had them long enough to draw the appropriate conclusions. the statistical sample is not big enough, but when it is we will draw those conclusions. this will butcher’s shop. we do not have enough time to go into detail in relation to this but i repeat what i said earlier that this is an issue that we will have to give very careful consideration to. in - the next item is the report (a5-0002/2001) by mr olsson, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending council directive 96/22/ec on the prohibition of the use in animal feeding of certain substances having a hormonal or thyrostatic action and of beta-agonists (com (2000) 320 - c5-0357/2000 - 2000/0132 (cod)).
commission. – mr president, first of all i wish to thank the rapporteur mr olsson for his report and also the committees who gave their opinion on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending council directive 96/22 on the prohibition of the use of hormones in stock-farming. the main purpose of the commission proposal is to increase our level of food safety and to comply with our international obligations deriving from the sanitary and phyto-sanitary agreement of the world trade organisation, the so-called sps agreement. this assembly is well aware that the current ban on use of hormones for growth promotion was challenged at the world trade organisation and that the final ruling in 1998 criticised the risk assessment on hormones used in food-producing animals presented by the european community. as you are aware, the commission initiated a complementary risk assessment on these hormones in the light of the clarifications regarding risk assessment provided by the appellate body of the wto. in april 1999, the scientific committee on veterinary measures relating to public health issued an opinion on the potential adverse affects to human health arising from hormone residues in bovine meat and meat products. this opinion was reviewed and confirmed in may 2000. the main conclusion was that no acceptable daily intake can be established for any of the six hormones evaluated when they are administered to bovine animals for growth promotion. as regards to the hormone oestradiol 17-b, the scientific committee found that it has to be considered a complete carcinogen insofar as it has both tumour and tumour initiating affects. for the five other hormones under consideration, the need for further information was identified. in the light of these conclusions the commission proposed firstly to ban definitively all the uses of oestradiol in farm animals in the light of the finding that this substance is a complete carcinogen. secondly, the commission proposed to maintain provisionally the current prohibition on the five other hormones until more complete scientific information is made available. this measure will be kept under regular review and is thus fully compatible with our international obligations. i am most satisfied that the report supports this approach. with this proposal the commission has also provided the necessary legal basis for adaptation of the lists of definitively and provisionally banned substances by the regulatory committee procedure in order to allow for rapid reaction to new evidence and thus further to enhance consumer safety. i regret very strongly that the introduction of the regulatory committee procedure for the adaptation of the lists of substances has not been supported by the report. many of you here know my view on this issue. i have discussed with you in bilateral meetings on a number of occasions the question of the use of the comitology procedure and i note that request by the commission is not being accepted in the amendments that have been put forward. i would ask parliament to reconsider its view on this issue, because i believe that it is of considerable importance that the question of comitology be seriously addressed in this issue. i believe that if parliament insists on the adaptation of the annexes to be done by way of codecision rather than comitology, that parliament will be guilty of not properly looking after the safety of the consumer health in this issue, an issue that parliament has discussed in this debate earlier today, both in the bse context and on this particular issue. how can we possibly justify a delay of a year and a half in the adjustment and adaptation of the annexes in circumstances where a scientific committee may have advised the commission to add for instance a further hormone to the list of annexes? how can that be justified? someone said that this is a political issue. i emphatically reject that proposition. it is a scientific issue. that is the very reason why this issue was considered in the wto. it comes as some concern to me that there is a risk if parliament adheres to the view that it appears to have on this issue, that we are going to have a situation whereby comitology will not be accepted in this way but rather there will be an adherence to codecision. i have been through this before. i have had this debate with parliament and i know what is going to happen later in the day. members of this house will arrive in here to vote on this issue and they will follow the whips. the vast majority will not know the detail that they are voting on because they are not informed on this particular issue. it is also a major concern to me that so many people today will vote on an issue which is of considerable importance to consumer without knowing that they are putting in place a procedure which would put at risk consumer health by delaying the procedure under which i can, on the basis of clear scientific advice, put something into an annex which will protect consumer health. i sincerely ask you ladies and gentlemen, to revise your view on this issue, give consumer health a greater priority. consider the question of consumer health as more important than the interinstitutional wrangling between parliament and the commission on the question of whether there should be a full codecision in cases such as this. this is a scientific issue, based on scientific advice: it is an executive decision which will be taken by the commission and put into an annex in circumstances where there is a full droit de regard by parliament on that issue. i have said here before when debating this issue that i will not lightly disregard the view of parliament on any issue where comitology arises. so i sincerely ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to give serious consideration to the rights of consumers, to the question of the proper protection of consumers and also bear in mind we are going to have a food and safety authority in operation hopefully next year. it will have a role to play in rapid reaction. if it identifies an emerging risk, it can advise that there should be an executive response to that risk immediately. sometimes that will mean a legislative response introduced by the commission. if that can be done by comitology we will get the kind of speedy response that the consumer requires. but if it can only be done by codecision we will have a delay. now allow me to address in detail the amendments which have been proposed in this report as well as the amendment tabled by mrs grossetête. i will begin with the amendments the commission cannot accept. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10 as far as comitology is concerned for the reasons that i have already identified. nor amendments nos 12, 13 and 14 which reject the introduction of the regulatory committee procedure for updating the lists of provisionally and definitively banned substances and which re-introduce the codecision procedure. amendment no 1 focuses on a well-founded decision on maintaining the ban. the commission cannot accept this amendment as it prejudges the outcome of any possible future research. under amendment no 2, the commission would be committed to fund research on the five provisionally banned substances. this is not acceptable. there is no legal obligation under either community law or the wto framework for the commission to finance research. rather the wto requires parties to evaluate the risk on the basis of all scientific data. nevertheless, such studies are not excluded from the european union’s programmes on food safety. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 3 and 11 which insist on the need to introduce effective monitoring systems to protect health. i would like stress that monitoring systems already exist both in the member states and at community level. for instance meat imports are already controlled, notably according to the directive on controls and residues, council directive 96/23. finally, the commission proposed that the provisions in the directive concerning oestradiol would not apply to animals treated for technical or therapeutical purposes before 1 july. amendment no 15 by mrs grossetête proposes that this provision be linked to the availability of suitable alternatives. the commission cannot accept this amendment on health grounds given the clear scientific evidence as regards oestradiol. in addition, a recent study indicated that there is no lack of alternatives to oestradiol for therapeutical or zootechnical use in the community. this study should be made available to parliament in the near future. on the other hand the commission can accept amendment no 8 as well as in principle the part of amendment no 10 dealing with scientific data because they introduce useful clarifications to the text. to conclude, i wish once again to thank mr olsson for the excellent report and his support on this important issue. in summary, the commission cannot accept amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10 as far as the point of comitology is concerned, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. on the other hand it can accept amendment no 8 and in principle the part of amendment no 10 dealing with scientific data.
- thank you, mr olsson. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 11 a.m.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0043/2001), on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the common position adopted by the council with a view to adopting a european parliament and council directive on the harmonisation of certain aspects of copyright and related rights in the information society (9512/1/2000 - c5- 0520/2000 - 1997/0359 (cod)) (rapporteur: mr boselli).
- mr president, before i begin i must acknowledge a twofold interest in this subject. on the one hand, i am an intellectual property holder, as the author of some books and publications, and on the other hand, i am a member of the internet foundation, which has several supporters in this parliament. this day coincides with an important event from the point of view of intellectual property in the information society, namely the judgment of the court of appeal of san francisco in the napster case, which brings us closer to the moment when the vexing issue of the use of the network to infringe intellectual property rights is finally resolved. the judgment of the san francisco court of appeals enshrines the right of intellectual property and establishes a kind of measures for the protection of intellectual property in the united states. the challenge we face is to ensure that europe too establishes a system under which intellectual property is guaranteed, because otherwise it could happen that, through installations in europe, the effective protection measures that are currently being adopted in the united states, under the millennium act, which has been in force for just over two years, would be violated. we are behind the united states and on this point i agree with the rapporteur that we should move this directive forward quickly. the socialist group is concerned that the child will not be thrown out with the toilet water. we have tabled two amendments which we consider very important. first, the amendment concerning what is called private copying. private copying, which was traditionally a right of every person who obtained an intellectual work, an intellectual property, at this moment, in the information society, has to be subjected to very strict requirements, because of the enormous ease of reproduction. this amendment proposes that private copying should be for the personal use of the person making it, because otherwise we run the risk that, with the ease of reproduction, many copies can be made for the private use of people other than the person making the reproduction. and secondly, another rather important amendment is the one concerning the incidental and transitory nature of reproduction. if, as a result of the processes established by the information society, it is necessary to make a copy of a transitory and incidental nature, this should be intended to be of an effectively transitory nature. what we cannot do is create large libraries of intellectual property so that, at a certain point, the person who has been using this property can dispose of it in his own way. we believe that the accumulation of the requirements of transience and accessibility is an essential condition for the maintenance of intellectual property. i hope that in tomorrow's votes the various political groups will be able to agree on proposing alternatives which will effectively guarantee the protection of intellectual property in the information society, since probably in a few years' time there will be no other intellectual property than that which is transmitted through the large communication networks.

question no 52 by mr göran färm (h-0122/01) subject: conduct of the commission following criticism by a former commissioner the echo humanitarian office scandal in 1997 (missing of european aid of a high amount due to irregularities and subsequent disappearance of documents relating to the case from the commission's archives) was followed closely in sweden and denmark. in a television programme broadcast in both countries, both anita gradin, the former commissioner, and her then chief of staff criticised the way the commission had handled the case. following these statements, commissioner neil kinnock wrote to the two persons to inform them that they had no right to criticise the commission as an institution. if, against all odds, there were any provision that they were not allowed to express criticism, this would be a significant setback for freedom of expression within the european union. what legal provision does the commission rely on to claim that a former commissioner and a former chief of staff are not entitled to make such criticisms of the commission?
commission. – mr president, i am very grateful to the honourable members for their questions about my correspondence with my friend and former colleague, mrs anita gradin, and her former chef de cabinet, mr christer asp. the questions enable me to report publicly and fully to this house on an issue that i know has aroused interest particularly in sweden. on 13 november 2000 danish tv broadcast a documentary programme in which statements were attributed to mrs gradin and mr asp that appeared to relate to an employee of the commission who had been unanimously acquitted of specific charges by the last commission after due disciplinary process had been followed. as a result of that broadcast, and as commissioner responsible for personnel and administration, i was obliged to write to mrs gradin and mr asp on 22 november to request confirmation and clarification of the reported remarks, in order to enable the commission to establish whether or not the remarks in question would require any action by the commission. that was the sole purpose of the letter. it did not, either in tone or in content, demand explanations, offer criticism, seek to gag anyone or imply in any way that either mrs gradin, as a former commissioner, or mr asp, as a former official, had no right to criticise the commission as an institution. in order to make that absolutely clear, i will readily provide copies of that letter and all other relevant correspondence to the honourable members as soon as i have confirmation from mrs gradin that she has no objection to that course of action. mrs gradin has indicated by an indirect route that she would be agreeable to such a release of correspondence but naturally, as a matter of courtesy to her, i prefer to have direct confirmation of her agreement. mrs gradin replied to my 22 november letter on 29 december and i wrote a further letter to her on 25 january 2001. as i pointed out in that letter to mrs gradin, and as the house will be aware, the staff regulations applicable to all eu institutions make it clear that the commission as an institution and as an employer is legally liable to assist employees in defending themselves against attack. that obligation also means defending an acquitted person against any questioning of their innocence of the charges on which they were acquitted. my 22 november letters to mrs gradin and mr asp therefore related entirely to such legal obligations and considerations and to absolutely nothing else. as i made clear in my letter of 25 january to mrs gradin, whilst all liberties of speech are precious and must be upheld, the expression of certain opinions – for instance those that may be considered to defame others – can have legal consequences in all democratic societies, and have specific implications for the commission as an employing european institution. in that letter i also made clear beyond doubt that my letter of 22 november was not in any way an attempt to limit free comment or to prevent criticism of the commission either by mrs gradin, or indeed by mr asp or anyone else. all this will be evident to honourable members when they have the chance to read the exchange of correspondence, as i hope they will. that will also enable them to see that the basis for consideration of the actions of former commissioners and former officials is the treaty and the staff regulations. mrs gradin has obviously always taken her duty of discretion provided for in the treaty seriously as a responsible and reputable person. i am sure that will continue.

- question no 53 by mrs maj britt theorin (h-0083/01): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the united kingdom. subject: candidates for the post of director-general the commission's memorandum on the recruitment and appointment of women targets for 2000 indicates that the share of women in a1 and a2 posts should increase by 20% by 2005. however, according to the latest information i have, only 3 of the 49 directors-general of the commission are women. it is therefore surprising that the commission has once again appointed a man to the post of director-general for development when there was a woman candidate who was perfectly qualified for this post. the selection committee consisted of eight men. how is gender equality checked when appointing director-general of the commission?
commission. – mr president, this question, as mr harbour will be aware, has direct relevance to the question raised by mrs theorin because we believe that amongst the many other justifications for making changes, as regards appraisal and the advance towards a more linear career structure, will be to give fairer treatment to women officials, and indeed to make the commission more attractive for the employment of women, particularly women who have family obligations. so far as progress is concerned, on 28 february 2001 the commission will give consideration to a series of eight detailed draft proposals which will then be submitted for consultation to all the staff, and for formal negotiations to the staff representatives, as well as to two orientation papers, one of which relates to pay and pensions and the other to the more linear career system. we are therefore at the point – on the linear career system, on systematic appraisal and on a host of complementary activities – of making formal proposals, and of beginning detailed consultations on them. this is with a view, by the summer break, to compiling finalised proposals either for commission decisions – which have the force of law – or proposals to this house and the council where amendments to the staff regulations are required. the support and interest of this house is invaluable in all of these reform activities, both those relating to improvement in the gender balance and, much more widely, those seeking to ensure improvements in the efficiency of commission staff and in professional support for them. i hope that this support and understanding will continue.
commission. – mr president, the commission seeks to fulfil its obligations to maintain a reasonable gender balance, not only in managerial roles but right throughout the staff of the commission. the reason we do this is because this is a unique multinational and multilingual union, and it is essential that the executive administration of the union reflects the diversity of cultures and languages in the staffing of the commission. the same applies to trying to secure a much improved gender balance. i can honestly say to the honourable gentleman that no preference is given on the basis of the sex of a person or the flag that they happen to be born under or the passport that they carry. consequently we will strive to maximise the premium allocated to merit, whilst trying at the same time, by a variety of practical means, to maintain an improved gender balance and also to sustain a regional geographical balance as befits our multinational organisation.
question no 54 by mr niels busk (h-0011/01) subject: measures to combat bse would the commission please report on the situation in the various member states following the measures taken to combat bse in december 2000? how are these measures implemented in each member state and how does the commission monitor their application? what are the control provisions? how does the commission verify that in a given member state the feed does not contain meat or bone meal? do all member states have sufficient residual capacity and have they established a comprehensive register of bovine animals, so that any contamination can be traced? how many animals are waiting to be cremated in each country? how much slaughterhouse waste has been accumulated in preparation for destruction, and how is it stored?
commission. – i am very concerned to ensure that we have community measures in relation to all of these issues and that all member states apply the community law in the same way. this was not necessarily the case earlier last year and towards the end of last year, but i see some signs that it might be achieved following the community measures that have now been brought forward. i have every hope that any differences that arise in member states will soon be a thing of the past.
- question no 55 by mrs manuel medina ortega (h-0019/01) subject: mad cow disease: the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the victims of the disease. what action has been taken within the commission and in the member states on the european parliament's 1997 report on mad cow disease and what action is the commission taking to enforce the community rules on the prevention of the disease in the various member states?
commission. – the commission replied in its final consolidated report to parliament's report on bse of 1997 by setting an ambitious work programme. in two more biannual follow-up reports to parliament it gave a broad overview of the emergency measures taken to combat bse, to increase the safety of animal feed and to implement the new approach in the fields of scientific advice, risk analysis and inspection. the commission services have since been restructured to assure the independence and transparency of the scientific committees, the reinforcement of the inspectorate and the separation of consumer protection from the markets. a solid body of legislative measures has been introduced on which the commission has regularly reported to parliament. these measures include, for example, the requirement to remove and destroy specified risk materials, to pressure-cook animal waste and to actively survey the animal populations for the presence of tses. the commission has also made use of the new legal provision of the treaty of amsterdam to propose regulations under the codecision procedure on the prevention and control of transmissible spongiform encephalopathies and on the processing of animal by-products. these regulations will bring together in a single substantive legal text a wide range of measures which are currently based on safeguard provisions of community veterinary legislation. if the negotiations run their course as expected, the regulation on tses should be adopted next month. the proposed regulation on animal by-products is expected to be voted on by parliament shortly. in the meantime, the commission continues to monitor the situation on the spot, requesting scientific advice and taking legal measures whenever needed. the evidence resulting from the very regular visits of the food and veterinary office and the scientific opinions of the scientific steering committee has become the basis for the consumer protection policy of the commission.
- mr president, i thank the commissioner for his answer and i note that the commission has indeed made considerable progress since 1997 from a legislative point of view. i would like to ask a supplementary question, because of the perplexity of my constituents in the face of the tremendous errors and contradictions of the spanish authorities. in particular, a regional minister for agriculture has ordered the dead cows to be deposited in an open pit mine. there have been statements from one minister saying one thing while another minister said the opposite. in germany, at least, there have been some resignations of ministers. my question is: apart from legislative measures, does the commission intend to take executive measures with regard to the states? can we see a greater presence of the commission in our states to give guarantees to citizens? has the commission ever considered using the infringement procedure, by means of the letter of infringement, to make community citizens aware that the commission is actually looking after their safety and health?
commission. – the implementation by member states of safety measures put in place at community level is of crucial importance. there is little point in passing legislation at community level if it is not fully and rigorously implemented by the member states. there are a number of responses available to the commission in the event that there is a persistent failure by any member state to properly implement these safety laws. these are, for instance, the initiation of infringement proceedings against that member state or, alternatively, by taking community measures which can be understood to mean the putting in place of safety provisions which would prevent the member state in question from exporting its product. in this instance i assume that when you are talking about these issues you are talking about beef. these are obviously very powerful measures. they are required to be brought into effect in circumstances where there is a failure by member states to implement the safety provisions. it is appropriate to bring these measures into place, however, only in circumstances where the breach has been persistent. there has to be a pattern of behaviour by a member state of ignoring the law. one or two incidents would not trigger the infringement proceedings nor require the taking of community measures. this is an issue which is kept constantly under review by my services and myself to ensure that there is full compliance and to ensure that the consumers are properly and fully protected, both by the laws and the implementation of the laws.
- mr president, i am not going to waste any of my time in replying or criticising any of the member states that comply with the legislation or do not comply with it, but i would like to ask the commissioner a number of specific questions on the subject of harmonization. if the member states are required, and i agree with that, commissioner, to comply with the rules that are laid down here, those rules must be clear and the same for everyone. what degree of compliance can be required when we are talking about the application of tests? the member states are required to agree to 30 months, but some member states already apply 24 months. what guarantees are offered to the consumer? do you not think that this issue is causing considerable alarm and insecurity among consumers? the same could be said about the issue of spinal removal, the issue of hazardous materials. we are talking about the removal of the spine for only two member states and for animals over 30 months old; there are derogations for some member states, but what are they, why are they being removed, why on 7 february this year did the standing veterinary committee carry out the evaluation to remove the spine in animals over 12 months old? where's the harmonization? it is very difficult, commissioner, to guarantee consumer safety in beef when there are these legislative dysfunctions.
commission. – it is important to understand what we are talking about. i understand that the honourable member is asking me about the measure that was introduced last week at the svc for the removal of the vertebral column as distinct from the spinal cord. the spinal cord has been designated as a specified risk material (srm) for a long time and has been removed in many member states as such for a long time; it has been removed now as a matter of law in the european union by all member states since 1 october 2000. if you are referring to the vertebral column, i will deal with that aspect of your question by saying that the proposal that i put before svc for their decision last week was firmly based on the advice of the scientific steering committee. the situation is that something over 95% of the infectivity is located in the srm in an infected animal. the removal of the vertebral column is regarded by the scientists to account for an additional couple of percentage points so that, in the context of the whole question of the removal of specific risk material, this is an ultra-precautionary measure. in advising whether this should be done, the scientific steering committee examined the available evidence from member states and came to the conclusion that it was appropriate to remove the vertebral column in circumstances where member states did not have a substantially bse-free regime or did not have control measures in place which would be equivalent to very low bse-incidence. bearing in mind that advice, a conclusion was reached that it was appropriate to grant waivers to the five member states that you are referring to, two of them because they had very rigorous control measures in place, and the other three because they were in category 2 of the geographical risk assessment that was published last july, thereby identifying those member states as being at very low risk. accordingly, the waivers were granted in those circumstances. it is a community-wide measure. it applies to all member states. however, in circumstances where it is appropriate, in the individual circumstances of an individual member state, and strictly on the advice of scientists who advise me, it was considered appropriate to allow for derogations. not only did the scientific steering committee give advice on which that decision was based, but the standing veterinary committee came to the same conclusion, as did the commission. this was a justifiable response. there are many member states which take the view that i went too far. there are member states that take the view that i did not go far enough. proportionate responses in these circumstances are what we tried to achieve. with regard to the 24 months, i assume that you are referring to the fact that there is a requirement to test animals above the age of 30 months. there is one member state that has reduced that on its own territory to 24 months, but that has absolutely no trade implications between that state and other member states; that member state has presumably concluded that it would be worthwhile reducing it to 24 months having regard to the age profile of a couple of positives that they have found. i substantially agree with the basis of your question, which is that it is better to have community measures right across the board rather than have individual measures, but sometimes individual member states or a particular measure that is somewhat different from the community measure can be justified in circumstances where a particularly unique situation is obtained in a member state.
- question no 56 by rosa miguélez ramos (h-0021/01) subject: bse and the consumption of bovine bones the spanish minister for health has thrown the spanish consumer into confusion by advising housewives not to buy meat at a discount and not to use marrow bones in the kitchen. does the commission believe that there is a link between the price of meat on the market and the guarantees that this meat offers to the consumer? does she think that cattle bones are dangerous and should be banned? is the sale of these products prohibited in any of the member states? if so, does this ban apply to all bones or only to a certain type of bone?
commission. – community hygiene legislation applies to all meat or meat products irrespective of their price, ensuring the same high level of consumer protection. it is not acceptable that cheap meat should be less safe than dearer meat. the commission is very carefully following all issues relating to material which could present risks as regards transmissible spongiform encephalopathies. in this context, it gave a prominent mandate to the scientific steering committee to review the current list of so-called specified risk material if new scientific evidence becomes available in this field. in june 2000 the commission adopted decision 2000/418/ec which requires the removal of a series of bovine, ovine and caprine tissues from food and feed chains. in particular it provides that bones of the skull from cattle over 12 months of age have to be banned in all member states. in addition, it extends the list of specified risk material to the vertebral column of bovine animals over 30 months of age in the united kingdom and portugal. following further opinions of the scientific steering committee, the commission presented a proposal at the standing veterinary committee meeting of 7 february, which designated the vertebral column as a specified risk material to be removed and destroyed for cattle over the age of 12 months. this proposal was accepted by the standing veterinary committee and, when it is formally adopted, member states will be required to ensure removal of the vertebral column. this may take place at the point of sale, that is in the butchers' shops, from 31 march 2001. the proposal included provisions for derogations from the obligation to remove the vertebral column, on the basis of scientific committee opinions, for five member states – austria, finland, portugal, sweden and the united kingdom. this derogation is conditional on continued and improved surveillance for the presence of bse in those member states, with increased testing of certain categories of animals required. the derogations will be reviewed if necessary in the light of the results of these tests and further scientific advice.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environmental impact of the community's activities is not undermined. this regulation, known as emas, introduced the use of market mechanisms for organisations to commit, on a voluntary basis, to a more proactive approach to improving their environmental performance. the success of the project was largely dependent on the concept that the environment can and should be integrated into the business strategy as a factor that provides added value to the business itself, in addition to environmental safety. it is a major change in the mindset of the business world to consider respect for the environment as a factor of competitiveness and progress, rather than as an annoying legal obligation, in many cases with a heavy economic cost and with a doubtful appreciation of the effort by the consumer. this revised and updated regulation is an important contribution to a modern environmental policy, in line with the principles of sustainable development, important for the real improvement of the environmental performance of companies and also for the recognition of this improvement by third parties, especially by the consumer. during these eight years of practical application, we have learned several lessons. the first of these is its usefulness as a market instrument. almost 3 100 industrial plants throughout europe have joined this system, which is growing at a rate of almost 50% per year. despite this important development, there is still potential for further progress. the new regulation therefore incorporates a number of considerations which facilitate the participation of european companies in this system of environmental improvement. the extension of the scope to all types of organisations, including the service sector, and the possibility of incorporating the public administration itself, the establishment of incentives and special consideration by public administrations towards certified companies when awarding public contracts, the promotion of the participation of small and medium-sized enterprises, the coordination between the european system and other international environmental certification systems should be highlighted. in the latter area, a major simplification and unification of nomenclature and requirements has been achieved, which will significantly clarify the role of emas in the european context. another lesson well learned was the need to maintain and even strengthen the credibility of the system. the text has strengthened measures to ensure its quality and credibility and public access to information. the role of the environmental statement is enhanced, as is the work of environmental verifiers, who have to verify that organisations comply with the relevant requirements of this regulation. these requirements have also been strengthened by parliament's amendments, including: the obligation for companies to comply with environmental legislation; the establishment of higher standards in the qualification and training of environmental verifiers who accredit companies; the production of public reports on the environmental performance of companies, with full credibility vis-à-vis third parties; greater involvement of stakeholders in the process of monitoring and monitoring the environmental performance of companies and, in particular, of workers and users; an extension of environmental responsibility beyond the company's premises to include indicators of the performance of products and services, in line with the approach of the new environmental directives; and also an increase in the role of the coordination bodies in order to facilitate the application of the system in a homogeneous way in the different member states. in order to achieve the results i have just mentioned, i must say that the conciliation process has been extremely positive and interesting. we arrived at the same time with 24 amendments, of which only 4 were accepted without amendment and 3 withdrawn during the negotiations. the amendments accepted by way of compromise formulas were 20, which gives an idea of the intensity and success of the negotiation. i would therefore like to thank the technical staff of parliament, the commission and the council for their work during this period, as well as the members of the conciliation committee for their willingness to give decisive support to this directive. i think the european parliament can be very satisfied with the final result of the conciliation, since the vast majority of its amendments have been incorporated in full or in a revised form into the joint text, and i therefore propose that it be adopted tomorrow in plenary in third reading.
