- mr president, commissioner, mr president of the eib, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr lipietz, for his excellent report. the european investment bank is a non-profit-making body because the governments of the member states decided so, since its mission was not to make economic profit but to contribute to the balanced development of the european community, by granting medium- and long-term loans and guarantees for investment projects in the poorest regions, promoting economic and social cohesion. if we look at the preferred focus of eib financing, where did the loans granted in 1999 go? we see that most of it has been used to co-finance investments in the four richest member states (germany, france, the united kingdom and italy), which received more than 60% of the eib's complementary resources from the community's structural funds, while the so-called cohesion countries, i.e. the poorest and most needy (greece, portugal, spain and ireland), received only 26%. even if i am told that the same inequality exists in the population of these states, i believe that it is necessary to reflect on this aspect, since balanced development will not be achieved by proportionality but by solidarity. this will be more necessary as we go deeper into enlargement to new member states. and let it not be said that the less wealthy do not submit projects to be financed; a better policy of information, transparency, support and accompaniment must be developed. and to do this, one could well start by facilitating communication with potential applicants, by encouraging the use of all the languages of the european union, including regional and minority languages, so that everyone can have access to the european investment bank.
- mr president, we must now rethink the future cohesion policy in view of the challenges arising from enlargement to include the countries of central and eastern europe. enlargement will result in a sharp increase in population and geographical spread, but also in a dangerous increase in territorial disparities. because statistics are misleading and a region which now has an income per head of 70% of the community average will not have improved its situation when, after enlargement, that percentage rises by 10 or 15 points. income is a defining element of regional development but it must not be the only one. for a new programming period we must have new indicators reflecting the growing complexity of our societies and the economies of our regions: the unemployment rate, especially that of young women and the long-term unemployed; the regions' dependence on crisis sectors such as steel or fisheries; the low qualification of workers; the lack of vocational training or education; the limited economic diversification; demographic reality; the low presence of new technologies or the low integration of women into society in the less developed regions, which is a cause of their backwardness. cohesion should not be limited to the structural funds. all union policies must respond to this objective by contributing to improving competitiveness in the most backward regions and by contributing to creating more jobs and more skilled workers. the union will have to act in those areas where stimulus is needed which does not constitute a large outlay. this is a stimulus to regeneration and to increased competitiveness and productivity. the commission must have more capacity to intervene and a more comprehensive view, and the community initiatives must be better equipped, in my view, in the coming period. we should also - in my opinion - rethink your number.
- mr president, on the report on the impact of liberalization and the process of economic reforms, our opinion can only be very critical. it is not because we do not share general ideas about the broad objectives of economic policy, but because here, under the pretext of liberalization, we are being led down paths which, instead of increasing the well-being of our societies, are deepening social inequalities in societies which are supposedly more advanced. in the report we are discussing there are enough generic references to the us model and phrases that have become the economic right's rule book that cannot be accepted uncritically by those of us who want to maintain a balance between the big economic goals and the building of fairer societies. and this progressive stance is irreconcilable with the claims made in this report. i am not referring only to the above but also to others, such as the claim made about labour market reform, which literally says 'to reform the labour market so that it promotes mobility and makes it worthwhile for the unemployed to accept job offers'. this is treating the unemployed - and i say this with all due respect to mr gasòliba i böhm - as if they were parasites. the key to achieving the balance between economic objectives, competitiveness and cohesion and social justice is not in this so-called liberalisation, but in designing and implementing policies that make our economic systems more efficient, drawing from other economies - copying if necessary - what can move us forward in this two-pronged direction. we do not want models like the united states, which lead to greater social imbalances and injustices or to outright disasters, such as the liberalization of the electricity sector in california. why do you not copy the policies of the american treasury and abandon the model of the european central bank, which has done us so much harm in the past? the rapporteur has referred, in passing, this morning to the existence of european countries with interesting models. of course there are, but why not emphasize that? because it is not of interest to those who talk about liberalization too much without thinking about the consequences.
the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. i'll try to make some comments. the debate was very rich in ideas, very varied and raised many issues. first of all, i would like to stress what i consider to be a fundamental point, namely that lisbon has obviously not changed its objectives, namely full employment and the modernisation of our society, without forgetting respect for our social system and a high degree of cohesion. when we look at the employment figures, it is clear what has been achieved. we can talk about public investment, as some of you have done. but what is relevant to us is the overall strategy. when we look at the overall strategy, and that is the content of the synthesis report, we stress the need to make simultaneous progress in the various areas in order to achieve the objectives we have set out in lisbon. for example, the broad economic policy guidelines of 2000 already substantially change their historical structure to include in the various policies those measures which are a consequence of the strategy defined in lisbon. the lisbon strategy is obviously based on the idea that all or many of you have highlighted of a society with a dynamic and cohesive economy to which i have just referred. and that means progress in innovation, in education, in training, in liberalization, also in proper regulation and, of course, in the whole social protection system. neither these instruments nor these policies are living by themselves; there is an interrelation between them all. it is not a balance between different policies, but rather a synergy between different policies which must ultimately enable us to achieve the desired results. if we analyse the report, it is clear that we have made progress since then. i think we cannot be as negative as some of you have been, saying, "nothing has been done". i think that a lot has been done, whether we are talking about liberalization or economic results. it is also true that not many other priorities have been set, and that is why we have set out in our report some of the priorities which we consider to be essential for the immediate future. there's one point i find interesting. it has been raised throughout the debate and especially in the early part of the morning, and it is the role of indicators in relation to the objectives we are seeking. it is true that the indicators should not be regarded as a kind of inventory of positions taken on specific policies. it is true that indicators are not objectives in themselves, they are instruments which should allow us to move forward and interpret reality more globally and more correctly. contrary to what some of you have indicated, it is important to have indicators that by themselves give us a reality of our own situation. comparison with other models is certainly useful. there is no doubt that comparing, for example, some rates of technological penetration in the european union and in the united states will give us a measure of where we are, relative to the most advanced country in these matters. a partial comparison, only in some things and not in the whole model, between the two economies can lead to interpretations that are not always correct. in any case, when we are talking about comparative indicators there is always a difficulty and that is that, on many occasions, we do not have indicators that are homogeneous enough so that the realities we are comparing can be known through these figures. you have also debated, throughout the morning, whether the number of indicators was excessive. it is true that a reduction in the number of indicators would give the report more visibility; it would allow, in terms of public opinion, to send clearer and more direct messages. but it is also true that a smaller number of indicators would make it much more difficult to interpret the reality we want to know. the existence of 28 indicators, classified under the four fundamental lisbon objectives, is the minimum necessary for a good understanding of where we are at the moment. it is true, however, that we conceive of indicators, as i said before, as a working instrument. it is not an instrument which necessarily has to be permanent, because reality and a better knowledge of it will require us to review the indicators on an ongoing basis, possibly changing some of them in the course of the process we have started with lisbon. a subject which i find interesting, and which has been raised by some of you, is to what extent greater involvement of parliament in this whole debate can be achieved through an institutional agreement. i think we have enough instruments at the moment, at least in the relations between the commission and parliament, to be able to make progress in our joint work. in any event, the institutional agreement should also include the council. i would like to emphasize one point: the participation of both parliament and public opinion in the european debate is always open. the commission has taken the initiative, for example, of economic interviews, which are held once a year and whose main objective is to analyse the european economic situation, precisely in a global world and in comparison with the context of those countries of reference for our situation. this is a matter which is always open to parliament and we naturally expect its cooperation this year as we have had in the past. another point which i find interesting is the scope of the synthesis report. i have seen at least two references which i find interesting: why are we not talking about sustainable development? what is happening with the enlargement of the european union? would it not be appropriate to make a reference to both subjects? sustainable development will be the objective of gothenburg, so there is only a clear reference in the present report to the fact that the economic and social dimensions of lisbon will have to be completed by integrating the environmental dimension, which will contribute to a european union strategy for sustainable development. we are therefore talking about a possibility that is open after gothenburg and that will undoubtedly be reflected in the reality of the future debates. a different problem is the enlargement problem, where there is also a clear reference: the economy of the european union must not only take account of this essential element, but our whole design must start from the consideration that the union will be enlarged in a relatively short period of time. the european union should take this as a reference point, but the candidate countries should also be involved in the lisbon strategy, taking on its objectives as far as possible. this text, which is almost exactly what i have just said, is included in our summary report. when we talk about lisbon, we also talk about the new method of coordination, the open method of coordination. while this method is interesting in that it allows good practice to be identified and a common approach to issues of interest to be developed progressively, it should not, however, replace existing community instruments of a normative or quasi-normative nature or existing guidelines in areas such as economic policy or employment. one point i would like to highlight is structural reforms. we certainly included some specific references to structural reforms. we consider that these have a very varied content and among them is the concept of liberalization of our economies. this should undoubtedly enable us to be more competitive and will benefit users and improve the quality of services of general interest. but it is clear that a process of liberalization will only be efficient and will not raise problems if it is carried out within an appropriate legislative and regulatory framework. we cannot think of liberalization processes that do not fit into a global framework. this regulatory process will undoubtedly be a key issue in the forthcoming debates and it is in this context that the references to services of public interest made this afternoon are inscribed. a point which i also find interesting in the debate which has been raised today is the extent to which an excess of bureaucratic burdens is having a negative impact on the european development process. i would simply point out that this is a point of concern to the commission; in fact, at some points, work has already been done on an indicator relating to bureaucratic burdens. it is obviously a difficult subject, which is being piloted by eurostat, where a working group is trying to define precisely elements of this nature that will allow us to know in more detail whether or not this feeling that exists today in a part of our society, about this excess of bureaucratic burdens, responds to a real situation. to conclude my remarks, it might be interesting to stress at this point that the synthesis report process is a global process which requires coherence between macroeconomic stability, which we consider to be a fundamental issue, employment, reforms and social cohesion. and within the concept of social cohesion, we must have a broad approach and vision, which should not be limited solely and exclusively to individual issues, but should also cover regional issues, as some of you have suggested. it is easy to highlight the progress that has been made in general terms, but it is somewhat more complex to highlight how these advances in each of our countries, or in each of our regions, can be compared with others. in any case, and this seems to me to be a fundamental point, the reforms we are embarking on will only make sense to the extent that we are able to increase economic productivity and efficiency. the introduction of elements of the new economy into the european union will be the key to our future development. growth, yes, growth with social cohesion, growth which will enable us to face the future in terms of the technological challenge; after all, those are the objectives of lisbon and those are the objectives which we intend to set out in our report. thank you very much for your contributions and for your participation in this debate. we shall try to take account of all the points raised today, which will undoubtedly be useful for our debate in stockholm.

the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i have listened to this debate with great interest. on the council's part, we fully understand the frustration expressed in many of the contributions to this debate. i can understand that you feel that the review of regulation 1408/71 since the finnish presidency in 1999 has been very protracted. i the commission is aware of the difficulties facing the member states in the implementation of the directive. the commission also welcomes your support for articles 42 and 308 of the treaty as the appropriate legal bases for this objective. we believe that such an enlargement is entirely in line with community policy, particularly in the light of the conclusions of the tampere european council on the situation of third country nationals legally resident in the member states. the commission therefore regrets that the council has not been able to support this and other commission proposals to amend the regulation and in particular the overall proposal to simplify and modernise. we welcome what we have just heard from minister danielsson in this regard and we hope that his wishes will come lambert's report, to whom i express my sincere thanks for her very constructive contribution to the commission's proposal. our proposal is a technical proposal, intended to fill, as you know, legal gaps due to legislative changes in national social security rules. in order to ensure the proper functioning of community coordination of national social security schemes, which is a means of promoting the free movement of workers, amendments to national legislation also require the amendment of regulation (eec) no 1408/71: this is what is at stake. the proposals of mrs lambert, whose understand correctly, to extend the regulation to early retirement benefits. in fact, the commission included the same provisions in its 1998 proposal for the simplification and modernisation of regulation (eec) no 1408/71. however, the amendments now before us propose a substantial modification of the regulation and clearly go beyond the technical character of the commission's proposed update and, in our view, the debate on the technical update should not be confused with a debate on the substantive amendments. for that reason, the commission cannot accept the other additional amendments on supplementary pensions. as regards amendment no 8, i would simply like to stress that the commission has undertaken to submit a proposal on its transferability during the course of the year. so, in summary, we can accept amendments nos 1 to 7, but we cannot accept amendments nos 8, 9, 10, 12 and 13. i thank everyone, and especially mrs lambert, for their general support of the commission's proposal.

- question no 3 by mr per gahrton (h-0031/01) subject: recommendation of the european parliament on the establishment of a european civilian peace corps on 17 january 2001, the european parliament, in a proposal for the creation of a european rapid reaction mechanism, stated that it considered that priority should be given to non-military crisis management and cited its own recommendation to the council in spring 1999 calling for the creation of a european civilian peace corps. unfortunately, the finnish, portuguese and french presidencies chose to ignore the parliament's recommendation. what steps does the swedish presidency intend to take in accordance with this unanimous recommendation of parliament?
the council. conflict prevention and crisis management, using all civilian and, if necessary, military instruments, is a very important priority for the eu. this has been reflected in the conclusions of the european councils up to and including nice. the swedish presidency is actively pursuing the mandate given to it by the nice european council. the work is quite complicated in both the civil and military fields, as the eu is creating new resources and structures. the civil work is now concentrated on achieving the concrete objective set at the feira summit of deploying up to 5 000 police officers for international missions in the full range of conflict prevention and crisis management operations by 2003. 1,000 police officers will be deployed within 30 days. work in other priority areas identified at feira, in particular strengthening the rule of law, but also the emergency services and civil administration, is progressing. furthermore, the swedish presidency has made it clear that as eu civilian crisis management continues to evolve, it is appropriate to identify other areas within the framework of civilian crisis management where eu resources may need to be developed or applied more effectively. such areas could include, for example, expertise in democracy and human rights, and monitors and observers of various kinds. mechanisms for improved cooperation with ngos involved in conflict prevention and post-conflict peacebuilding, as well as improvements to the eu's diplomatic instruments for conflict prevention, will also be highlighted in the european programme for conflict prevention, which is expected to be endorsed by the european council in gothenburg. in addition, the union has reformed and concentrated the work of its monitoring missions, placing them under the control of the secretary-general. the monitoring mission also proved its worth recently when it was deployed in the presevo valley. all this work is in line with the european parliament's recommendation to set up a civilian peace corps and has the same objectives. the council prefers to complete the work mentioned above, i.e. an operational capacity in the field before the end of the year with the objectives and deadlines set by the european council. the council will then be better able to assess what further arrangements may be justified or necessary.

question no 7 by mr camilo nogueira román (h-0027/01) subject: tragic death of african immigrants of both sexes on the southern coast of spain faced with the inaction of the spanish authorities, an attitude which is both serious and reprehensible, what initiatives has the council taken to prevent immigrants from tragically dying every week while trying to enter the community through the andalusian coast (in southern spain) in order to look for work?
the council. the honourable member's question concerns the council's action both on the control of the member states' external maritime borders and on the measures that can be taken in the country of origin to prevent illegal immigration and to stop the activities of smugglers. the measures to improve the effectiveness of member states' controls at external airspace and sea borders have been developed mainly in the context of schengen cooperation and are now integrated into the union acquis following the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam. these measures are implemented by the member states themselves, but the council monitors their actual implementation through its competent bodies. practical measures are being implemented, for example, in cooperation with selected african countries to prevent illegal immigration, by air or sea, on the basis of the decision of the schengen executive committee of 18 december 1998 on a coordinated action of the document advisers. in addition, by decision of 28 april 1999, the same executive committee approved a plan for the mutual secondment of liaison officers to provide advice and assistance in carrying out security and control tasks at the external borders. apart from issues relating to the schengen acquis, illegal immigration into the european union is one of the major issues dealt with by the council, as is clear from the conclusions of several european council meetings - tampere, feira and nice to name a few. as the honourable member is well aware, the european council committed the union to intensifying cooperation to combat trafficking in human beings following the tragic incident in dover last year. following the conclusions of the european council, which stressed the importance of controlling migration flows, the council discussed both operational measures and rules to combat trafficking in human beings. in this connection, on 30 november last year, the council adopted conclusions containing various operational measures to combat illegal immigration, such as mutual information on observed migration flows, optimisation of the early warning system, the transfer of information on illegal immigration and human trafficking, and the coordination of networks of member states' liaison officers in the countries of origin of illegal immigration. as regards the root causes of flight or migration from certain african countries, we refer to the action plan for morocco, which was approved by the council on 11 october 1999 and which i hope the european parliament is well aware of. in the context of the implementation of the action plan for morocco, and since the union is aware that the implementation of the action plan must be carried out in partnership and in cooperation with the moroccan authorities, a delegation of the european union led by the presidency paid a second visit to rabat to open a dialogue with the moroccan authorities. the message that the presidency wanted to convey during this visit, which took place on 3 october last year, was that the action plan for morocco was the result of work initially undertaken by the member states and the commission and that it was now time to ask for the reactions of the moroccan parties and to make the necessary adjustments to the action plan so that it could be implemented jointly. i note that the moroccan authorities welcomed this approach and the idea of opening a dialogue with the european union on immigration issues. this dialogue will take place within the framework of the association agreement with morocco, when it the council. the council fully shares the commitment of the honourable members to the plight of afghan women under the taliban regime. the council regrets that the sad reality in afghanistan shows afghanistan. the council has often raised the issue of the critical situation of afghan refugees with the host countries in the region and will continue to do so. the community and several member the basis of the union's policy towards afghanistan. the union will continue its efforts to achieve lasting peace, to bring an end to foreign intervention and to encourage internal dialogue in afghanistan. the union stresses in particular the importance of promoting respect for international humanitarian law and human rights, including the rights of women and children. the union will signatory. we will continue to call on the afghan factions to end discriminatory policies and to recognise, protect and promote equal rights and dignity of men and women, including access to education and health facilities, employment, personal security and the absence of abuse and harassment, and to highlight the negative impact of discriminatory policies on the delivery of assistance. the union will continue to support the un secretary-general's proposal for civilian human rights observers, and will also continue to support assistance programmes in afghanistan that integrate gender issues aid to afghanistan. the council hopes that the latest sanctions, on the basis of un security council resolution 13033, which the council is currently considering with a view to adopting the - mr president, before i begin my speech on this report, i would ask you to note in the minutes that, in accordance with rule 161, the explanatory statement for the report under discussion is the sole responsibility of the rapporteur and reflects only her personal opinion, not the opinion of the committee on industry. the citizens do not have to know our rules of procedure and certain statements may be confusing and give rise to misunderstandings. thank you, mr president, and i now begin my speech. the draft decision contained in the commission proposal, which is the subject of the report we are debating, is the culmination of a long process which began in 1995 with the signing of a joint declaration between the european community and mexico, which set out objectives to be reflected in an agreement to replace the cooperation agreement, signed in 1991, in order to strengthen and develop political, economic and commercial relations between the european union and mexico. the agreement on economic partnership, political consultation and cooperation, also known as the global agreement, was signed in december 1997. the commission's proposal, on which parliament has been asked to give its opinion, must therefore be seen in the context of the comprehensive agreement between the european union and mexico, the most important agreement the european union has ever signed - and i think it is worth recalling this. the same situation prevails in the case of the interim agreement on the economic and trade aspects of the global agreement, the purpose of which was to enable negotiations to be opened as soon as possible on the liberalization of the trade aspects of community competition contained in the global agreement. as regards the draft decision in question and the agreements which it contains, my group regards them very positively because they increase the possibilities for action in areas of particular interest to community operators, by guaranteeing them access to the mexican market under conditions equal to or even better than those of the nafta countries in terms of services, investments, payments and respect for intellectual property, with the consequent benefits and legal guarantees which this can entail for the european union. these considerations alone would justify the adoption of the draft decision by my group and, i hope, by this parliament. in addition to the economic advantages, my group is very much aware of the political advantages of adopting this draft decision and of the need, therefore, for the eu-mexico joint council meeting at the end of this month to be able to adopt it, because only after it has been adopted can the provisions on political dialogue and cooperation in the fields of education, the fight against poverty, social issues and the environment enter into force - all of which are issues to which my group in particular and this parliament in general have always been very sensitive, because they are the guarantee that the economic benefits, which will undoubtedly flow from the agreement as a whole, will contribute to promoting a more democratic political system and one which respects human rights and is more in line with social justice.

- mr. president, i'm sorry, but i was out of time. first of all, i would like to congratulate mr ceyhun on his work and his efforts to address all the sensitivities that existed around these two initiatives. secondly, i must insist before this house on something which is absolutely paramount for the future of the european union, our society and the political project we are building here. it is the need for a community policy on immigration and asylum, something which we cannot achieve without the commitment, effort and work of the political institutions of the european union. i would like to reiterate a number of points which this house and the council must clearly take into account when taking future decisions. it is essential to distinguish between disinterested and humanitarian aid to illegal immigration and the activity of criminal networks, as specified in article 27 of the schengen convention. it is also important to distinguish clearly between the direct and active beneficiaries of illegal immigration, such as the organisers of the transport of illegal immigrants and those who participate in it, and the passive and indirect beneficiaries, who are those who profit from the labour activity of illegal immigrants. it should also be noted that the economic benefit can also be a direct or indirect benefit, depending on the nature of the action itself. i also understand that carriers cannot be held responsible for the transport of persons who, immediately after arriving in the territory of a member state, apply for political asylum. the carriers have neither the capacity nor the authority to assess the suitability of an asylum application and therefore i understand that they cannot in any case be persuaded, directly or indirectly, through these instruments to assess such suitability. the sanctions must be proportionate and balanced, and we must seek that proportionality between sanction and infringement. the measures and their objectives must strictly respect the obligations assumed by the states signatories to the 1951 geneva convention with regard to asylum seekers entering a state of the european union. such measures can never be intended to dissuade asylum seekers from exercising their legitimate right to seek protection in a signatory state, since that would be a breach of the geneva convention. finally, i would like to draw attention to the need for the member states to be aware that certain areas of the european union are particularly affected by illegal immigration and that, because of their geographical location, they are bearing a large share of the burden of immigration policies, so budget lines should be developed to allow for compensatory payments, which will generate increased solidarity within the european union in this area.

and if there is one area where the european union needed a decisive impulse to integrate policies, to widen the space of cooperation, coordination and synergies, it is that of research, development and technological innovation. the european research area initiative is therefore one of the main priorities of the present college of commissioners and it is up to commissioner busquin to promote and promote this ambitious idea. the european research area introduces new instruments which have the potential to be very beneficial, such as cooperation and coordination between the research policies of the member states, concentration on a few strong priorities, the full exploitation of the concept of european added value, the idea of large-scale projects and networks of excellence. all of them, if properly applied, will undoubtedly contribute to improving the quality and competitiveness of our research, development and innovation system. our amendments, mr president, were motivated by a number of concerns: the promotion of the mobility of researchers, which we consider essential, the openness and permeability of the research systems of the member states, the strengthening of basic research and the clear definition of the criteria which will enable us to set priorities. the european research area opens up new prospects, it is a source of great enthusiasm for all. we wish you success, mr commissioner, because your success in this field will be that of parliament and of the european union. do not doubt that, at all times, in the line you have so positively thrown, you will find us at your side.

facilitate and encourage open coordination between the member states. how are we going to promote, facilitate this coordination? it is therefore clear that this is a long-term task, one that will require a partnership between the commission and the member states, with the support of the european parliament and, mr alyssandrakis, the support of the entire scientific community. this is a project which concerns all european scientists. there is no distinction; there are subsidiarity elements, of course, there is research that is done in the member states and there is value-added research. we are therefore far, light years away from the monopoly concept to which you have just referred and which is certainly not in the mind of any of the members of this house. we must adapt new forms of work. it is in this spirit that the instruments proposed by the commission have been defined. but i also understand your concern about the need to ensure that these instruments provide equal opportunities for all. the instruments should not appear to be reserved for one or the other category, one or the other group, with a size effect, and it is in this spirit that the new instruments should be better defined. as regards networks of excellence, i think it is quite clear that this is a key point, but i also feel that we need to agree on the definition of networks of excellence capacity. it is appropriate to use this term rather than mammoth centres. they're not mammoth centers of excellence. these are networks of excellence, by theme and by research subject. the objective is therefore to set up virtual centres of excellence integrating excellence capacities in priority areas. it follows that it is certainly not a tool for small and mediumsized enterprises and the least advanced countries in research. there are centres of excellence in all european countries, with the criterion, which we will discuss, being: where is the european added value for the programme? this - the report (a5-0022/2001) by mr korakas, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council regulation (ec) amending for the sixth time the arrangements for cotton introduced by protocol 4 annexed to the act of accession of greece (com (99) 492 - c5-0049/2000 - 1999/0202 (cns)); the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's agricultural policy is not affected by the crisis.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we must begin by saying that we are talking about a product which is in short supply in the european union, since its supply rate between 1995 and 1999 was only 42%. it is also worth adding that, as mr korakas has very well said, and i congratulate him on his report, it is a crop located in particularly disadvantaged regions of spain and greece and its production absorbs a large amount of labour. on the one hand, this means that their maintenance is essential to the socioeconomic fabric of these areas and, on the other hand, it justifies the two fundamental requests of this parliament: that the penalty for excess production not be increased from 50 to 60% and that the maximum guaranteed quantities be brought closer to the production reality; i am talking about approximation, not equalization. when the commission put forward its proposal, it was alarmed by excessively low world prices, the lowest in the last ten years, and consequently by an increase in aid expenditure, in line with the cotton aid system. but, commissioner, the circumstances have changed: the price has risen to almost historic levels, the budget devoted to paying farmers has been reduced and the proposal for a regulation is no longer justified, while the amendments adopted unanimously in the committee on agriculture are justified. an increase in penalties would lead to the disappearance of many of the smaller farms, with the social effects that would follow. the gap between actual production and the maximum guaranteed quantities is currently causing the tremendous penalty that farmers are suffering. as mr korakas has rightly said, we could also invoke protocol 4 of the greek act of accession, which calls for the maintenance of cotton production in those areas where it is considered important for the agricultural economy, and for farmers to be allowed to receive a fair income, which stabilises the market by improving agricultural infrastructure. with the amendments it has tabled, the committee on agriculture calls for the launching of collective environmental actions, through the producer associations which we intend to promote and encourage in this sector. we hope that the commission will take these amendments and arguments into account and agree to amend this proposal.
- mr president, the rapporteur, mr korakas, has done a very important job in recent months, and i am very grateful to him for being open, from the outset, to all kinds of proposals, to dialogue, with great receptivity. if we add to this the work done by the committee on agriculture, we can understand that we are dealing with a magnificent report from the european parliament. if the commission were to accept the amendments which we are proposing in this report by mr korakas, we would have a cotton regime with major improvements in the adjustment of national guaranteed quantities, in the aid regime and a new permanent system of recognition of producer groups. in addition, these amendments by parliament encourage the adoption of measures which are much more environmentally friendly, allow water savings, reduce the use of pesticides and provide for proper management of plastic waste. however, i think that the commission's proposal is too minimalist, it is only concerned with saving money and it is inconsistent with what is said to be the european union's first priority, the defence of employment. it is not consistent because it is not sufficiently sensitive to the maintenance or promotion of jobs when deciding between one or the other. that is why i recommend that you vote in favour of amendment no 20, tabled by mr garot and myself on behalf of the socialist group, because it contains a very important proposal. we call on the member states to take account of the employment factor when they adopt measures to adjust the areas eligible for aid. at that time it must be taken into account how many jobs depend on that area. we also propose that the situation of substitute crops be considered and whether or not there are alternatives. in short, mr president, this is called social and economic sensitivity. i hope therefore that you will support our amendment and i congratulate the rapporteur again on this excellent report.

important sector of european agriculture and, in particular, of very important areas of greece and andalusia, productive areas par excellence. cotton is a traditional crop which is the main economic and i cannot dwell on other matters - mr korakas' report develops a framework for the promotion of producer organizations and, above all, a system for implementing actions to reduce the environmental impact of cotton cultivation. because the commission is talking about possible environmental problems of cotton growing, but it is not proposing solutions. i hope, commissioner, that the commission and the council will complete the legislative procedure including the amendments unanimously adopted by the committee on agriculture, as requested by the previous speakers.
the rapporteur. - mr president, this proposal concerns nuts, that is to say, nuts and carrots. we are therefore talking about walnuts, hazelnuts, almonds, pistachios and chestnuts, products which are usually served with other fruits at the table and in supermarkets, but which are not treated fairly and equitably when decisions are taken in relation to other fruits and vegetables. mr president, with this proposal the european parliament is consistent with its own acts, because on two occasions already, on 16 june 2000 and 26 october 2000, the european parliament unanimously supported the maintenance of this aid and proposed an extension until the adoption of a new aid scheme. i would also like to say, mr president, that i think that this aid is well-targeted, because it benefits the farmers who need it, because it compensates for a fall in income. and i think that aid which is overly generous to good market situations should be avoided. this has happened, for example, with cereals, where the commission and the court of auditors itself have insisted that there has been overcompensation, because in this cereals sector the commission estimates that there has been an overcompensation of eur 8.5 billion and the court of auditors speaks of eur 13.1 billion for the period 1993 to 1997 as overcompensation. i am not in favour of aid in the form of a lottery. the measures we are proposing are necessary. moreover, mr president, this proposal is in line with agenda 2000, because when it was adopted, commissioner fischler himself repeatedly told us that the criterion was to maintain all aid. the council agreed with parliament's position and therefore invited the commission on 17 july 2000 to extend the aid. the commission's proposal is a good one, because it corrects the previous mistake of wanting to cut this aid. it is all right that it should be corrected, but that is not enough to maintain the future of the sector; mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament will accept this supplementary and amending budget in virtually the same terms as the other institution has presented it. we accept that we are facing a real budgetary emergency here. we need that extra €900 million to deal with the plan the commission has drawn up to combat bovine spongiform encephalopathy. above all, we need to convey to our farmers and to the public that the european union is a common solution to their problems. we would do irreparable damage to the process of european construction if, in the face of this general crisis - the first truly general crisis of the union - we did not find a common response. and this response must be primarily financial. we can discuss later when we should apply all the principles of agenda 2000 to agriculture, but now - again - is not the time to talk about the future of the common agricultural policy. we must now give real answers, financial answers, we must help european livestock farming with real euros. it is not the time to discuss cofinancing rates, and that is why there is a majority in this parliament which, in principle, rejects the budgetary amendments to the haug report, despite the opinion of some colleagues such as mr stenmarck. there is a financial issue that remains: will there be enough money in category 1 for additional measures when they are needed there by may? agenda 2000 sets out a multiannual budgetary framework, which was unanimously adopted by the council and by a sufficient majority in the european parliament. so, is it not time to say why the actual budget for 2001 is by a significant percentage lower than the one approved in berlin's financial perspective for this year? commission. – i would first like to thank the three rapporteurs, mr brunetta, mr paasilinna and mrs niebler. these are not just any reports. firstly they cover three directives which will be central to the future competence of the european economy. secondly, the amount of knowledge of technologies, markets and regulation which is needed for drawing up these reports is exceptional, so let me sincerely salute the reports for their high quality. i am not able to cover, due to the time-limits, all the issues of crucial importance that i would like to. i apologise for this and will try to concentrate on the very core issues. first, on the framework directive, the commission is very pleased with the paasilinna report, in particular as regards the consultation and transparency mechanism contained in article 6. this is the key provision to ensure that not only national interest drives regulatory decisions but that european interest is also taken into account. after all, if we do not take into account european interest, we do not serve national interest in this business either. this legislation will ensure a level playing field for operators across the single market. its application will lead to a european regulatory culture in the telecommunications sector which will help to even out those differences in national decisions that can threaten the single market and the whole sector. i am referring here, as many here have already done, to different licensing conditions imposed by member states for the third-generation services. the commission is happy to support those parts of amendment no 33 which aim at strengthening the transparency and consultation procedure and the commission is strongly against amendment no 78 which would weaken this procedure. however, we consider that the requirement to consult other national regulatory authorities on draft measures is necessary for the creation of the european regulatory culture. the second key element is the smp definition. it is the commission’s view that the definition in amendment no 56 is too wide. we are concerned that it could lead to over-regulation, which would lead to fear of over-regulation by the operators, which could in turn hamper investment. we also believe that this definition could undermine consistency of regulatory action. the commission considers that its original proposal would better serve the fundamental objective of the whole package, which is to minimise regulation but provide regulators with flexible tools to ensure effective competition in every market segment. on institutional issues, i am convinced that we must involve the european parliament closely in the process of implementing the new framework. we must seek together the most efficient and flexible mechanisms for involving parliament but for institutional reasons we cannot go against the agreements on comitology. thus i regret that the commission cannot support amendments nos 72 to 74. finally, on digital television, i will soon be inviting the market players to discuss how best to ensure that digital television systems are rolled out swiftly in europe so that digital television becomes a viable alternative platform for internet access. for the time being, the commission considers that voluntary industrial standardisation is the best process, and it is not ready to support amendment no 63. as far as the report of mr paasilinna is concerned, the commission can accept in full amendments nos 4, 12, 29, 32, 34, 55, 65 and 68 and the commission can accept in part or in principle amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21, 22, 25, 27, 28, 30, 31, 33, 35, 36, 37, 38, 40, 45 to 48, 53, 54, 57 to 61, 66, 67, 69 and 75. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 5, 8, 14, 16, 18, 20, 23, 24, 26, 39, 41 to 44, 49 to 52, 56, 62, 63, 64, 70 to 74 and 76 to 79. on mr brunetta’s report on access and interconnection, i am thankful for the support for the basic principles of the directive. in competitive markets interconnection of and access to networks should, in principle, be agreed on the basis of commercial negotiations. if this does not happen regulatory intervention is warranted but we have to ensure that regulatory intervention is done on the basis of a market analysis. we have to prove first that the market is not competitive and only then impose ex ante regulation if necessary. therefore, i believe that imposing straightforward price regulation on mobile call termination or on roaming charges would be over-regulating. the commission cannot support amendments nos 39 and 40. however, there is a field where all service providers have been subject to access regulation. this is the conditional access for digital television. this regime has worked well. moving away from the regime of directive 95/48 would require wide consultation and careful analysis. therefore, the commission does not support amendment no 46. to sum up, the commission can accept in full amendments nos 7, 8, 15, 21, 29, 41, 44 and 48. the commission can accept in part or in principle amendments nos 1, 6, 9, 12, 16 to 18, 19, 23, 24, 26, 28, 30 to 34, 37, 38, 42, 43, 45 and 47. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 2 to 5, 10, 11, 13, 14, 20, 22, 25, 27, 35, 36, 39, 40, 46 and 49 to 51. concerning mrs niebler’s report on the authorisation directive, the commission is very pleased with the support for the basic principles of its proposal. the move from individual licences to general authorisations will greatly improve market access and cut red tape. in many respects, mrs niebler’s report strengthens and improves the commission’s proposals. for the key issue of usage fees for radio spectrum i welcome the elements that seek to strengthen coordination and to eliminate the possibility of unproportionate and potentially disastrous licensing conditions. the idea of annual instalments for the payment of one-off amounts is a possible solution. we will, however, have to look carefully at the exact wording. the obligation on member states to take account of the policy objectives of the whole framework in their systems for frequency pricing is likewise welcomed. it is also one of the key objectives pursued in the commission’s proposal for a regulatory framework for radio spectrum policy. specifying that frequency pricing mechanisms are subject to the consultation and transparency procedure of the framework directive is also useful. all in all, we are happy to accept most of amendment no 21, subject to some redrafting. however, on the matter of administrative charges the commission cannot support amendments nos 7 and 20. they would delete the provision that aims to ensure that such charges will not have a discriminatory effect. maintaining turnover as a key for dividing administrative charges seems the most appropriate way. the commission is willing, however, to consider some of the elements proposed in the new amendment no 27 tabled by mr van velzen. to sum up, the commission can accept in full amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 23 and 25. the commission can also accept in part or in principle amendments nos 8, 11 to 14, 16, 18, 20 to 24 and 26 to 28. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 4, 6, 7, 9, 15, 17 and 19. finally, i should like to touch briefly on the situation on the telecommunications markets and licensing for third-generation services. of course we are all worried – europe is the world leader in mobile communications and we have to maintain this lead. we know the facts. the current legislation leaves member states the choice of licensing methods and licensing conditions. we know that it has led to a wide divergence in the sums paid for the licences. the single market is fragmented. frequency actions which coincided with the peak of the new economy stocks led to price levels which would be unimaginable in today’s market conditions. i am ready to reply positively to mr paasilinna’s request for a commission report later on the licensing issue. there is uncertainty and preoccupation in the market now, but we have to remember the fact that third-generation mobile communications will offer enormous potential for totally new types of services. there will be a strong business case for it and public authorities must ensure that the right conditions are in place, and here we need to work together. we have to safeguard europe’s lead in mobile communications. there is no magic wand but we absolutely must get the future regulatory framework right. our proposals, with parliament’s support, provide for procedures that allow for coordinated or even harmonised assignment of radio frequencies. the consultation and transparency procedure of article 6 of the framework directive, the authorisation directive and the commission’s proposal for a regulatory framework on radio spectrum policy provide us with the necessary instruments. the new framework will also allow for secondary trading of radio spectrum which enables more flexible management of this resource. more than ever we need to work together. the european parliament and the commission should try to convince the member states to take a more coordinated approach to frequency assignment. i urge parliament to debate soon the proposal for radio spectrum policy and thus send out a strong signal on the importance and the urgency of the matter. finally, on the proposals made by mr van velzen, i strongly agree with him that we need firm actions to stimulate the use of mobile internet and take steps to keep the european lead in third-generation. we have to see that new internet protocol version 6 will be rolled out swiftly. we have to stimulate european content production and we also need to increase the availability of public sector information for these purposes. we have to see that sufficient research funding is available for future wireless technologies as foreseen in the commission’s proposal for the sixth framework programme for research and also, the other proposals which he made, i am ready to look at them and the commission will come back to this area. together we must guarantee that europe’s lead in mobile communication will be safeguarded.
the rapporteur. - mr president, this own-initiative report which we are debating today in the house is at the request of the euro-mediterranean forum of women parliamentarians and forms part of the overall concept of globalisation which will be discussed throughout this weekend at the meeting which starts tomorrow in malta. the european parliament was responsible for producing this report on the influence of globalisation on migrant women. migration is an old phenomenon but one which has recently acquired a distinctive character. in other words, it is not only men who emigrate, women being the ones who use the regroupment to join their husbands with their children later on, but women are themselves immigrants, they are the heads of families and it is they who, by changing countries, by coming to the european union, are seeking a better personal situation, a better future for themselves and their families. the woman comes as a person looking for possibilities that she does not find in her home countries. in general, she works in the service sector, has no good training and is in a helpless situation for the double reason of being an immigrant and a woman. it often does jobs that nationals of different countries do not want, but which are necessary for the economy to run smoothly. recently, migrant women have also been very important in maintaining jobs, the labour force, given the ageing of the population in some member states, and future prospects. they do not come temporarily to solve a problem, but they come determined to stay, to start a new life in a country that they feel will welcome them. in most cases, they come without sufficient information. on many occasions, deceived and victims of human trafficking mafias, in which they find themselves without possibilities of getting out, ending in many cases in prostitution. this lack of information is one of the most important aspects we highlight in this report. these women need to know what the labour market situation is, what legal requirements are required, what their living conditions will be and what they must contribute to be able to work legally in the country they are going to. there are also cases of highly qualified women who have to do work that is not in keeping with their training. the situation of abuse is precisely because of the defenselessness of women in a country whose language and legislation they do not know, living in isolation in a world that is difficult for them. we want these women to be in a legal situation and with decent work contracts so that they cannot be victims of exploitation. this means that they must have more information in their countries of origin. we therefore ask that there be offices to solve these problems so that they are perfectly informed about the work they are going to do. i should like to point out that some amendments to the report have been tabled in the committee on women's rights, with which neither i, as rapporteur, nor my group agree. they refer to the concept of 'euro-mediterranean citizenship'. it's a concept with legal problems. there is no precedent for this concept in any report or statement, either of this parliament or of the national parliaments. citizenship is a national competence of the member states and it seems to me that introducing this concept in the report does not add much, but could create legal problems. we have therefore asked for a split vote because we would like to see this concept removed from the report so that we can support it without any problems. if it is upheld, i think it is very difficult for us to vote in favour of the report, which would be unfortunate, since the report has very positive aspects for women and is very much needed because of the situation in which most of these women find themselves. i would like to call for reflection so that, by avoiding these terms, we can have a report that is approved by the whole house.
mr president, allow me to begin by congratulating mrs avilés perea on her excellent report. i would like to congratulate you on the fact that you have managed to take a full and balanced view of the consequences of globalisation for the world of immigration, specifically for women and particularly for women in the southern mediterranean region. i think the rapporteur has tried to produce a text which is balanced, necessary and possible, between the different perceptions and sensitivities, avoiding maximalist and dogmatic positions, and a text which takes account of the different opinions and the seriousness of the situation. certainly, globalization is not the panacea for all our ills. globalisation does not necessarily imply well-being and wealth and, in many cases, it is or can be a source of inequalities and a source of greater poverty. the treaty of amsterdam established, for the first time, the union's competence in matters of immigration and asylum, and the tempere european council agreed that the separate but closely related issues of asylum and migration require a common policy of the european union, which implies the need to assess present and future migratory flows in all their categories: humanitarian reasons, family reunification and economic reasons, as the rapporteur has already anticipated, and demographic changes, the situation of the labour market and the regions of origin of migrants. in political terms, i think it is a choice between continuing to hold the view that the union can continue to resist migratory pressures or accepting that immigration will continue and must be properly regulated, working together to maximise the positive effects of immigration, both for the union and for immigrants themselves and for their countries of origin. the situation is even more critical when it comes to migrant women. they are more vulnerable to abusive practices. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a good example of the need to ensure that the protection of workers from the risks related to asbestos is not jeopardised by the introduction of new technologies. all this should be considered within a balanced framework of rights and obligations for all third-country nationals residing in the union. i therefore believe - and i appeal to the generosity demanded by the seriousness and rigour of the subject - that it would be good to abolish concepts such as 'euro-mediterranean citizenship', which i think create confusion and which, in my view, are presented as exclusive. the mediterranean, a source of civilisation and culture, must be an element of integration and not an element of exclusion. i think we must therefore focus on the integration and dignity of women, who in many countries - and it should be remembered - are not even considered citizens. the broadest consensus will undoubtedly give greater force to our demands and our actions.
mr president, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr gemelli, on the work done in preparing this report, in which all the groups have finally reached a consensus in committee, although, as has already been said, it has not been easy. this report deals with an area of increasing complexity, such as globalisation, particularly in the environmental field and the problem of migration flows, which is becoming increasingly important in defining the role of the european union in the world. the socialist group has always argued that development policy must be an essential dimension of the external action of the european union and its member states. and this for two fundamental reasons: first, because the underdevelopment in which at least eight hundred million people live seems to us inherently perverse, socially unjust and economically inefficient. secondly, because we believe that the principles of solidarity and cohesion on which the european union is founded must guide the management of globalisation, so that it is sustainable. in this regard, i recommend that those who are not convinced of this should read susan george's latest essay. but we do not support any development policy. if the objective of development policy is poverty eradication, as you and the council have repeatedly stated, you should not, in your preliminary draft budgets, squander funds on the least developed countries in favour of other external commitments. if that means raising the ceiling on the financial perspective, then do so, and if you do not, change your speech. if we follow the oecd development assistance committee (dac) approach to the rationalisation of anti-poverty strategies, we will also have to follow the dac approach to budgetary structure, in order to be able to assess the effectiveness of our policy in relation to our objectives. that is what this parliament has approved and what we want. if the commission wants new forms of governance for europe in which dialogue with civil society plays a key role, we must help those organisations which are most representative of development in the european union. in short, we cannot manage this policy as erratically as we are doing. mr. gemelli's report is good. the commission's communication also lacks, as the report has already said, concrete action and quantifiable commitments. both documents are dry paper if they are not put into practice. in the coming months, several world conferences will be held and the debate on the major development issues will be reopened: the world conference against racism, the united nations conference on the least developed countries and the first aids conference. all these issues affect us in our daily politics. for example, racism is closely linked to immigration problems, which in turn have to be looked at from the perspective of the development of the countries of origin, and aids is closely linked to everything that is patent policy and the pharmaceutical industry. the socialist group in the european parliament calls for the european union to participate actively in these conferences and, to this end, the european community's development policy must be effective, coherent and cohesive. in this respect, we hope that this report will be positive.

development fund and for the rest of the world we also have, as part of the financial perspective, clarity and certainty as to the budget level for development cooperation. this is quite important, challenge to live up to this. to mrs sauquillo, i would just give the information that on 9 february we had a very good meeting with a whole range of different development ngo networks in europe and and this will be very useful. however, i find it more important to have a substantial debate, an ongoing discussion, with parliament than with anybody else. one does not exclude the other but it should be remembered in any discussion about the role of ngos that this house has the legitimacy and representation which gives any opinion from here a somewhat bigger weight than any from anywhere else. this is also part of my approach in dealing with these issues. mr rod pointed out the problem of whether we or our partners are deciding what we are supposed to do. this is in any case a complex issue. we can only offer to do those things in the developing countries that we know how to do. we have had to limit ourselves to some extent because there are many things we do not know enough about to be delivering good assistance in those fields. there are some limits to what we can make our obligation and we also have to ensure that it fits in with what other donors can offer. it is not correct to say that we have designed our priorities by thinking how we could help ourselves by doing these things in the developing countries. this is simply not fair, especially when we look at the new policy and the very strong focus on poverty. mr rod also mentioned access to medicines. it should be noted that the commission has recently taken a number of steps in the follow-up to its communication on aids, malaria, tb. we decided two weeks ago in the commission on a programme of action which follows up what we did in the autumn. this actually includes some very strong ideas on opening up for a more focused attention on tier pricing and also opening up for bidding and becoming a supplier across the geography for non-oecd companies from, for instance, brazil, india, south africa, china which should have access to bids on all our agendas relating to malaria, tb and aids. mrs sandbaek, the opening up for exports from ldcs has been an issue which i assume everybody is well informed about now. i listened carefully to the different evaluations concerning how member states finally decided on monday. there was very little doubt as to the commission’s views and its original proposal. the member states have now decided. i take some relative satisfaction in looking at comments from everybody outside the eu, as well as comments from third world representatives, that they now sincerely hope that other big trading partners and players in the global trade policy discussions will now do something as good or comparable to what europe has done. there is absolutely no doubt that europe is now in a better position than before the ldc conference and in the effort of creating a basis for a new global round in the wto framework. we can always discuss whether we have
