to mrs maes, i would say you are right that the battle against poverty is not over and has not been won. one of the reasons why development assistance has not worked is, quite simply, because there has not been enough of it. some of it has not been good and the crazy conflicts, the problem of corruption, all these problems are there. but we are in a situation where, for once, it is reasonable to say that more of the same is part of the answer. we know what good development cooperation is and the sigh of relief, the sense of getting things in order now for the eu, reflects that fact that there is a global consensus to relate to. otherwise we would have invented something very new and exciting which we could choose to call a wheel or whatever, but the interesting thing is that there is not really much new in what we have done. but we have become mainstream. we are hooking into the priorities and the ways of working which reflect best practice in the understanding among donors and partner countries in the south. this is why i feel so confident that the priorities that we have listed, the policy paper and the support it has got is strong, real stuff that we can use. getting it done will be quite a challenge but we will face up to it. to mr howitt and mr van den berg i would say, on the issue of priorities, that it is pretty well established that we agree on the aims of actually being able to deliver something that more than lives up to the 20-20 principles from the social summit in copenhagen for instance. giving priority to health and education agreed and so on. but our problem, and this also comes back to what mr imbeni said, is strangely enough the fact that we do not know what we are doing. to some extent we do know what we are doing but we have no record of the composition of the different activities. we are not able to say how much we are doing on environment because the labelling of our different projects was never organised in such a way that we can take out the files and say, “well, this is it”. we are not able, as of now, to say how many kilometres of roadway we built last year. this is something i am trying desperately to produce – clear, tangible, real, down-to-earth statistics, telling people what we are doing. but it is all obscured by commitments and long-term programmes etc. and there is no link between the spending and the commitment. this is where we are now. so delivering, technically, in the manner that parliament would like will require more homework than we are able to perform in a very short time. this is the core of the discussion that is still outstanding, not an issue of substantial disagreement. honestly, at the beginning i myself had some doubt as to the importance of writing the overall policy statement for development cooperation because in my view it was not really that new. today, almost a year after we did it, i am of a different opinion because first of all the actual process of writing it and having it accepted showed that it was definitely worth the trouble and that debate was necessary to create real ownership in the commission throughout the different services with regard to these principles. the next thing was that member states were much more enthusiastic about having one paper covering the whole geography saying what our policy is. we never had that before. so, even if it is not revolutionary, i see a strong meaningful value in having it and certainly, as i sense in our discussions over the months between the commission and parliament in this field, we have real value in having this shared framework of what it is that we think about when we talk about the development policy paper. so it is valuable. the next thing now is that we are going to use it and the moment is important because together with the launching of the cotonou agreement, the hammering out of country strategy papers for each and every one of the 77 acp countries, we are in business, and we are going to use these principles. for the rest of the geography we are going to move from country to country applying the same rules. this is where we will be calling the bluff on the reality of the acceptance of focusing on poverty when we come to middle-income non-acp countries and start looking at the real distribution of what we are spending our money on in these countries. so, we will have tons and tons of work and a lot of political challenges to correct the course of what we are doing in the coming months and years in this area. another big drama will be the actual delivery. i will continue being very open and frank with parliament, not to reduce our own responsibility for executing the budget but rather to make sure that there are no misunderstandings as to the size of the challenge and its nature. we now have a good policy and we are fortunate to have the backing of this house for that policy. the next thing is to move forward hand-in-hand and implement it and make sure, as i have said before in this parliament, that we change the situation from what it is today, where we can say that as europeans we are proud that we do this, to some years from now when we should also be proud as to how we have done it.
- doc. a5-0047/2001 by mr varela suanzes-carpegna, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the proposal for a council regulation (ec) laying down certain control measures applicable to fishing activities for certain highly migratory fish stocks (com (2000) 619 - c5-0585/2000 - 2000/0253 (cns)); - a5-0046/2001 by mr varela suanzes-carpegna, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the proposal for a council decision on a financial contribution by the community to certain expenditure incurred in implementing certain measures for the management of highly migratory fish stocks (com (2000) 651 - c5-0556/2000 - 2000/0268 (cns)) - a5-0051/2001 by mr piétrasanta, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the proposal for a council regulation laying down certain technical conservation measures for certain highly migratory stocks (com (2000) 353 - c5-0016/2001 - 2000/0149 (cns)) i give the floor to the chairman of the committee on fisheries, mr varela suanzes-carpegna.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are again having an important debate today - and again at night - on the common fisheries policy, and more specifically on the external aspects of it, on what we might call the external fisheries policy, that is, the participation of the european union in multilateral fisheries organisations - hereafter, for short, i shall refer to the rfmo - and the renewal of a fisheries agreement with a third country, in this case equatorial guinea. i would first of all like to congratulate the rapporteurs who are with me tonight, mr piétrasanta and mr gallagher, on the excellent work they have done. focusing on the first of these aspects, the role of the european union in the stecf, we are dealing here with the stecfs which regulate the stocks of highly migratory species, that is to say tuna and related species such as swordfish, fishery resources of the highest commercial value on which we must put our greatest effort and zeal for the enormous economic interests of these, both for the union and for third states. i would also like to draw attention to the community decision-making procedure in this area. we have tabled an amendment to the regulation on control measures in committee, so that the commission will submit to us an annual report on the control and surveillance activities carried out in the context of these orps, to which the european union belongs, and that this report should include the provisions adopted by the management committee for the fisheries sector in implementation of the provisions of the regulation itself. there is a huge lack of information to the european parliament or, what is even more serious, there is a sense of the futility of these consultations with the european parliament, whenever we are consulted - if you will allow me the expression - at the last minute, that is, with facts that have already been done and when the measures have already been adopted, thus reducing to ridicule the role of the first democratic institution of the european union. we must change this system, commissioner. as we are already trying to do de facto with the iccat meetings, a system which we must extend to all the other stecfs in which the european union is involved, which - we hope - are increasing. we want to know in advance, in our committee on fisheries, what proposals the commission is going to defend in these forums, to discuss them with us and then defend them, thus fully associating the european parliament with meetings in which it will continue to participate, or i hope, as an observer, as it has been doing in recent times, thanks to the code of conduct established between our institutions. i shall not dwell on the enormous role of the orps, on which our committee has already made several reports. i would remind you that we are preparing another own-initiative report which has a lot to do with stecf: i am referring to the control of illegal fishing in international waters, to the report on vessels flying flags of convenience, which unfortunately also occur so frequently in the fisheries of large-scale migrants. the european parliament wants to be involved, together with the fao, in defining new, more precise and more developed concepts of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, catch declarations, inspections at sea and in port, landing bans, etc. for this irresponsible fishing. that is why, commissioner, we have asked to be present at the previous meetings on the control and inspection of the stecf, and also at those on the criteria for allocating quotas, since these must be linked to the stecf, so that in future one of the main criteria for allocation will be precisely the capacity to comply in practice with the control and inspection measures imposed by the stecf, since it does not seem advisable or reasonable for a state to increase its catch quotas if it does not have the means to control them. in short, we welcome the commission's efforts to consolidate the wide-ranging and scattered rules on large numbers of migrants, even though it is submitting to us decisions which have already been adopted and are already binding at international level, since they are not subject to objection, and only for greater legal certainty. but we are calling for greater involvement of the european parliament in the proposals which the commission must defend in these forums, bringing them to the committee on fisheries beforehand. secondly, i cannot, not only as rapporteur for these reports, but above all as the current chairman of the committee on fisheries of this parliament, fail to reiterate here once again, commissioner, the request of our committee, which was endorsed by the house, that the administrative structure of the directorate-general for fisheries should include in its organigram a specific unit to deal with the management of the stocks of these highly migratory species. the many existing stocks of these species, and those which may still be created in the future, together with the importance of the european fleet fishing for large migratory fish, plus the high commercial value of these, to which we have already referred, are calling for greater material and human resources to be provided to the directorate-general for fisheries, creating a specific unit within it. if you, commissioner, were to attend a meeting, either a preparatory working meeting or an annual meeting of one of these tens and saw the deployment of resources from other delegations and the resources available to the community delegation, you would immediately give the order to set up that unit. parliament therefore reiterates that in this context and in the reform of the directorate-general for fisheries' organisational structure which is currently taking place, parliament's request should be taken into account. finally, i would like to refer to the amendments adopted by the committee on fisheries concerning the management costs of the european union's membership of these large migratory stecfs. our committee on fisheries has considered, in line with what it has already said, that if we are faced with an exclusive competence of the european union in the field of the common fisheries policy, the international financial commitments acquired by the commission, in the exercise of precisely that exclusive competence, must also be assumed exclusively by the commission, via the community budget, and not be transferred to the member states themselves. the commission's own competence must imply its own financial capacity to deal with it. and a policy which is called common - as in the case of the fisheries policy - must fully apply the principle of the adequacy of the resources which govern it. these are the considerations, mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, which i have been pleased to make in connection with these two reports for which i have had the honour of being rapporteur.
mr president, as we all know, the great migrants have a number of characteristics which require that their fishing be subject to particular monitoring. their movements, both through exclusive economic zones and through open waters, their regulation at present by four regional fisheries organisations, their high economic value, which makes them the target of many fleets, and their association with species which are not the target of direct fishing, such as dolphins and other marine mammals, explain the fact that even the united nations has decided to intervene through the agreement for highly 'experimental' fisheries, the commission's claim is simply irresponsible, and the tactic of transposing a recommendation in one paragraph to empty it of content in the next is unacceptable. we already council itself by quota transfers. the aim of limiting the presence of vessels, whether they like it or not, with tradition in the fisheries to open the doors to new fleets cannot be accepted in any way and therefore i ask for full support for the amendments tabled by the committee on fisheries. i can only thank the rapporteur again, mr president, for his cooperation and i congratulate him sincerely on his excellent report.
- mr president, we are talking today about a type of fishery, the large-scale migratory fishery, which requires a strong international presence from the european commission. the growing activity which the european commission must carry out in the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas is being supplemented by that carried out in the indian ocean tuna commission and must be commission. – the presidency has just explained the background to the recent air raids. i do not wish to go over the same ground so let me just say that i agree fully with the assessment of the situation which we have just heard. i agree very much with the distinction, which i thought was nicely made, between the first efforts to create a common foreign and security policy and the ambition suffering which that stalemate has caused is extremely unsatisfactory and we should do all that we can to avoid it continuing. we must bear in mind, however, that the sanctions were put in place originally for a purpose. as a result of the gulf war the un security council established through a number of resolutions that iraq should dispose of all weapons of mass destruction and that this should be verified by unscom, the un special committee with responsibility for dismantling iraq’s arsenal of weapons and maintaining a monitoring programme to ensure that it was never rebuilt. until this was achieved it was agreed that iraq would be subject to various economic sanctions though exceptions were allowed for essential humanitarian supplies. although they could have done it straight away, back in 1991, the iraqi government did not take steps to set up an arrangement with the un before 1995, when iraq agreed to the ‘oil for food’ facility as set out in the un security council resolution that year. the ‘oil for food’ facility has since then been extended every six months with improved conditions. in principle the ‘oil for food’ facility should provide basic humanitarian aid without recourse to outside assistance. however, the management of the programme and cooperation with the iraqi government in implementing it, is not effective. there is no shortage of funds available to the iraqi authorities through the ‘oil for food’ facility to buy food and medicine for their people. it is the iraqi regime which has chosen not to do this, not to use the opportunity offered to them by the international community. the issue of sanctions, worsened of course, when unscom was expelled from iraq in november 1998 and it took a year to agree to a common approach to deal with this problem. the un security council adopted resolution no 1284 in december 1999 which allowed for a suspension of the sanctions against iraq following arms monitoring. however iraq did not accept the resolution and resisted any cooperation on verification of dismantling of weapons of mass destruction. iraq has not therefore complied with the un security council resolution, a point made i recall in the european parliament’s resolution of april last year. we have now reached an important point in our dealings with iraq. the sanctions which have been in place for 10 years have clearly not achieved their desired objectives. they are perceived to be exacerbating the humanitarian condition of the iraqi people. the recklessness of saddam hussein and his regime has resulted in malnutrition, ill-health and widespread degradation of the physical and social infrastructure of the country. this policy will have consequences beyond the present which will be borne by future generations of iraqis. these dire circumstances have brought into focus the plight of the iraqi people and the problem of dealing with a regime which is as ruthless as it is reckless. we all agree that there is clearly a need to re-think the whole iraqi issue and to identify the best course of action to take. the new us secretary of state, colin powell, has said as much. we must not lose sight of the basic objective. we must make sure that we will never again give saddam hussein the means to pursue aggression against his neighbours, or indeed against his own people. the sanctions remain in place but we should look at how we could make them more effective in pursuit of the basic objective. we want to focus on the iraqi leadership and their weapons, not on the iraqi people and iraqi society. the international community should explore the possibility of replacing the present sanctions regime by, what is called in the jargon, “a smart sanctions programme” and other appropriate measures whilst seeking to ensure that weapons of mass destruction are not manufactured. the suffering of the iraqi people is very much a concern of the european union. since the gulf war in 1991, europe has been the major donor of humanitarian aid to iraq with over eur 250 million. for the last two years, the european union has provided assistance of between eur 8 and 10 million on an annual basis. for 2001 the amount may be somewhat higher at around eur 12 million. the assistance, through echo, focuses on provision of clean drinking water and health facilities, with special emphasis on institutions for the handicapped, for orphans, and with emphasis as well on street children. the echo assistance is provided through international non-governmental organisations and through the appropriate un agencies. mr president, apart from being an evil against the civilian population, sanctions can, when maintained for a long time, become a harmful political instrument and turn against those who imposed them. now, colin powell says that the us administration is considering a system of sanctions that is not against the people but against the iraqi regime. however, it has been recalled precisely these days that this is what president bush sr. said ten years ago, when the theory was put forward that the tyrant in baghdad, thanks to sanctions, would be overthrown by his own people. today, with few exceptions, arab states are ranked among those more concerned about the risk of an extension of the israeli-palestinian conflict than about applying sanctions to iraq and among those others who wish to resume relations with baghdad. and all this coincides precisely with the new anglo-american bombing. frankly, i think the more iraq is bombed, the more the arab public opinion is radicalized, which it already is, and also the palestinian public opinion, which is also radicalized. and at the same time, we must remember, a favour is being done to saddam, who is morally and politically strengthened within his country - at least according to a certain conception of morality and politics - and in the eyes of the majority of arab public opinion. this may lead to a growing sense in those arab public opinions that the arabs are suffering from a war on two fronts: one, american against iraq, and the other, israeli against palestine. i hope that these public opinions do not consider that this is an anglo-american war against iraq. finally, i would like to say that it is not only in the arab countries that the west is held responsible for the prolonged suffering of iraqi children. many in the west feel the same way. i am one of them, mr. president.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the role and influence of the european union in the international arena is becoming increasingly important thanks to the consolidation of the european union process itself. alongside this process of globalisation towards the east, towards the mediterranean, towards north america, towards africa, relations with other regional blocs are being strengthened. the agreement recently concluded with mexico, which has been very positively assessed by the foreign minister, mr castañeda, is moving in this direction. the agreement, according to mr castañeda, is a kind of stimulus for mexico to improve its living conditions, since it can count on the opinion of parliament and the european union. within latin america, the association agreement with mercosur, an agreement based on the treaty of rome, is of particular importance as a response to the process of globalisation and as a means of improving relations with north america. this process began in 1995 and was embodied in the declaration of the first summit of heads of state of latin america, the caribbean and the european union, held in rio de janeiro from 25 to 29 june 1999. from that moment on, meetings with organised civil society were also held. in this respect, however, it is regrettable that the european parliament does not participate in the definition of the mandate for the negotiation of agreements with third countries, in which, it is true, the trade and economic development are given the highest priority, but in which the fight against poverty, cooperation, the development and consolidation of democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights also play an important role. this agreement marks the transition from the third generation agreements to a larger, interregional agreement which is at the same time political, economic and trade liberalization. that is why the commitment of this agreement to mercosur and to chile is unique. the summit referred to above is the point at which the directives are put into effect at the general affairs council meeting on 13 september 1999. but we thought it would be a good idea to make some modifications. the european parliament, in this report, - taking into account that the european parliament represents the will of european society, which is not only a commercial and economic society, but also a society full of social, justice, equity, solidarity and cultural concerns - intends to introduce new directives expressly containing the following:first, that the legal basis for the new agreement is to be article 310 of the treaty on european union (formerly article 238) in conjunction with the second sentence of the first subparagraph of the second paragraph of article 300 and the second subparagraph of the third paragraph. it is important to give it a legal guarantee and to state that the partners have a whole legal framework behind them. secondly, it is necessary to provide for specific mechanisms for future arrangements which will enable international cooperation, the development of democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights, which are the objectives proposed by the cfsp, to be based on the principle of economic and social cohesion and to tend towards the reduction of imbalances. thirdly, the new directives must be based on international agreements - i am thinking of the agreements on ethnic minorities and indigenous peoples, which are important in mercosur as well as in other countries - and agreements relating to the international labour organisation, to provide for control mechanisms which can specifically improve the functioning of trade unions and workers and which provide not only for joint participation in the un and other international bodies, which would give greater importance to this agreement, but also for explicit mechanisms of dialogue for european security and defence policy, as the institute for relations with latin america has recently advised. it is also necessary to extend and improve the specific involvement of civil society and to examine the subordination of this agreement to the world trade organisation, whereas both the european union and mercosur have sufficient authority to reach concrete agreements. it is also necessary to improve relations with other countries and to eliminate, as far as possible, the current two-stage division of the process. it is therefore important that the house should be able to approve this report, which was adopted unanimously in the committee on foreign affairs and with considerable assistance from the commission's secretariat.
the rapporteur. mr president, mr marset campos has already mentioned the main points and demands of parliament which are common to both reports. if i could sum up this debate in one word, i would say that parliament, commissioner, is calling for a revision of the negotiating directives through these reports. why would you do that? firstly, because it is inconceivable that negotiating directives should not mention the legal basis of the agreement. in the opinion of this parliament - and mr marset campos has already said this - the only possible basis is article 310 of the association agreements. this parliament, while recognising that these are mixed agreements by virtue of the subject matter - that is to say, where there are competences which are those of the member states and of the community - understands that the division of the negotiation into two stages, the first concerning general issues on trade, which has already begun, and the second concerning the tariff and services negotiations, which will begin on 1 july, is discriminatory and should be corrected, although i understand that for practical purposes it would not make much sense to ask for a modification of the directives only for this purpose, given the proximity of the date. more serious, mr president, is the inclusion of a clause making the conclusion of these agreements conditional on the conclusion of a new round of negotiations at the world trade organization, which we do not know whether will take place and, if so, when. this condition has not been imposed on any other country or group of countries and therefore, commissioner, we in parliament believe that this obstacle should be overcome. parliament therefore calls for a review of the current negotiating directives so that they can eliminate and overcome this anomaly. i would like to know what the commission's view is on this point, in particular on the connection between the conclusion of these agreements and the completion of the new round of the world trade organisation. during the discussion of the report - on which we have had excellent cooperation, mr patten, with the latin america directorate and the mercosur and chile division - we heard that one of your colleagues, mr lamy, in charge of trade relations, was not in favour of revising the negotiating directives unless there was prior acceptance by the council. as this agreement is an agreement on political association, economic concertation and cooperation, and with trade liberalization, but in which political will must prevail - and i understand that it does - i would like to know what the impression is of the commissioner responsible for the political impetus of this negotiation. i would add, commissioner, that if this aspect of political dialogue is to have credibility, it must respect an inescapable requirement, namely that the discourse be adapted to the reality of cooperation, and that words be met with deeds so as not to be reduced to mere rhetorical statements. what latin america needs is not gifts but solidarity and opportunities, and an excellent opportunity to demonstrate political will with action is in the field of trade relations. i would like, mr president, that, with a view to the next summit of heads of state or government of the european union and latin america, these negotiations with chile and mercosur should be sufficiently advanced and, if possible, be concluded. i know that the case of chile and the case of mercosur are different, and i would like to ask publicly (we already do so in the reports to be voted on this morning) that these negotiations be conducted each on its own merits, but with the aim that they are advanced or completed with a view to that summit which will have to be filled with content in the next six months. the european parliament believes, and has said on many occasions, that the commitments of the madrid summit and these agreements are an urgent imperative and a sign of the european union's renewed credibility towards latin america. the comments i have just made on trade, mr president, are just as valid as regards cooperation, because, while recognizing the importance of the effort made in favour of the region, which in absolute terms reaches important figures, we consider that there is some unjustified discrimination for the subcontinent in relation to the andean pact and central america and the priorities resulting from the rio summit. i would therefore ask the commissioner responsible, at this point in time before the drafting and presentation of the budget, to send a signal - i understand that the pressure on our budgets is really great on the eve of the birth of the euro - an effort to send a signal contrary to that which was sent in last year's preliminary draft budget in favour of the region, with a view to enriching the next madrid summit. mr president, we in parliament, one of the two arms of the budgetary authority, are also fully aware of the difficulties involved in this exercise, but if in the last budgetary debates we have been able to demonstrate that the european parliament remains in solidarity with this region, i the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. mr president, first of all i would like to refer to a small error of annotation in relation to the opinion of the committee on industry, for which i was rapporteur, since point 2 in particular should end with the acronym gatt. the following sentence is from the draft report and was deleted during its hasty preparation, for which i had only 24 hours. turning to the text in question, i would like to refer to the trade aspects of the association agreement between the european union and mercosur, which will bring together almost 600 million consumers, i.e. 10% of the world's population. the annual trade volume in 1998 - the only year for which statistics are available - was eur 42 billion, growing by 125% over the last eight years, with a surplus for the european union of eur 6.4 billion. in the same vein, it should be noted that the community remains mercosur's largest partner, five points behind the united states, and its main supplier. in addition, if we look back, the presence of european countries in this area has been the largest in all of latin america, no doubt due to the particular historical and cultural ties that unite us. in short, it is an agreement of enormous importance, unprecedented in the world, by which the only two subregions in the world which have constituted common markets are associated in the commercial field. finally, i would like to express my support for this interregional association agreement, which may mark a milestone in the history of world trade.
mr president, in the european parliament's resolution of 14 december 2000 on the prosecution of general pinochet and the consolidation of democracy in chile, we insisted in the same terms that the best support that the european union can give to the process of democratic consolidation in chile is the conclusion of an ambitious agreement on political consultation, economic partnership and cooperation, with particular emphasis on the human rights clause. i think we can today be pleased with the speed, consistency and high degree of consensus with which this parliament, through the committee on foreign affairs, has responded to that demand. the two rapporteurs have already outlined the characteristics of the proposals. i would therefore like to emphasize only two points. firstly, as has already been said, the importance for the committee on foreign affairs of the legal basis of the new association agreement and the fact that that basis is article 310 of the treaty, among other reasons already mentioned, because that legal basis guarantees parliament its assent. secondly, i would like to stress that the committee on foreign affairs attaches great importance to the fact that the conclusion of the negotiations on these agreements is not conditional on the conclusion of the world trade organisation round. on this second point, perhaps commissioner patten could give us his position on how to resolve the differences in agriculture, especially in the case of mercosur. another aspect i would like to stress in these two recommendations is the fact that the committee on foreign affairs, perhaps favoured by its transversal character, has succeeded in giving both proposals a strongly political character, emphasising their foreign policy and cooperation aspects over some tendencies to maximise the importance - by no means less, but not exclusive - of economic and trade relations. it is not hidden from us that strengthening the political character of our relations with mercosur and strengthening the process of integration could be an attractive force for chile, whatever the pace of the negotiations, perhaps compensating for the attraction of the united states in trade, economic and political relations with that country, as well as its project to relaunch the free trade agreement of the americas. i would also like to congratulate mr patten and the commission for having taken up the testimony of his predecessor, commissioner marin, and for having followed faithfully and responsibly - i would say politically - the steps of the initiative he had launched. finally, i would like to ask mr patten a question, although i think he has just left. it is not hidden from him the importance which the model of parliamentary cooperation to be established between chile, mercosur and the european parliament will have for the institutional development of the agreements. i anticipate that i, like many other members of the committee on foreign affairs, will be in favour of a model similar to that established for the europe agreements, a model based on joint parliamentary committees which improves the current system of delegations. i would like to know what the commission and mr patten think about this.

mr president, although mr patten is back in the chamber, we cannot say that his lack of presence in the chamber is an expression of the commission's fondness for these matters. but in any case, those of us who have recently been in the area in question - and this member has just arrived from argentina and chile - do want to convey the great scepticism with which the european union's involvement in relations with latin america is seen, which is absolutely insufficient. this scepticism is particularly acute in the world of the social economy of small businesses and trade unions, with which i had the opportunity to meet this week in argentina and chile. i agree in general terms - and we certainly will! - with the report that is being discussed here today and, in general, with everything that is involved in increasing economic and trade relations with the countries of the region and also with the involvement of civil society in this and other aspects of the association agreements. but it is obviously a critical support, because although the international pacts on ethnic minorities have been mentioned - as mr marset has done - we find them to be absolutely inadequate in this and other areas where our group's amendments have not been echoed. although progress has been made in the field of labour rights, with the adoption of ilo conventions, there is no mention of the code of responsibility for multinational enterprises adopted by the oecd, arguing that this is not europe, when in fact it is european enterprises that are setting up in these countries. nor have environmental measures been adopted, and the new negotiating mandate does not include specific references to the structured and institutionalised participation of civil society in this political dialogue, as we requested. we therefore support, in general terms, what we are discussing here today on the association agreements, but we are, once again, critical of other aspects which we consider essential.
mr president, the agreements we are discussing will in future form the backbone of the european union's cooperation relations with mercosur and chile, and they constitute a homogeneous body of one is closer to us than the latin americans in terms of democratic values and aspirations. no one like them shares with us an ambition for social justice and national dignity, reconciling this with many decades of project of supranational integration and of responsible and coordinated participation in the international community. the horizon opened up by these agreements is that of ever closer cooperation, including political cooperation, between europe and latin america. with it, we may be able to chart our own paths more than has been the case in recent decades, when we were much more commission. – let me first start by congratulating the rapporteurs for their excellent and very helpful reports. we are clearly entering a crucial moment in the negotiations for association agreements with chile and mercosur. the negotiations are well on track. we have had three negotiating rounds, part of the last of which i attended myself. it was a considerable success. preparations for the fourth round of negotiations to be held in the second fortnight of march are in full swing. it is fair to say that after one and a half years of negotiations, we are approaching the most intensive phase. political dialogue, cooperation and trade issues figure very high on the agenda of the next session. negotiating texts have been exchanged. work has even started on the preparation of the tariff and services negotiations, including agriculture, which are going to begin in july. this has all been possible thanks to our serious commitment to these negotiations. no-one doubts that the commission wishes to do all we can to strengthen ties with mercosur and chile. during the course of this year i want to accelerate these negotiations. much progress has already been made in the political and cooperation fields but major progress is still needed on the trade side. i hope we will see a leap forward on non-tariff barriers and business facilitation in march. in july, we expect progress with negotiating offers on both tariffs and services. as my honourable friend pointed out earlier, the second european union – latin-america summit will take place in madrid in spring next year. it is still too early to speculate on what concrete progress we should expect by then but it is always clear, as the honourable gentleman said earlier, that by the time of the summit, negotiations must have established a critical mass. this critical mass should be sufficient in some areas to finish discussions. it should also be possible in other areas to conclude negotiations as soon after that as reasonably possible. our objective is to attain a high and ambitious level of political and commercial interaction with mercosur and chile. as parliament knows, no sector is excluded from the negotiations. our main guidelines are achieving a strategic political partnership, strengthened cooperation, and a wto-plus deal on the trade side. it is no secret that while chile fully shares this comprehensive approach, mercosur has a rather more limited objective, aiming primarily for greater market access in agriculture. we should continue to insist on a comprehensive global and balanced agreement which aims at a deeper political and cooperation relationship as well as wide and far-reaching trade liberalisation. the two reports that we are discussing are both comprehensive and extremely useful. they make a number of sound recommendations – most of these are based on the possibility of modifying the current negotiating mandate provided by the council. that may be desirable at some point over the coming year but, at that this point in time, we are naturally focused on achieving successful rounds of negotiations in march and july rather than on stopping the discussions and going back to the drawing board with the council. we had a full internal debate on this two or three years ago. at present, the commission is keen to get down to work and do the job it was instructed to do. let me just make a few concrete comments as regards the specific recommendations. first the matter of the legal base. the final agreement will be an association agreement not a mere trade deal. our future strategic partnership goes well beyond trade. however our legal advisers tell me that the exact articles for the legal base could only be determined at the end of the negotiations. i agree with this opinion. for the time being we only have the outline of agreement. we need to wait for the final result, as we have done in other similar negotiations, before we look at our own legal base. then there is the question of democracy, the rule of law, respect of human rights and good governance. these are all basis tenants of our negotiating position and they are the cornerstone of the agreement that we want to reach. these issues have already been discussed during the third round in brasilia and santiago and we have reached consensus with mercosur and chile on them. i am personally committed to ensuring that these essential elements underpin our future association agreements with mercosur and chile. then labour rights. these are also an integral part of the negotiations. they are currently being discussed in view of the fourth round in march. we need to ensure that labour rights and greater prosperity advance hand-in-hand. greater prosperity should help lead to a deepening of democracy and that should mean greater respect for basic rights, including of course labour rights. so we support an approach in the association agreement which assures labour rights through cooperation and promotion of the relevant ilo conventions. i come to greater political cooperation including security. this was already established during the third round in brasilia and santiago. we will work together for the promotion of peace and international security on the basis, of course, of our own internal rules and procedures. civil society was mentioned in the reports and by a number of speakers. transparency and accountability are essential. civil society should be part of the agreement. we have already agreed on proposals during the third round to include civil society in the institutional framework of the agreement. in addition, the commission organised a successful conference with civil society last october to promote discussions on the negotiations. we have also created a website in august of last year which provides a full breakdown on the negotiations for the general public. so as the house can see we are making a real effort to enhance the transparency of the process. several members and the reports themselves refer to the possibility of eliminating the link to the proposed new wto round. i certainly do not rule out this possibility but this will depend first of all on whether we have a new wto round at all. we obviously hope that happens, and the sooner the better, but we have not yet got that proposal off the ground. it depends as well on the progress we achieve in future negotiating rounds with mercosur and chile. we might consider this option if sufficient and substantial progress is made. it is suggested that we should eliminate the two-phased negotiating approach. the house will know as well as i do that this approach was the result of a compromise solution between ministers during the general affairs council of june 1999 in luxembourg. this compromise formula broke the deadlock in council and opened the door to the approval of the negotiating directives. i very much appreciate parliament’s support on this important issue but it is presently more a matter of principle than practice. i am afraid we are now too far into the process to turn back. we only have four months more to go and only one negotiating round until july when the second negotiating phase is meant to start. so i think we should get on with the job and prepare meaningful global negotiations from july onwards. let me finish by underlining once again that the commission is absolutely committed to successful negotiations with mercosur and chile. we are determined to get on with the job and make as much progress as possible. negotiations are in full swing. preparations for the next round are on track. with or without changes in the mandate, the commission is working to make these negotiations a success as quickly as possible. i hope i can count on parliament’s support to that end. lastly, can i refer to two questions which i received during the debate. first of all, mrs díez gonzález asked me a question. i am afraid i left the chamber for about 60 seconds of her speech. i will not go into the details as to why, but if i tell the house that i am present in parliament the whole of the morning she will perhaps appreciate why i needed 60 seconds outside the chamber, but i can respond very positively to her remark. she asked whether there would be a joint interparliamentary committee. the commission strongly believes that there should be. we can respond very favourably to the honourable lady’s request and we will be discussing exactly the mechanism that we can use shortly with mercosur and chile. so we can give a very positive response to that important proposal. secondly, the honourable gentleman mr knörr borràs, asked me about the oecd code. we cannot oblige countries that are not members of the oecd to follow the oecd code. i understand the importance of the point he raised but we cannot make it obligatory for non-oecd members to follow the oecd code. i repeat i hope that we can count on parliament’s support in the weeks and months ahead, and i am sure that the close attention being shown in this debate underlines the fact that we will able to do so.

mr president, telecommunications networks, in my view, are nothing more than highways of social communication, just as air corridors, railways or motorways are. if, in the latter, we find a model which guarantees equal opportunities and in which transport service providers, even when competing with each other, share networks built and maintained primarily with public resources, reducing the environmental impact of these civil works to the minimum possible, i think it would be wise to opt for a similar scheme for the development of telecommunications, where competition is not for the construction of overlapping infrastructure networks, but for the provision of more efficient and cheaper services for the user. in the 1980s, as mayor of bilbao, i witnessed a struggle between companies for more and better networks, each of them wanting to open their own ditches and install their own antennas to have their own pipes and exclusive coverings in all the streets of the city. i opposed this, considering it more rational that through a single ditch, pipeline, network and public antenna all the telecommunications services of all the private operators could run, in the same way that buses and trucks of different companies do it on the same highway, without the need for each to build its own. mr president, if we wanted the final networks to be private too, i am not against it, but i think it would be better, in any case, to separate the functions of owner and operator of these networks from those of user and provider of telematic services.
in writing. - (es) after terminating a previous agreement which was part of the so-called third generation agreements, the european union has had an interregional framework agreement with the mercosur countries since the end of 1995. this framework agreement should have been replaced by a comprehensive agreement on interregional political, economic and trade liberalization association, including chile, as requested by the heads of state and government of the two parties at the rio summit at the end of june 1999. this new association treaty is being delayed by endless partial negotiations, slowed down by our demand for a prior compromise in the wto. on the other hand, some want the new agreement to be only an instrument of free trade between the two sets of states. i believe that, whatever the importance of the economic and trade association that is sought between mercosur and the european union, the political, social and cultural aspects that must govern the new association agreement, which must now be a top priority in the union's foreign policy, are of greater value. we must not forget the history of latin america, nor the links that have been forged over the centuries between the various european countries, which discovered what was then called the "new world", and which have made this part of the planet imbued with the same cultural, religious and identity substrates as the europe we are building, to the point of sharing our membership of this great family of values and customs called the "west". we must therefore strengthen the bilateral dialogue at all levels, institutional, economic, civic and social, parliamentary, intergovernmental and executive, to ensure that the new full association agreements with mercosur and chile become a reality as soon as possible.

commission mr president, i would first of all like to reassure both mr chichester and, certainly even more so, mrs isler béguin, that my presence on the commission's benches is not due to the fact that the transport of nuclear materials has been transferred to the sprawling and insensitive domain of the head of foreign trade. it is a much more innocent exercise of temporary transfer of files without storage - i should like to say this - among members of the commission who are anxious to lend a hand from time to time. the transport of nuclear materials, as you have just said, is often approached with a certain amount of passion, given the context and environment of this industry. the commission therefore understands the great difficulty you have had in synthesizing sometimes contradictory positions. we believe that the rapporteur, as well as the members and members of the committees who have contributed to this effort, should be congratulated on this very remarkable synthesis work. as many of you have pointed out during the debate, the nuclear industry, whether we like it or not, is responsible for a considerable part of the security of our energy supplies, and so we must accept that this industry must resort to the transport of radioactive materials. the report which we are presenting to you is essentially a confirmation that the measures taken at international and national level ensure a high level of safety in the transport of these materials. however, it is clear that transparency is very important in this area, as in all activities in the nuclear sector. we recognize and support, and are fully committed to promoting, accurate and transparent information on all risks that people may or may not face. despite the difficulties of the subject and the limitations imposed by security, we share your view that it is important to strengthen this information. it is clear that this is an area where the optimum and perfection have never been achieved and, as mr piecyk has said, it is true that the member states have the primary responsibility in this matter, but this does not prevent us from working on actions which would, for example, improve the documents accompanying the transport of the materials in question. it is not for us to decide whether or not to use reprocessing technology. it is a solution of an essentially industrial nature, which must be chosen on the basis of rather technical and economic criteria and the need to reduce high-activity waste. we can and we intend to support research and development efforts. this is what the commission has proposed in the context of the sixth research and development programme, with priority given to innovation in waste management. it is also our responsibility to ensure that the obligations of the euratom treaty, chapter 3, on radiation protection are met. you want to include a chapter on energy in the treaty on european union in your report. we all know that this is a question which has been discussed several times in intergovernmental conferences and which has so far not been resolved. as our green paper on the strategy for energy security and supply points out, we believe that the euratom treaty fulfils its objectives in a number of areas. it is true that it does not contain any specific reference to the transport of radioactive materials. we believe, however, that the provisions of this treaty allow us to play a supervisory role while maintaining the primary responsibility of the states. that is what the commission wanted to say about this report. we will of course give careful consideration to all the suggestions in the report in the spirit i have just indicated, namely to improve our own intervention to the extent of the means we have and the possibilities offered to us by the treaties. as i said at the beginning, we consider this report to be a useful document. it is a means of providing european citizens with an informed opinion and, after the many debates you have had among yourselves on the question of the transport of radioactive materials, it seems to us to contribute to a reasoned approach to this activity, which will undoubtedly lead to improvements in transparency, and so we welcome this report.

the commission mr president, i thank the three members of this parliament for their comments. i would first like to emphasize that the commission fully recognizes the importance of european shipyards and understands the particular difficulties faced by many shipyards. we are perfectly aware of the nature of these difficulties. the expansion of the already over-indebted south korean yards was made possible by additional loans from financial institutions which do not operate on market terms. various forms of indirect state intervention have allowed south korea to maintain in operation capacity which, if normal commercial criteria had been applied, would have had to be reduced in order to meet the actual market demand. this excess capacity is a dead weight on the world shipbuilding market and even threatens the existence of some european shipyards. the commission considers that unfair competition practices in the shipbuilding sector at international level should be addressed through appropriate mechanisms. this means first of all through negotiation and, ultimately, in the world trade organization. although commissioner lamy is in a better position than i am to give you detailed comments on the current state of this negotiation, i can assure you that the commission is continuing to do its utmost to find a negotiated solution to the problem. it is of course prepared to raise the matter with the world trade organisation and is currently making the necessary preparations to initiate the procedure. commissioner lamy made this very clear to the south korean authorities at the meeting with them in mid-february. if the international negotiations currently under way do not lead to a solution, the commission has undertaken to report to the council by 1 may and to propose a temporary defensive support mechanism. this does not mean reintroducing the old operating aid provisions in article 3 of regulation 1540/98. the third report from the commission to the council on the state of the world shipyard industry clearly states that operating aid, which is authorized under the aforementioned regulation, is not a solution to the problems of international trade. the typical negative effects of operating aid have led the commission to express a generally negative opinion on this type of aid. the shipyard was the last industrial sector in which this type of aid was still authorized. you are certainly aware that the commission is in favour of aid where the distortion of competition resulting from state aid is offset by positive incentive effects. the commission therefore decided in its decision of 29 november not to extend the operating aid provided for in article 3 of regulation (eec) no 1540/98. the third report from the commission to the council on the situation of the world shipyards, referred to above, confirmed that operating aid linked to contracts had a number of negative effects on the single market. the aid was onerous, untargeted and distorted intra-community competition. the commission is considering very carefully the form that the temporary mechanism should take in the event that we fail to reach a satisfactory solution in the negotiations with south korea: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this mechanism should specifically address south korean unfair practices for the period of time necessary for the conclusion of the wto proceeding and should target those market segments where the european industry has been directly penalised by south korea's unfair trade practices. i can assure you that we are working diligently on the preparation of the proposal. we will do everything possible to ensure that it can be ready by the deadline set by the council, should it be necessary. parliament will of course be kept informed of the progress made. in the meantime, there should be no doubt about the commission's determination to take a stand in defence of those community shipyards which are suffering the consequences of internationally unacceptable and distorting commercial practices. specific references were made to aid for research and development.

- mr president, illegal trafficking in human beings has become one of the most despicable crimes that must be prosecuted and repressed by the law and by international cooperation. the governments of the european union have committed themselves to this in the tampere agreements and this also requires the necessary cooperation of the countries of origin and especially of the agents involved in the transport and transfer of travellers. the problem is how to harmonize the laws of the member states and to seek ways of approximating them. it is clear that carriers have an obligation to check that the aliens they carry meet the entry requirements. the formula proposed by this initiative of setting a minimum amount, as a penalty, of not less than eur 5 000 per person transported does not seem unreasonable, although the confiscation of vehicles and means used by carriers should also be imposed, not as a possibility but as an effective penalty. it also seems necessary that the transport of a person who, under the geneva convention, is in a position to be granted asylum should not be considered as punishable. in short, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a question of the union's governments making every effort to ensure that the carriers, the border police and the customs police carry out their duties in a properly coordinated manner and prevent mafia networks from being able to traffic in human beings. this is not the only way to combat illegal trafficking in human beings. it is a matter of sharing responsibility for a serious problem which european society as a whole is obliged to face. that is why, ladies and gentlemen, it is urgent that this initiative, which has been under discussion for many months, should be implemented as soon as possible.

the commission is aware of the fact that the court of justice has already ruled on the question of the right to a fair trial in criminal proceedings. following this express reference in the treaty, this issue was included by the council in the vienna action plan, in the conclusions of the tampere council, and subsequently included in the commission's scoreboard for the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice. as the rapporteur has pointed out, and i would like to congratulate him on his excellent report, this issue has been dealt with in the past in the 1970 hague convention on the taking of evidence abroad in civil and commercial matters, which, however, has only been ratified by eleven member states of the european union. the increased mobility of persons within this common area of the european union has been one of the factors which has contributed decisively to an increase in the number of cases with cross-border implications. in the field of taking evidence, legal proceedings before the courts of one member state increasingly involve, for example, the hearing of witnesses resident in another member state. it is therefore necessary to adopt clear and effective rules on cooperation between the courts of the member states in order to facilitate the taking of evidence in such situations. such rules will undoubtedly represent a significant step forward in the ongoing work to improve access to justice for both individuals and businesses, as well as in the pursuit of the overall objective of creating a european judicial area in civil matters. this regulation thus adds value to european citizenship, to the protection and guarantee of the individual rights of citizens, and has a considerable economic value in that, by allowing and facilitating the taking of evidence, it makes possible a faster and more efficient administration of justice, and above all an administration of justice more in line with the new needs of economic reality, the internal market, the single currency and electronic democracy. in view of these considerations, the commission welcomes the german proposal for a regulation in this field. the commission is not prejudiced against initiatives by the member states, especially when they are in line with the priorities defined by the tampere european council. the german proposal also gives us the opportunity to advance and modernise the rules of the 1970 hague convention with the added value of the action of adopting a community instrument which applies uniformly and directly in the legal order of each of the 15 member states. this is a first stage whose central objective is to create the necessary mechanisms to strengthen mutual trust between the legal and judicial systems of the 15 member states. this first stage should, once the implementation of the regulation has been assessed, open the way for more ambitious objectives, in particular those which would result in the possibility for the requesting court to request a special procedure to be used in the enforcement of a judicial act by the requested court, as well as the possibility for the requesting court to be associated with the participation in the enforcement of the judicial act by the requested court. we therefore welcome the support given by the rapporteur to this initiative. the commission shares the general considerations advanced by the rapporteur and the content of the amendments he has proposed. and i can assure you that we for our part will be following closely the discussions on the proposal in the relevant council committee in order to find a text which exactly corresponds to the concerns which parliament has expressed in the marinho report.

flax - and record some figures for this house. figures such as the fact that in my country, spain, 3,376 hectares of flax were grown during the 1994/95 marketing year, whereas in 1998-99 there were already 100,000 hectares of flax cultivated. the initial grant for 1994-95 was pta 411 million, while for 1998-99 it was pta 10 billion. the fraud was denounced by the spanish regional authorities and in 2001 the area under flax cultivation miraculously dropped from 100,000 hectares to less than 1,000 hectares and, of course, to a subsidy of less than 100 million pesetas. despite these facts, the then head of the ministry of agriculture maintained that it was all a campaign of the opposition and, of course, recently changed his mind and said that it was not so, but that it was mainly the fault of the opposition. i would like to focus, mr president, on what kind of responsibility this parliament can ask for. first, the question of criminal liability. a criminal responsibility that is around certain owners of processing plants, who are the ones who had the privileged information - office olaf as a whole, and i would like to begin by addressing the points you raised in the debate here and in mr bösch's report on olaf. the council and parliament created the legal basis for olaf in 1999, and this is of course also the basis for the commission's action. this legal basis has created olaf as an office which is administratively part of the commission, i.e. olaf officials are commission officials and are subject to the staff regulations. this also means that if, for example, problems or irregularities arise with regard to the behaviour of commission officials at olaf, the commission would be sued. to take this into account, the commission has said that it wants to have a transparent procedure for the selection of management positions at olaf, just as in the other commission institutions and departments. this means that an advisory committee first reviews the applications and makes recommendations to the person who ultimately makes the decision. in the case of olaf, the decision on recruitment and appointment is ultimately taken by the director. the composition of the advisory committee is now such that the persons not directly attached to the commission or coming from olaf clearly have a majority. the court of auditors, the european court of justice and the monitoring committee are represented on the advisory committee, and i think that the solution we have found is a very good one. i would remind you that this solution is designed to make the appointment of managers transparent, whereas the appointment is ultimately made by the director or the director-general of olaf. i hope that in this sense the question of the continuation of olaf posts will be resolved very soon, because i can only say once again that it is in my own interest, but also in the interest of the commission as a whole, that olaf should make available all the posts that were actually decided upon as soon as possible. i think it would also be in the interests of the various parties concerned to have a dialogue with each other, since the monitoring committee has now laid down further conditions so that the amending budget can finally be tabled and this question the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the best environmental results are achieved when all concerned citizens are given the opportunity to participate in the process. improving access to environmental information for the public leads to increased environmental awareness. citizens must therefore be at the centre of environmental policy if we are to be able to cope with the changes needed to guarantee sustainable development. the rio declaration already stressed the importance of public participation in the formulation and implementation of environmental policy. without access to environmental information, it is difficult for citizens to participate and exert pressure. that is why this proposal for an extended right to environmental information is so important. in 1998, the member states signed the unece convention on access to information, public participation in decision-making and access to justice in environmental matters - the aarhus convention. the convention is a major step forward in implementing principle 10 of the rio declaration and in continuing the process of transparency initiated by directive 90/313/eec on the right of access to environmental information. before the community can ratify the convention, the existing community acquis must be adapted. that is also one of the main aims of this proposal. another main objective is to correct the shortcomings identified in the practical application of directive 90/313/eec, which was adopted in 1990. one of the key elements of the commission's proposal for a new directive is to provide a right to environmental information instead of free access to environmental information. it also provides a broader definition of environmental information and sets a shorter deadline by which public authorities must disclose information. it also provides clear definitions of the exceptions and proposes that public authorities may refuse to disclose environmental information only if it could harm private or public interests protected by the exceptions, and that public authorities should also actively provide environmental information to the public. since the question of authorities has been raised, i can say that the commission has accepted mr korhola's amendment with a definition of 'authorities'. it is fully in line with the aarhus convention. when public services are privatised, as they are in the united kingdom, it is up to the national authorities to ensure that environmental information is still made available to citizens. the commission's proposal covers the main obligations of the aarhus convention and goes beyond in some respects. the proposal, however, leaves it to the member states to decide how these obligations are to be applied in practice. the commission's proposals have definitely improved in recent months and i would like to thank mr korhola and the european parliament for the work that has been done. i am convinced that, thanks to good work, a common position will be adopted at the council meeting in june. some of parliament's amendments seek to adapt the commission's proposal to the precise wording of the aarhus convention. the commission can accept these amendments in general. however, we cannot accept amendments which significantly depart from the aarhus convention. however, we think that some of the amendments lead to too much detailed regulation of the issues covered by the proposal. i would like to emphasize that this is a framework directive. the main objective is to establish the basic conditions for ensuring public access to environmental information. i therefore believe that the member state should also be given some flexibility in transposing the directive into national law. one issue that came up in the debate was how we deal with registers. the proposal provides for the possibility of setting up registers in the member states, but it is not an obligation - it does not lay down any mandatory rule for member states to set up registers. finally, i would just like to say a few words about public access to environmental information held by the eu institutions, as this issue has also been touched upon in the debate. i am now examining various options to ensure that the community institutions also fulfil the obligations arising from the aarhus convention and intend to return to you as soon as possible. of course, we must first await the examination of the proposal currently under discussion. the commission cannot accept the amendments on this particular issue, as they fall outside the scope of this directive, which is addressed to the member states. i also want to say a few words to bernié about the life programme and the various life projects. i personally think it's incredibly important that we disclose information and be completely transparent about the life projects. however, we have the problem that member states say that this is information which they have produced and which they therefore do not accept the commission to disclose. this is the very problem that is being dealt with in the context of the debate on article 255. these are the questions on which we must come back with a proposal on how to bring the eu institutions into line with the aarhus convention, and i promise we will come back to this as soon as possible. in conclusion, the commission can accept amendment no 3 in its entirety and can accept amendments nos 1, 11, 15, 19, 21, 24, 25, 26 and 28 in part. the commission can accept in principle amendments nos 13, 17, 19, 20, 21, 23 and 24. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 16, 18, 22, 27, 29 and 30, which are not in line with the commission's proposal.
