- question no 47 by mr lennart sacrédeus (h-0191/01): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the french company, subject: indication of origin in the labelling of meat in february, a eurobarometer survey revealed a marked decline in support for the planned enlargement of the european union to the east in several member states. in the three most populous countries, germany, france and the united kingdom, a majority of respondents were against enlargement. this is happening at a time when mad cow disease is at its peak in most member states. the enlargement of the union and the arrival of new members will considerably increase the geographical area from which our agricultural products originate. as a result, european citizens will have even more difficulty than they do today in knowing the origin of their products. in order to reverse the decline in confidence in meat producers, could the commission consider proposing the introduction of a compulsory indication of the origin - national or regional - of meat in order to better inform consumers?
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. when the european parliament and the council approved in july 2000 a mandatory labelling scheme for beef marketed in the community either in fresh or frozen condition, this was an important step forward in improving transparency and regaining consumer confidence. today, as we are experiencing a second serious crisis in the beef sector, the mandatory beef labelling system is already proving its worth, because now every piece of beef is traceable, and it is also clear where the animal has been slaughtered and cut up. the place of birth and the place where the animal was raised will be added to this mark from the beginning of the following year. with regard to the labelling of beef products covering all types of food preparations containing beef, the commission is to comply with the timetable laid down in article 21 of regulation (ec) no 1760/2000, which requires it to submit a report to the european parliament and the council by 14 august 2003 and, if appropriate, to submit proposals for the labelling of those products. the commission is, however, working on a proposal on the indication of the content of meat and offal in all foodstuffs, within the framework of the general labelling rules. this proposal would then be another important step towards greater transparency in meat products.
commission. - mr president, to make this point a little clearer, why is there this distinction? what came into force on 1 september last year concerns information on the labels about things that can be found at the slaughterhouse. each animal has an ear number, and when i pass that number on to the meat, i can trace the path from the meat to the animal. secondly, clearly i know from the slaughterhouse where the animal was slaughtered, and i can also determine where it was dismembered. the other problem that becomes acute from 1 january 2001 is that we also want to provide information on upbringing and place of birth. i cannot see that at the slaughterhouse, but the animal must, so to speak, bring its history with it, and that requires a corresponding database and also a corresponding computer registry for this to work. the problem we have here - and this is why we can only start with this system in general later - is that not all member states have sufficient data going back to the time when the birthplace of all animals was already recorded by computer. it will also be the case on 1 january 2002 that you will not have this data for every animal, but you can then distinguish very precisely. quality meat and meat labelled as such will have this information on the label, which will normally be a code and not a spelled name. the other meat may not be marketed as quality meat. that's the procedure.
- question no 48 by rosa miguélez ramos, substituted by medina ortega (h-0193/01): subject: aid to the livestock sector in the member states affected by bseseveral member states have discovered in recent years that their herds are affected by bse after the united kingdom exported animal meal to these countries, whereas the marketing of animal meal was already prohibited in the united kingdom itself. the european union had then given the united kingdom considerable aid to deal with the crisis. now that other countries are experiencing cases of mad cow disease, public opinion expects community aid similar to that granted to the country at the origin of these ills, otherwise we would again be faced with the paradox stated by president prodi before the ep during the presentation of the programme for 2001 'of a europe ever more necessary and yet perceived as ever more distant'. what were the volumes and percentages of eu funding for the measures taken to address the bovine spongiform encephalopathy crisis in the uk? what resources are available and what percentage does the european union intend to co-finance support measures for the countries affected by this new bse crisis?
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. in order to solve the problems of the first bse crisis, when the export of live bovine animals and beef from the united kingdom was prohibited, the so-called 30-month scheme was used to destroy all meat from animals older than 30 months at slaughter. in addition, the calf processing premium for the early slaughter of calves has been offered not only in the united kingdom but also in france, portugal and ireland. in the four years from 1996 to 2000, when the uk now has this 30-month scheme, the cost to the eu budget was €1,275.4 million. this amount is equivalent to 70% of the purchase price for these animals, as 30% of the purchase price and the total disposal costs have to be borne by the united kingdom. 80% of this amount was paid when the animals were slaughtered and the remaining 20% when it was established that the animal meal produced from these animals had been burned. however, it should be noted that the full costs of killing and also of harmless disposal were borne by the united kingdom. the calf processing premium was financed 100% by the community budget. for the four member states in which it was offered, this resulted in expenditure totalling eur 326.6 million, of which eur 235.4 million went to the united kingdom. the community's response to the first bse crisis also includes full financing of public storage and an early marketing premium for calves, as well as direct aid of eur 1 309.9 million. these direct aids - the early marketing premium and public storage, which collectively accounted for over 700 000 tonnes of meat - benefited all member states. in order to deal with the current crisis, the commission not only provided eur 238 million for intervention in 2001 and eur 700 million for the destruction approach, but it also recently proposed to the council and parliament a package of measures for the beef sector, including both intervention and specific market measures to reduce beef production in the period 2001-2003. this means additional expenditure to the approximately 1 billion already approved for the 2001 budget, of 157 million in 2001, additional expenditure of 1 145 million in 2002 and 181 million in the 2003 budget. the cost of the campaign and the special schemes is also borne by the community at 70%, all other costs being borne by the member states. the community will continue to finance 100% of intervention stocks.
- commissioner, thank you very much for the information you have given us. in view of the exponential growth in community expenditure in this sector, does the commissioner think that the various member states affected by the second mad cow crisis will be able to meet these needs with the means which the commission is expected to have at its disposal in the coming years, 2002 and 2003?
the commission. we have also included a financial statement with the package of measures we have presented, and it shows very clearly what expenditure will be incurred and how we intend to finance it. in this way, we are sure of the funds. we expect that in the 2002 budget we will remain below the limit decided in berlin, mainly because of the unforeseen development in the dollar/euro ratio in berlin and mainly because exports of wheat in particular are still very favourable and because there is not as much need to spend in some other areas. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter.
- commissioner, there is a great deal of concern in galicia. it is an objective 1 region which is suffering from bse and is strictly implementing a plan to combat this disease. i would like to know whether these measures, of which the commissioner speaks, are enabling or will enable direct aid to farmers. and, in particular - because i am asked to do so - whether specific measures for female bovines aged between 9 and 24 months can be authorised or are planned and whether the special premium for male slaughter can be changed, changing the age criterion to the weight criterion: 185 kilograms. this is what they are asking me to do and it would be important from the point of view of fighting this disease.
the commission. i'm sorry if it always takes a little longer, but the translation takes a little longer than the speaker. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. firstly, we are already spending all the available funds under the items we have proposed. we have no more funds available in the 2001 budget to use for direct aid to farmers, for example. it is also a different situation from that which prevailed in the first bse crisis, because in the first bse crisis the old agricultural guidelines, which were much more generous, still applied. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission has no way of going beyond this limit. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i therefore see no possibility of paying a specific income aid to farmers under objective 1 funding. thirdly, i would point out that this fact naturally leaves a possibility open, but only within the framework of the national aid scheme. within this framework, national aid may be granted by the member states. however, they are subject to the condition that they are notified and that they do not exceed the limits laid down in the state aid schemes.
- mr president, i have asked the commissioner two very specific questions. one has been answered, but the question on bovine premiums has not been answered and it is a question which perhaps the commissioner did not get through interpretation and i would like to repeat it, if i may: are you going to authorize the specific measures for female bovine animals aged between 9 and 24 months and amend the special slaughter premium for male bovine animals, changing the age criterion to the weight criterion, 185 kilograms? you haven't answered that.
commission. - mr president, there is only one slaughter premium. the slaughter premium is regulated by the market rules and is the same for all animals. i cannot therefore give you any further answer to what has been translated as a question.
- question no 49 by mary elizabeth banotti (h-0137/01): the council has not yet adopted the common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer. subject: convention on the protection of children, 1996 the 1996 convention on the protection of children is generally regarded by those concerned with child protection as a very useful instrument which will be of great help in many aspects of child protection. it is imperative that any new introduction of a child protection regime in the eu does not impede the implementation of the 1996 convention. given that some conflicts of jurisdiction have arisen at eu level in this area, can the commission give an assurance that the member states will ratify as soon as possible the hague convention of 19 october 1996 on jurisdiction, applicable law, recognition, enforcement and cooperation in matters of parental responsibility and measures for the protection of children?
commission. – i totally agree with such an approach but, as the honourable member will recognise, it will be extremely helpful if we clarify first of all the conditions under which the community as such can accede to the convention. there are some legal problems because the drafting of the convention only provides for member states to be part of the convention. so we need to incorporate the fact that the communitarisation of the subjects of the convention give the commission and the community exclusive external competence. once we clarify that, it will pave the way for member states to ratify the rest of the convention with the full support of the commission because the commission is committed to solving its own problem without delay.
question no 50 by mr juan de dios izquierdo collado (h-0149/01) subject: cost of bank transfers does the commission not consider, as has been repeatedly requested by consumer associations, that bank transfers within the european union, in the eurozone, should have the same cost as national transfers? does the commission not consider that the current upstream and downstream costs of bank transfers, which are high and do not take account of the single currency or the single market, are excessive? what regulatory measures or strategy does the commission intend to implement to ensure that the costs of these transfers are kept to a minimum in the euro area and across the union?
commission. – i wish to begin by thanking the honourable member for his question. the commission shares his concerns. it is our political goal to have the fees of cross-border and domestic transfers converge so that it will be no more expensive to transfer money abroad than to transfer it within the borders of a single country. this statement and objective has been repeated by the commission on numerous occasions. for example, in the communication entitled "retail payments in the internal market" of january 2000; in my reply to parliament on the peijs report of 26 october 2000; and further in the commission's round table conference entitled "establishing a single payment area" of 9 november 2000. i should like to stress that it is intolerable in a single-currency zone that charges for cross-border transfers exceed those for domestic transfers by several orders of magnitude. however, the determination of charges and fees should be left to competition and market forces: european legislation should not aim at price regulation. the introduction of the euro has only limited effects on transfer costs. the reason is that the convergent costs of currency are only one element of the total transfer costs. in fact, the currency convergence costs represent about 20% of the total. the remainder – the other 80% – of the persisting high fees for cross-border transfers are mainly due to insufficient automation and standardisation. there the commission supports, and indeed promotes, the initiative aimed at changing and improving the present situation. the commission will continue to monitor the situation and keep pressure on the eu banks for the establishment of more efficient cross-border retail payment systems.
- commissioner, i know that you have already spoken on more than one occasion about my question, but i echo the views of the consumer and user associations in this respect. they are not happy just because we talk; what they usually appreciate is that we solve problems. they have brought this problem to the table in quite a few cases and they still know that their consumers are complaining about a reality that is really hard to accept, because transfers not only have a high origination cost, but they also have a high destination cost, to the point that the bank is now charging unjustified costs when it issues the transfer and the receiving bank is charging unjustified costs of the same level when it receives the money. in other words, we are taking action which does not seem to correspond to the objectives of the single currency which will enter into circulation on 1 january 2002. what concrete negotiating action can the commission take in this respect to satisfy consumers?
commission. – mr president, i am not at the moment in a position to agree with mr titley's statement that there is less and less competition in banking. that is something that would require further research. however, it is certainly the business of the commission to see that fair competition prevails. as mr titley will appreciate, it is my colleague mr monti who deals with competition. i know that mr monti has made certain investigations, but they were more concerned with the exchange of currency. there are two different aspects involved here: first the cost of transferring money, which was the original question put to me, and secondly the cost of currency exchanges. the commission's investigations on this have not yet reached their conclusion. the latter will, of course, be a thing of the past for the twelve "euroland" member states as from 1 january 2002.
- question no 51 by mrs laura gonzález álvarez (h-0226/01): what is the commission's position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer? purpose: saving jobs after the merger between aceralia, arbed and usinoraceralia, arbed and usinor announced in brussels the merger of the three steel groups and the formation of a new company, which will capture 60% of the european steel market. according to statements by the president of the new company, francis mer, the merger will create a number of synergies, which should lead to savings of eur 300 million in the first year and to savings of eur 600 million by 2006, thanks to improved costs and productivity, with workforces that will gradually become reasonable. these statements have caused concern among trade union organizations. on the day of the merger, usinor announced the closure of the charleroi blast furnace. there is also considerable concern in spain, with the risk of job losses in asturias, the basque country, aragon and the autonomous community of valencia. in view of the commitments made at the lisbon summit on full employment, what measures does the commission intend to take to ensure that the new steel group will retain the existing production centres and workforce? question no 2 by mr verheugen
commission. – mr president, it is true that we live in an era of industrial change and reconstruction. it is true that every day there are new acquisitions and mergers and that sometimes restructuring is synonymous with job losses. this can have tragic consequences for the social fabric of any region, but particularly those regions where there is little potential for job creation. the commission appreciates that citizens and workers need to feel secure in this difficult time. we believe that the cornerstone of successful adaptation to change is dialogue at all levels, based on full and transparent information. the basic ideas that the commission intends to highlight are as follows. the first one is that decisions and corporate restructuring are both a prerogative and a responsibility for the management. this means that, when considering action that will have social consequences, companies should always actively try to find less negative and less damaging solutions. secondly, when dismissals prove to be inevitable, everything possible must be done to assist with the redeployment of those concerned. this requires forward planning, timely preparation and effective management of these processes. thirdly, nothing is more important than the social dialogue. there must be timely, effective and comprehensive information and consultation with workers' representatives and this must, of course, be before initiatives are launched or publicly announced. worker participation is not only a basic right but also a necessity if corporate restructuring is to be accepted. under the existing european legislation, employee representatives in merging companies may be informed and consulted on the potential social consequences of the announced measure. there are concrete european directives which have been transposed into national law relating to collective redundancies, transfers of undertakings and european works councils. but it is not for europe to intervene at this stage as regards compliance with the directives. they have been duly transposed into the national law of the member states and any conflict or litigation arising from the application of the rules should be assessed by the relevant national authorities. in my first point i concentrated on the social dialogue and the implementation of the existing european legislation. my second point concerns the three enterprises concerned by the merger in particular, because they have considerable experience with restructuring and dealing with the social consequences and social dialogue and social partners. in particular, if social measures were to be taken to assist the workers affected in order to redeploy them, to provide them with temporary income support or remove them from the labour market by early retirement before the ecsc treaty expires on 23 july 2002, the commission could, at the request of the government concerned, provide additional aid under article 56 of the treaty. this is the aid commonly known as readaptation aid.
- mr president, i would like to thank the commissioner for her extensive explanation. i fully share many of the things he says. like her, i think that dialogue is necessary and that the directives relating to labour rights and european works councils should be implemented. however, you will understand our concern if i tell you that i live in asturias. asturias is a region that has undergone the conversion of coal, mining, arms manufacture and shipbuilding. there has been dialogue and agreements with the workers and there have been retirements and early retirements, which is what one of the presidents of these three companies we are talking about today is proposing for, for example, the charleroi furnace, which seems to be one of the first to be closed. the very specific question, madam commissioner, to which you probably already have an answer, is: if the lisbon agreements spoke of full employment, is it not terrible to use public resources for this job creation and, on the other hand, to lose jobs continually through restructuring, privatisation and mergers of companies? the problem in asturias, where there were retirements and early retirements, is that today young people have no future because more than 30,000 jobs were eliminated.
commission. – of course i share with you the concerns we have just mentioned because it is an area with big problems. but you know that the entire area – valencia and asturias – belongs to objective 1 of the framework support. within this framework the government of asturias can possibly make some changes to the proposed programme for the next six years and maybe they could acquire some money, according to the regulation on implementation of the european framework programme and according to the governmental rules. there is a need to combine the social fund, the employment strategy and the finance of the employment strategy and the implementation of the european and national – in that case, spanish – laws. what we are trying to do in this case is to find a combination of actions within the framework of this information and consultation. this would mean that we can organise training courses and we can finance them; we can support people in organising their own self-employment activity or small sme. in some cases – and this is one of the cases in which it can be permitted – we have the early retirement system. so we must find this combination and address the situation. obviously we cannot prevent companies from merging or making acquisitions.
- mr president, you too were born in the asturian region and it is therefore normal that you should be concerned about the issues of our region. a supplementary question to the commissioner: do you think that the main role of the commission in this area of setting up or helping large enterprises is to create a sufficiently efficient and competitive economic environment? i mean, we think it is much easier to guarantee employment through companies that are in an environment that is efficient enough to allow competition with companies from other places than to maintain a restrictive social policy that is often against the interests of the workers themselves.
commission. – your question is the fundamental question of how we can combine economic and social policies. this is the main problem we face in europe: how to combine competitiveness and cohesion. as far as this merger is concerned, this is a field with many problems. we have major acquisitions and mergers across europe. the only way to address this is not through legislation or restrictions concerning jobs. after every merger or restructuring in the industrial field we must see not only the number of jobs lost, but also the number of jobs saved. in some cases mergers, modernisation and acquisition are very important for the future of the sector. so what we have to do now is to address both: to support the competitiveness of our companies and to see how we can address the implications of these mergers in our societies. this is what i have just explained. in this case there are three main elements. you can use the ecsc treaty. we only have one year now to use it. the asturias can be subsidised under the treaty. secondly you can use the european framework. and finally, you can use national money in order to organise or to implement social policies in the area.

this exploitation covers several problems which it is necessary to distinguish. as regards player agents, a competition procedure is still ongoing before the commission and discussions have led fifa - as their objects are related, i call questions 56, 57 and 58 simultaneously. question no 56 by astrid thors (h-0219/01) subject: impact of the european year of languages on regional and minority languages as we all know, 2001 is the european year of languages, which has just been officially inaugurated. what impact does the commission consider the year of languages will have on regional and minority languages and, in the light of the follow-up, what does it intend to do to ensure that this impact continues to have a beneficial effect on the situation of these languages? question no 57 by mr michl ebner (h-0239/01) subject: multiannual programme for minority languages many people and organisations representing minorities had hoped that the nice summit would decide to use qualified majority voting in the field of culture and that a member state would no longer be able to block decisions concerning minorities and their languages, as has already happened on several occasions. how does the commission view the current (post-nice) situation with regard to minority languages and a multiannual programme in their favour? question no 58 by concepció ferrer (h-0245/01) subject: european year of languages 2001 the year 2001 has been designated by the european union as the european year of languages. the aim of the year is to promote knowledge and learning of the official languages of the community, as well as irish, luxembourgish and other languages specified by the member states. since the preamble to the charter of fundamental rights of the european union states that 'the union shall contribute to the preservation and development of these common values, while respecting the diversity of the cultures and traditions of the peoples of europe', could the commission indicate which languages the member states have considered eligible for the measures planned for the european year of languages? questions to mr barnier

- the president-in-office's statement on foot-and-mouth disease is on the agenda.
- mr. president, we are facing a problem that has a very high potential to become explosive. although draconian measures have been taken in the various member states, the risk of the disease spreading must be acknowledged. we are facing an extremely virulent strain and in environmental conditions that make us fear the worst. the problem of foot-and-mouth disease can be approached from three angles: actions to be taken immediately or in the short term, determining responsibilities and preventing these problems in the future. let me make three points. firstly, in the short term, the economic effects of a vaccination campaign would be equivalent to those of its absence and the consequences would be extremely heavy. but if the vaccine is abandoned, the measures taken by canada will have to be met with a harsh response. the european union cannot tolerate in silence widespread and unjustified embargoes such as canada's or retaliation such as the united states's. secondly, commissioner, will there be compensation for farmers for this tremendous crisis? where are we gonna get the money? i have calculated that there is only 50 million euros left for compensation to farmers, after the last budgetary revision proposal, for foot-and-mouth disease and even for bse. and thirdly, the final reflection. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the spread of the disease, including the introduction of a new vaccine. we should also reflect on the risks posed by a community livestock system based on the transport of live animals and large concentrations of animals. the crises that surround us should lead us to design a cap geared more towards the consumer and the producer than towards trade. it is therefore necessary to target aid to ensure the viability of farms which present the least risks to the environment and to the consumer and which are most necessary for the maintenance of the social fabric in rural areas, rather than reducing or eliminating aid.
- mr president, mr commissioner, mr president-in-office of the council, the disease which now threatens a europe without frontiers may contribute to the increase in the crisis of confidence of citizens in both national and community institutions. the health risks of the cattle shed, the changes in dietary habits and the collapse of the productive sector are more than enough elements for us to make exceptional decisions. the measures have economic and political costs, and i would like to know what costs both the council and the commission are prepared to bear. are they prepared to increase support measures in all the countries of the european union? what do the european institutions think about mass vaccinations? what is the position to be taken with regard to third countries? will any action be taken against the unilateral restrictions imposed on us by countries such as the united states, canada, bulgaria and saudi arabia, as well as against non-rigorous imports from countries which are vaccinating, such as argentina, chile, brazil, etc., which may put our whole hut at risk? as for the wild animals, what's going to happen? what measures are planned, commissioner, for wild animals, zoos, circuses and so on? what happens if it affects deer, wild boar, goats? finally, i would like to know whether the european commission will take account of these health crises when it presents its budget for the european veterinary emergency fund which is so poorly endowed.
commission. – a number of different issues were raised. perhaps i might deal briefly with those, rather than go through the individual questions, and hope that i touch on all of the issues, particularly the important ones. first of all, regarding globalisation, it should be stressed that foot-and-mouth disease was prevalent – even endemic – in many member states in the past when trade was a tiny fraction of present levels. so to identify trade as being the cause of this is, in my opinion, a simplistic response. foot-and-mouth disease is endemic in the developing world. the eu has a huge trade surplus in food and agricultural products. so do we wish to surrender the resulting benefits? trade in agricultural products is one of the areas where the developing world has real potential to increase trade. i am personally asking my own officials to advise me about raising the standards in developing countries so that they are in a position to trade with the european union. this is an important issue. we must not lose sight of that. are we to tell these countries that we do not want their products for the reasons that we have discussed here this afternoon? the other route is the better one. intensive farming is another issue that was raised. i should repeat that the foot-and-mouth disease is endemic in the developing world. conversely, it is extremely rare in the oecd countries: the united states, canada, the european union, australia and new zealand. that is an important issue to be taken into account. there farming is at its most intensive. so, once again, to identify the debate as being one that focuses on intensive and extensive farming is also, in my opinion, an inadequate response to a complex issue. intensive farming has a lot to answer for but it is simplistic to see this as the cause of the current outbreak. transport was another issue that was raised. it is a commission policy and priority to reduce the incidence of long-distance live animal transport. a number of you asked the question "is this under control?". the restrictions on animal movement will minimise the risk of transmission of the disease. this will, in turn, eventually ensure that the outbreak is brought under control. it remains to be seen, however, how long this will take. a lot depends on the amount of trade that took place before we first knew about this outbreak. we will have to wait for the passage of incubation periods before we get a better picture of the situation. many measures advocated by members such as restrictions on sporting events, for example, are simply outside the competence of the commission and outside the treaties. with regard to controls, i should also emphasise that it is likely that this outbreak commenced in the united kingdom as a result of illegal activity. i must stress this. a number of people have asked why the commission does not bring forward more proposals. that is always the standard response when something happens. the legislation is there. it was a breach of the legislation which caused this illegal activity to spark off this particular infection in the uk. i should also emphasise that it is the responsibility of member states to seek to properly enforce the legislation relating to this and other matters. i can only draw your attention to the discussions we have had here before in relation to questions surrounding bse. controls and enforcement are important. we must not lose sight of that. i hope i have dealt with most of the issues you have raised. - question no 3 by mrs ewa hedkvist petersen (h-0229/01): the council has not yet adopted the common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer. subject: strengthening the dialogue with the european citizens european citizens are keenly interested in european issues. as a swede, i have seen this in informal ministerial meetings in sweden and more recently at the meeting of the ministers for telecommunications and employment in luleå. as elected members of the european parliament, we meet regularly with the citizens in our constituencies. the european commission, for its part, meets regularly with citizens from all the member states as part of its 'europe dialogue'. the council's role is more complex: in intergovernmental cooperation, european issues are competing with national affairs and, at the same time, the council takes the major decisions. we all know how important it is for confidence in the eu that there is a dialogue between the council and the people on the content of european policy. in this context, could the council indicate what measures it is considering to strengthen its dialogue with european citizens on european policy, for example at a ministerial meeting?
the council. the council agrees with the honourable member that the dialogue with the eu's citizens must be improved, as decided by the european council in nice in december 2000. in particular, the declaration annexed to the final act of the conference on the future of the union recognises the need to improve and monitor the democratic legitimacy and openness of the union and its institutions in order to bring them closer to the citizens of the member states. as regards council meetings, efforts are being made to make discussions more open and transparent. this is done through public debates, which involve, among other things, making the discussions open to the media and citizens by means of live broadcasts on domestic television or, unfortunately less frequently, directly via television stations. efforts are also being made to make press conferences and press releases more informative. other positive measures to raise public awareness are to improve access to information, both through conventional and electronic channels. in this context, the council is expected to adopt a decision on 19 march 2001 on the publication of certain categories of council documents. the aim is to publish as many council documents as possible on the internet without waiting for a request from the public. this decision shall enter into force on 1 may 2001. so a lot is being done. nevertheless, the council will of course continue its analysis in order to further improve the dialogue with the citizens of the eu in the context of the council's work.
the council. the honourable member may have noted in this morning's debate on the future of the union that one of the many concrete measures now being taken to stimulate further debate is precisely the opening of a website to be managed by the commission but to which the council, the member states, parliament and all interested parties can submit written contributions. i do not know whether it is possible, as the honourable member proposes, to extend the initiative by also opening a chat room. however, i think it is an interesting idea and i would be happy to discuss with representatives of the commission whether it can be put into practice.
the council. let me stress that we think now i am speaking on behalf of the presidency that the ombudsman's recommendations on the publication of documents are a very important step towards the increased transparency for which this parliament, in particular, has worked hard. the decision which we expect to be taken on 19 march does not go as far as the ombudsman proposes, but can be seen as a step along the way. the presidency is very much hoping that the necessary further steps to increase transparency will be taken as soon as possible. we shall not, however, be able to get to the end of march, i am happy to say.

the council. the honourable member gahrton uses a common debate technique, namely putting things in the mouth of the counter-debater. i thought i made myself pretty clear. i did not argue that passports are not needed for travel in general after sweden has joined the schengen area. what i said was the rules of internal control between the nordic countries, and i stand by what i said. secondly, as mr gahrton will understand, it is impossible for me to comment on the information contained in individual journals and publications. it is not within the scope of a presidency to do so. of course, any major change such as the entry into practical schengen cooperation requires that public authorities and others - primarily national authorities - inform citizens of the consequences. i can assure mr gahrton that the swedish government will do everything in its power to ensure that the citizens are as informed as possible. however, this is a debate that should take place outside this house.

- doc. b5-0016/01 by mrs randzio-plath, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, to the council, on the final report of the committee of wise men on the regulation of european securities markets; - b5-0017/01 by mrs randzio-plath, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, to the commission, on the final report of the committee of wise men on the regulation of european securities markets.
- mr president, i would like to join mrs villiers in her comments on the presence of commissioner bolkestein and i think we are fortunate that in such a short debate as this we have the commissioner, who will be able to answer almost immediately. i am speaking not as a member of the committee on economic affairs but as a member of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market and i would like to join the demonstrations of mr cox, mr goebbels and mr herzog. we have a legislative problem. we all agree that community legislation is very complicated, very baroque and very complex, but the reason why community legislation is so complicated and so baroque is the intergovernmental procedure used for the adoption of the rules, because of the lack of a genuine community legislative body which could have the power to adopt clear rules. so while we agree with mr lamfalussy and the committee of experts on the substance of the matter and with the need for clear and rapid community legislation, we cannot agree with the solution that he arrives at because it involves more committees, more use of the famous comitology procedure. in this respect i must recall the famous phrase that 'a camel is a horse drawn by a committee' with many humps, and community legislation is camel legislation, 'camelist' legislation. the committee procedure proposed by the lamfalussy report will create many more camels and will not create adequate legislation. the solution is not therefore to insist on comitology in this type of proposal. the solution lies in creating a clear legislative procedure which effectively enables parliament to exercise its powers. otherwise, all we would be doing is letting governments play games with each other to continue drawing up community legislation.
commission. – to begin with i should like to answer some of the points that were raised this afternoon. first of all, mr von wogau said that he welcomes the use of regulations and also the fast-track procedure. i would agree with him in his sentiment. certainly regulations and a fast-track procedure would help to speed up legislation. mr von wogau said that perhaps as a pilot project a pension fund could be used to show how quickly these procedures could be used. certainly, the commission would like to see the pension fund directive become a reality as soon as possible. however, certain articles in the treaty concerning the internal market mention directives and not regulations. naturally we have to stay within the confines of the treaty, so where the treaty says "directives" we cannot use regulations. but i agree with parliament that regulations are usually – although not always – faster than directives. mr goebbels asked if the new procedures would speed up legislation. as i have explained, they would. also the comitology procedure provides for short deadlines and therefore it would also speed up the whole process. mr goebbels then asked whether the securities committee would consist of secretaries of state. i am afraid i cannot answer that question. the securities committee has delegates coming from various member states and it is up to the member states to decide who represents them on that committee. so i cannot comment on that. as i said, member states will nominate their own representatives. what is important is that these representatives should show a real european spirit, are prepared to work closely together and are technically competent. i now come to the matter of transparency, which has been raised by a number of members of parliament. i agree with all those who have emphasised the importance of transparency throughout the legislative process and indeed the report by mr lamfalussy and his colleagues makes various references to the need for transparency. the commission wholeheartedly endorses that. mr herzog said this is a cumbersome intergovernmental procedure instead of a single european regulator. the procedures set out in this report are not intergovernmental. for example, the securities committee – which is an important committee in this respect – will not be a council working group. it will be a regulatory committee in the sense of the 1999 comitology decision; it will be chaired by the commission. so it is not an intergovernmental committee. the decision of the lamfalussy committee not to propose a single european regulator at this stage is the result of a full and thorough consultation process. as the report states, it may be necessary to look at the possibility of a single regulator when the whole procedure is reviewed in 2004 if the process that is currently proposed is not satisfactory, but not before. let me now answer a few points that were raised this evening. i am grateful to mrs villiers and mr medina ortega for their kind words, although to me it is only natural that i should be present here when a subject falling within my portfolio is discussed. mr medina ortega said that the european union's legislation is complex, which is true. normally there is a government and a parliament. we have a triangular relationship, the commission, parliament and the council. that makes it more difficult. the fact that there are 15 member states further complicates the procedure. he said that the whole system for dealing with executive measures under the comitology procedure is like the horse designed by a committee which turns out to be a camel. indeed there was a committee, the lamfalussy committee. but the whole idea of a comitology procedure is to get the implementing measures through more speedily. that is a purpose i share. i must say, however, that the matter of secondary legislation is a very important one. in many member states – in germany and the netherlands for example – there is a definite procedure for dealing with secondary legislation, which the european union lacks. there is no provision in the treaty for dealing with secondary legislation in this way. parliament, the council and the commission would be well advised to think about the need for a proper system of dealing with secondary legislation. since this whole process will be reviewed in 2004 let us hope that at the same time we can look into the matter of secondary legislation. then if we manage to work out a clear plan it can be taken up in the intergovernmental conference which will hopefully start in 2004. the commission is grateful for the support mrs kauppi has given to the report of the lamfalussy committee. there is no difference of opinion. she want speedier legislation. she is right. the commission wants it, mrs randzio-plath wants it, everybody wants it. she gave the example of usits, which it look a long time to agree upon. fortunately, agreement has now been reached but i would agree with mrs kauppi that it has taken a very long time. central to this whole discussion is the possibility of having a callback mechanism as parliament has requested. i do not have to explain what it is; everybody knows. the commission firmly believes that we ought to find a solution within the treaty – which means articles 202 and 211 – and that we should stay within the confines of the comitology decision of june 1999. therefore we cannot see our way to granting parliament a callback possibility. having said that, i would ask parliament to remember what is on the table. firstly, the commission will take full account of a resolution approved by parliament. secondly, as mr cox said this afternoon, it is parliament – and the council – that decide on the scope of levels in implementing measures. if the directive contains broad principles and executive measures and parliament does not agree that a certain executive measure should be called that and relegated to level 2, then parliament should say so and amend the directive to say that a particular implementing measure should be elevated to the status of a general principle and therefore be dealt with under level 1. so it is in parliament's own hands to decide on the distinction between general principles and executive measures. that is the second point. thirdly, if parliament thought the commission was abusing the system, what do you think would happen the next time the commission made a proposal concerning a certain directive? parliament would surely then be in a position to say "look, you fooled us the last time, now we are going to be extremely strict with you". so parliament can be certain that the next time it is dealing with a directive under this whole plan it can tighten the screws. the commission knows that. so why should the commission frustrate the wishes of parliament by doing something that is not really proper? that is the third point. fourthly, in the year 2004 there will be a review of the whole process and this – my fifth point – will be steered by the monitoring committee, an interinstitutional committee on which parliament will be represented. the monitoring committee will not keep silent if it thinks that the procedures are being abused and the commission is allowing itself too much latitude. my sixth point is parliament can pass a resolution saying that the commission is ultra vires, that it is going beyond what is consistent with the law. again, the commission would take full account of that opinion and reconsider the whole proposal. these six measures should allay the fear, which i understand but which is not justified, that the commission would disregard parliament's opinion. the commission cannot and will not do so. therefore, i do not think there are any grounds for wanting a callback possibility. i can find no provision for it in the treaty or in the 1999 comitology procedure. lastly, two members of parliament have mentioned something they think has happened in the council, namely that the council wants to have a stronger position for itself than is consistent with a balanced relationship between the three institutions. i cannot speak for the council. the council proceedings are not open and therefore it is very difficult to comment. but if there should be any attempt to lower the bar of a qualified majority vote to a simple majority vote, that would meet with the strongest objections from the commission. after all, a single majority vote is almost never mentioned in the treaty. we know what unanimous votes are and we know what qualified majority votes are. simple majority votes are perhaps used for procedural matters, but not for anything of substance. so the commission will firmly oppose any moves towards lowering the decision-making system from a qualified majority vote to a simple majority vote. as i said, i cannot speak for the council and it is only with great reluctance that i am commenting on something that may or may not be true.
commission. – mr president, may i express the gratitude of the commission for mrs randzio-plath's remarks. i reiterate that the commission is basing itself on two particular articles in the treaty and on the comitology decision. when i look not so much at article 6 but at article 5 and article 8 of the comitology decision, i am sorry, but i see no room for a callback procedure. mrs randzio-plath referred this afternoon to a callback procedure or equivalent measure, or words to that effect. the commission is here to try to find a balance and if mrs randzio-plath is willing to come forward with a new suggestion, the commission will, of course, listen to it but once again it must be within the framework of the comitology decision. if mrs randzio-plath or any other member of this parliament then says it is time we changed the comitology decision, i am out of my depth. it is not within my remit tonight to pronounce on the possibility of changing the comitology decision, although if we are considering the question of secondary legislation, we might also consider comitology. however that is a big step and i do not think i can make any comment on changes to this delicate and complicated interinstitutional balance tonight. once again, if mrs randzio-plath wants to put forward a new proposal which we might not have considered, we will certainly look at it and try to be positive in our reply, always provided that it is within the confines of the comitology decision,
- thank you very much, commissioner. i have received a motion for a resolution tabled on the basis of rule 42 (5) of the rules of procedure. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.
- the agenda calls for the report (a5-0082/2001) by mr von wogau, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the situation in the european economy, preparatory report for the commission recommendation on the broad guidelines of economic policies [2001/2008 (ini) ].
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to express, on behalf of the liberal group and myself, our congratulations and our support for the report by mr von wogau on a subject which, although very important - the broad economic policy guidelines - is nevertheless a substitute for what we would like. we have always argued that the euro area should have a genuine and well-defined economic and monetary policy. it is known that, at the moment, it is shaped by relations between ecofin and the commission itself, with the intervention of parliament. the broad guidelines are obviously a basic element, but - i repeat - they are still for us a substitute for what a genuine economic and monetary policy at the level of the european union should be, with the possibility of acting in a more direct way. of the various aspects dealt with in the von wogau report, i would like to highlight three which, from our liberal point of view, are particularly important. the first is to continue the process of liberalization in sectors such as telecommunications, postal services, railways, etc., which still disturb the possibility of higher levels of competition and a better functioning of the internal market. the consequence of this process would also be to bring about, as mr bolkestein rightly claims, a better functioning and the disappearance of obstacles within the european internal market. and, within this better functioning - as parliament has already approved in my report on structural reforms and liberalisation - the fact of ensuring in particular a thorough reform of the labour markets, an essential element, firstly, to better adapt them to the economic and social needs of european society and, secondly, to achieve what we need, that is, higher levels of productivity to be competitive at international level.
the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. this year, for the first time, the procedures for debating the broad economic policy guidelines have been changed as a result of the lisbon procedure and you yourselves have had the opportunity to introduce a parliamentary position on this debate which is the one which, in principle, should help us to define that economic policy to which some of you, including mr trentin, have referred and to which we are not giving sufficient importance. the commission's view is that we can share the fundamental criteria in the report, both the first and second paragraphs, which refer to the social market economy and an economy based on a democratic system, price stability, sustainable growth, subsidiarity, solidarity, etc., objectives which we fully share. i also share the reference that some of you have made to the importance of the present moment, as we are now less than 300 days away from the introduction of the euro. however, as always, i would stress that we often confuse the introduction of banknotes and coins on 1 january next year with the introduction of the euro on 1 january 1999, from which we have already obtained clear benefits and positive results, as some of you have pointed out. among these positive results is the good economic result that the european union is enjoying at the moment. it is true that we must not be complacent because this good economic result, however, conceals some shortcomings, some problems caused by external factors, some lack of ambition in budgetary considerations and, above all, poses some risks as a consequence, above all, of the development of economies such as the north american one. however, even on this specific point, i would like to stress that the euro is also protecting us from the slowdown of the economies outside the european union. the commission's position, which remains relatively optimistic as regards the growth process in europe in 2001, is based on the fact that at the moment in europe we still have clear confidence in consumers and producers at historical levels, that employment is still very clearly progressing, that inflation has reached a peak and, in this context, we believe that the obligation of those responsible for economic policy is above all to maintain economic expansion in the short term and, therefore, we insist on our view that budgetary policy must continue to be directed towards the objective of public finances close to balance, we also believe that wage policies must be compatible with non-inflationary growth and with clear job creation and that monetary policy must maintain its commitment to price stability. we will certainly ease monetary policy to the extent that we have a coherent fiscal policy and further liberalisation of the markets. some of you have also raised the problem of concern for employment as a fundamental element. that is certainly a key point. we therefore also insist - as we did in our presentations of the reports for stockholm - on increasing the union's growth potential. in our report on the 2000 review of the union economy, the commission services analysed the impact of spending and production on information and communication technologies and the advantages they could give us in terms of potentially increasing our growth potential. the structural reforms - mr gasòliba has referred to them - are obviously a fundamental point, but there are also other shortcomings which we must stress. firstly, in lisbon we insisted on the knowledge economy as a key and fundamental element. if we are to move in this direction, we must also create good conditions for private sector investment in r & d and new technologies. we must also improve research and, on the other hand, we must increase vocational training for the new technologies. structural reforms are one of the subjects we usually refer to. we have certainly made progress, and it is quite clear in the report on the implementation of the broad economic policy guidelines this year, but we must not regard this progress as entirely satisfactory. the commission continues to insist on the need to make further progress on these issues and, as you know, just yesterday the commission made new proposals to move forward with the liberalisation of the energy market. we are aware that a balance must be struck between liberalization and regularization in order to obtain the best economic results from this process. we also agree on the need to make progress in all areas of achieving more efficient and integrated financial markets. you have just had a debate with mr bolkestein on the need to put in place the procedures deriving from the so-called lamfalussy committee. it is certainly moving in the direction of speeding up the process of liberalizing financial services, but we believe that this is not enough and that further progress must also be made in terms of risk capital and the improvement of risk capital in europe. the labour market is another of our fundamental concerns if we are to make progress in employment. a better combination of tax reforms and benefit schemes can undoubtedly have a positive influence on the behaviour of the working population, as well as helping to achieve a better balance between wages and productivity at local level, to improve employment in some areas or elements such as labour mobility or better work organisation. we are also concerned about the problems of the long-term sustainability of public finances, which is one of the points which we do not think the report has stressed enough. the problems linked to the ageing of the population will be one of the key issues and, of course, to deal with it we will have to take measures related to public debt and linked to the improvement of the labour market by achieving a higher activity rate, a higher employment rate and, in particular, of women and older workers, which can also help to counteract some of these effects, as will help reforms in the current social security systems consistent with employment and with a sustainability of the model. i thank all of you for your speeches, your comments, your positive contributions to the report, which we will take into account when drawing up our draft broad economic policy guidelines for next year.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.

- the next item is the report (a5-0060/2001) by mr fava, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, on the commission communication on eu electoral assistance and observation missions (com (2000) 191 - c5-0259/2000 - 2000/2137 (cos)).
- mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate mr fava on his report, which i believe is a key element for the coherence and visibility of the european union's external action. i believe that electoral observation and support for electoral processes are an extraordinary element in supporting the european union's action in favour of human rights, democratic freedoms, democratic values and the rule of law. it is important - mr fava has said it very well - that we do not isolate the electoral observation processes from their general context. citizens are called upon to express their views at the ballot box on certain occasions, but democracy is built every day. i therefore believe that the european union's action must be directed towards achieving long-term democratic stability in the developing countries by effectively financing the relevant programmes in which the commission has a key role. i should like to make a very brief comment, mr president, on the role of the european parliament in these processes. i think that paragraph 9 of the motion for a resolution in mr fava's report points very clearly to the fact that these missions should preferably be chaired by members of the european parliament. this is for three fundamental reasons: firstly, because the european parliament can bring a very particular experience, knowledge and vision to the table on this subject, since all the members of the european parliament have been elected in open and democratic electoral processes in our member states; secondly, because the european parliament legitimises our integration project and i believe that the european parliament is therefore very well qualified to represent the european union better - i would say - than the national parliaments; and thirdly, because, after all, the european parliament is one of the two arms of the budgetary authority. the european union is the largest donor of development aid in the world and i believe that it is therefore the european parliament's responsibility to participate in such processes. i therefore hope, mr president, that this report on the commission communication on mr fava's eu election support and observation missions will contribute to an effective, visible and coherent improvement in the european union's external action.
the commission. - mr president, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr massimo carraroa, for his excellent report. this report is full of technical details, but carraro has done an objective is indeed an international, balanced and impartial regulatory system. but we must admit that we have not yet reached that goal. the us government still has special powers and icann's board the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are talking about the activities of the acp-eu joint assembly in the year 2000 and this report may have a slightly different character from those of previous years on the same subject. firstly, because in the year 2000 specific events took place which marked the life and even the very identity of the joint assembly, but also because we deliberately wanted to give the report a certain innovative flavour. in addition to the traditional reminder of the specific facts about the assembly's activity in that year, we have opened a debate of a more political nature on the role of the assembly itself and, more importantly, on how the activities of members of the european parliament in the assembly should be understood. beyond formal or legal considerations, we believe that the members of our parliament who are part of the acp/eu assembly are not there for free but are delegates and therefore our action in it must be guided and then judged by our parliament. we believe that it would be essential in a democratic perspective for this annual report on the joint assembly to cease being a more or less routine and bureaucratic procedure and to become an accountability to the european parliament by its delegates. the debate on this annual report should also be the occasion for parliament to give its representatives in the joint parliamentary assembly a guideline for the work to be done in the months to come. the year 2000 was marked by the adoption, after lengthy negotiations, of the treaty of cotonou, which ratifies the assembly in its legal legitimacy and elevates it to the status of a joint parliamentary assembly. above all, it marks a before and after in the european union's cooperation reflect on how we can achieve this effectively and without confusion, keeping everyone in his or her place. another challenge is to explore the great potential of the assembly to coordinate the positions of the acp and eu partners, in order to make the cooperation and development process and the treaty itself effective and perhaps also to establish consensual positions for action in other forums such as the wto, for example. the first condition for this is that the european parliament should take full responsibility for the work of the joint assembly and give it the priority it commission. – mr president, the water framework directive will protect all our waters and improve the quality of the environment, for example through environmental quality standards, mandatory participation by civil society and tackling pollution at source. it applies the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle. the directive does not prohibit water transfers per se. however it imposes a binding legal requirement that they should not harm the environment. it seems particularly important in this context that since the directive entered into force on 22 december 2000 a strict non-deterioration clause has applied, which should prevent a repetition of past errors. the possibilities for derogation are restricted and subject to mandatory conditions. the directive points out the importance of integrating the protection and sustainable management of water into other community policy areas. when a natura 2000 may be affected, the normal procedure as provided for in article 6 of the habitats directive should be applied in sequence: a search for alternative solutions, assessment of the overriding public interest and as a last resort, compensatory measures.

the framework directive says that no movement of water can take place without first rigorously assessing the need for it and exhausting all possible alternatives. yesterday we spaniards learned that the government is now considering cutting the flow of the ebro by half through measures such as saving on agriculture and reuse. we very much doubt that this reduction is a counter-proposal. we think it is more a modification of concessions to finally share the same volume of water, but in any case, it goes without saying that measures such as water saving and reuse are considered fundamental in the alternative plan put forward by our party, the socialist party. if such a transfer could be done from the outset, allegedly, with the same amount of water as is now proposed, i.e. half, does this fact not demonstrate that the government has not thoroughly studied all the socioeconomic implications, alternatives and availability of the resource before its proposal? on another matter, you know that the framework directive says that citizen participation is very important and so far associations such as adena, ecologists in action or groups of experts have not received an official response to their well-documented allegations. let us also talk about the deterioration of water, a point which is dealt with in articles 1 and 4 of the framework directive. these articles set out the objective of not deteriorating the current state of the waters and add that this must be achieved as from the entry into force of the directive, i.e. 22 december 2000. this means that the current spanish national hydrological plan is already incompatible with the framework directive because, as the works it includes are planned, there will undoubtedly be serious changes to the ecosystems and the quality of the waters. finally, let me briefly set out the position of the european socialist group on the subject of water management. we believe that water is a common heritage and therefore a good, more subject to solidarity than to marketing. any water management plan must be more than a set of infrastructures and transfers. water transpiration should be a last resort, to be undertaken only when all possible alternatives have been exhausted and when it is shown to be environmentally sound. any water management measures must be accompanied by parallel plans on irrigation, forest resources and taking into account climate change. i know that i have a lot to say, but i can assure you that what mrs wallström did say in the february plenary session is that the european union will never finance, will never agree to any plan that is not environmentally friendly. southern africa. it neglects the plight of many very poor black people in zimbabwe. secondly, on trans-nationally abducted children: the commission shares the concerns expressed by the honourable members in the case of international child abductions, often by one of the child's parents. within the community the brussels ii regulation entered into force on 1 march this year. this regulation sets out rules on jurisdiction, automatic recognition and simplified enforcement of judgments in matrimonial matters and matters of parental responsibility for children of both spouses. therefore custodial decisions at the time of divorce taken in the member states in accordance with brussels ii can now be enforced throughout the community. admittedly the regulation does not go far enough in that it is limited to custodial decisions for the children of both spouses taken at the time of divorce. later this month, the commission plans to present a working document on the mutual recognition of decisions on parental responsibility, to be followed by a proposal for a regulation extending the scope of the brussels ii regulation to cover all children and situations. as far as cases that transcend the borders of the community are concerned, the commission also supports the ratification, or the correct application, of the 1980 hague convention on the civil aspects of international child abduction, which is indeed a very valuable instrument. on cabinda: the commission agrees and deplores the situation of the eight european citizens who have been kidnapped in cabinda. the kalimantan, which resulted in injury and serious loss of life. clearly several factors have influenced the outbreak of violence and massacre: a decade-old and badly implemented policy of the commission has in place development projects in southern and eastern kalimantan, which include support for sustainable management of tropical forests. the indonesian leadership currently faces some extremely difficult policy choices. they must establish temporary shelter for the refugees in kalimantan. however, they also need to consider whether to assist those who want to leave kalimantan permanently and return to madura. they must also show determination to restore law and order and pursue the perpetrators. failure to do so would send bad signals about the commitment of the indonesian leadership to the rule of law. the commission is closely following the situation and would stand ready to assist if the situation justified it. however, our current assessment is that most of the 50 000 refugees intend to return to their place of origin – madura – where they have families who will be able to support them. on turkmenistan: the commission is fully aware of the case of mr atakov, a and mr nurberdy nurmamedov. the release of these two prisoners was ordered by president niyazov later in an amnesty allowing the release of 12 000 prisoners. the commission fully supports parliament's
