the council. the charter of fundamental rights of the european union has been signed by the european parliament, the council and the commission. at the present stage, the three institutions have recognised the political value of the document within the framework of the union's action. however, if the aim is to make existing rights more visible, some of the rights proclaimed in the charter already exist in international conventions or in national constitutional traditions. the fact that these rights are included in the charter does not alter their legal value independently of the existence of the charter, since the basis for their observance in union law is article 6 (2) of the treaty on european union. the fact that the rights are formulated in the charter does not therefore affect their value. as regards the question of whether the charter as a whole should be considered legally binding, as the honourable member is aware, the nice intergovernmental conference adopted in december 2000 a declaration on the future of the union, which states that the question of the status of the charter is one of the issues to be addressed in the context of the preparatory work to be carried out before 2004. it was agreed that, once this work was completed, a new intergovernmental conference would be convened to discuss, among other things, the status of the charter.
the council. the council has the duty to follow, discuss and monitor the status of the charter. this was decided by the european council in nice and the council will of course follow that decision. let me remind you that the various articles of the charter are based in part on a number of rights derived from other already existing instruments. several of these rights are already 'judiciable', i.e. they can be an appropriate basis for a decision in a court of law, not because they are included in the charter of fundamental rights, but because they are derived from other instruments. the charter also contains a number of articles which express general political objectives, such as articles 37 and 38 on environmental and consumer protection. they are not designed to be immediately admissible. however, i agree with the honourable member that it is an important task for the council, parliament and the commission to continue to monitor this matter as stated at the nice european council.

the council. the council assumes that the honourable member is referring to the regulation on total allowable catches and quotas adopted by the council in december 2000. in the light of the scientific opinion of the international council for the exploration of the sea, which recommended that the minimum catch for 2001 be maintained and that a recovery plan be drawn up for this stock, the council fixed the total allowable catch for hake, the so-called northern stock, at 22 623 tonnes and 4 kg. on the basis of article 15 of council regulation no 3760/92, the commission is currently considering a series of measures to restore the stock. the council would point out that the northern stock is a biological concept. the catch allocation of member states is broken down according to the management areas of the international council for the exploration of the sea, in order to respect the principle of relative stability as laid down in the abovementioned regulation and in the 1985 act of accession. under this principle, only denmark and sweden may fish in the area comprising the skagerrak and the kattegat, and only belgium, denmark, germany, france, the netherlands and the united kingdom in the areas comprising the north sea. article 161 of the 1985 act of accession sets the share of spain in the northern stock of whiting of vb, vi, vii and viiiab, that is to say, the western waters including the bay of biscay, at 30%. spain has no rights in the areas comprising the skagerrak, kattegat and the north sea. article 349 of the act of accession limits the access of portugal to the southern stock of kummel.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, it is well known that, despite successive reforms, article 73 of the treaties remains in force, which means that coordination between the different modes of transport remains a community obligation. it could not be otherwise, otherwise the chances are, given the current trends we face every day, that the roads will end up overflowing with trucks. this coordination between the different modes of transport was being exercised through a regulation which had been in force for thirty years and was becoming obsolete. that is the commission's excellent opportunity to put forward this proposal which, in due course, will replace the old regulation. this was his intention, which we applaud. we believe, however, that the commission has displayed a certain sense of caution in its proposal. he's advanced, but with too much temptation. moreover, it seems that most of the political groups in this house also feel that way, period and for those emissions, there would be an increase of 40%. it has also been calculated that moving goods by rail requires four times less energy than by road. the same could be said of water proposal on the valuation of such external costs so that they can then be internalised, and then we will have taken a giant step forward in this matter.

commission. – mr president, members of parliament, today we have an opportunity to discuss another important food safety issue which is the labelling of compound feedingstuffs. i appreciate the work and consumers. this includes full transparency in giving livestock farmers details of the composition of compound feedingstuffs that they buy for their animals. one of the lessons of the dioxin crisis was that there was often a lack of such information. this is clearly not satisfactory. this information should be available, not only to ensure transparency but also to assist in the traceability of products. the labelling of compound feedingstuffs must be sufficiently accurate to allow the stock farmer to make an informed choice as to which feed to use and many of you have already made that point in your contributions. i am satisfied that this objective is met in the council's common position. while it falls short of the commission's original proposal of full and precise listing of the quantities of all ingredients, it nonetheless strikes an acceptable compromise. in my opinion we have an excellent instrument for improving the existing labelling rules for animal feed. the common position provides for all ingredients to be precisely named and for the quantities to be expressed in five percentage bands. it also requires operators to notify the exact composition of the compound feedingstuff on the request of the stock farmer or any operator. i would also like to remind you that, from the very beginning, there were difficulties in the council in reaching an agreement. a majority of member states were opposed to the obligation to indicate on the label the precise composition of a given compound feedingstuff. for this reason, the commission accepted the french presidency's compromise which had the unanimous support of all the member states. i also consider that the common position provides us with a level of safety equivalent to that set out in the commission's initial proposal. the most important fact is the presence of an ingredient in the compound feedingstuff and not necessarily its exact quantity. these exact quantities have a commercial value but they are not linked to health protection and that is the important issue in this consideration. i would ask mr graefe zu baringdorf to reconsider seriously what he said earlier in his - the next item is the commission statement on the impasse in the negotiations on the fisheries agreement between the european union and the kingdom of morocco. i call mr fischler to speak.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. i have been personally very involved in the fisheries agreement with morocco from the very beginning, since i took over responsibility for the fisheries sector. i had already contacted morocco before the expiry of the previous agreement in order to start negotiations on a new fisheries agreement. but for many months this was strictly rejected by morocco, and concrete talks on a new agreement were only possible after a meeting with king mohammed vi in casablanca last october. since then, seven rounds of talks have taken place at political level and 13 at technical level. the community has from the outset sought to be as flexible as possible in order to meet moroccan wishes and interests. however, after my visit to rabat in february of this year, i found that the gap between the two positions was unbridgeable, particularly because of morocco's financial ideas as a compensation for the fishing opportunities offered. there were also some major divergences in terms of fishing opportunities, particularly in terms of the technical framework for fishing, i.e. in which zones and at what times and with what vessels fishing in morocco would be likely to take place. i therefore immediately informed the council of the situation on my return in february, in order to explore alternatives with the fisheries ministers. the council has asked me to make a final attempt to reach an agreement within the framework of the present negotiating mandate. i met mr chbaatou in brussels on 26 march to discuss this. but unfortunately, this meeting was also completely unsuccessful. the commission, for its part, has made several proposals during the negotiations to promote the development of the moroccan fisheries sector, for example by providing financial resources for the development of port infrastructure and the service sector in morocco, by promoting and developing coastal fisheries, by providing training and research and by developing aquaculture. we would also have accepted very large landing commitments in moroccan ports, which would have meant a radical change in the traditional fishing activities of many spanish and portuguese fishermen, but would also have contributed to the development of the moroccan sector. we have also agreed to increase the proportion of moroccan nationals on the crews of vessels in order to improve the employment situation and the level of training in the moroccan fishing sector. in addition, we would have accepted further and far-reaching restrictions on fishing opportunities to ensure the conservation of resources in moroccan waters. just to give you a few examples: we would have accepted a drastic reduction in the community's presence in moroccan waters in the first year of the agreement, and in the remaining two years we would have practically phased out cephalopod and shrimp fishing. we would also have accepted new technical conditions which would be less favourable to the community fleet and would reduce fishing effort. despite all these concessions and the progress made by the moroccan side in the course of the negotiations, the following fundamental differences of opinion have remained. firstly, the fishing conditions proposed by morocco would mean that the economic benefits for our fishermen would be lost, because we would have had to fish with far fewer vessels in less rich areas and accept a longer cessation of fishing. secondly, the community considers that the financial compensation must be in reasonable proportion to the fishing opportunities offered. this is not only our general policy line, it is also the negotiating mandate of october 1999. we have, of course, not only evaluated the financial part purely economically but also included political considerations, such as the need for good relations with morocco at the political level. we have offered morocco a financial contribution of eur 70 million for the first year, eur 60 million for the second year and eur 40 million for the third year for our proposal for a fisheries agreement. this offer was very, very advantageous for morocco for several reasons, because firstly, we have calculated our financial contribution on the basis of fishing opportunities in the last year of the previous agreement and not on the average of the last agreement. this alone gives morocco a price advantage of 15%. secondly, we have not made any distinction in our calculations between species of fish, although we would have accepted greater reductions for the more expensive species of fish which are of more interest to the community, such as cephalopods or shrimp. this also gives morocco a price advantage. thirdly, we have not included the landing obligation in morocco in our calculations. fourthly, i have increased the financial compensation resulting from this calculation by 20% to show that we understand morocco's concern about the development of its own sector. in addition, at the last meeting i made it clear to the moroccan minister chbaatou that our offer, as i described it earlier, was not only a fair price for the fishing opportunities, but i even promised him that we would be willing to add another 5 million euros a year to prove once again our goodwill for the conclusion of an agreement. the moroccan minister for fisheries, however, stressed that morocco had no room for manoeuvre. in view of this moroccan attitude, i therefore see no possibility of concluding an agreement on the basis of our mandate. i shall report to the fisheries council on 25 april. the question of what will happen to the shipowners and fishermen concerned, who have been condemned to inactivity for more than a year, is now all the more important. as you know, we have been making compensation payments to shipowners and fishermen from the fisheries fund since 1 december 1999. we have made all the preparations in accordance with the conclusions of the nice european council. the commission proposal is currently before parliament and the council to extend the compensation payments until 30 june this year. at the same time we have proposed that the 4% ceiling should not be applied to compensation. we estimate that a total of about 80 million euros has been paid to the fishermen and shipowners concerned so far, of which 20 million euros has been paid by the member states themselves, i.e. a community share of 60 million, of which about 51 million euros has gone to spain and 9 million to portugal. but one thing is clear: additional measures and resources are now needed for the future of the spanish and portuguese fisheries sector. i believe that we must be active in three main areas. firstly, we should try to look for alternative fishing opportunities in other third countries, at least partially. secondly, we must help to develop alternative employment opportunities for the people affected, for example in aquaculture or tourism or the service sector or wherever there is an opportunity. thirdly, we must also support the scrapping of ships for which there is no alternative use, as we do in other cases. we shall certainly make full use of the commission's margin of manoeuvre. but here too, with the 2002 budget in mind, the budgetary authority is called upon. the next step is to report to the fisheries council first. in conclusion, i would like to say that i very much regret the rigid attitude of morocco, which has prevented an agreement which is mutually beneficial.

the rapporteur. - mr president, the proposal for a council decision is the continuation of a policy of financial support to the member states to finance their infrastructures for this fundamental pillar of the common fisheries policy. the proposal gives priority to the introduction of new technologies, the use of computer networks, the possible widespread use of satellite monitoring systems, the training of control staff and the intervention systems which are necessary to meet the european union's obligations towards regional fisheries organisations. although the commission's proposal is acceptable in general, there are two aspects which clash with the line taken by the committee on fisheries and the european parliament on other matters closely related to the one we are dealing with. in recent reports on regional fisheries organisations, parliament has stressed that the community should have exclusive competence for control and monitoring and that the institutions of the european union, in particular the commission, should be responsible for taking the necessary measures to meet these obligations. the financing of these measures should therefore be borne by the community budget. since regional fisheries organizations are destined to become increasingly important in the future of the common fisheries policy, it is appropriate to follow the line defined by previous reports adopted by this parliament. the commission proposal makes it clear that in future the contribution to the work of regional fisheries organisations would also be entrusted, at least in part, to the member states, as would inspection and control missions. as long as there is a common fisheries policy and the community has powers in the fisheries sector, it must act as such and equip itself with the human and material resources to meet its obligations, as required by the principle of the sufficiency of the resources of the common fisheries policy. the application of this principle has financial implications and requires legal developments and perhaps the transfer of sovereignty, but if a particular model of political construction is accepted, it is necessary to provide the means for that model to be put into practice. the present situation does not exactly correspond to this model, since the core of the control competence lies with the member states, and a reasonable period of time is necessary to adapt the structures to the model announced above. it is for the member states, on a transitional basis - perhaps during the three years to which the duration of the programme contained in this decision is targeted - to continue to represent the union in these areas. this does not prevent the member states from being reimbursed in full and immediately for the expenditure incurred in respect of these community obligations, and therefore 100% of the expenditure should be reimbursed instead of being co-financed. that is the meaning of amendment no 1 to the draft report. it is surprising that the statement in the explanatory memorandum to the decision mentions that a reduction of eur 41 to 35 million per year is foreseen in expenditure on control operations, since it is very likely that the adequate infrastructure to cover control and surveillance programmes will require in the future, not a reduction, but an increase in the current financial burden. amendment no 2 raises the community's share of financing for the purchase or modernisation of inspection and control equipment from 30% to 35%. most of the investments in this direction have already been made and most of the future actions will relate to the area of modernisation. in any case, since the investments are costly and - let us not forget - we are talking about control of the common policy, the percentage of community financing should be increased slightly. i must confess, in conclusion, that i have been tempted to enter into a more in-depth discussion on the future of the control system after the reform. however, the experience of recent reports which, in the face of the prospective, have lost some of their effectiveness, has led me to take a more modest and immediate approach.
- mr president, again what strikes me most about the commission's proposal is the imbalance between the importance it says it attaches to certain issues and the means it then puts to solve them. if we were to rely on declarations of intent alone, it would appear that the commission is indeed giving fisheries control policy top priority. the explanatory statement for this proposal is a tribute to the importance of this policy within the common fisheries policy, which it calls crucial, a qualification we all share. the green paper, recently presented, goes even further, stating that either the system is improved or the credibility of the cfp will be dealt a fatal blow. however, when it comes to the truth, we see once again that, after the great declarations, the two legs of the bank are missing and that neither the necessary means are provided to carry out the measures nor the essential policy of transparency is followed to make them credible. it is therefore difficult to understand how, given the priority given to this policy and the need to strengthen it, the budget allocated to it this time has not increased but has decreased from 41 to 35 million euro per year. moreover, this being the third commission decision to this effect, the commission has not yet made public the report on the results of previous actions, so that we are left with no idea whether, apart from the fact that the choice of the financing measures was more or less correct, they have achieved practical results, including those which are so desirable as to link the sector to this policy which has so far eyes of the world the credibility of its alleged commitment to the sustainability of resources.

the rapporteur. - mr president, the report i am presenting to this house today on safety in fishing and the causes of accidents in this sector analyses, ladies and gentlemen, the reasons for the high incidence of accidents in this sector and examines aspects such as the european legislative framework, the problems affecting the work of fishermen and the prevention of risks. although the initiative to deal with this matter in parliament was taken by the socialist group, the work before you today is the result of many contributions, including those of my colleagues, members of the committee on fisheries in the european parliament, who worked hard and well with me and who finally approved this report unanimously; also the hearing with experts, which we held in september, or the invaluable contributions that officials from the directorate-general for employment or the directorate-general for studies of the european parliament sent me; or also the contributions made by the advisory committee on fisheries. all agreed that the fishing profession (270,000 in the european union) is a very dangerous profession, and they shared much of the diagnosis of the reasons why fishing has an accident rate up to 25 times higher than the rest of the economic sectors, and why one in seven fishermen in the european union suffers an accident at work every year. this very high rate is due to a combination of very different causes: bad weather, long working hours with very intense rhythms, pay systems such as the so-called "a la part", which are not very homologated, the absence of collective bargaining, difficult working conditions, poor conditions for the ship's habitability, isolation, separation from the family and the social environment, distance from the fishing grounds, ageing of the fleet, etc. i reject the skeptical and fatalistic view of those who think that fishing accidents are irreversible and that the victims of these accidents are a tribute we have to pay to the sea. i think we should look for the causes of these accidents and fight them. we have to put safety first. we are suffering from intolerable accident rates and we must increase controls, raise the awareness of shipowners and fishermen and, if necessary, promote legislative changes to reduce them. the social and working conditions of seafarers must be taken into account and their working conditions improved, since they are able to cope with rest periods and irregular working hours of more than 14 hours a day. the right of this sector to continuous weekly and daily rest must be recognised and, if necessary, the public authorities must intervene to enforce this basic right of any worker. these harsh working conditions lead, for example, to young people not wanting to embark, which prevents generational change. it is necessary to establish a social dialogue in the sector at european level in order to reach collective agreements incorporating these safety issues at work, to consult more with the sector, to extend to fishermen a social coverage similar to that of other workers and to develop a safety culture among employers and workers. the european union does not even have statistical data; only five countries provide figures, and these are not homogeneous. this issue should be taken into account when the third phase of the european statistics on accidents at work project is launched, so that the community can have reliable and complete data, harmonised at european level. my group has always felt that it is necessary to discuss in this parliament not only the issues relating to fisheries resources but also the human problems affecting seafarers. i therefore call in my report for the conclusions to be incorporated in the regulation for the reform of the cfp so that the triangle of legislation, training and social dialogue can be included. i also urge those member states which have not yet done so to ratify the international conventions and to improve the community directives which, at present, exclude more than 90% of the fleet from their coverage. i also point out in my report that flags of convenience do not offer any guarantees of employment or safety for their crews, which entails serious risks for the fishermen on board these vessels. in short, ladies and gentlemen, this is a report on a subject which has not been dealt with until today. it is the first of these reports; possibly a second and third reports on fisheries accidents will follow. i hope that, as the first, you will look at his shortcomings with tolerance and support him.
- mr president, i hope that this report will help the commission to abandon once and for all its obsession with the idea that a modern fleet is incompatible with the protection of resources. the protection of resources is a priority objective of the cfp which, in no case, can be put before the safety of fishermen, because it is also a false approach from the very beginning. there are a number of measures to maintain or even reduce fishing effort, while improving the living conditions and safety of crew. the report we are discussing today, like all the reports on safety, shows that the ageing of the fleet is the main cause of both accidents on board and shipwrecks, and that shipwrecks often have such serious consequences. the commission's claim that structural measures are reserved for the fleet and are almost exclusively designed to destroy it is therefore unreasonable, while the surviving fleet is in fact condemned to navigate in increasingly precarious conditions. the only thing that this policy unfortunately achieves is that the community fleet is more present on the events page than on the economy page. on the other hand, a battery of safety standards is of no use if compliance with them is not required. this is doubly worrying because the fact that we have to monitor and enforce this makes us question the perception of the sector of its own security. the latest fao report on the state of fisheries and aquaculture in the world states that a safe working environment is not something that can be easily imposed and that measures to improve safety can only be effective if there is a willingness to put them into practice. it is therefore necessary to recall the responsibility which we all have, politicians, administrations and fishermen, to put an end to the fatalism which seems to be engulfing this sector, a responsibility which the commission and its narrow vision of fleet modernisation cannot escape.

- the next item is the recommendation (a5-0132/2001) by mr swoboda, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, on the proposal for a council and commission decision on the conclusion of the stabilisation and association agreement between the european communities and their member states, of the one part, and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, of the other part.
- mr president, thank you. the reason for my intervention is simply to support and emphasize, if possible, the essential elements expressed by the rapporteur of this report, our colleague charlotte cederschiöld, whom i congratulate on her rigorous and excellent work. i would like to begin by recalling the revolution that will be the materialization of the euro on 1 january next year. the euro will be the symbol par excellence of european identity, and alongside the yen and the dollar it will be one of the guide currencies used not only in europe but also, as our colleague has said, on a world scale. it will be the cornerstone towards the building of a political union. the euro is therefore embodied in a banknote or coin, so there is clearly a very real risk that it will be counterfeited, and prevention policies are therefore essential. with this objective in mind, we must be very much concerned with the need to train, through courses and other procedures, those who will work with money on a daily basis, especially banks, exchange agencies, so that they are familiar with the euro. they're going to be the key players in detecting the counterfeit currency. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the euro against counterfeiting. finally, i would also stress the importance of effective criminal protection to eradicate all evidence of counterfeiting. since i do not want to dwell on the fundamental issues already raised by mrs cederschiöld, such as the inconvenience and confusion caused by having legal instruments dependent on different pillars for the defence of the same objective - the fight against the counterfeiting of the euro - i shall concentrate on two or three issues which i consider important. one is the reference in amendment no 23 to a database on counterfeit money, unlike the regulation, which omits any reference to it. i believe that this will add to the effectiveness and accuracy of the fight against counterfeiting. as regards the status of the european technical and scientific centre, which, as stated in article 5 of the proposal for a regulation, will be the channel for the fight against counterfeiting, i would like to stress the need to defend, from the outset, its independence from the paris mint, as stated in amendments nos 20 and 26. the functional link of this body should relate exclusively to the european institutions and in no case to a national institution. finally, amendment no 27 adds to the original text of the rules the idea which i expressed at the beginning of my speech. the key role that money professionals should play in the fight against euro counterfeiting. it is important that they have not only the obligation to withdraw from circulation those banknotes and coins of questionable authenticity but also to exercise authenticity control themselves. we are aware of the doubts this requirement may raise, since it will require major investments in instruments, machines and elements to ensure the legality of money, but it is essential from the point of view of defending the citizen. and it's also a guarantee that the money distributed by these entities will actually be genuine.

- the next item is the report (a5-0127/2001) by mr katiforis, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the annual evaluation of the implementation of the stability and convergence programmes. the rapporteur, mr katiforis, has seven minutes.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this debate gives us an opportunity to consider the current situation of the european economy, which, although it presents a positive balance sheet for the year 2000 - with high growth, job creation and monetary stability - now raises much more acute questions about the evolution of these magnitudes. this means that there will be clear pressure in some countries, as there is already on the european union as a whole, to act by provoking more expansionary policies. this situation could of course run counter to the commitments made in the stability pacts to the various member states. we therefore consider the parts of the report we are discussing here to be particularly appropriate, in which a number of points are reiterated: the need to maintain budgetary rigor; the avoidance of promises of tax cuts - sometimes due to the proximity of elections - if there is no corresponding counterpart; and an aspect on which mr katiforis always stresses, namely that there should always be a counterpart in productive investments which will lead us to improve the productive structure of the european union, thus enabling it to be much more competitive. i would like to end by drawing attention to the need to maintain this coordination and the commitments set out in the stability programmes. i would also like to stress the need to increase the level of management of economic and monetary policy, which in our view is still too fragmented and whose capacity and coherence will obviously be demonstrated in a time of greater difficulties such as the present.

the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been asked to submit a report on the stability and convergence programmes. the third round of programmes we have presented was finalised by the ecofin council in march. the increased vigilance in budgetary policies, as a result of the implementation of the stability and growth pact, is proving to be hugely positive and appropriate. i do not know whether, as mr karas said, it is an element for achieving political stability or simply an element for maintaining a clear commitment from the point of view of public deficits. the member states, in a clearly coordinated approach, have achieved better budgetary consolidation. according to our current figures, of the present member states, 10 are projecting a surplus or a balance in their public accounts. and all but the united kingdom will have a balanced situation by the year 2004. the public debt is clearly falling and we expect it to be below 60% this year in 11 of the 15 member states of the union. i therefore believe that we have made very clear progress and that we have achieved, as mr katiforis said, a situation of economic stability in europe in budgetary terms. it is true that the problem of the consolidation of public finances, which has allowed us to make considerable progress, raises some problems of long-term sustainability and of the quality of public finances; on both points the commission essentially insists that progress must be made. further progress is needed to reduce current deficits and achieve a balanced position in public budgets as soon as possible. we still have in some cases excessive debts which need to be corrected, particularly to deal with some of the budgetary problems we will have to face in the future. in this connection, i would also like to point out some of the points made by several speakers, including mrs randzio-plath, but not only, when she referred to the need to improve the quality of public finances. when we talk about the quality of public finances, we are referring not only to short-term problems but also to medium- and long-term problems; in the short term, of course, to fiscal reforms which will enable us to manage taxes better; in the medium term, to everything connected with better public spending - and then i will refer to public investment, as mr katiforis argues in his report - and, of course, in the long term, to the problem of the ageing population, which must undoubtedly be one of our main concerns at this time. the medium-term strategies defined by the member states in their programmes allow us to know very clearly what their priorities are. and in that sense, to reconcile our views in order to achieve a better coordination of our budgetary policies. i would like to refer specifically to some of the problems raised by mr katiforis in his report. first of all, i would like to make a few specific comments on the very important subject of public investment, to which mr katiforis has devoted a substantial part of his report. firstly, i agree with him completely that in many member states public investment has been reduced, we might even say unduly, during the budgetary consolidation of the 1990s. secondly, it is true that the improvement in the situation should also allow us to give priority to public investment spending; we would thus be consistent with what we agreed in lisbon and, in this sense, the basic idea is to improve our growth potential. the third point i would like to stress is that public investment is not incompatible with private investment, that there can be synergies and interrelationships between them and that there is room for innovative methods of financing; that often the public sector does not necessarily have to propose action in the sense that it traditionally did, in isolation. this greater priority for public investment, which i fully share, should not, however, make us forget the other side of the coin: greater public investment does not necessarily mean greater deficit. we insist that the problem must be solved by reorientating certain types of expenditure and keeping the public deficit under control. we consider budgetary control of the public deficit to be essential. it is essential to achieve that balance in the medium term and it is true that measures such as the golden rule, proposed in the united kingdom, are useful insofar as it is consistent that public investment can be financed by deficit or debt, but it is also right that this deficit or debt should not exceed the ceilings we have agreed and, therefore, that priority should be given to one type of expenditure over another. so when we talk about encouraging public investment, we are in no way talking about uncontrolled indebtedness or a clear increase in public spending. an increase in investment which could lead to a surplus of the deficit or expenditure levels currently envisaged will certainly not be supported by the commission. paragraph 10 of the motion for a resolution refers to a more harmonized timetable for the submission of member states' programmes. we agree on this point and have always considered the need to update the programmes before the budgetary procedures. we have insisted on this point and will continue to insist on it and we hope that in the future we can at least get these programmes updated at the same time as the budgetary procedures are started. mr katiforis also raised the need to have the commission's documents available. this is an old debate. we as the commission consider it important that parliament should have as much information as possible, but we are also aware that what is not relevant from the point of view of public opinion in many cases are the small nuances or the small differences that may exist between the commission proposal and the final decision of the council. we believe that the debate should focus on the elements which are finally adopted by the council and that is why we believe that disclosure of previous documents would complicate rather than facilitate the process. the commission's macroeconomic forecasts are set out in paragraph 9 of the final report. these are prepared separately from the evaluation of the programmes, as you know, twice a year and are published when they are ready. the last ones, the spring ones, which we have just published, were sent to parliament on 25 april and raise some of the issues which have been raised today. on the irish problem, our position is known: in ireland, only the rules currently in force have been applied. another topic of interest is the problem of lower growth as a consequence of the american situation. and let's say, in some of you, i've seen the idea of a change in budget policy being planned as a positive element to improve growth. in our view, with forecast growth of 2.8% as included in the commission's forecasts, there is still a clear margin for progress in the stability programmes as planned; and therefore the commission continues to insist on the need to make progress in the implementation of these stability programmes, which does not mean, however, that we do not accept that automatic stabilisers can operate in a situation of lower economic growth. these are the elements i wanted to highlight in my speech. i can only thank mr katiforis for his efforts and all of you for your comments, criticisms and suggestions. thank you very much.

- the next item is the report (a5-0116/2001) by mr harbour, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the future generation of the internet: the need for an eu research initiative. i call mr harbour, the rapporteur, who has seven minutes.
mr president, we are certainly not dealing with the most exciting report we are going to discuss in this sitting, and i am not referring here to the excellent work of lord inglewood, for which we must congratulate not only him but all of us. when the european parliament's work in a codecision procedure improves, as in this case, the commission's proposal and does so in terms of a high technical level, not only is there a positive contribution to the process of producing legislation, but we are also increasing the prestige of the european parliament and making arguments in favour of the generalization of the codecision procedure. the fact that - as i have just said - this is a report which does not arouse passion does not mean that it is not an important report from a technical point of view. and in that order of things, the proposal to modernise the accounting directives is not only of great importance, but can be described as a totally necessary proposal to improve the transparency of companies' accounts. traditionally, the accounting valuation rules of companies stipulated that assets should be valued at cost price, in short, what was called the historical value. consequently, that was the criterion which was set out in the accounting directives; and it is logical if one wants to avoid accounting manipulations which prevent the accounts from reflecting the true image of the company. the aim was ultimately to prevent the managers of a company from artificially revaluing parts of the assets in order to distort the image of that company. it is true that certain accounting irregularities which were not allowed to companies have been allowed, in the case of public accounts, to some member states to join the euro. that's right, by euphemistically calling them, instead of irregularities, "creative accounting". but ultimately, those accounting criteria referring to historical value were not immutable, and the complexity of today's financial markets and the increasing use of sophisticated financial products make it necessary to change historical value to fair value. this reasonable value, which is the one included in the proposal for a directive which we are adopting, is obviously not as fixed as the historical value, as it has much more ethereal limits, and requires more precise instruments for its incorporation, criteria which are set out in the proposed amendments, to which we are going to vote in favour.

commission. – mr president, honourable members, it is with great pleasure that i reply to this debate on the report of the conciliation committee concerning the tobacco products directive. this directive is the culmination of several years of hard work by the commission on the basis of the best scientific advice. we have developed and proposed a qualitative step forward in protecting public health, working within the confines of the legal basis for completion of the internal market. the directive before you today will represent a significant improvement on our current legislative position and fill many of the gaps, which have made the current rules ineffective. the present directive will put the european community at the forefront of efforts to control the death and disease caused by tobacco consumption. in this way, the addiction of future generations of young people has been taken seriously, and a framework created to reduce the enormous harm caused by this product. i need hardly remind parliament of the level of health damage from tobacco to our population which exceeds that from more widely debated causes. the world health organisation estimates tobacco-related deaths in the community to be more than half a million a year. this does not include the number of smokers who suffer from serious and debilitating illnesses, such as respiratory disease and heart disease. this makes tobacco control the most import tool in reducing death and disease in our midst. i must here compliment parliament and in particular the rapporteur, mr maaten, whose amendments have substantially improved and completed this measure. the commission was happy to accept many of these amendments. mrs maes, in her contribution to parliament, made a statement that this was a textbook example of cooperation between the three great legislative institutions of the european union; i would echo that, but refer also to the role of the court of justice in its judgment in the case relating to the advertising directive. i would go further and, say echoing what mrs maes has said about this being a textbook example, that this issue – the story of tobacco and the legislation of tobacco – both in the first advertising directive that i am bringing forward soon and this particular directive, is worthy of close examination by any serious student of the european union or law student. it provides a clear example of how all the institutions can work well together in formulating policy and bringing forward that policy in the form of valuable legislation within the confines of the competences laid down in the treaties amending the treaty of rome, and will allay the fears of anybody who has concerns about the european institutions becoming too powerful, because the lines of demarcation are clearly set out by the court and respected by the institutions in respect of this legislation. in short, this is a textbook example as mrs maes has said, worthy of further study by young students. this directive recasts several existing directives from the late 1980s. we have used this proposal to update and complete existing instruments on the basis of scientific developments, including, for the first time, several important harmonisation measures. i should like to mention the setting of a reduced tar ceiling in cigarettes and the creation for the first time of a ceiling for nicotine and carbon monoxide. these ceilings will directly attack the agents in cigarettes responsible for cancer, addiction and cardiovascular disease. we are not, however, aiming at producing a safe cigarette, since such a product cannot exist, but simply to reduce the most dangerous product constituents. importantly, these rules now apply to all imported products and to all products manufactured in the community. thus, we will not export products, which are considered inappropriate for our citizens. equally, given the significant amount of smuggling, we do not run the risk of unsafe exports coming back onto the community market. i have been particularly upset at the cynical efforts of the tobacco industry to use the spectre of job losses to threaten this measure. the same threats were also expressed when the original tobacco directives were adopted in the late 1980s. they were not true then and they are not true now. there is no room for double standards for our own citizens and for others when we are talking about an addictive and deadly product. another innovation in this text is to require the declaration of additives in tobacco products – potentially the most important single measure contained in this legislation. currently we do not know what these additives are at community level and, more importantly, why they are added to the product. manufacturers and importers will in future be obliged to declare these constituents. we will then move towards preparing a legislative proposal when these data are provided. this will be done before 31 december 2002. i am happy to say that preparations for this consequent legislation, arising from the furnishing of this data, will be undertaken during my mandate as a commissioner. in the meantime, member states remain free to protect their consumers. another important component of this directive is the substantial increase in the size of health warnings on packaging. they will be increased to ensure that consumers are fully informed of the health risks they run and, for the first time, information will be provided on how to get help to stop smoking. the previous rules were worded too loosely and the new directive makes sure that the warnings will be printed in colours that are clearly readable and cannot be disguised as at present. as a result of an amendment from this house, the introduction of colour photos on warnings is to be introduced for the first time. this will greatly increase the impact of these warnings. in recent years research has shown the importance of avoiding misleading product descriptors on tobacco products which may make the consumer believe that a particular product is safer than another. this directive introduces a requirement not to use such misleading terms on tobacco products. as such, it aims to protect smokers and non-smokers alike from misleading representations of the dangers posed to them by such products. in order to provide a mechanism to keep these rules up to date, we have also included a provision for regular commission reports and a committee procedure. in a previous declaration when the first reading took place, i undertook to consult with tobacco experts in drawing up this report and any subsequent proposals. i can inform you today that work is already under way to reconstitute the commission's advisory committee on cancer prevention and to create its working group on tobacco. however, i must draw your attention to the difficulty the commission envisages in respecting the deadline imposed in article 5(3) of this text, which leaves little time to consult these committees and subsequently to adopt rules for the use of colour photographs on warnings. in the coming weeks, i also hope to meet my undertaking to present a new proposal on tobacco advertising and sponsorship. this will replace the directive annulled by the court of justice last october. i also regard the community's legislative activity as complementary to that under way in the world health organisation framework convention on tobacco control. i welcome the presence of an observer from the european parliament in the community delegation, appropriately mr maaten, which early this month met in geneva when the second round of negotiations for this convention took place. finally, let me again express my appreciation for your support and confidence in ensuring the rapid adoption of this important directive and for the words expressed in respect of the commission's involvement. i should like to play tribute in particular to mr john ryan and the significant contribution he has made to this issue over the years. i hope it will be seen in coming years that this directive is a keystone of our efforts to reduce the damage to health by smoking.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow, tuesday, at 12 noon.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0115/2001), on behalf of the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a recommendation of the european parliament and of the council on the mobility within the community of students, persons undergoing training, young volunteers, teachers and trainers (13258/1/2000 - c5-0029/2001 - 2000/0021 (cod)) (rapporteur: mr evans)
commission - mr president, mobility is one of the subjects which the commission is particularly concerned about. we attach fundamental importance to this - as my colleagues have said - both for the personal enrichment of the individual and for the building of the great european family. being mobile means getting to know each other, working together better, even after school. mr evans, i would like to thank you very much for the work you have done, for your commitment and your efforts to find solutions to problems which are not always easy because of institutional barriers which unfortunately prevent us from moving forward as quickly as any of us would like to. the european parliament has shown excellent cooperation. i would like to thank all the members of the commission, apart from mr evans, who have helped parliament, the council and the commission to find solutions together after a long process. the text of the council's common position on which parliament is to take a decision is the result of a long debate between the three institutions; i think the final text meets the expectations of all those involved in mobility in europe, even if i agree with the members that a text is not enough, that it must be followed by concrete action. but by continuing the debate on the recommendation, i think we are nonetheless moving in the direction proposed by the lisbon and nice summits, which advocated that education and training policies play a major role in economic growth and european social renewal, and which therefore made mobility one of the issues in those policies. it is also in this perspective, mr president, that the action plan for mobility endorsed by the nice council should be understood, since it provides an operational complement to the measures provided for in the recommendation and is the expression of a new commitment by the member states to mobility. as regards commitment, i would like to emphasize that of my colleague, mr busquin, who is actively working to ensure that the mobility of researchers follows the same logic. before i explain to you the position which the commission intends to adopt at this second reading, i should like to return to the amendments adopted by parliament at first reading because your rapporteur has mentioned them. i am pleased to note that both the commission, in its amended proposal of 9 november, and the council, in its proposal of 19 january, have accepted, in whole or in part, a large majority of these amendments, especially those which clarified the text in order to strengthen community action. the text of the common position thus incorporates 40 amendments out of the 56 voted for by parliament at first reading. now, at second reading, mr evans has tabled six amendments to the common position, on which i shall be voting. some of these amendments add an explicit reference to the mobility action plan as a new legal act in the field of mobility; amendments nos 1 and 3 are the ones that are being proposed. they therefore aim to create synergy between these two initiatives; and when we say synergy, we also mean the commission's agreement, because we agree with both texts. i would, however, like to add to the recital as amended by amendment no 1 the reference to the nice council which was originally provided for in amendment no 3. this is, in fact, a minor correction which does not alter the content. i also agree with amendments nos 2 and 4, which provide for clarification of the follow-up to the recommendation, in particular the timing and content of the reports by the member states and the commission on the implementation of the recommendation. i also believe that the clarification requested by parliament in its amendment no 3 as regards the profile of the members of the group of experts is entirely appropriate; finally, i agree with the view of the committee on culture of parliament that the time limit - i quote - of up to one year should be removed in principle from the definition of mobility and voluntary activities in amendments nos 5 and 6. this amounts to a more flexible wording, whereby the mobility covered by the recommendation is the limited-term mobility as it appeared in the commission's initial proposal. so you see, mr rapporteur, that the commission can accept the six amendments proposed at second reading with a slight rewording of amendment no 3. in our view, this convergence of views between parliament, the commission and - i am sure - the council shows that we are all moving in the same direction. i would also like to thank parliament, mr president, for always having understood the importance of mobility and for always being willing to cooperate throughout the procedure, even in difficult times - is that not so, mr rapporteur? we have reached an agreement which is not political but which addresses the deepest needs of our students and teachers. i would also like to recall the important role assigned to parliament in community initiatives on mobility, such as the communication on the new european labour markets which provides for the creation of a high-level task force on skills and mobility, and in the social agenda which calls for the modernisation of the rules to ensure that workers' social rights in the field of mobility are maintained. i would remind the members of this text, who have very rightly pointed out that one of the great unresolved problems is that of the social field. finally, i would like to say how much i am committed, on behalf of the whole commission, to the rapid implementation of the mechanism provided for in the recommendation. this mechanism will enable us to monitor the situation in the context of joint action by the member states; i am therefore responding to the legitimate concerns that parliament has expressed throughout the procedure about really effective monitoring.

- mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the commission, the college of commissioners and, in particular, mrs reding, on the work they are doing to break down the boundaries of limitation and the principle of subsidiarity, in order to create joint programmes that go beyond this very specific world in which the educational system is evolving. i believe that one of the most complex aspects of the history of europe - where the same phenomenon is being repeated - is the tendency to convergence and fragmentation, the tendency to unite and to distance oneself, to divide into a thousand pieces. we are in an era where once again there is a process of nationalist involution against globalisation, which is clearly misunderstood and tends to fragment states and regions. and culture and education are the great victims, because they are held and limited to their own borders. however, certain programmes can only be implemented from above. the principle of subsidiarity is also being misinterpreted and, in my view, to a great extent perverted by the states and by many regions, which use it to increase their own power and - why not say it - to exercise control over thought and the educational system by the state apparatus. now, the state should provide free education for all, but it should not exercise absolute control. let us imagine that airplanes could only fly to the border of a province, to the border of a region or to the border of a country. well, in the educational field we are pretending that our cultural knowledge only flies to the limit of the frontier and, of course, the result is a broken and fractured project. i therefore commend, applaud and think that the commission's idea that it is the only supranational body capable of acting in this field must be supported with ideas, articles and means. i think one of our first debates should be on subsidiarity, because there is a lot of legal literature on subsidiarity and not just this peasant interpretation of it that is being made. and on the other hand, i understand that there is no europe but a common thought or at least the ability to communicate. in this sense i believe - and i also commend the forum which has recently been set up with the companies - that we cannot carry out this project without private initiative. the states, by virtue of the very limits of their powers, cannot go beyond their borders. and we are seeing exactly the same phenomenon in the regions: each region makes its own intranet (everyone is proud!), or its own egonet. in this way, the result is a product that is the sum of many things, but the whole is never the sum of the parts. i therefore call for a debate on the principle of subsidiarity, to examine to what extent we are often deprived of our citizens' freedom. and only companies, with the help of the commission, are capable of carrying out projects that fly like eagles over the mountains and have a global vision. i believe that only in the spirit of a europe which converges and not a europe which fragment, can we make this programme a reality and not a source of many frustrations. we have to avoid two years from now we're talking about what we wanted to do and they didn't let us.

doris pack: the initiator of this whole policy was indeed the european parliament - these ideas have, at least partially, been put into practice. recognition of skills: i know that there is still a fundamental wave will also be felt in the daily practice of our teaching. investment in education: i leave it to subsidiarity and i share the regret of the members who say that budgetary resources should follow the fine words. but there is no doubt that either most of these 1995 ideas are now being implemented or we have a toolbox to take them forward. so i am not as pessimistic as many members of parliament are in this area, because i have seen, i have felt that the situation has changed since the lisbon summit. there is a fundamental change, which, of course, is too slow, but at least things are moving, and it's already a very big step forward. lifelong learning: yes, 1996 was the year of the first steps in this field. i have presented my memorandum on what mrs maes says: 'learning helping us to put our ideas into practice. the elearning action plan is also helping to change this. finally, we are also in the midst of the european year of languages. i have said it before and i conscience. some colleagues have spoken of subsidiarity. i think the interpretation of subsidiarity is very clear. i respect it, but i want to create european added value, networking, exchange of information, dissemination of good practice. i would like to draw your attention, ladies and gentlemen, to the quality analyses of primary and secondary education. this is a revolution! would you have imagined in 1995 that ministers would have agreed to a foreigner coming to their country to see where they stood in terms of the quality of education? - no , please ! today, it is done. the system is not yet perfect, but comparisons enable ministers to see where their strengths lie and where their weaknesses lie, and they work to fill those weaknesses. financial provisions: no such provision was - mr president, the proposal for a council and european parliament decision under discussion must be understood in the wider context of the water directive, with its immediate objective of limiting and reducing pollution of the european aquatic ecosystem by classifying 32 substances in the group of priority substances, of which only 11 are substances falling within the legal category of priority dangerous substances. in my view, the list of priority dangerous substances contained in the annex to the commission's proposal should not be altered and it is necessary to maintain it as drawn up by the commission. in order to reach a consensus on classification, cooperation between the commission, the european parliament and the council is of course essential. i believe that only on the basis of the work done by the commission in this field will we be able to articulate a classification system which applies clear and comprehensible criteria for the identification of substances. we all share the desire to eradicate water pollution as soon as possible and this requires a twofold strategy: on the international level, ratification of international commitments, especially the ospar and commps conventions, although we do not consider it appropriate to make any explicit reference to these agreements in the text of the proposal; on the member state level, ensuring that the commission is provided with the necessary means to know exactly the situation of our water bodies, so that a detailed and constant monitoring of the evolution of the quality of our waters can be carried out, comparable between states. it is also important to encourage future eu member states to tackle pollution by moving closer to european targets, especially in those countries which share river basins with the european union. finally, i would like to emphasize the exceptional circumstances of certain substances, such as cadmium and mercury, which cannot be completely eliminated at present, as amendment no 2 in the report of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy points out.
- mr president, commissioner, in the field of water policy, the final agreement of june 2000 provides for the commission to identify, among the dangerous substances, the priority dangerous substances, whose emissions, discharges or losses must cease or be progressively reduced within 20 years. the european commission has amended its proposal so that, through groups of experts, firstly the priority dangerous substances are identified; secondly, a review clause is introduced that would apply to some of them and, thirdly, the terminology and the final text are adapted. of the 32 identified priority substances, 11 are proposed as priority hazardous substances, 11 more as priority substances under study - this within 4 years of the entry into force of the framework directive. there are no data on toxicity, persistence or bioaccumulation for the remaining 10. the committee on agriculture, whose three amendments should be supported, points out that natural nutrients should not be priority hazardous substances and that there is already an established procedure on the phytosanitary issue: directive 91/414, which should be respected, and the decision which should be adapted at the same time, not before or after. finally, the various definitions, such as river basin district, or the management of these districts should be reorganized, as this would prevent different rules from affecting the same territories and problems in different ways, as could happen when applying the wfd, commps and ospar conventions.
the rapporteur. - mr president, we are discussing the revision of directive 92/59/eec which concerns general product safety and there is a priority which we share with the commission, the council and the european parliament, namely improving the health and safety of consumers. it's a wish that's always been there but now, given the situation, it's more firm. the proposal is designed to ensure the safety of products placed on the market and to encourage compliance with the obligations of producers and distributors. producers should only place safe products on the market, provide consumers with reliable information, prevent risks and, if necessary, ultimately withdraw dangerous products already on the market. and distributors should not supply any product that they know is unsafe, and they should cooperate with the market surveillance network, which also includes the authorities responsible for ensuring product safety. the method we believe to be appropriate for this review includes consultation with non-governmental organisations and social actors, businesses and others before the proposal is made. more than fifteen of these organisations were consulted before the proposal was made and it was intended to correct the gaps, the inadequacies in the implementation of the directive in the past years. some of these suggestions are contained in the first council proposal put forward by the commission. we agreed with most of the proposals that were made to us. however, we tabled 30 amendments which we believe could improve this proposal. more than 21 of these were adopted at first reading, in whole or in part. these clarified the concepts of 'safe product' and 'recovery', recognised the need for regular reports to the european parliament on the success or failure of the implementation of the directive, as well as for labelling in the language of the country where the products were marketed, and proposed, among other things, the inclusion of the candidate countries in the rapex system. however, some issues remained of concern to the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, the alternative rapporteurs and the commission itself. and in this second reading we have tabled only eleven amendments, which were discussed in the committee on the environment, and which were adopted at the last sitting by a rather large majority, and which in the various informal meetings - there were many, and i have to thank the commission and the council for their interest in this report - we have tried to reduce. i think we can easily reach agreement on five of these amendments. these amendments concern the possibility of external certification of safe products, the possibility of harmonization in the surveillance programmes of the various member states, the inclusion of the precautionary principle in such an important issue as this and the establishment and strengthening of a network of competent authorities in relation to product safety. there are more difficulties in other amendments, such as those relating to the export of unsafe products to the third world and to the safety of services. we think it is very important that there should be specific legislation. i am not sure if this is the case in the rest of europe, but in my country it is. services such as tourism, academic courses and telecommunications are being discussed very much, because in many of them there are flagrant abuses. we therefore want to ensure that there is legislation on this subject in the near future and also on the nature of committees. mr president, i think it will not be difficult to reach agreement on the 11 amendments adopted by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy. and i will emphasize one which we believe should be a hallmark of europe. it is an ethical attitude which means not exporting to third countries products which we europeans consider unsafe. we think that is a very important amendment because if they are not safe for europeans, they are not safe for anyone else in the world, even if there are more flexible rules in other countries. we therefore believe that by defending the proposal of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, we are also defending very important principles of the european union.
- mr president, as has already been said, the reform presented to us by the commission on 13 february 2001 as a package of seven measures to overcome the problems created on the beef market by the bse crisis undoubtedly merits critical reflection on the part of our group. firstly, while the community's livestock sector is waiting for measures to solve the crisis in its sector, there are only two in this package that seem appropriate to solve a crisis, namely the budgetary crisis that the commission has in relation to it. the abolition of the 350 000 tonnes public intervention ceiling for meat, in order to prevent the so-called safety net intervention system from becoming operational, seems to be a crisis measure, as does the measure - already approved by the meat management committee on 16 march - of a new intervention method for the purchase and storage of animals over 30 months old. i would also like to say, commissioner, that this measure will do little to improve consumer confidence and solve the problems on the market, since we are storing meat which will have to be brought to the market later, thus introducing important elements of imbalance into the market. the other five measures are indeed targeted at the sector, but they are not urgent and can come into force and have their effects in the short and medium term. these measures should have been taken with the calmness that any reform in a sector affected by such a deep crisis demands. however, i must be absolutely critical of two of them. one is the abolition of the national limit on male bovine premiums for individual rights; i think this is not the right measure, it would lead us to a closed, narrow quota market, which would do nothing to help the transparency and simplification of the cap or to a future reform of this sector. the other is the limitation of production, as is intended, through the reduction of the suckler cow premium. i would like to say, commissioner, that this proposal, which makes it compulsory that, in order to be able to collect the suckler cow premium, between 20 and 40% of the animals for which the premium is claimed must be heifers, is intended to reduce the quantity of meat available on the market, but what it does remove is quality meat from herds of suckler cows reared under extensive systems. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's agricultural policy is not distorted by the fact that it is not able to meet the needs of the community's agricultural population.

- question no 46 by mrs maría izquierdo rojo (h-0360/01) subject: association agreement with algeria and the situation of women will the next eu-algeria association agreement include a section on the protection of human rights for women (including the right to education in rural areas) and the improvement of their family status? what advances are planned ? what will be the eu's support for women's access to the democratic process? question no 2 by mr solbes
commission. – the association agreement currently under negotiation with algeria sets out among the priorities in the social and cultural field the promotion of the role of women in economic and social development and the improvement of women's access to education and training. gender questions also figure within cross-cutting priorities in the meda national indicative programme for algeria. the potential impact on the situation of women is examined before a decision is taken on the financing of each programme. women are among the primary target groups of the assistance project for the development of ngos. they had received about eur 5 million under meda by the end of 1999. an important social fund programme is in the final stages of preparation. it will finance activities for poor women in rural areas through training and micro-credit schemes. for 2001 we are preparing an education and health infrastructure rehabilitation project and a vocational training reform programme. these projects will have a direct and positive effect on the living conditions and on the employment situation of women. the programme european initiative for democracy and human rights has funded several seminars and projects concerning human and economic rights of women in algeria since 1996. in the year 2000 for example a eur 1.4 million regional programme was launched in the three maghreb countries. it aims to promote activities to enhance the participation of women in political and economic life.
