question no 48 by mr papayannakis (h-0322/01) subject: fight against poverty in greece it is clear from a commission communication (com (2000) 0594 final) that greece has a considerable gap between rich and poor and that, as confirmed by the recent commission report on social cohesion, it is in second place in the indicator on the persistence of poverty. in section 2.2 'poverty', it is noted that 21 to 22% of the population in portugal and greece have incomes below the poverty line and that in greece 10% of the population suffer from persistent poverty. could the commission state whether and when the greek government has communicated to it concrete programmes and action plans to combat poverty, since the utilization rate of the previous operational programme in this field was only slightly above very low levels? given that greece also has a very high unemployment rate, virtually no training programmes and the lowest expenditure on education - all of which are directly linked to poverty - does the commission believe that the root causes of this phenomenon can be tackled by the payment of social benefits to the poorest?
commission. - i think my initial position and your comments do not differ much. i have pointed out that economic growth helps to improve the context and you conclude that it does not necessarily reduce the differences. that is correct, and i do not think that this debate will go far enough. it is true that in the case of greece the differences between the richest 20% and the poorest 20% of the population are very high compared to the average. what is the commission's position? i think the commission has been very clear. first of all, i think growing up is important. within growth, it is essential to increase employment. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation of the unemployed. we also think that adapting labour markets in such a way as to create more jobs is fundamental to the fight against poverty, but we believe that this does not include the specific actions to combat poverty referred to by the nice council and which you are obviously very familiar with. the necessary actions concern a number of areas which are well covered. i believe that is the position of both the european union and the commission.
question no 49 by mr jonas sjöstedt (h-0361/01) subject: warning from the ecofin council to ireland earlier this year, the ecofin council criticised ireland's budgetary policy, saying that ireland's economic policy was leading to far too high inflation. what action does the commission intend to take in this case? does it intend to take further action against ireland for not heeding the ecofin council's warning?
commission. - mr president, i shall be very brief in my first speech. what the recommendation says in its second paragraph, and i try to explain it, is that the commission is invited to report throughout 2001 on economic and budgetary developments in ireland and that the council will follow these developments and in particular assess their consistency with the broad economic policy guidelines. we are in may, and we have a number of economic and budgetary data at the moment, but i would not dare to draw too definitive conclusions just yet. the commission hopes to obtain this information with, i would not say more precision, but with more value from the point of view of compliance with the recommendations, in order to subsequently present its assessment to the council. we believe that working with data which corresponds solely and exclusively to the first months of budget implementation, which are traces of the previous budget, is not the best method.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, which are not in line with the commission's proposals. and if we apply classical monetary theory, it's clear that those countries with higher inflation rates, with higher growth rates, need more restrictive monetary policies to avoid overheating processes. the conclusion is obviously clear from the comments i have just made. the problem of the exchange rate is a problem which has given rise to a great deal of debate and discussion, since the exchange rate cannot be changed, because it is an irrevocable exchange rate, since the solution in ireland would be solved by a change in the exchange rate. it is not through higher inflation and, to some extent, a re-evaluation of the exchange rate that their problems can be partly solved by achieving a greater balance in terms of the current account balance. this is a debate which certainly has some bearing on the fundamental debate of expansionary or non-expansionary fiscal policy, but there is no doubt that, if the argument used by some economic theorists is true, it is no less true that an expansionary fiscal policy would force that adjustment by real revaluation of the exchange rate to be even more violent than it would otherwise be. that said, i will only say that, according to our information, growth is clearly going to be lower at the moment. inflation is still high, although lower than last november, and the budgetary measures which will most interest us in assessing what is happening in ireland in the future will undoubtedly be the savings plan enacted by the irish government, the impact of foot-and-mouth disease in ireland, which is very significant, and of course the development of revenue and expenditure which so far does not correspond to what is budgeted. but as i said before, drawing conclusions in april on the end-of-year figures seems to me to be too risky.

mr president, i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission is concerned that the court of justice is adopting a particular judgment in one way or another for breach of community rules. i think we've all established a few rules of the game. i think the fundamental rule is that we must keep our promises. the commission has the task, not always easy, of highlighting breaches of the agreement. the commission has in this particular case emphasized this fact, which has also been unanimously endorsed by the ecofin council. so i understand that there is interference of this kind, but i think we cannot be held hostage to such situations. secondly, does the commission intend to take the irish hostage to its decisions? no, the rules of the game are very clearly defined in the treaty. there are general guidelines to be respected and those general guidelines include a number of elements of coherence with the general policy. ireland, like other countries, is part of monetary union and the development of interest rates and exchange rates is a matter of concern to all member states. we must therefore all be consistent with this national economic policy which we must adopt in accordance with the treaty, but also coordinated in accordance with the treaty. the debate on the relative weight of ireland has already taken place in this house on other occasions. i stressed at the time that, from the commission's point of view, the rights and duties of all the member states are the same and therefore the economic concept - economically relevant - of the different weight of one or another member state is not so important from a legal or regulatory point of view. that said, the irish government has a wide margin of manoeuvre to increase what it deems appropriate in terms of public investment and to improve its services. the problem is that this must be compatible with respect for the broad economic policy guidelines and the stability pact. it is obviously up to the irish government to define its spending priorities.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. but from a legal point of view, from the point of view of our legal commitments, the situation is the same for all countries, whether large or small. the treaty does not provide for different treatment of countries in one situation or another. what should we do if a small country acts as a free-rider, enjoying the advantages of the union but without any of its disadvantages, and what if instead of one country there are two, three or four small countries? what dimension must a country have to be relevant? i think that this argument, although attractive from an economic point of view, is unfortunately not acceptable from a political and legal point of view.
- question no 50 by mrs astrid thors (h-0385/01): subject: coordination of the european union's positions within the imf and the world bank informal interviews with europeans working at the world bank and the international monetary fund have shown that there is no coordination of european union action within these bodies. could the commission state whether it has taken any initiatives to address this shortcoming, which prevents maximum use of the union's influence? questions to mr fischler
- commission. - the commission has made several attempts to improve the coordination of the european union and monetary union in order to solve the problem of external representation in the international monetary fund. in vienna, an agreement was reached at the end of 1998 on the basis of a commission proposal, but the member states did not accept it. the commission's proposal was that, in accordance with article 111 (4) of the ec treaty, it should be decided that the community would in principle be represented by the euro area presidency, the european commission and the european central bank. however, the member states reached an agreement of a different nature, reducing the validity of this proposal, especially as regards the role of the commission, which was reduced to a kind of support for the presidency of the euro area. but these proposals, already limited, are not being implemented in practice. in practice, what has been achieved so far is some improvement in the framework for the coordination of economic policies and an exchange of views through the economic and financial committee on the positions adopted at the international monetary fund. this coordination is taking place both in brussels and in washington and i believe that it has allowed some progress to be made in the coordination process. if you ask me whether the commission is satisfied with this process, i must say that we are not satisfied with this process or with the level of coordination achieved, although we are aware of two limitations: firstly, the international monetary fund is made up of states. the union is not a member of the fund as such - a fact which presents us with some interesting difficulties. secondly, the fund itself is currently undergoing a revision of its statutes, which is also something that needs to be taken into account in order to move forward with the external representation process.
the commission - it is true that these channels exist and, at the moment, we have at least three instruments that are useful. the commission is of course present at the meetings of the economic and financial committee, where the positions to be taken are discussed, the actual rules we take into account for the positions of the various constituencies in washington - and let us not forget that we are made up of countries which are not members of the union. as a representative of the commission is also present in washington at the meetings of the executive directors of the european union areas or constituencies which concern the european union in the fund. secondly, whenever the commissioner attends meetings of the international monetary fund, which is usually every six months, he has bilateral contact with the executive director of the fund, with whom we also have very developed cooperation, not only for the euro zone but also for other areas outside the european union. in the euro area, at the moment, we have accepted the application of the so-called article 4 fund analysis which is produced every year with the international monetary fund. outside the euro area, we have a great deal of cooperation with the fund, not only in the candidate countries, but in all those where we are implementing macrofinancial assistance schemes, because we always do so in cooperation with the fund. finally, it is true that the president of the eurogroup acts on behalf of the euro area in the monetary and financial committee of the fund, the former interim committee. it is true that the speeches of the president of the eurogroup are agreed speeches, which include the elements of common agreement between all the countries of the euro area and are the germ of something that we would like to have more content and more precision in the future. we think it's a good step to move forward.
- question no 51 by mr josu ortuondo larrea (h-0326/01): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the victims of the earthquake in the azores. subject: cod fishing for cod the cod fishery rules for cod in the bay of biscay allow a minimum mesh size of 70 millimetres. in view of the available resources and with a view to improving the operating system, it is proposed to increase this mesh to 100 millimetres. such a measure would result in a 50% reduction in the catches landed by this fleet for an equivalent effort and an increase in the operating costs of the vessels in view of the efforts to be made to achieve the same level of catch and to meet the cost of new nets. in these circumstances, could the commission state whether it has assessed the potential gains in terms of long-term performance? has it taken into account the post-escape mortality phenomenon common to other lizard species and to the colin? has it taken into account that the widening of the mesh involves a multiplication of efforts to achieve an identical catch level, which in turn leads to an increase in post-escape mortality and the cost of operating the fleet? has it considered what the cost of the new nets might be and what measures could be put in place to facilitate the transition of the fleet to the new meshes? would it not be better, before making any changes to the provisions on technical measures, to ensure first of all that the existing regulations are strictly observed?
the commission. - mr president, the commission will adopt the emergency measure referred to by mr ortuondo larrea in his oral question at the end of may. there are a number of scientific opinions, in particular the one of the international council for the exploration of the sea last november, which were confirmed by the commission's scientific, technical and economic committee for fisheries earlier this year. all these reports indicate that the sea-buck stocks in the bay of biscay and south-west of the irish coast are facing an imminent collapse. the main problem for this stock is the high number of young fish caught. the number of adult fish is declining and it is feared that the stock will not produce enough offspring to replenish itself. one way of reducing the catches of juvenile fish is to use nets with larger mesh sizes. at a mesh size of 70 mm, sea bass are caught from a length of approximately 25 cm. a mesh width of 100 mm, on the other hand, brings sea depths of 40 cm into the net. the proposed regulation does not require that all hake be fished with nets with a mesh size equal to or larger than 100 mm. we have deliberately set aside certain exceptions in clearly defined areas for vehicles of less than 12 metres in length on daily journeys and also for vehicles catching crayfish. this exemption covers about 1 500 vessels, or about two thirds of all vessels catching or by-catching hake. i am aware that increasing the mesh size will result in short-term losses in catch weight. but without such action, the stock will not grow back to a size that would allow a sustainable fishery. scientific studies have also shown that increasing the mesh size to 100 mm and maintaining the current fishing effort will increase yields by at least 70% in the long term. of course, the fishermen need a certain amount of time to re-equip their nets, and we will give them that time until 1 august this year. those fishermen who then wish to continue to operate with a mesh size of less than 100 mm - this is also possible - may then not report more than 20% of by-catches of hake. we want to create an incentive for fishing with larger, more selective nets. i am not sure that the commissioner has been able to answer this question. we want to present a long-term reconstruction plan to the european parliament and the council later this year. once this proposal has been adopted by the council, member states may pay their shipowners ex post subsidies for the new acquisition of networks in accordance with the provisions of article 16 (2) of the structural regulation. unfortunately, there is no such possibility under the urgency regulation. i also regard this as a major shortcoming and i have ordered that we should make an adjustment to the structural regulation in this direction as soon as possible. now, the argument is that sea urchins are very sensitive and some of the young fish that escape the nets again eventually die anyway. i'll be honest with you. our experience shows that larger mesh openings over a longer period of time lead to more adult fish. that is the main point, namely that the stock can be replenished for reproduction. this is perhaps the best proof that this measure is a sensible one.
- commissioner, i appreciate the breadth of your answer to this problem of cod fishing, but if i have not misunderstood you, you said that you are considering an exception for vessels of less than 12 metres in length, including lobster and shrimp vessels. the information i have from the fishermen confirms that these vessels, although small, are fishing with long nets and that, in addition, the capture of the cichlid also has a great impact on the juvenile cod, because the areas of distribution of the cichlid and juvenile cod, which are the exploitation areas, are very overlapping. i would like to ask you whether, in making these considerations, you have considered the serious impact of smokers on the juveniles of cod.
the commission. perhaps there was some problem with the translation. so let me get this straight: what i said was that firstly, there should be an exception to the 100 mm net for vessels of less than 12 m in length and not for those of more than 12 m. the additional condition is that they are small vessels on a day-cruise. secondly, there should be an exception for vessels fishing for lobsters. i would like to say to you that i do not think that it is these smaller vessels that use very long nets. i think that we can live with this - as i have to admit - compromise that we have made here. we believe that, on the one hand, we must make it a top priority to ensure that the sea-buck stocks are restored to normal. we cannot, however, ignore all the social implications of this measure, which is certainly very strict, which we are proposing. we therefore think that we are the most responsible, especially for the owners of very small vessels, who are directly dependent on these economic activities and have no alternative to provide an exception. we cannot go any further, because that would make the measure de facto ineffective.
question no 52 by mr camilo nogueira román (h-0331/01) subject: reform of the structures of the directorate-general for fisheries why has the commission changed the structures of the directorate-general for fisheries in defiance of international agreements with third countries from the south, in order to favour the positions of the countries of northern europe in european waters as if they were their own, even though this is detrimental to the positions and contrary to the interests of the southern member states, to the extent that they feel they are intruders into community waters and the international fisheries policy of the european union?
commission. - mr president, first of all, i should like to clarify the wording of your question, mr president, that your claim that we are looking down on the southern part of the community is simply not true, and i therefore reject it, as do your allegation that the commission regards the southern member states as invaders, as you have said. the commission is not guided by such motives when it comes to ensuring the best possible management of the directorate-general for fisheries, but is concerned solely with optimising its work. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this is how we ensure that they are managed in a uniform and coherent way. we are thus in line with the council's conclusions of 1997, the court of auditors' position set out in a special report and the demands of the green paper on the future of the common fisheries policy. on the other hand, the inclusion of agreements with third countries, which mainly concern the exchange of fishing rights, in the section dealing with tucs and quotas at the same time makes sense because the fishing rights under these agreements are already part of the tucs and quotas. the advantage of this new structure is particularly apparent in norway, where we are now negotiating long-term technical measures to restore the cod stock in the north sea. the commission has not been unfair in its treatment of the applicant countries, but it has been unfair in its treatment of the applicant countries.
- mr fischler, according to my data denmark has 44% of the fishing quotas in community waters, the united kingdom has 16% and the spanish state only 6%. this is exactly the opposite of what happens with extractive capacities, where the spanish, mainly galician, share is 35%. these figures serve to prove the deep-seated discrimination and state selfishness on which the principle of relative stability is based, which you do not want to call into question. the same discrimination is now applied within the structure of the directorate-general for fisheries, favouring denmark and the united kingdom. do you not think, commissioner, that it is time to apply the european union's founding principles of equality to the fisheries sector, which you administer? do you not think that the southern states, like spain, should be given their rightful place in the union's fisheries sector?

- question no 61 by mr richard howitt (h-0363/01) subject: the next commission green paper on the social responsibility of enterprises does the commission still share the views expressed on 30 october 2000 by anna diamantopoulou in her address to the european union committee of the american chamber of commerce, which stated in essence that when voluntary action is deficient, the demand for regulation grows and that there are a number of violations of fundamental rights which voluntary action simply cannot remedy? how will this concept be defended in the green paper on corporate social responsibility currently being prepared within the employment dg? what control system does the commission envisage to allow both voluntary action and legal regulation to be deployed?
the commission. i would like to highlight two key dimensions in the green paper. the first concerns european policy and the second the international dimension of the problem of corporate responsibility. at european level, breach of the law is clearly a matter for the member states and we have the power, through both the european parliament and the commission, to impose sanctions on member states which do not enforce the law. as regards the international dimension and issues such as child labour to which you referred, there are proposals concerning either social etiquette or codes of conduct for companies, but we want to link them to independent evaluation of the operation of these companies on a global level. the public debate which will begin with the green paper in june raises, among other things, the question of how we can activate international evaluators, international and independent bodies, in cooperation with governmental organisations, and with what specifications, so that we can refer to an evaluation at international level in an objective way. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of the information it receives from the public, and i am sure that the commission will be able to take this into account in its future work.
the commission. the best practices for business action in the social field are of course largely relevant to large enterprises. and the existing corporate social responsibility network is made up of large companies. but we must also note that one of the chapters in the green paper is about cooperation between large and small enterprises and best practices, examples of which we already have in several european countries where large enterprises set up networks with medium and small enterprises both to support them and to train workers, but also to inform them about new practices. i believe, and i agree with you, that the green paper and the new role of business can be very positive in supporting small businesses in particular.
question no 62 by maj britt theorin (h-0365/01) subject: equal treatment in the field of pay i believe that next year the commission will launch a campaign on the principle of equal treatment in terms of pay. i welcome this, since it is the commission's responsibility to monitor the implementation of the equal pay directive. although the directive has been in force since 1975, the results have been striking in their absence. wage gaps are still at 1980 levels - in the union, men in full-time employment earn on average 27% more than women in full-time employment. in some countries the gap is as high as 30%. it is important to explain the difficulties faced by member states in combating discrimination in pay and to determine whether a revision of the directive is necessary. could the commission state whether it is prepared to examine the application in the member states of the directive and the case law of the court of justice of the european communities and the need for updating the directive?
the commission. as mrs theorin points out in her question, the issue of gender pay inequality in the european union remains one of the major problems, despite longstanding national and community legislation and case law. it is one of the first principles we find in the treaty of rome, it is one of the first legislation that has been made since 1975, we have it repeated and strengthened in the treaty of amsterdam. the situation is, however, the same as in the early 1980s. what the commission has done so far, beyond legislation for the implementation of which there is a serious problem - i must stress that governments have not succeeded in mechanisms for the proper implementation of existing legislation - so beyond this key issue of implementation, the commission has made proposals and, in the 2001 guidelines, this issue is being looked at very seriously, it is one of the guidelines, and in the evaluation of the national action plans we will have a more complete picture not only of the situation in the member states but also of the actions and initiatives they have taken to deal with this issue. it is also worth mentioning that at the stockholm council this year the commission undertook to develop indicators to ensure that these differences between men and women do not exist because of discrimination. the fifth programme on women also includes a call for proposals, initiatives and innovative ideas from transnational partnerships to help us understand the phenomenon better, and proposals to governments and businesses to achieve results faster and more substantially than in the previous decade. in the light of these results and the initiatives i have mentioned, the commission will assess, with the help of parliament, of course, the need to update the directive on equal pay for men and women.
the commission. the policy in sweden on equal pay is, i think, both innovative and highly effective, because it is the only country that has managed to reduce the pay gap to a minimum. i would say that as a model it is ideal and i fully agree that it would be particularly positive if it were implemented by other countries and that is why i think that in a first phase it could be used as a best practice among governments, which could adopt it on a voluntary basis at the outset and in a pilot way. such a european dimension of the swedish model could later lead to binding decisions.

and the only thing that is done, of course, if missile shields are created is to have more missiles, that is, to go against all the efforts made since the abm treaty to reduce missile armaments in the world. another point which we also think should be mentioned to our american allies is that in relation to the un we must act jointly, but not through unilateral measures. i say this because, particularly in the case of the commission on human rights, we must start from the fact that all countries are taking part in an election and that one or two are elected at a time, and we cannot propose retaliatory measures such as the possible suspension of a debt that has already been paid and has been unilaterally reduced. finally, mr president, two weeks ago i had the opportunity to lead a visit by my group to the congress in washington. we believe that, apart from what they tell us, we too must speak directly. the visit was very positive: i was able to speak before the house of representatives subcommittee on european affairs, we had a dialogue as it should be: frank, direct and at times hard, but we believe that this is also an element that must be part of our future. and in this connection, mr president, i would like to conclude by saying that my group regrets that at the last moment - and this concerns you as rapporteur for the echelon commission - the american authorities were not able to confirm an appointment which is also important for maintaining and building confidence between us.
- mr president, i think we can say today that history is now merging with the present and that in this historical present we have to live in, the european union and the united states are two main actors. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we have to talk about the kyoto protocol, the missile shield - which will not only affect our security but also our pockets - the issue of the death penalty, the issue of drugs - in which i believe we have to act with full respect for international law and take on this problem from a regime of shared responsibility - the issue of globalisation - to use the terminology used by the commissioner. i would say that the united states and europe have a great responsibility to make sure that this ship produces far fewer castaways than crews. and we must also put emphasis on the development of trade and welcome this initiative of the united states at the quebec summit to create a free trade area for the 'americas' and congratulate ourselves on the fact that they have discovered that this trade initiative must have a democratic substrate and basis, as we have shown through our cooperation agreements with third countries which, as we saw yesterday in the committee on foreign affairs with mr patten, include a democratic clause and have a tradition of ten years. i would just like to ask one question, mr commissioner, madam president-in-office of the council, and that is whether the bush administration will continue the practice which the clinton administration had followed of exempting european companies from the application of title iii of the helms-burton act and whether this matter will be discussed at the transatlantic summit.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0155/2001), on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a european parliament and council decision establishing a programme of community action to encourage cooperation between member states to combat social exclusion (13740/1/2000 - c5-0046/2001 - 2000/0157 (cod)) (rapporteur: mrs figueiredo)
commission. – mr president, first i would like to assure mrs kratsa-tsagaropoulou that all the national action plans on exclusion and poverty submitted to the commission will be examined in the framework of the indicators and concrete goals agreed in the stockholm council. i would like to congratulate mrs figueiredo on the excellent work she has done, which is both helpful and useful. i believe that since we all agree how important this programme is, we can agree as soon as possible to start implementing it. as you will recall, in its amended proposal the commission accepted in full or in part 31 of the 47 amendments that were tabled by the european parliament. the common position that we have been examining incorporates 25 of these amendments. with regard to the amendments which are now under consideration, the commission can accept six of them in full or in part. i refer to amendments nos 2, reference to the social charter; 4, reference to the compatibility of the proposed budget with the current financial framework; 6, strengthening the comparability of indicators; 7, as it refers to the involvement of the local and regional level, 11, reinforcing the monitoring of coherence between this programme and other policies; and, most importantly, amendment no 14, referring to raising funding to ngos under exceptional circumstances to 90%. the following amendments cannot be accepted. amendment no 1 proposes adding solidarity among member states to the list of relevant community tasks. the fight against poverty and social exclusion in each member state is a national effort and should be placed in the context of promoting national action plans underpinned by community-level objectives and policy-oriented cooperation. so it is obvious that these are national efforts and national targets. amendment no 5, in which the european parliament is proposing to be involved in the agreement of targets, is not in line with the decisions of the european councils of lisbon and nice. as regards commitology, referred to in amendments nos 3 and 10, despite the fact that our proposal referred to the creation of an advisory committee, i believe that the mixed committee is a fair solution. this is the option that is applied in two other programmes: the equal opportunities and the anti-discrimination programmes. the commission is assisted by a management committee for horizontal issues concerning implementation, and by an advisory committee when dealing with individual funding decisions. amendments nos 8 and 12 refer to the role of the european parliament in the open method of coordination in the social exclusion field. i am ready to explore with you all the appropriate means of making sure that the european parliament can play its full role within this framework in this context. for example, i have already accepted the setting up of a round table, which will bring together the relevant actors. amendments nos 7 and 13 propose to open funding under the programme to innovative projects with a european added value in combating social exclusion. as i have already stressed, the aim of the programme is to encourage close national policy cooperation and mutual learning, and not to fund actions on the ground. moreover, innovative projects on the ground can be funded by the european social fund and by the new equal initiative. my next comment relates to your proposal in amendment no 14 to name the actors to be consulted in the preparation of the annual round table conference. i feel that such a list risks being more restrictive, incomplete and less flexible than the admittedly more general term "all the actors concerned". as regards amendment no 9, as i said at first reading, the commission has carefully examined all the questions concerning the budget and is of the opinion that the original proposal for eur 70 million is an appropriate one. i cannot accept at this stage an increase in the budget. amendment no 18 seeking to delete article 7 is not acceptable to the commission because it will make the execution of the programme very difficult. amendment no 15 attempts to restrict the implementation of measures, under strand 1 of the programme, to tenders only, in fact excluding the possibility of promoters of the innovative projects participating in the call for proposals. amendments nos 16 and 17 seek to curb the role of the commission by preventing it from using external expertise as well as technical and administrative assistance. to summarise, the commission can accept amendments nos 2, 4, 6 and 11. it can accept parts of amendments nos 7 and 14. it rejects amendments nos 1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17 and 18.
commission. – the role of the european parliament is a very important one but, of course, this role is defined by the decisions of the council. according to the lisbon and nice councils, there is a role for parliament and cooperation between parliament and the commission, but nothing more than that – if you mean the commitology issue. of course, we can find other ways of cooperation. i have already said that we can organise a round table. there can be cooperation between the commissioners and the high-level social protection committee, which deals with exclusion issues. of course, the european parliament has a very important role to play in the joint employment report, which will evaluate all the programmes. as far as the budget is concerned, i insist on the original proposal of eur 70m. it is very difficult to change it. we have to be realistic about what the council will accept and how this programme can be implemented with the human resources at our disposal.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow, wednesday, at 12 noon.
- the next item is the report (a5-0147/2001) by mr cercas, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the commission communication entitled 'the future of social protection in the long term: secure and sustainable pensions' (com (2000) 622 - c5-0011/2001 - 2001/2003 (cos))
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission has given us the opportunity to do so in its communication on the future development of social protection, as mandated by the lisbon european council. i would therefore like to begin by welcoming this communication, because of the importance it attaches to the problem, because it gives parliament a chance to speak and because of the breadth of perspectives with which it analyses the ageing of europe without limiting the debate to mere financial considerations. it is right to congratulate commissioner diamantopoulou, and i am doing so at this moment, for bringing the representatives of the european citizens, the members of the european parliament, into a debate which is crucial for the future of the union. i should also like to begin by sincerely and not just on paper thanking my colleagues on the committee on employment and social affairs, not only because they have been so generous in approving this report by an overwhelming majority, but also because i have received a great many contributions in the exchange of views and a very broad set of amendments, most of which i have been able to incorporate into my report, as they have provided valuable insights. i do not want to be too bombastic, but i think that the committee on employment has reconstructed a broad area of agreement that crosses all the groups in the house. and it is obvious that this has been possible because instead of each of us imposing his maximum programme on the subject, we have sought the space of consensus on the most relevant points. we are all aware that the ultimate responsibility lies with our states, but we also know that in the europe we want there is room for common criteria, objectives, values and principles for all europeans, and that we have the obligation and the right not to remain silent on this great problem. i would also like to say, in the first approach, that i am absolutely convinced that this is a problem which requires a broad debate and a social and political consensus. the european social model was built on the premises of the great social and political agreement, and the reform of the european social model will not be possible from new enlightened despotisms such as those which claim that some expert groups, high bureaucrats or certain finance ministers rule the world. the question of modernising the european social model has such social and political consequences that it cannot be left to those who have only a financial perspective and forget the social dimensions of the problem. it would be irresponsible to close our eyes to the data on economic requirements. but we would be making an even greater mistake if we limited our perspective to the impact on the economy, forgetting the impact on people. europe is ageing, and unless there is a radical change in fertility rates, this will have serious consequences for us, affecting the financial capacity of the system, the balance of public accounts and also the people. we risk, if we do not tackle the problem, or if we tackle it from an unsolidarist perspective, a wave of poverty and social disruption spreading across our continent. the first message i want to convey, or which i think parliament should convey, as our committee has done, is that we must take into account in a balanced way all the challenges arising from ageing, the challenge to public finances, and also the challenge to the way we have been building europe in previous generations. our committee has seen that the demographic dependency ratio is a very relevant figure, but it is not the only one. there is another fact that is even more relevant, which is the economic dependency rate, which means that our main problem is not going to be the rate of pensioners we have, but the employment rate. the real problem is whether europe will grow, create jobs, create businesses capable of ensuring that this rate of economic dependence does not deteriorate. europe has a long way to go, because we do not have sufficient employment rates, but we can have them if there is economic growth and if economic growth is directed primarily at creating the jobs our continent needs and which are infinitely lower than those of our main competitors, the united states and japan. in fact, if we were to achieve the lisbon objectives, the objective could be observed with much less drama than the available data suggest. the data, on the other hand, are long-term projections and therefore subject to change. they're not some biblical curse that has to fall on our backs. we can find ourselves on the way to a solution because we still have time to change certain information which is worrying us at the moment. and that data will certainly have to be monitored, on an ongoing basis, with increasingly rigorous criteria, so that it does not become the beating heart of those who are trying to gain advantages. one last thought, mr president. if we want to create the jobs that europe needs, that the protection system needs, we have to think about women and older workers. there are the large bags we have to put into action. we must put all the union's economic and social capacities into action, and in the committee on employment we believe that this is the best way of tackling the problem of our continent's ageing.
the commission. i would like to congratulate mr cercas, who has worked very well with the committee on economic and monetary affairs and the committee on women, and whose work has resulted in the impressive consensus we have had in the debate that has preceded it. the issue of pensions is a major political, economic and social issue and concerns all governments. other reforms are under way, others are being discussed and others were completed only a year or two ago. it is therefore a european problem and the sustainability of pensions is the bet for the next generation. there is a set of policies which, if achieved at european level, will facilitate and enhance the sustainability of pensions. these policies are aimed at increasing the rate of growth, increasing employment, effective policies to support parents in reconciling work and family life, and immigration policies. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one, but it is not the only one. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the information it receives. i think it is particularly important, as several speakers have pointed out, that pensions have been excluded from the ecofin agenda and budgetary discipline and have been the subject of the ministers' discussions, as well as the committee on employment and social affairs. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the social security system is not distorted. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. but let us not forget that, under the treaty, we are obliged, we have a specific objective, to ensure a high level of social protection and sustainable, non-inflationary economic growth. it is therefore important that, for the first time since lisbon, the heads of state agree on the need for cooperation on pension issues. it is a very important shift in european policies, which also highlights the scale of the problem. it is certain that cooperation between member states will make reforms more effective in all countries. after lisbon, a first commission communication was commissioned and adopted. the question of pensions has been discussed at all the councils, at faira, nice, stockholm, and now the newly created committee on social affairs is preparing the study to be presented in gothenburg. this study will analyse all the problems per member state and make proposals on the basic principles for sustainable systems. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. it was said by many members that there can be no neutral approach to pensions because women face major problems and poverty in europe is closely linked to the pension system and the position of women in the economy and society. it is important that after stockholm it was decided to examine the method of open cooperation on pensions, taking into account the issue of subsidiarity and the particular problems of each country. we are preparing, and will present before the summer, a commission communication in which we will try to approach the issue of the open method of cooperation in pensions in more detail. i must say that this resolution of the european parliament, if adopted tomorrow in the form we know it to be today, is a strong support for this coordinated effort to reform pensions in the european union. i hope that in this new chapter opening up at european level, the chapter of cooperation on pensions, we can find new ways of cooperation between the commission, the council and parliament. i should also like to remind you that the commission has strongly supported the need for the european parliament to cooperate with the high level committee on social protection, and that cooperation is under way. ladies and gentlemen, i believe that the fact that we have opened this chapter and given a european dimension to the pension issue will support and help governments in all member states in particular to achieve reforms which will be sustainable, taking account of the economic and, above all, the social dimension.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow, thursday, at 12 noon.

question no 1 by mr bart staes, substituted by mrs maes (h-0323/01): subject: community organization of the sugar market on 30 june, the sugar regulation in force is to be extended or amended. last year, the cost of overproduction in the sugar sector reached 800 million euros. this is almost as much as the amount that was released for the bse crisis. despite the strong criticism of the court of auditors and the negative effects on consumers and producers in the third world, the council does not seem at all prepared to make the amendments to the sugar regulation proposed by the commission. several member states of the european union are threatening to capitulate to the short-term vision of the sugar industry. does the council intend to endorse the commission's proposal, in view of the court of auditors' strong criticism of the current sugar regulation and the negative impact of its provisions on consumers and third world producers? if not, why does the council advocate the maintenance of sugar regulations which have been strongly criticised by the court of auditors and which have a negative impact on consumers and third world producers?
the council. as the presidency, we will do what we can, i.e. ensure that the matter is constantly discussed. there are differences of opinion between member states. this is a sensitive issue in many member states. we will now take it up at the agriculture ministers' meeting in a few weeks' time, and i promise that we will continue to give priority to the issue. at the same time, it is unfortunately not possible to predict what a possible compromise might look like.
- question no 2 by mr per gahrton (h-0325/01): subject: euro councilalthough the council has decided in the past that the preparatory meetings for the meetings of the ecofin council between ministers from the 12 euro area countries would be completely informal and would deal exclusively with euro-related issues, there are increasing signs that these meetings are becoming formalised to become a kind of 'euro council' and, in practice, by preliminary decisions on all sorts of economic and financial issues, to take away the real power from the ecofin council. belgium, for example, has proposed to 'develop' the informal euro council. in these circumstances, would the council indicate what measures it intends to take to put an end to all attempts to formalise, in contravention of the treaty, a sort of 'euro council' and to transfer the powers of the ecofin council gradually to it?
the council. - the so-called eurogroup is an informal body set up in 1998 on the basis of a resolution on the coordination of economic policies in the third stage of emu. resolution adopted by the european council in luxembourg on 13 december, the feast of st. lucia, 1997. the resolution states that 'the ministers of the euro area states may meet informally to discuss matters relating to the specific responsibilities they share for the single currency'. the resolution also reaffirms that 'in all cases where a decision is to be taken, this will be done by the ecofin council in accordance with the procedures laid down in the treaty'. i would also point out that the nice european council last december welcomed the improvements made in the way the eurogroup operates and in its visibility. it also welcomed 'the intention to broaden the number of issues, in particular structural issues, addressed in that forum, taking due account of the conclusions of the luxembourg european council'. that is to say, informally and without decision-making.
the council. - i would be happy to tell mr gahrton that when the swedish presidency took over the presidency club on 1 january this year, it was quite concerned about how it would work with the eurogroup versus the ecofin council. we were afraid that we would end up in a situation where - as gahrton suggests - decisions would be taken in a room to which we had no access. then there would be a fait accompli which we would have to implement only in the ecofin council. i must say, however, in all honesty, that this has not been the case. the principles laid down in the luxembourg decision i have just quoted, that is to say, the decision of the european council of december 1997, have been respected to a very great extent. it is quite natural that there is a need for discussion in the circle of finance ministers who share the common currency. but there's no real decision making in that circle. the position of the ecofin council has been respected and there has been a very strong unity of principle on this. can you be sure of what the future holds? it's hard to tell, and especially about the future, as someone once said. i think there is every reason to believe that the members of the council will continue to feel solidarity with the principles laid down in previous european council decisions, namely that the position of the ecofin council should be maintained. that, after a representative has expressed a personal opinion that the eurogroup's position should be extended, the representative concerned may be responsible. we are trying to assess how things have been in practice, and then we feel that we can say without trembling at the vote that the ecofin council's position has been respected.
- question no 3 by mrs yasmine boudjenah (h-0329/01): subject: western saharathe united nations has decided to extend the presence of minurso in western sahara for two months, but the settlement plan signed between morocco and the polisario front has not yet been fully implemented. on the contrary, the threat of a renewed armed conflict between the two sides is greater than ever. several facts thus testify to the moroccan desire to rearm. such as the announced acquisition of us or french fighter planes through the investment of part of the sums provided for in the recent agreement between vivendi and maroc telecom (i.e. usd 3.5 billion). moreover, the british press has recently revealed that morocco has been able to benefit from trade agreements with the united kingdom which have enabled it to acquire new weapons and to renew its military power: mirages and spare parts which would have already made it possible to manufacture 56 guns. this weaponry would now be stationed on the border along the "defense wall". if confirmed, the transaction would be illegal as eu law - the arms export code of conduct - prohibits the sale of arms to countries or areas in conflict. can the council confirm this information ? does it intend to intervene in this member state?
the council. - it is now the case that the code of conduct concerning war material is not legally binding. there can be no sanctions; there is no legal basis for this. however, the swedish presidency is seeking to promote greater openness and transparency in this area, as in most other areas. i think we have seen several positive, constructive steps towards greater transparency, including in the application of the code of conduct on arms exports. we will try, together with all the other forces of good in the council, to take further steps to increase transparency in matters relating to arms exports. the conflict in western sahara has been going on for far too long. right now, i think we all feel a clear frustration at the lack of progress. however, the council is of the firm view that we will best serve the quest for a peaceful solution by continuing to give clear support to the un, to the un secretary-general's special envoy mr baker. this is the line which the council will continue to pursue.
- the presidency is quite right to reply to mrs boudjenah, not only on the code of conduct on arms but also on the sahara conflict, because the president-in-office of the council knows very well that behind mrs boudjenah's question there is concern about the conflict between morocco and the sahara. and in his answer, which is very clear, he speaks of support for the united nations and james baker, he speaks of the need to reach an agreement acceptable to all and he says that, indeed, europe is the largest donor of humanitarian aid, with 20 million euros. the question is, as the largest donor of humanitarian aid, should we not play a fundamental political role in this conflict, to prevent the saharawis from taking up arms again and from further escalating this conflict, and not just support james baker and the united nations? the acceptable agreement, mr president-in-office of the council, was already reached in 1992 when the saharawis laid down their arms to go to a referendum which should have been held in that year. will that not be the best agreement, to hold the referendum with europe's contribution?
the council. the western sahara conflict is very difficult and has a complex background. i believe that the union, which wants and must play an active political role in important and difficult international conflicts, would do well to give strong support to the efforts of the united nations. i note from the report presented by mr baker in april this year that some progress has indeed been made in developing various proposals for selfgovernment for western sahara. i think that at this stage it would be very unwise for us to take any other route than to continue to give this constructive support to mr baker.
- mr president-in-office of the council, i would like you to follow along with me on the following line of reasoning, which is very simple. you tell us that the council has dealt with the situation in the western sahara conflict and that a series of measures have been taken to restore confidence between the parties. do you think that a measure of confidence between the parties is that a member state, which is as important as the united kingdom, sells arms to one of them when there is a ceasefire? secondly, and this reasoning is also simple, what code of conduct are we talking about? because i have the impression that many people, many organizations, speak of a different code of conduct than the one you have referred to. because you've referred to a code that may or may not exist. thirdly, i would like you to abandon a sort of metaphysical stance whereby you support mr baker's efforts but never say how you support them. please, how are you going to support them?
the council. the council has not had occasion to discuss the possible sale of arms to the region by any individual member state. i cannot therefore comment on this. however, i think i have tried to emphasize clearly enough the council's view on how best to move forward in the conflict itself. the council has, for example, deplored the deadlock on the question of a referendum. the un secretary-general has proposed that the parties should discuss alternative solutions to reach a solution to the conflict, now that the referendum issue has proved so difficult. i repeat that i think it would be very unfortunate if the union did not wholeheartedly support the collective international efforts being made to resolve this difficult conflict.
subject: death of four african emigrants on the beaches of tarifa, on the andalusian coast (spain) on 21 march, the bodies of four new people were found, two men and two women, including a pregnant woman, who drowned in tragic circumstances, as so many others before them, while trying to reach european territory in search of work and a new life. when will the european union decide to act and put pressure on the spanish authorities to put an end to this extremely serious situation, which should be a source of shame for all european and spanish institutions?
the council. the council has on several occasions had the opportunity to reply to similar questions from the honourable member. the council's position should therefore be well known. i would refer the honourable member to the reply given to his oral question h-27/2001 of 14 february 2001. i would also like to emphasize the efforts made by the council together with the commission to implement the action plan for morocco. let me also point out that the fight against human smuggling is a priority. i would also like to emphasize that the spanish authorities have no jurisdiction in morocco and therefore cannot control when vessels of various types leave morocco.

- question no 5 by mr carlos carnero gonzález (h-0335/01): what is the commission's position on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work? subject: requirement of a visa for entry into the european union for colombian citizens a leading group of colombian intellectuals, led by nobel prize winner gabriel garcía márquez, expressed their indignation at the council's decision to require a visa for colombian citizens to enter the european union. these intellectuals went so far as to say that, until the decision was revoked, they would refuse to travel to a country as close, culturally and linguistically speaking, as spain, whose government did not oppose the council's decision. 187 spanish intellectuals expressed their solidarity with the position taken by their colombian counterparts. in view of the concern and rejection aroused by the council's decision, could the council answer the following questions? does he know the position of the group of intellectuals led by gabriel garcía márquez? does he really believe that the visa requirement is an effective means of combating crime committed by colombian nationals? does he intend to contact nobel prize winner gabriel garcía márquez to inquire about his arguments? is he prepared to reverse his wrong decision, as is being demanded by a large part of public opinion, with which the author of this question agrees?

the council. - i consider that a procedure such as that described by mr sjöstedt is out of the question. i note first of all that it is expressly agreed in the preamble to the act that the regulation has neither the purpose nor the effect of amending national legislation on the publication of documents. secondly, sjöstedt refers to the principle of loyalty. it's not new. the so-called loyalty principle, which is enshrined in article 10 of the ec treaty, has been with us all along. it has not changed from the agreement reached here and approved by parliament earlier this month. i would like to emphasize that the consultation procedure introduced by article 5 of the new act is only advisory. if we are talking about swedish conditions, it is not in itself new that when applying the rules on foreign secrecy, swedish authorities may need to consult the institutions in order to make a correct assessment of the damage. this is well known in swedish law and nothing in this respect is changed by the new act.

- question no 11 by mr william francis newton dunn (h-0348/01) subject: weu satellites located at torrejón following the decisions adopted by the european council in nice, what are the plans and timetable for the transfer of these weu facilities to the european union?
the council. - the european union confirmed at the nice summit its intention to take over the crisis management functions of the weu. the council took note of the decisions in principle taken to incorporate the relevant western european union data into the st petersburg data. they included the establishment of a satellite centre and a security studies institute in the form of bodies, which would incorporate appropriate elements of the existing parallel weu structures. the swedish presidency was invited to continue work on this issue in the general affairs council, together with the secretary-general of the council. a draft joint action on the establishment of a european union satellite centre is currently being examined by the council's bodies. the swedish presidency intends to have it adopted by the council before the end of june. a satellite centre is of the utmost importance for strengthening the early warning and crisis monitoring capabilities in the context of the common foreign and security policy, in particular the european security and defence policy. the centre must have a statute and structure which enable it to respond flexibly to the requirements of the union and its member states and to carry out its tasks in close cooperation with existing community institutions at national and international level. the staff and infrastructure of this centre should initially come from the weu satellite centre. the precise arrangements for this have not yet been determined. the newly established satellite centre, to be located in torrejón de ardoz, spain, will start operations on 1 january 2002.

- question no 13 by mr lennart sacrédeus (h-0353/01) subject: remembrance of the holocaust following the initiative taken by the swedish prime minister, göran persson, to organise the important stockholm international forum on the holocaust in january 2000, the european parliament adopted a written declaration on the remembrance of the holocaust on 7 july 2000. in this declaration, the european parliament called on the council and the commission to increase efforts to promote education, remembrance and research on the holocaust, to encourage the study of the holocaust in all its aspects, to promote appropriate forms of remembrance of the holocaust, including by establishing an annual european day of remembrance of the holocaust, and to take all appropriate measures to facilitate the disclosure of archives, in order to ensure that all documents relating to the holocaust are made available to researchers. what action has the council taken to respond to the requests made by the european parliament? are there any plans at present to establish a common european day of remembrance or national days to commemorate the holocaust?
the council. - as regards the question of teaching and raising awareness of the holocaust, i would just like to remind lennart sacrédeus of the answer given to a written question from joan colom in naval in march 2000 and which i know you have also had the opportunity to read. as regards the establishment of a european holocaust commemoration day, the council would only point out that it has not received any concrete proposals in this area. the member states involved in the international working group on holocaust remembrance, education and research have followed the recommendations of the committee of governmental and non-governmental representatives to establish unilaterally and nationally holocaust remembrance anniversaries. this has happened this year in germany, sweden, the united kingdom and italy. from next year, finland will also have such an anniversary. the council stressed that the lessons of history, including the holocaust, show the need to actively combat racism and xenophobia in all their forms, now and in the future. in this context, the european monitoring centre on racism and xenophobia in vienna will play an important role, not least in terms of cross-border action. it should also be noted that the council and the representatives of the governments of the member states will adopt a statement on combating racism and xenophobia on the internet on 28 may. it is a sad fact that new technology is being exploited by anti-democratic forces. as part of the further efforts to spread knowledge about the holocaust, so that conclusions can be drawn, among other things, on how to combat intolerance in our time, an international conference on the fight against intolerance was held in stockholm in january this year. representatives of all eu member states, the commitment of the european parliament in this area. i would like to thank in particular lennart sacrédeus himself for his work on the important position adopted by parliament on this subject in july last year.
the council. this is a very pressing issue that lennart sacrédeus raises. it has also been discussed in depth in the council. one conclusion is that, unfortunately, there are many historical events in the 20th century in which atrocities were committed. unfortunately, this is not just the case with the holocaust we have just discussed, but there are also events which we want to remember and use as a starting point for the fight against intolerance and xenophobia. we have therefore concluded that it is probably most appropriate to leave the question of a national memorial day to be a national question, to inspire national authorities to take such a decision. perhaps we should refrain from recommending a specific day, for example, that 27 january should be a european day of remembrance. there are so many other dates. for example, we have kristallnacht, which is important to remember in many countries, and we have the days around the end of the war in 1945 that can also be such days. we therefore believe that the best way forward is to inspire national decisions rather than to try to put forward proposals for decisions at european level.
- question no 14 by mr josu ortuondo larrea (h-0356/01): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the french overseas departments. subject: cod fishing: significant discrimination resulting from the reduction of catches decided by the fisheries in subarea viii (gulf of biscay) in december 2000, the eu fisheries council of ministers set the annual catch rates (tacs) and quotas for the 2001 cod fishery, i.e. a very significant reduction in catches in sub-area viii (gulf of biscay) of around 45% compared to the reductions for the northern areas (58.9%), without any justification based on the scientific management board, especially in terms of scientific monitoring and evaluation). this is the largest reduction since the late 1970s, and the stock is uniform and does not lend itself to regional differentiation. what was the criterion used by the council to justify this differentiation? in the absence of any scientific evidence indicating that there is any distinction in the composition of this stock, since it is a single population occupying vast areas of the sea, is the council aware that the subjective political criteria it uses constitute a serious discrimination against some of the community fleets? does it not consider that this should be taken into account in order to rectify the situation when the tacs for 2002 are next set?
the council. - i would first like to refer to the answer given by the council to question no 280 by the honourable member during the april part-session of this year and to make the following additions. in the light of scientific advice from ices, which recommended a minimum catch and the implementation of a recovery plan for this stock, the council fixed the total allowable catch for hake at 22 623 tonnes, compared with 42 090 tonnes in 2000. the commission had proposed a tac of only 11 000 tonnes for 2001. the total allowable catch for hake is divided into four management areas. according to the scientific information available to the commission, the situation of hake in management areas vii (a), (b), (d) and (e) was worse than in the three northernmost areas, and a proportionately larger reduction in tacs was therefore applied there. action for 2002 is necessary in the light of the ongoing discussion on a recovery plan for kummel.
- i do not understand your answer because, according to the information i have, scientific studies of the northern hake consider it to be a unique stock. i therefore do not know where they have got the data to differentiate the situation or the decline of the stock in one part or another: in the bay of biscay or elsewhere. and secondly, i would like to say to the president-in-office of the council that perhaps the council should have taken into account socioeconomic and commercial factors, safeguarding as far as possible the viability of the cod fishery, demanding radical compliance with the technical fisheries management measures that the common fisheries policy has not been able to put into practice in recent years, despite the continuous warnings from the bodies providing scientific management advice.
the council. the allocation of quotas is based on biological and scientific advice, not socioeconomic advice. the scientific advice provided requires drastic measures to address the serious situation of the herring stock. since there is clear scientific evidence that the stock of hake is currently severely overfished, a number of measures have been proposed by the scientific advisors in this area. this, of course, has short-term socioeconomic effects, but hopefully also positive long-term effects on the stock.
- question no 15 by mr esko olavi seppänen (h-0357/01) subject: president of the military committee of the european union what institution pays the salary of the person who takes up these posts? how is this one determined ? is it intended to seek the consent of the european parliament on this post and the corresponding salary?
the council. the chairman of the european union military committee is part of the delegation of the sending member state in the same way as the chairman of a committee or working group within the council. this also applies to non-presidential posts, such as the chair of the economic and social committee or the economic policy committee. it is therefore for the sending member state to determine and pay the salary of the chairperson. the procedure for appointing the chairman of the military committee of the european union shall not require the consent of the european parliament.
the council. - i can assure the honourable member that i have at least signed the reply. i hope it's on its way. sometimes it's a long way from stockholm to strasbourg, but i can promise you that the answer is on its way.

- since the two questions are related, i shall refer to questions 16 and 17 at the same time. question no 16 by mrs maría izquierdo rojo (h-0359/01) subject: association agreement with algeria and the situation of women will the next eu-algeria association agreement include a section on the protection of human rights for women (including the right to education in rural areas) and the improvement of their family status? what advances are planned ? what will be the eu's support for women's access to the democratic process? question no 17 by mr niall andrews (h-0377/01) subject: algeria it is estimated that 200,000 people have been murdered in algeria over the last ten years. these murders continue at a rate of about 200 a month. can the swedish presidency state what steps it has taken during its mandate in conjunction with an independent international inquiry into these killings and what initiatives it intends to take at eu level to put an end to these killings and the alleged use of torture?
the council. - first of all, let me say that the negotiations on an association agreement between the union and algeria are proceeding as planned, but there are still a number of important issues to be resolved. the negotiators meet almost every month with a view to concluding the negotiations this year. much has been accomplished. algeria has already given its provisional approval to the following human rights text: 'respect for the democratic principles and fundamental human rights as set out in the universal declaration of human rights shall be a guiding principle of the internal and external policies of the community and algeria and shall be an essential element of this agreement.' this broad reference covers human rights for all people, regardless of gender, and all areas of civil, political, as well as social, economic and cultural rights. another provision in the draft gives either of the contracting parties the right to take appropriate measures if it considers that the other party has failed to fulfil an obligation under the contract. the ongoing negotiations have also reached agreement on two important issues relating to the situation of women, namely a particular emphasis on providing the female part of the population with access to education, including technical, higher and vocational training, and to give priority, in the context of social the killings that have taken place in algeria over the last ten years. the presidency, through the swedish foreign minister, raised the issue at the meeting of the political dialogue between the union and algeria held in algiers on 24 april. we expressed our concern about the disappearances, arbitrary arrests and torture. a further list of such cases was submitted to the algerian authorities, and we requested information on these cases. the union has also expressed its concern along similar lines at this year's meeting of the un commission on human rights in geneva. as part of its technical and financial assistance to algeria, the eu is supporting a project to modernise the police. the programme includes training on respect for human rights in police arrests. eur 8.2 million has been earmarked for this purpose. the union also provides support to selected institutions to strengthen civil society. once the association agreement with algeria, which i have just mentioned, has been concluded, the political dialogue with algeria will be institutionalised. we will then have a framework within which we can express our concern and criticism of algeria.
