the council. - as i mentioned in my reply, the general wording on human rights is included in the draft association agreement now on the table. the general declaration on human rights contained in the association agreement must cover not only women but also minorities. you mentioned the berbers yourself. there are many other groups that need to be mentioned as well. i can assure you that on the basis of this general formulation, the swedish foreign minister, who is a woman, made clear references to the need to draw attention to the situation of women in algeria. this is something that is constantly being repeated in the dialogue with algeria, and we will be able to repeat it even more forcefully when we have an association agreement. the agreement will provide a framework for addressing all human rights problems. i think we share the same view of the need to improve the situation of women in algeria. i also think we share the same view that we must also ensure that algeria respects not only women's rights but all human rights. let us work together to achieve this.
the council. - i do not want to prejudge the council's final position on the association agreement, but i think it is important to ask the question: why does the union have an instrument such as an association agreement? it is not that an association agreement gives a government or a country carte blanche to do anything. the reason for having an association agreement is that the union wants a framework, a form, within which it can, among other things, conduct a political dialogue - also on matters on which it does not agree. that is why we want an association agreement. the council believes that this is a more effective instrument than simply letting things happen. the association agreements are, as the case of turkey shows, an effective instrument for the union to be able to point out and criticise conditions which it does not accept. it is slow at times, and we can all feel frustrated, but dialogue is always more effective than isolation in these contexts.
question no 18 by mr manuel medina ortega (h-0366/01) subject: agreement on 'everything but arms' what will be the consequences for community banana producers and traditional suppliers of acp countries of the recent agreement on 'everything but arms' which provides for the abolition of customs duties for the least developed countries?
the council. - it is an important issue that the honourable member is raising. i shall therefore give a relatively long answer, despite the late hour. as the honourable member is aware, the so-called 'everything but arms' regulation was adopted by the council on 26 february 2001, extending duty-free access without any quantitative restrictions to all products originating in the 49 least developed countries of the world, with the exception of arms and ammunition. the regulation entered into force on 5 may 2001. we believe that this measure constitutes a meaningful contribution to the economic development of the least developed countries and that it is also a concrete demonstration of the union's political goodwill towards the developing countries in the context of the preparations for the next round of wto negotiations. the regulation was the result of intensive discussions in the council, which took full account of the impact assessment prepared by the commission and of the member states' need for assurances on the detailed rules for the implementation of the proposed system. these assurances concerned not only the interests of the member states but also the implications of the proposal for the acp states not belonging to the least developed countries and the desire to ensure that the least developed countries themselves rather than third parties benefit from the new system. the doubts concerned mainly three particularly sensitive products: bananas, rice and sugar. the final text took account of the doubts in these respects, while maintaining the main principle that the eu should take meaningful action to improve the economic situation of the least developed countries. implementation was therefore delayed for bananas, rice and sugar, while agreement was reached on the principle of duty-free and quota-free access. for bananas, full liberalisation was postponed until 2006. in the meantime, annual tariff reductions of 20% will be introduced from january 2002. in view of the infrastructure problems currently faced by potential banana exporters in the least developed countries, it is difficult at this stage to assess with certainty the immediate impact of the regulation on the banana market. as mentioned above, the regulation has been adapted to take account of the concerns in this respect in the union and in the acp banana-producing countries not belonging to the group of least developed countries. in addition, the commission has undertaken to monitor the application of the regulation in order to detect and address any difficulties as soon as possible. the commission will examine the extent to which the least developed countries benefit from the regulation and whether the instruments available are sufficient to address, where justified, more severe disturbances on community markets and in the regulatory mechanisms, in particular for rice, sugar and bananas. on the basis of this study, the commission will present a report in 2005 and make the necessary proposals. as the honourable member is well aware, the council is fully aware of the problems of its acp partners in the functioning of the banana market and is doing its utmost to take account of these concerns in all relevant initiatives. in the context of the cotonou agreement, the eu recognised the 'overwhelming economic importance' of exports to the eu for acp banana suppliers and agreed to take measures, if necessary, to ensure the continued profitability of acp banana exporting companies and the continued availability of their bananas on the eu market. the council therefore, when acting to meet the need to amend the banana regime to bring it fully into line with wto rules, also seeks to introduce safeguards to prevent acp bananas from being excluded from the market. on this point, i would also like to mention the agreement in principle reached just before easter between the commission and the united states on the longstanding dispute between the eu and the united states over the banana trade regime. in general, the provisions of the agreement concerning acp suppliers are designed to protect their position by ensuring more reliable and favourable conditions for acp access to the eu market. the proposed introduction of a quota reserved exclusively for acp suppliers and of a historical licensing system, which is proving to favour acp suppliers more than the earlier proposal of 'first to mill first to grind', is of particular importance in this respect. in this context, i would also like to recall that when the community's banana market organization moves to a system of customs duties only in 2006, a tariff preference will still give the acp states a relative advantage. the commission proposes that the council should formally comment on certain details of the agreement of principle with the united states. the european parliament will of course be consulted on any possible amendment to the council regulation on the common organization of the market in bananas. finally, i would like to recall the council regulation establishing, from 1 january 1999, a special support system for acp states which are traditional suppliers of bananas. this system offers technical and financial assistance to help acp suppliers adapt to new market conditions and increase their competitiveness, while encouraging more environmentally friendly production and marketing practices. the financial and technical assistance provided under this regulation amounted to almost eur 45 million in 2000.

the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the commission, hoping to have more and better information on the real situation in the sector, has postponed the definitive reform for two years and has put forward a proposal which affects aspects of quality and market measures. although this intention is laudable, certain shortcomings in the proposal cannot be ignored, which concern three issues: the market situation, controls and the marketing of oil blends. in the 1998 reform, and against the wishes of this parliament, public intervention purchases were abolished, even though their average cost was the lowest of all existing ones. the effects of their abolition have led to a huge fall in market prices and a consequent reduction in producers' incomes. the mechanism of private storage is very slow; the committee on agriculture therefore proposes that it be automated, without altering the conditions for opening it. this is not the subject of the commission's proposal, but that is no reason to close our eyes to the consequences of the latest reform. the commission, in its replies to the court of auditors, stated that it would introduce elements in this proposal to strengthen controls. it is clear that, in general, it has not done so and that is why the report makes proposals to improve the effectiveness of controls by increasing the frequency of submission of information by the distilleries and by introducing similar obligations for the aid for olive oil. since 1996, this parliament has denounced the problems arising from the marketing of olive oil mixtures with other fats and has called for protection similar to that which exists for milk and butter, for example. unfortunately, these demands have never been met by the adoption of regulations. this time, this shortcoming in the proposal is all the more striking because the commission proposal is focused on the quality strategy. for this reason, the committee on agriculture of the european parliament proposes that the marketing of olive oil mixtures with other fats be banned, as is already the case in most producing countries. as regards the contents of the proposal which refer to quality, the names proposed by the commission have been modified somewhat. the report also proposes a number of measures on labelling. the most important of these is to prevent the name 'olive oil' from being used as an advertising claim to mislead consumers. in other words, if olive oil were not the only fat in any food product, the use of the name 'olive oil' would be limited to the quantitative description of the ingredients. the proposal also includes two other aspects of labelling: the indication of the origin of the oil, reflecting the place of origin of the olives, and, in the case of ordinary oil, the obligation to indicate that it is derived from virgin and refined olive oils. on all these questions i expect a more positive response from the commission than on other occasions. on 25 october, for example, the commission rejected some 30 of our amendments to the proposal on the common organisation of the market in fruit and vegetables, because it said it would include them in a subsequent report. the report has been published, but the content of our amendments has not been taken into account. the commission's proposal is based on the principle of subsidiarity, and it is not a matter of the member states being able to take the necessary measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. the commission plans to launch it within two years, by means of a call for tenders from what it calls 'organisations of economic operators'. since the planned measures would be partly financed by a percentage of the production aid, it is natural that producers would be represented for their management. for this purpose, there are already well-defined figures such as producer organisations, their unions and inter-branch organisations. under these conditions, a two-year period would not be necessary to implement the measures envisaged. in the same way, in order to provide legal certainty and to speed up and facilitate the preparation of programmes, it is proposed that a clear list of actions be drawn up which cannot be included in the programmes. finally, i should like to thank all the members of the committee on agriculture for their cooperation, which has enriched the report considerably with their amendments, allowing it to be adapted to the requirements of producers and consumers in all the member states concerned, as was shown at the meeting recently organized by the italian ministry of agriculture in verona last april.

- madam president, i should like to stress first of all the excellent cooperation between commissioner busquin and the european parliament, through the commission which i chair, in research matters. i would also like to take this opportunity to convey to you a twofold concern of the scientific community, which is practically unanimous, on two issues. the first is that the scientific community unreservedly supports the idea of a common research area. but on the other hand, it has serious doubts that the effect of synergy and added value at european level can be lost through a concentration of the different research projects; that is, that the smaller the core, the more these projects are concentrated, the more difficult it is for these synergies to occur at european level. the second question concerns the instruments. three instruments are envisaged: networks of excellence, integrated projects and the use of article 169. the scientific community is concerned about the fact that these three instruments are new and are the only ones being used. he fears that others will be lost, that they have been used and that the scientific community has already become accustomed to them. it is also concerned that a whole series of research teams which have been set up may suddenly be lost because of the exclusive application of these three instruments. i would therefore like the commissioner to respond to that double concern.

if you have any - of this resolution and of this report that antonio seguro and i have tabled is that it is a balanced document, which is what characterizes a parliament that has gone from being merely a promoter to being a co-decision-maker. and a co-decision parliament means a responsible parliament and therefore a parliament which has to do things in a balanced way. i would like to pay tribute at this point to all the members of the committee on constitutional affairs who have done a tremendous job of achieving consensus, starting with its chairman, giorgio napoletano, and also my good friend, antonio seguro, who has been not only a solid and intelligent but also a loyal member. we are therefore talking about a balanced document, in which we make clear what we do not like and what we would like to see changed in the future, because agreements, and the treaty of nice is an agreement, do not last forever - it is always only a matter of time - and they are subject to reform. the treaty of nice itself contains the germ of such a reform. i believe that this resolution looks to the future, to declaration no 23, which sets out the reform guidelines. and we have wanted to help the swedish presidency in this constructive spirit, with which we have had many contacts over the past few months, so that it is precisely at this european council in gothenburg that we can see what the future of the european union is in its institutional responses. we are committed, madam president, to the setting up of national committees in all the member states so that people can debate in truth, not in lies, so that we can know what the citizens want for the europe of the future. this parliament is also committed to a democratic method of preparing the intergovernmental conference. we believe that this democratic method is the model of the convention which drew up the charter of fundamental rights. and now that we are seeing so many proposals from all sides, all on the convention - which is already a positive fact - i would like to say that what the european parliament wants is a convention based on the model of the charter of fundamental rights which it drew up: on that one and not on another; because that one proved to be a successful model and brought together various legitimacies to achieve the desired result. on the basis of the convention's model, we want the outcome of the convention to be the role that governments will be considering at the intergovernmental conference. we are going to make constitutional proposals, and we should not be afraid of the term constitutional because when we talk about competences or institutional architecture, we are talking about constitutional issues. the result we are seeking is a european constitution, and i want to be very clear about this, a european constitution, in which it is very clear what the powers of each are and, above all, what the various institutions do in the institutional architecture. we want it to be ready before 2004, before the european parliament elections, so that the political groups in this house can go to those elections defending our options. madam president, i believe - and i repeat what i said at the beginning of my speech - that this is a path of hope. we are facing the europe of the euro, we are facing the europe of enlargement, and whether we choose a path of hope or a path which leads to a situation of blockade in the european union - which nobody wants - depends on us. i therefore want this resolution to be a constructive contribution to making this road of hope ever wider and, thanks to it, to making us ever more european.
, the council. president. - the debate is closed. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the future of europe is being shaped as the european union gathers for enlargement. it is a historic task to unite europe and to welcome the applicant countries back into the european family. in the western balkans, the union is doing everything it can to prevent new wars in europe, another srebrenica or another ethnic cleansing. so far we have been able to help prevent full-scale conflicts in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia and in southern serbia. the future of the eu lies in coordinating our foreign policy so that we can prevent armed conflict. the union is also developing cooperation with africa. an eu troika is currently visiting west africa. the eu's responsibility and its future also involves a global responsibility. cooperation is now being deepened in a number of areas in europe. europe must be more than a market. full employment, gender equality and social and economic balance are the objectives of the future eu. the union's working methods are now being developed with the act on public access to documents and with the reform work within the institutions. the future of the eu lies in an open and democratic union. at the same time, we know that much remains to be done in the field of fair and free trade, the fight for human rights and the work on environmental issues. the debate on the future is about how to succeed with these questions of the future and how to create institutions that will make us successful. the treaty of nice prepared the union for the accession of new members and at the same time made clear our commitment to further deepening. we succeeded in moving from unanimity to majority voting on some 35 other provisions. however, i myself, and many others with me, would have liked to have gone further in the social field and the third pillar. we also succeeded in extending the codecision procedure to new areas where the european parliament, together with national governments, can ensure the democratic anchoring of the decisionmaking process. these were important decisions and we succeeded in going beyond the three issues that were raised in amsterdam. at the same time, most people agree - and i am sure we will have many examples here today - that the next igc needs to go much further than nice and that we therefore need this broad debate on the future of europe. a major objective must be to involve citizens more closely in the european project. the swedish presidency, which, together with the forthcoming belgian presidency, was given the task of launching the debate, has taken it very seriously. the common website, which is managed by the commission, was launched at the beginning of march. it already contains contributions from many heads of state and government and a wealth of comments from european citizens. the website will be extended to cover all 11 eu languages and i hope it will live on in the debate that will continue up to and in parallel with the igc. the institutions are also planning a series of joint seminars and conferences. in addition, all the national initiatives have been launched, both in the member states and in the candidate countries. we are now addressing the citizens of europe directly for the first time in the run-up to an intergovernmental conference. their expectations and hopes will certainly go beyond the four institutional issues identified in nice. i think that's good. i believe that the debate on the future is primarily about politics and secondarily about institutions. before we try to define our tools, we need to know what the tools are to be used for. at the same time, we must of course also make the fundamental reasoning about the nature and essence of the union. that is why, as president-in-office of the council, i welcome the longer-term visions that we are now beginning to see in the debate. it can be tempting to simplify the debate by looking too much at the concepts themselves and too little at what the concepts actually stand for. we see, for example, that many people want to draw a clear line between the radical 'federalists' and those with more modest ambitions on institutional matters. however, each country has its own history and frame of reference, which also determine how the concepts are viewed there. the very concept of 'federalism' is interpreted positively and as decentralisation in some countries, while it can be a red-eye and seen as centralisation in other countries. the same applies to the debate on a 'constitution'. the existing treaties already constitute, as has been said, a kind of constitution. they contain provisions on the tasks to be carried out, the allocation of responsibilities between the various institutions and the rules of procedure. what is interesting is what the basic rules contain, not what we choose to call them. similarly, a contrast is often drawn between those who believe that democratic legitimacy is based on popular elections in their own country and those who believe that it must be sought in a new political model for european cooperation. i believe that we must try to find ways of strengthening the link between european policy and national policy. democracy is not a zero-sum game. i am convinced that we can do a great deal to strengthen european democracy without rebuilding the union from the ground up. when the interaction between the european and national levels develops, democracy wins and the influence of citizens is strengthened. we must get away from the artificial division between european and national. both national and european parliamentarians have a direct popular mandate. what is the reason why national parliamentarians do not appear more regularly in the european parliament and european parliamentarians do not appear more regularly in national parliaments? the requirements of popular support and the extensive agenda will place particular demands on the preparations for the next igc, and many have suggested that a more open approach than in the past must be found. some feel that a small group of so-called wise men would make suggestions. such a group can work quickly, but at the same time it would mean that not all countries could be represented. many, not least in this house, have proposed the use of an open forum, similar to the convention which drew up the charter of fundamental rights last year. however, several countries have stressed that an open forum, a convention, must not restrict or prejudge the debate with the citizens. after the completion of the work of an open forum, the result must be open to debate, comment and consolidation. if i may speak for a moment as the swedish president and swedish foreign minister and not just as president of the council, i would like to say that i would very much like to see an open forum set up at the beginning of 2002. the purpose of such a forum would be to work for about a year, to make recommendations on the issues to be included on the agenda of the igc and to make proposals for the answers and views to those issues. at the same time, it is important that the broad debate continues and that we also take account of what is happening in the national debates. one way of ensuring this is to summarise national debates and to report to the european council every six months. it is also certain that technical investigation will be necessary, since the issues raised in nice are quite complex. in conclusion, i believe that, in the light of the discussions i have had with the member states and the candidate countries, it will be difficult to find a single form of preparation which is appropriate for all issues. we need a combination. i think we need a convention, we need technical preparations and we need to report on the national debates. the swedish presidency will continue discussions with the european parliament, alongside the council's deliberations. the resolution you are adopting today - i really want to thank méndez de vigo and seguro - will be a very important contribution to that debate. this will of course also be an important basis for the presidency when we present a report in gothenburg. these issues will be given prominent place and will hopefully provide new impetus for the further discussion. i look forward to hearing your views! (applause) i would like to thank you.

- mr president, the treaty of nice represents both a failure and an opportunity. failure, because it does not contain the reforms needed to ensure that the union can adequately meet all the challenges of the present and the future. it does not include, for example, codecision as a rule or the charter of fundamental rights. but nice is also an opportunity, because the convening of the next igc opens the door to a new cycle in european construction, the objectives of which are to respond to citizens' demands, to end the democratic deficit, to develop the european social model, to intervene with ideas of their own in globalisation to regulate it and to complete enlargement without turning the eu into a mere free trade area. today, more than ever, we must make a commitment to a bigger and better europe, to a greater political europe with more european policies, to an enlarged federal political union with more democracy and greater efficiency. the future does not lie in weakening the existing system by renationalizing policies such as cohesion, but on the contrary in adding to the euro an economic government of the union, building a social europe and providing a sufficient and progressive budget that is up to the task. the key to this new cycle must be the adoption of a european constitution through a radically democratic process that goes far beyond nice and whose protagonist is a convention, made up of the council, the commission, the european parliament - whose final composition would have to be fixed in this framework - and national parliaments, which will draw up a constitutional proposal that must be formally adopted by an igc before the european elections. tomorrow, when we vote by a majority on the excellent report by mr méndez de vigo and mr seguro - whom i congratulate on their work - parliament will call on the governments, as we hope the national legislatures will do, to take up this challenge in which - we hope - now, yes, these governments understand the message: no more constitution and convention - no more treaties and no more intergovernmental drift - and do not again respond timidly to the shameless challenges we have ahead of us.

- mr president, for some unknown reason i have not been able to speak at the turn of the opinion-makers from the various committees, but i will state the opinion of the committee on agriculture. the committee on agriculture and rural development considers that the non-introduction of codecision is one of the main issues pending in nice. this is a way of maintaining discriminatory treatment for agriculture in relation to related areas such as public health, consumer protection or the internal market. we believe that the nice summit has left in public opinion the image of states overly concerned with the distribution of internal power within the institutions and has cast serious doubts on the council's ability and political will to reach the necessary agreements needed for agricultural policy. these reforms must respond to the growing demands of european citizenship, to the challenges posed by enlargement and to our commitments in the world trade organisation. we also believe that after nice the complex decision-making process will become even more complicated, if necessary, and this may paralyse future cap reforms. we do not want this situation to jeopardize the safeguarding of the european model of agriculture which - we must not forget - is a fundamental element of europe's social model. we therefore ask that the next intergovernmental conference take account of the adaptation of the agricultural chapters of the treaties to introduce codecision. we sincerely believe that the new agricultural policy, based on the principles of multifunctionality and sustainability, requires and requires codecision in order to achieve the greater democratic legitimacy, greater transparency and also - of course - greater coherence in the agricultural policy that european society is demanding.
- mr president, how do we preserve our resources, win in environmental health and social welfare in a balanced way, without hurting any of the three pillars of sustainable development? the gothenburg summit will seek to answer these questions and will demonstrate the political maturity and capacity of our governments to meet the challenge of a new order of peace and prosperity for the 21st century. the first step is to achieve a decoupling between economic growth and the intensity in the use of resources, and in the production of undesirable effects such as pollution. in this context, i think that the reports by mrs hulthén and mr blokland should be welcomed. making europe's economy more competitive and dynamic, based on knowledge rather than resource-intensive use, will require better and greater use of market instruments to achieve the highest levels of efficiency for our processes and products, but it will also require other factors to be taken into account simultaneously. if we want to eliminate forever the specter of loss of competitiveness or the threat of industrial conflict in europe, we need more than ever, and urgently, to make the way uniformly and consistently across all member states. moreover, we need to do so from a global perspective, with international agreements that allow us to resolve the legal and practical difficulties that many of our legislative acts face. we also need to set realistic timetables, which allow businesses and society at large to adapt to new market conditions and introduce the necessary reforms, thereby reducing the chances of undesirable effects if they are approached with too narrow a margin of manoeuvre. finally, i believe that, in order to bring the process of change under way to a successful conclusion, it is essential to have a broad social consensus which includes commitments to the social partners and the - not progressive but firm - replacement of social values belonging to the old order - based on the possession and accumulation of goods - by other values which are typical of a more ethical and civically advanced society, based on the enjoyment of the more immaterial aspects of life.
, draftsman of the opinion of the committee on petitions. - mr president, we share with the rapporteur and the commission the priority objectives of this programme, which is very important and which will shape the european union's environmental policy over the next ten years. these priority objectives are now in the spotlight every day, and they are the subject of daily press coverage: climate change, the promotion and preservation of biodiversity, sustainable management of resources and the protection of health and the environment. these are the priority objectives and it is therefore essential to take more drastic measures than have been taken so far. first, the legislation must be enforced. as the rapporteur said, environmental policies must be integrated into other policies: agriculture, transport, energy. it hasn't been done properly yet. and more sustainable production and consumption models. i believe that the pattern of production and consumption must be changed, otherwise we shall not achieve the objectives set by the commission and the rapporteur. the interest of this programme is obvious. the proof is that we have been voting for hours on more than 350 amendments and that even today, despite the fact that many of the amendments tabled by the various rapporteurs have been collected, almost 300 amendments are to be submitted to the plenary for approval. i think that from the point of view of the committee on petitions - and i am referring now to the practical experience in this committee - the fundamental issues are two, which the rapporteur has mentioned. the first is the application of community law. the member states do not apply it and the evidence of this is that the european commission has had to take several member states to court for various reasons (e.g. nitrate pollution). spain is specifically being sued at the moment for the existence of more than seven illegal landfills. the first fundamental issue, therefore, is compliance with environmental legislation. the second is to encourage citizen participation. we in the committee on petitions find that of the 1100 to 1200 petitions that are registered in this committee every year, 40% concern the protection of the natural environment. this shows that not only environmental groups, but also platforms of ordinary citizens have a huge interest in preserving the environment in which they live and are the ones who denounce. they are concerned with studying community law, they lodge complaints here and they have the holy patience to wait for the outcome of processes which are sometimes too long. that is another problem: when a complaint or a request is made, there are delays in the response of the governments and the processes are so long that sometimes the damage is already done, it is irreversible and, at other times, the citizens who denounce these irregularities lose patience. the committee on petitions considers that this is the key issue: citizen participation, simplification of procedures and, above all, compliance with community law. we had a debate in the committee on the environment a few months ago on the fact that while there is excellent environmental legislation in the european union, it is not being complied with. we must find a way to fulfill it. we are proposing here some amendments to penalize those who do not use the structural funds and the cohesion fund for projects which preserve the environment. unfortunately, this is the only thing that governments understand. other mechanisms must also be found to speed up the processes so that citizens do not lose their patience. i think, mr president, that this is an extraordinary programme. i hope that tomorrow the majority of the amendments tabled by the rapporteur and by some of the groups will be adopted and i believe that what we have to achieve is that the programme will be put into practice properly over the next ten years.

- the next item is the report (a5-0173/2001) by mrs hautala, on behalf of the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending council directive 76/207/eec on the implementation of the principle of equal treatment for men and women as regards access to employment, vocational training and promotion, and working conditions (com (2000) 334 - c5-0369/2000 - 2000/0142 (cod))
- mr president, commissioner, the 11th annual report on the structural funds, which for the first time examines community measures to promote equality between men and women, points out that although the active participation of women in the labour market has been steadily increasing over the last three decades, significant differences between the sexes still remain. in almost all member states, unemployment rates are higher for women than for men. the difference in employment rates between the sexes in the member states is close to 20% on average. the employment of women decreases with the number of children. women do most of the unpaid work in the household, including caring for children and other dependants. even in countries with high employment rates, women are overrepresented in parttime jobs, often unintentionally. the gender pay gap remains considerable, at 28% on average at community level. in short, in this europe, the champion of human rights, women do not enjoy the same rights as men in practice; their representation in public institutions and decision-making positions in private bodies remains low; and they continue to be the first victims of ill-treatment within the couple and sexual violence. i am convinced that women cannot be truly free, equal to men, unless they have the same opportunities to find a job, receive equal pay and achieve real economic independence. and the day i achieve these goals, the rest of the inequalities will also be gone. it is true that the lisbon european council has already set a target of increasing the female employment rate from the current average of 51% in the community to over 60% by 2010. but when i think that, for example, in spain the rate of women in employment is now barely 35%, it seems to me that not in 10 years but even in 20 years we will be able to speak of real equality between the sexes, especially if there are still significant unemployment rates in general. it is perhaps time we took more seriously, for example, the proposals of orio giarini and patrick liedtke in their report to the club of rome entitled 'the employment dilemma: the future of work' - where they advocate the division of the working day - or also the proposals of peter hall which orient taxation towards business consumption and free the labour cost factor from burdens and levies. the challenge of equality is above all the challenge of employment. i therefore welcome the initiative to amend the 25 year old directive 76/207/eec on the implementation of the principle of equal treatment for men and women. i also congratulate mrs heidi anneli hautala, president of the green group, on her excellent report.
- mr president, commissioner, we have here today the proposal to amend the directive on the application of the principle of equal treatment for men and women as regards access to employment, vocational training and promotion and working conditions. the amendments are being tabled in the light of the treaty of amsterdam and the judgments of the court of justice in recent years. the main aim is to adapt the directive to social reality and to take account of women's demands in order to solve the problems of different treatment in the workplace. sexual harassment in the workplace is considered for the first time as discrimination on grounds of sex. we call for preventive measures and measures to help women whose working lives and careers are affected by sexual harassment. the support given to women in pregnancy and maternity by the amendments introduced is noteworthy, as it guarantees their return to work and the benefit of any improvements which may have occurred in the workplace during their absence. positive action measures to balance representation in the different sectors of employment will also be an effective aid. women, especially younger women, have today a high level of vocational qualification, which is not matched by the development of their working life, generally occupying low-skilled jobs which do not allow them to fully meet their professional expectations. the directive will help to solve these problems, but it is the member states who must finally ensure that women can work fully without having to face problems in their personal and family life. those of us who believe that the family should be supported know that it is essential to start by supporting women in order to facilitate the reconciliation of family and professional life as a principle of community legislation. i have to say that it has been really difficult to work on this proposal, but we have made an effort to highlight the points of agreement and the objectives pursued by the directive over the logical differences between different political groups.
- mr president, commissioner, we are today extending the frontiers of equal treatment to all aspects of women's working life, not just employment but also the whole training and vocational training system and working conditions. since equality between men and women is an objective and also a mission of the european union, it is necessary to adapt, update and also imagine new strategies, new legislative texts that will enable us to cover this task effectively. the article on sexual harassment is noteworthy, and i will not dwell on this point because it has already been highlighted sufficiently. it is also important - in my view - to define direct and indirect discrimination and to establish positive action as a tool for balancing inequalities, a transitional tool until equality is achieved. the european community has always sought to eliminate inequality of treatment, but unfortunately today there are still glaring inequalities in this respect, which i shall not go into too much. some international organization has recognized that, at the rate things are going, we could achieve equality in about four or five centuries, and i don't think any of us here are prepared to wait that long. we must intervene with positive measures like this to change an order of things which is profoundly unjust and contrary to the development of our societies. the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities has done rigorous and thorough work which substantially improves the commission's proposal. i congratulate all of us on this, and especially mrs hautala.
- mr president, the report by mr antónio josé seguro and mr iñigo méndez de vigo is ambivalent. we recognize that, after the amendments introduced, it contains a clear commitment to the convening of a convention for the proposed reform of the treaties and that the report accepts the launching of a constitutional procedure. but we must also say that the report is not as critical as it should be of the outcome of the intergovernmental conference in nice. with this report parliament is sadly moving away from the feeling of failure which prevails in a european society which has realised the inability of the heads of state and government to agree on the way forward in building the political europe now more than ever required by enlargement to include the eastern and mediterranean states. once again the majority of members of this parliament have ignored their full status as representatives of the european citizens, subordinated their positions to those of their national governments and, paradoxically, have let themselves be overtaken in the last instance by those responsible for national policies. so now that president rau, chancellor schroeder and prime minister jospin have spoken, i have the conviction and the hurt feeling that if the majority of members had known the positions of these relevant state leaders beforehand, the report that has just been adopted would be very different. the european parliament is the central institution of european political union, and we consider it to be a shame. i hope that in the future constitutional process this parliament will maintain a position of self-respect, more responsible, especially with regard to the interests and aspirations of our citizens. i hope that we will learn this lesson and be aware of our role in political europe.
- mr president, i believe that the treaty of nice will go down in history as a clear example of a lost opportunity, due to the particularism of the irreducible defenders of the power of the states. states are political structures which have their origin in the increased capacity for production and mobility, which was brought about by the discovery of the steam engine, the second great technological revolution of mankind, according to the american thinker alvin tofler; which left small and useless the political framework of the old kingdoms, counties, duchies and lordships that, until then, had structured societies. but ever since marshall mcluhan spoke of the world as a global village and tofler himself referred to the third human revolution as information technology, the globalisation of political relations, trade, the economy, defence, leisure and so many other things has made states equally small and insufficient and no longer fit to meet the current needs of citizens. the future path for the european union is therefore not decided by the measures adopted in nice: what is needed is less powers from the member states and more from the european institutions. we need a constitution, a parliament, a european government and a president elected by the people.

the rapporteur. - mr president, we are facing one of the few but serious problems caused by the abolition of our internal frontiers. from the very beginning of the single market, it was established that the free movement of goods had to be compatible with the protection of the artistic and cultural heritage of each member state. it was and still is the responsibility of each state to define its national heritage and protect it. but from 1 january 1993 measures were necessary, such as the approval of the requirements for sale or the uniformity of the control procedure for export outside the community. the regulation and directive we are discussing today were adopted in 1992 and 1993 to this end. the philosophy of the regulation can be summed up as follows: each state is obliged to control the export of not only its own heritage but also that of another of the 14 remaining states, which is located on its territory. nine years later, the text and approach adopted in 1992 are still valid, with the exception of some minor changes. and it must be said that the problem of illicit trafficking in cultural property and the impunity in which it takes place is more serious than ever. the forecasts are even more pessimistic if the integration of the rich heritage of the candidate countries into the single market, when the time comes, is to be met by the same community legislation that now prevails and which has proved insufficient. in 1993, the commission undertook to report every three years on the progress and effectiveness of the two standards applied and to propose any necessary corrections. it tried to do so in 1996, but the information it requested from the states was not replied to by most of them. in some cases, the delay in transposing the regulation into national law was scandalous; in four of these cases, the regulation did not come into force until 1998. finally, in 1998, the commission obtained some data, opinions and experience and with them has prepared the report on which we are speaking today. this communication is purely informative, i.e. it does not propose any new measures or changes to existing ones. it is a voluntary report which lacks sufficient data to allow measurements to be made objective and which also lacks, in my view, its own criteria to propose any improvement to the current procedure. some conclusions can be drawn, however. the less positive aspects are that the mere existence of the two rules has been sufficient to raise the awareness of the administrations and of public opinion and to force extrajudicial solutions. other, more negative, arguments can be summed up in one: the general practice continues to be that the state which grants the authorization to export cultural goods does not ask the state of origin whether the goods are lawfully or unlawfully imported. the commission has also been asked to draw up a report on the situation in the member states, which is to be submitted to the council in the near future. i identify one of the core problems here: on the one hand, these units of the administration have other frontier priorities related to organized crime. and on the other hand, as you know, this is cooperation in the third pillar, which is so difficult to achieve. the situation is therefore serious on two fronts, the increase in the intra-community illegal trade in historical and cultural goods and the increase in their exit through our external borders. the emergence of organized networks in the business, the unlimited proliferation of antique dealers without sufficient professionalism or control and the almost usual impunity of those responsible, either because of the early prescription of the crime - only one year - or because the simple allegation of the good faith of the buyer is the cause of the oversight are some of the reasons for this serious situation. in our report we therefore consider that there is an urgent need for better regulation and a qualitative change in community treatment. we believe that this is a cultural issue which the council must address through the cultural authorities of each member state; these are crimes or failures which must be detected by community units specialising in artistic and historical heritage; the commissioner for culture, better than any of her colleagues, must make a diagnosis and propose a solution to the situation. all this without prejudice to the integration of trade, police and customs officials into the various teams, but, i repeat, from a predominantly cultural point of view. the report also identifies some difficulties, such as the existence of an unknown heritage held by institutions such as the church. we propose some specific measures which are considered to be very urgent - such as the use of the internet to make images and forms of stolen objects publicly available - or we ask the commission, under the direction of the commissioner for culture, to draw up a green paper describing the current situation, assessing the effects of the regulation and the directive, carrying out a comparative study of the definition of heritage in each member state and, above all, proposing concrete measures to improve the situation. the commissioner for culture, whom i have admired for many years, has for some time been as enthusiastic and determined about future work as she is cautious and indecisive about the present. he has the capacity and equipment to make sure that's not the case. with this report parliament is anxiously warning against the present situation which, although it is the consequence of the abolition of internal frontiers, which is so beneficial in all other respects, is not being sufficiently addressed by the community's leaders.

- commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate mr whitehead on his good work and his contributions to the rules of procedure. i would like to refer to two of the controversial issues in the regulation: the procedure for choosing the seat and the criteria. the proposal for a regulation does not designate a seat or nominate candidates; article 63 sets out the criteria which any nomination should meet and also lays down the procedure for the election. i think the rapporteur's proposal that the decision on the seat of the authority should be taken by the council after consulting the commission and the european parliament is correct. however, i do not think it is appropriate to add to the criteria of independence and integrity, scientific judgement, adequate infrastructure and easy access to communications the criterion that the number of cases pending before the court of justice in the member state is an indispensable condition for the choice of the seat. i would like to know, commissioner, what you think of this new criterion, which i consider discriminatory. the french, italian and barcelona applications would be dismissed in advance. i think that this new criterion is nonsensical and does not fit in with the objective of the future food authority, which is above all consumer and health protection.
- commissioner, ozone concentrations in the atmosphere are a serious problem, not only for the environment but also for public health, as they have an impact on the health of citizens, with a particular impact on the population at risk such as children and the elderly, causing allergies and cardio-respiratory difficulties, among other manifestations. ozone concentrations are affected very unevenly in the member states. and because of their transfrontier nature, they often affect places far from the source of production. to date, member states have not sufficiently studied and dealt with this phenomenon, nor have they systematically and coordinatedly assessed it. this has resulted in a lack of reliable and comparable data and in insufficient short- and long-term action plans. i therefore consider the adoption of this directive to be very necessary and i very much appreciate the work of mr davies, particularly his approach to the problem, emphasising the study and monitoring aspects and his willingness to incorporate the suggestions of other groups, which has made it possible to put to the vote in the plenary a proposal with important compromise amendments, which enrich the commission's proposal and maintain the sense of reality and the viability of the proposed measures. the first important result of this directive is that it will finally encourage the member states to pay more attention to the problem of tropospheric ozone, by strengthening the study and control of it; secondly, it establishes the obligation to draw up short- and long-term action plans and to improve early warning systems and information to the public. in this connection, i think it is very important that these plans should, in each case, strengthen the study of the local conditions in which concentrations occur, so that they can be combated more effectively. i also think that it is necessary to set target dates as an element to stimulate progress in controlling the problem. however, we cannot ignore the current difficulties in ensuring full control of tropospheric ozone concentrations and therefore strict compliance at all times with the values and deadlines set. our group has therefore insisted on formulae which, while tightening the obligations of the member states, set realistic objectives and deadlines, allow for some flexibility in cases where it has been physically impossible to achieve the objectives and take into account, in the comparative reports, the meteorological and local circumstances of the points where the target values have been exceeded. we have naturally been opposed to amendments which do not correspond to the scientific possibilities of controlling the problem.

the rapporteur. - mr president, despite the avatars, or perhaps precisely because of them, we need the community institutions to reaffirm our political commitment to deepening our integration. and the european parliament has repeatedly stressed the need for the european union to assume a strong role on the international scene and to be able to speak in that context in a coherent way. the maastricht reform designed the cfsp for this purpose and several proposals are now being put forward with a view to 2004. however, if the european union is to consolidate its external role, it is first necessary to organise and strengthen the external policy instruments already at the disposal of the union and, in particular, its foreign service. it must be admitted that the foreign service, which today has such important responsibilities, suffers from many shortcomings which have not been overcome, despite the reforms which the european commission itself has promoted, and that is why this parliament adopted last september the own-initiative report on 'common european diplomacy', with the aim of providing greater efficiency in the exercise of the union's foreign policy. we therefore proposed decisive progress in three areas: firstly, improving the training of community officials to be responsible for the exercise of external activity by creating, ultimately, a community diplomatic school and linking national diplomatic bodies with a system of gateways to be set up for this purpose; secondly, we proposed clarifying and developing the legal status of delegations, their role and their relationship with the institutions; and, finally, we proposed improving coordination between the delegations and external services of the member states, for which we suggested, among other things, promoting the grouping of the missions of the member states which so wished with the commission delegation, wherever and whenever possible. commissioner patten then told this house that the commission would consider these recommendations very carefully and would prepare a communication on its external services during the first half of 2001, which we are looking forward to with great interest. but, pending more ambitious initiatives, parliament must now take a position on the latest commission communication on the development of the external service, which of course has a much more limited objective, since it focuses mainly on the network of delegations and their staff. it is, however, a welcome communication, as it opens up a debate on this important issue. in this communication the commission confirms its willingness to move forward with decentralisation and the decentralisation of external aid. this can only be considered positive, even if it requires more human resources and therefore more costs, which i believe we must help to bear. we would point out, however, that not all the difficulties in the functioning of the delegations and in the management of external aid stem from a lack of resources. the commission should also adopt complementary measures, such as recruitment policies, training plans or revision of procedures. as regards the network of delegations, the commission's proposal to move forward with regionalisation seems appropriate, but it is nevertheless necessary to consider the opening of new delegations in some countries in south-east asia, the gulf area and latin america, as well as in switzerland. in this context, it is necessary to express the concern aroused by the recent rumour that the commission is considering the possibility of closing its delegation in costa rica. the rapporteur therefore welcomes this communication from the commission, which i think is on the right track, but which clearly does not address the issue in its entirety. we hope that in the coming weeks the commission will adopt a new, more ambitious communication which takes account of the views of this parliament and will finally allow the external service to be rationalised, organised and improved so that it can be an effective instrument of a sound european union foreign policy.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's forests are protected against fire. the latter regulation, which established a framework for the observation, assessment and monitoring of damage to european forests, established a network of observation points, conducting a regular damage inventory and publishing an annual report, as well as a complementary network for the monitoring and control of pilot demonstration projects. the general trend observed is the increasing deterioration of leafy species such as beech and oak, an intense defoliation due to the severity of air pollution, mainly in central europe, and which also causes soil acidification. atmospheric deposits cause serious concentrations of nitrates in the soil and increase the risk of drinking water pollution, thus threatening the filter function of water resources in forest soils. the budget for this regulation in the commission's proposal is reduced from eur 40 million for the first five-year period to eur 34 million for the second five-year period, from 1997 to 2001. the committee on the environment again proposes to increase the budgetary allocation to eur 44 million, in line with the increase in the area under trees and the cost of living. the usefulness of the programme and its monitoring networks is beyond doubt, and its strengthening would exponentially increase the service that forests provide to european society as a whole. as regards regulation (eec) no 2158 on the protection of forests against fire, a framework for action was established to reduce the number of fires and the area affected by them, allowing for the cofinancing of actions mainly of a preventive nature, including the creation of protective infrastructure - fire barriers, forest tracks, water points, etc. - as well as the improvement of systems for monitoring and identifying the causes of fires. article 10 of the regulation provides for an allocation of eur 70 million for the period 1992-95, whereas the proposal put on the table for 1997-2001 estimates that eur 50 million is sufficient. that's 10 million a year. in addition to being contrary to the council's recommendations to the commission in points 5 and 6 of the forestry strategy for the european union, which call for the possibility of improving community measures to protect forests, this reduction is contrary to common sense, since since 1995, the date of the last enlargement, the area covered by forests has gone from 21% to 36% of the total community territory, and the equivalence between more forest to protect and less money to protect it escapes me. the amendments therefore propose an increase in the budget to 77 million euro, which i believe is justified and which we must not renounce in any way, since the protection of the landscape, nature, biodiversity, traditional cultures and multifunctional activities and, in short, what we all see when we close our eyes and think of the forest is at stake. in europe there are 60 million hectares declared at risk of fire. the commission's proposal is eur 0.16 per hectare. the parliament's request is for 0.23 euros per hectare. the difference is 0.07 euros per hectare. gentlemen, we are almost talking about parrot chocolate in terms of protecting our forests, and this is denied us. there is a special mention in the report, which i do not want to omit, of the mediterranean mountain, which is much more affected by fires because of its location in hot areas with long periods of drought, and also very affected by desertification. in this area, particular attention must be paid to properly weighing the different tasks of action in the forest environment: prevention, improvement, conservation and restoration of burned areas and afforestation. i therefore ask the commission to make a statement of acceptance of these arguments in the forthcoming proposals so that the members of this parliament can accept this report at this second reading.

- madam president, the truth is, and we have just had proof of this, that it is often said from conservative political positions that we socialists are opposed to the process of liberalization. nothing could be further from the truth. we are fully committed to a process which presents a number of progressive perspectives. one of them is that when a sector is liberalised to the extent that the market is shared among a larger number of firms, this is putting a stop to the concentration of economic power and this is a progressive objective which is fully accepted by these ranks. we cannot agree with monopolies that offer goods and services of lower quality and at a higher price than if they were offered under competitive conditions. but if public monopolies are unsatisfactory, private ones are totally unacceptable and unbearable. we therefore believe that services should be provided under a competitive system, but that system should be corrected to ensure that only those who, because of their income or place of residence, are profitable to the providers of such services have access to services, leaving out those who cannot afford the price of them, however basic the services may be, or those who live in areas that are not profitable for businesses. the need therefore arises to impose universal service obligations, but naturally the discussion about the size and conditions of universal service is a discussion of strong ideological content. the right wing, always in the interests of business, insists that these universal service obligations be kept to a minimum. progressive positions must insist that the greatest number of services reach all citizens at affordable prices. and these applications are reflected in this report. the rapporteur, mr harbour, has done a magnificent job, but i cannot forget that he is a member of a political group whose positions seem to be more oriented towards defending the interests of business than the - mr president, commissioner, i will begin by saying that our group very warmly supports all the arguments and all the amendments that the rapporteur, mr hughes, has made for this second reading. i shall take my time in stressing the problem of the selfemployed, because i believe that the good intentions of the commission and the council on the health and safety of mobile workers can have a bad effect if the inclusion of selfemployed people in the directive continues to be hampered. because it is a fact, ladies and gentlemen, and not an opinion, that the three basic principles used to justify the need for the directive (the safety and health of workers, road safety and fair competition) become mere rhetoric if we exclude the selfemployed. it could well be said that the safety and health of most workers in countries like mine, who are selfemployed, is of no concern to us in the least if we exclude them from this directive. the council has the opportunity to avoid being held responsible for situations such as those in my country, where more than 400 drivers lose their lives every year, without distinguishing between selfemployed and salaried workers. this figure is increasing by 20% each year. why is it that only the risk of a minority of these drivers is taken into account? the selfemployed are not people, as mrs smet used to say. of course they are. why forget most of them? are not these drivers and the citizens who drive on the roads exposed to the same risks? let's get serious about this. if we really want road safety, safety and health for workers, it does not matter whether they are employed or selfemployed. independents are not a different breed. they have even more work to do than the salaried workers. they have to take care of their trucks, their business, they have to do loading and unloading, adding these tasks to their peak hours, while the salaried workers deduct all of that from their peak hours. if this argument were not enough, ladies and gentlemen, and if you want to use the argument of free competition, of fair competition, think that salaried drivers will drive fewer hours, the lorries they drive will make shorter daily journeys and will arrive later at their destinations. how will these companies in the sector be able to compete with those who will have much tougher conditions and much less economic burdens? our conclusion is therefore that excluding selfemployed people will have negative consequences for these workers, but also for the sector. we therefore call on the council to complete the efforts already made and to include the selfemployed if it really wants to ensure - and this is not rhetoric - the safety and health of all drivers, to ensure road safety, to promote fair competition at community level and not to break up the sector. if you want to preserve jobs and businesses, if you want, in short, the directive we deserve in the 21st century.
- mr president, commissioner, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur for the good work and the efforts made to arrive at a balanced, flexible recommendation for the second reading which can lead to the success of a conciliation which will probably not be easy. nor is it easy to achieve the general objective of the organisation of working time for persons who carry out mobile road transport activities as a profession, because the health and safety of the worker driver, as well as road safety and therefore collective safety, must be taken into account. and because another objective must be to avoid unfair competition. i think the directive should include the selfemployed. 'every worker has the right to work in conditions which respect his or her health, safety and dignity', says article 31 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. and the selfemployed is a worker, by definition, by concept and by content. and "every worker has the right to limitation of maximum working hours and to daily and weekly rest periods and to a period of paid annual leave", says the second paragraph of the same article. i believe that the text, by providing for inclusion in the terms in which it does so, is intended to achieve both the elimination of unfair competition and the granting of a reasonable period of time for the selfemployed to adapt to the new situation and to ensure their protection. at the same time, the prudence of the deadline will not encourage companies to dismantle and resort to the figures of the false selfemployed. in short, i believe that the recommendation should guide us and help to create a fairer and more transparent society, one in which unfair competition is difficult to tolerate and in which due attention is paid to the health, safety and dignity of the selfemployed and those employed by others.

the rapporteur. - mr president, the two reports i am presenting concern seven regulations whose reform we are discussing and which concern the outermost regions of the european union, namely: guadeloupe, martinique, réunion and french guiana; the azores and madeira in portugal; and the canary islands in spain. the reasons for remoteness, internal dispersion and climatological conditions have been important obstacles to their development. the distance and transport costs for imports and exports, as well as the small size of these territories, have prevented significant investments from being attracted and made profitable. in its declaration of its duty of community solidarity to respond to the needs of these outermost regions, the european community adopted between 1989 and 1991 a number of other action programmes, for reasons of remoteness and insularity, the so-called posei. the aim was to promote sustainable development and to strengthen the productive and job-creating sectors. this was done on the basis of the use of the structural funds and of a particularly favourable modulation of common policies, and in particular the cap. special aid was introduced for certain local products and the supply of raw materials was improved by means of specific supply schemes included in the respective posei. the community's support measures have been combined with very considerable efforts by the states directly concerned, france, portugal and spain, and by regional and local administrations. the commission has therefore taken note of the progress made, but there are still some shortcomings. in any case, in order to make further progress in the integration of these regions into the european area and to deal with the phenomena which have recently emerged with the increasing process of globalisation, it is necessary to provide a firmer legal basis and to strengthen the regulations with which it has operated so far. we have been working on this for months, and we also know that the treaties, starting with amsterdam, introduced in article 299 the recognition of the specific nature of the outermost regions and the commitment to support them in overcoming their difficulties. the reform proposal that was presented to us was going in the right direction, but it fell short of its proposals. for example, it did not propose the necessary change in the legal basis to refer to the new text of the treaties, to which i have just referred, but it was certainly a good starting point for the work of our committee on agriculture and rural development, which had the best cooperation of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism and the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, the latter precisely to encourage the change in the legal basis. we also listened to the authorities and social sectors in the areas we are dealing with here and thus came to a number of amendments which were discussed and adopted in committee. in addition to the amendment on updating the legal basis, there are amendments which respond to common demands from the different regions and others which are specific to each of them. the common ones include the possibility of these regions being able to export, with the right to a refund, products manufactured with raw materials introduced on the islands under the res, the need to increase support for the livestock sector and the desirability of strengthening agri-food smes. the amendments concerning sensitive products specific to each region concern tomatoes in the canary islands, livestock, dairy products and the sugar industry in the azores and the wicker industry in madeira, and support for rice in some of the french territories. with these amendments we are expressing our desire to overcome once and for all the problems of our outermost regions. it is not a question of subsidizing the economic and social backwardness of these territories, but of acting decisively to overcome these backwardness in an irreversible way and thus to offer those living there living conditions and prospects for the future on a par with those of other citizens of the european union. the costs of the improvements we propose are, moreover, certainly insignificant within the budgetary dimensions of the union. i would like to end by thanking the dedicated and professional staff of our committee on agriculture and also express my gratitude to the commission and the council for their interest and understanding. if, as i hope, the house approves what the committee on agriculture submits to its judgment, it will be the council of the union that will have the responsibility not to disappoint our expectations, which are, in short, those of the people of the canary islands, madeira, the azores, martinique, guadeloupe, réunion and guyana. it is in actions like this that the confidence of citizens in the action of the european union and, in short, the credibility of our project is at stake.
the rapporteur. - mr president, as i think you all know, the negotiations to renew the fisheries agreement with morocco have come to an end without such a renewal having taken place. they will also know that negotiations have been going on for an extraordinarily long period - 15 months - which has put the community fleet in a truly unprecedented situation, with activity being suspended for a period not provided for in community legislation. article 16 (1) (b) of the fifg regulation allows for the financing of the temporary cessation of fishing activities in the event of non-renewal of a fishing agreement for a period of six months, renewable for a further six months, following the submission of a conversion plan. that deadline and its extension expired on 31 december last, while we were still in the middle of negotiations with morocco. the commission then felt that shipowners and crew could not be left unprotected while these negotiations were going on, and so it put forward the proposal for a regulation which is now before the house for a vote in order to change the legal basis of the fifg regulation with two objectives: on the one hand, to allow such aid to be extended for a further six months, until 30 june next, and on the other hand, to authorize the member states concerned to exceed the 4% threshold of the fifg budget which they can allocate to aid for the paralysis of the fleet, a deadline which, as is evident from the extraordinary nature of the situation, had already been greatly exceeded. it was therefore a perfectly reasonable proposal. however, when the report we are discussing was practically finished, the council of ministers in april declared the negotiations closed, and in may the commission had not yet presented its proposal for the measures to be included in the conversion plan. we know that the commission intended to present a proposal for a regulation to this effect at the next council of fisheries ministers on 18 june, but for technical reasons it cannot be adopted before 3 july, and the timetable will be considerably delayed, since the european parliament is also due to be consulted. in addition, shipowners should be able to carefully consider the options available to them, depending on the type of vessel they own, as choosing between scrapping, relocating the vessel to another fishery or setting up a joint venture with a foreign partner are business decisions that cannot be taken lightly. on the other hand, the workers concerned will probably have to wait even longer, since it will depend on the decision of their companies whether they will leave one fishery to work in another or whether they will simply remain unemployed if the formula chosen is scrapping. it is clear that these decisions cannot be taken before 30 june, as the formulas which will finally be offered are not yet known. i therefore tabled an amendment before the vote on this report in committee to change the dates of the commission proposal from 30 june to 31 december. the committee on fisheries fully understood the situation and, taking into account that the extension of the deadline has no financial implications for the community budget, since the aid will continue to be paid by the fifg of the member states concerned, decided unanimously to support the modified content of the report. i therefore hope that, in view of the reasons i have set out and with the unquestionable support of the committee on fisheries, this house will also be able to approve the text which is being put to the vote today. on another matter, i would not like to finish without congratulating both rapporteurs and, as far as i am concerned, the committee on fisheries, mr poignant, and i assure him that our group will support his report and i want to emphasize amendment no 5 to it, because i think it is much more in line with article 29 (4) of regulation (ec) no 1260/1999, which allows a maximum contribution of 50% to smes in the outermost regions. we must not forget that measures to modernise ships are often what makes the difference between a competitive company and a company in difficulty, and also ensure a more dignified employment for its workers. that is why they should be the last public investments to disappear or to become economically unsound.
