- mr president, the posei programmes were proposed more than 10 years ago as instruments to help develop what we now know as the outermost regions. in its three versions for the regions and departments of france, spain and portugal, the posei programmes were conceived and implemented as an expression of the political will of the council and the commission to stimulate the development of these regions, which are among the most disadvantaged in the union because of their remoteness and insularity. with the inclusion of the new article 299 (2) of the treaty, the outermost regions now have a solid legal basis which has enabled the commission to propose these new posei. in the budgetary context defined by the stability agreement reached to make economic and monetary union possible, the financial perspective proposed by the commission is strictly in line with the criteria of budgetary neutrality. and i must say that virtually all of the additional expenditure is offset by the savings from the agenda 2000 reform. the commission's proposals, however, reflect its desire to honour the commitments it has successively acquired over the last few years, such as the cattle and dairy farms in the azores and the inclusion of tomato production in the canary islands, to name just two examples. there are, of course, some unresolved issues, such as the specific supply arrangements for certain products, especially those from the agro-food processing industry, which will have to be resolved by the competent management committee, since if the terms laid down at this stage are maintained, the result will be unsatisfactory.

the rapporteur. - mr president, community cooperation in the field of civil protection began in 1985 with two programmes: one lasting two years - 1998-1999 - and the other running until 2004. in recent years, disasters, often misnamed natural disasters, have had serious consequences for people, the environment, natural heritage and cultural heritage. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster is a very important one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. i think it is worth remembering that, according to the un intergovernmental panel on climate change, there is already evidence that if the current trends in increasing greenhouse gas emissions are not corrected, these catastrophes - floods, droughts, storms and so on - will become more and more common. this mechanism is therefore to be welcomed. the commission's proposal is based on the following elements: the identification of available resources for intervention, the formation of assessment and coordination teams to intervene in emergency situations and a common system of immediate communication. these are the elements on which this proposal is based in order to achieve the objectives of protecting citizens, the environment, natural resources and cultural resources. the four priorities defining the operation of the mechanism are: accident prevention, immediate reaction capacity, emergency response and disaster recovery measures. and to achieve these objectives, the most important elements are: the creation of a management, coordination and information operational centre; the identification of available resources in the member states; training programmes for response teams, experts in needs assessment and coordination of transport, resources and equipment; the establishment of a common emergency communication system, linking all available civil protection teams. it is clear that there are different realities in each of the member states, in germany and spain the autonomous communities are very well delimited, the regions have their own civil protection mechanism, also in the mayorships and in the town halls. in the other countries, civil protection is more centralised. in any case, it seems clear to us that this mechanism will be very useful, since it can coordinate and put into effect all the resources at our disposal in europe in the event of clear emergencies, such as those which have occurred in recent years - i remember very well what happened in the doñana national park, when a toxic waste raft broke, flooding a river and a huge meadow, and causing the loss of more than 5 000 farmers' jobs. and so it is very important that such a mechanism is fast and effective. the need for rapid communication and coordination may also be supplemented by the need to train and educate citizens for self-protection. there are in europe - and i was surprised by the number - about five million people who are volunteers, who come without any remuneration at a certain time when there is a catastrophe. the need for a minimum of training for these people would go a long way in helping them to cope with such catastrophes. i think we should remember what happened with the erika off the french coast and other catastrophes of this kind. i think that the proposals made by parliament are acceptable, that they improve this mechanism and that in the future it will be very important to have a clear and concrete mechanism, with a coordination centre for communications and resources in the field of civil protection.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the report adopted unanimously by the committee on agriculture and rural development on 25 april on community measures to combat classical swine fever proposes an early diagnosis system and the maintenance of the community method of combating the disease and slaughter, given that progress in marker vaccines is still not sufficient. the reason for the non-vaccination policy is based on the fact that in case of infection vaccinated pigs can become carriers of the viruses, especially pregnant sows, which without showing signs of the disease can transmit the disease horizontally to the rest of the holding and vertically to their offspring, which may result in persistently infected piglets. furthermore, as regards the differentiation of animals which have been vaccinated or have suffered from the disease and which have generated antibodies, this differentiation between vaccinated and infected animals is not yet reliable. we must continue research in this direction until these marker vaccines are effective and we are able to have differential methods that tell us whether the animals have been vaccinated or have contracted the disease. the directive improves certain prophylactic rules, clarifies definitions and proposes to include the diagnostic manual as an annex to the directive. the amendments also concern animal welfare rules on the farm and during transport, and they propose emergency solutions in cases of serious health crises that immobilize animals for long periods, such as intervention purchases, which the commission has never carried out. it is also proposed that these health rules be extended to the ceecs and included in the plans for the control of classical swine fever. there are a number of amendments to this document which the rapporteur feels she should comment on in some way. there is an amendment, amendment no 34, tabled by mr mulder on behalf of the eldr group, which is intended to be logical, but at a time when the health control authorities are national, to try to divide the european union into regions belonging to different nations and not coinciding with national borders seems unrealistic. i would ask mr mulder, who is in the chamber, whether the dutch are going to be able to control german farms or whether the germans are going to control dutch farms. i don't think either of us will agree. amendment no 35 tabled by mr mulder is contrary to the spirit of the rapporteur and the report. if the animal is not killed, the suppressive vaccination is not, and the marketing of meat from vaccinated animals in the european union would be less safe for our consumers than for those in third countries. we cannot export in principle and, moreover, this news in the press would sink the sector. fresh meat from vaccinated animals carries viruses, and could infect healthy animals that feed on the animal's waste. i cannot therefore accept amendment no 35. as regards amendment no 36, also tabled by mr mulder, we are again faced with the issue of co-financing and the rapporteur is also against it. there are two other amendments, amendment no 33 by mr böge, on behalf of the ppe group, and amendment no 37 by mr graefe zu baringdorf, on behalf of the green group. these two amendments go a little further than the rapporteur's spirit would allow, since the use of waste has been prohibited in my country for more than 20 years. however, in this very house, in mrs paulsen's report, amendment no 102 has been adopted as revised in this very house and i do not want to go against the spirit of this house. i therefore believe that both amendment no 33 and amendment no 37 are acceptable because they can lead us to a more realistic solution for the control of animal feed.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the agreement we are going to vote on today is both a continuation of the previous one and at the same time a similar philosophy to most of the agreements of this kind that the european union has signed. the present agreement, which, as i said, is in continuity with the previous one, introduces only slight quantitative changes in the number of vessels authorized to fish and in the volume of catches, and also slight changes in the amount, but significant changes in the structure of the financial contribution by the union and the companies benefiting from the agreement. the volume of authorized catches is fixed at 4 600 tonnes, slightly above the previous agreement of 4 500 tonnes, but well below the historical levels of 6 000 tonnes from 1988 to 1994. the number of vessels authorized to fish is fixed at 65: 40 tuna vessels and 25 surface longliners. there is an increase in the number of vessels from 60 to 65. of these, the tuna vessels are from the following countries: france, 21; spain, 18; italy, 1. as far as surface longliners are concerned, most of them are from spain, with some from portugal. it should be noted that although the number of vessels has increased, the number of tuna vessels, which produce the largest volume of catches, has decreased from 44 to 40 and that of longliners has increased from 16 to 25. these figures reflect precisely the rate of utilization actually achieved during the period of the previous agreement, which was 75 to 80% for tuna vessels and more than 90% for longliners, which are precisely those that are now increasing in number. turning to the financial contribution, it should be noted that it is set at a figure of slightly over one million euro: namely, 1 050 750 euro, i.e. the equivalent of 350 000 euro for each of the years of the agreement. the main change in this section concerns the structure of this financial contribution. whereas under the previous agreement, 50% of the funds were allocated for each of the two tranches, between the funds allocated for compensation and those allocated to specific targeted measures, i.e. measures to help develop the local fisheries sector, technical programmes, etc. in the new agreement, however, the funds allocated to these specific or targeted measures account for 60% of the financial contribution. in other words, there is a greater emphasis, so to speak, on contributing to development to the detriment of purely commercial aspects. the distribution of the cost of the agreement is also changed. the contribution from the community budget is reduced by 2.7% and the contributions from shipowners are increased by 35%. in particular, the quota is increased from eur 20 to eur 25 per tonne caught. it is a fair and balanced agreement which brings together the different interests and the different elements which are inevitably affected by such agreements. that is to say, the interests, first of all, of the islamic federal republic of the comoros, the interests of the european union, the interests of the companies which will benefit from the agreement and, last but not least, of course, the aspect of conservation of resources. as i said, this is a fair and balanced agreement which was voted by a very large majority in the commission and for which i am asking the house to vote at this moment.

- the next item is the report (a5-0134/2001) by mrs wallis, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the commission working document on the out-of-court resolution of consumer disputes.
commission. – mr. president, i am not only an advocate but a convinced advocate of the benefits of arbitration. this largely comes from my experience of legal practice, both in the area of domestic law in my own member state and in the area of international commercial arbitration. i had the honour of being a member the international court of arbitration of the international chamber of commerce for seven years, and drafted the last piece of legislation in my own member state on international commercial arbitration, so i am a convinced advocate of the benefits of arbitration, as distinct from court procedures. therefore, i believe that the establishment of the eej net is an essential step in ensuring that consumers have practical access to simple, low-cost and effective means of resolving cross-border disputes. it is the natural follow-up to the 1998 commission communication on access to justice and the notification by member states of their out-of-court bodies applying the principles set out in recommendation 98/257. in addition, this is a significant step forward in fulfilling the tampere council conclusions in providing better access to justice in europe. the continuing expansion of economic activity within the internal market means more and more that consumers' activities are not confined to their own country. the continued growth of e-commerce, coupled with the introduction of the euro, underlines the urgency of the need to actively promote consumer confidence to ensure a truly competitive and effective internal market. the involvement and support of all the community institutions, including the european parliament, is essential to raise the profile of this initiative and to ensure its effective delivery and to guarantee its eventual success. member states, in close cooperation with the commission, have already made substantial progress since this initiative was proposed in march last year. all, with the exception of germany, have now informed the commission of the body that will perform the functions of their national clearing-house and the process of setting up these bodies is under way. the commission is providing financial assistance for the start-up costs and will examine how best to provide further infrastructure and targeted support. in addition, both norway and iceland have expressed their wish to participate and have been attending meetings with member states' experts and with the commission. we are also examining how best the enlargement candidate countries can be brought into the network. much work has been completed with member states' experts and with wider stakeholders to turn the network into a successfully functioning reality. in particular, one result of this work has been a memorandum of understanding, setting out the minimum functions and operational guidelines for the clearing-houses, which is now close to finalisation. this document marks an important step in ensuring coherent cooperation throughout the network. it includes requirements for the provision of practical information and advice to be given to consumers, a general system for complaint handling, based on the european complaint forum, its translation, and monitoring to ensure the network operates efficiently, the requirement for either the clearing-house or the national authority to make practical arrangements with national adrs to ensure smooth cooperation and the need to monitor their compliance with the principles in the commission recommendation. network cooperation is envisaged through regular meetings, the development of network strategies and continual review of the network to ensure constant improvement. uniform methods for collecting data on the performance of the network, for its evaluation and to identify specific consumer problems are also part of the plan. the group of member state experts meets tomorrow to finalise these details. it is also provisionally agreed that the network should become operational on the 16 october of this year. this coincides with the launch in belgium of their euroguichet, which will act as the clearing-house, and with the annual general assembly of the consumer associations that takes place on 18 and 19 october. i see the eej net initiative as a priority. it is an essential component of a number of initiatives currently being developed by the commission aimed at creating confidence to enable consumers to actively take part in and benefit from the internal market. it will also be important for businesses in facilitating greater cross-border trade, particularly of course, for smes. it will put the practical framework in place to allow the adrs' potential for resolving cross-border disputes to be fully exploited. the organic nature of this framework will enable it to be sufficiently flexible and adaptable to meet new challenges and be kept under constant review to ensure the delivery of an effective mechanism for all citizens and for the effective operation of the internal market.
commission. – mr president, these are amendments to the excellent text that has been put forward by the rapporteur. as they stand, i do not have any objection to them, in particular the first one which identifies the need to have access to legal staff. that is desirable and included in our proposal. the others seem to me to be perfectly reasonable. for instance, amendment no 3 makes reference to the involvement of the eea states. some of them are already involved and we want more of them involved, including the applicant countries. so the commission fully supports this.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.

question no 30 by mr william francis newton dunn (h-0546/01) subject: police capabilities the first police capability conference was held recently with a view to creating, as agreed, a police force of five thousand men which the european union would have for civilian peacekeeping operations. could the commission report to parliament on the progress made and inform it of the next steps? second part
commission. – that will need to be determined case-by-case and situation-by-situation. let me explain one of the problems we have in providing the policing capacity which is needed. what we are looking for is not a conventional community police officer. what we require is a trained officer – man or woman – who is capable of the traditional policing functions of detection, who is capable of providing community policing, and capable, from time to time, of the sort of paramilitary policing which is needed, for example, in parts of the west balkans. in the country i know best there are very few police forces who have that sort of capacity, which includes the regular use of arms. the police service in northern ireland is an example of a service which has that sort of all-round capacity. that is one reason why it is difficult to provide exactly what is required, but whether or not arms will always be necessary will depend on the circumstances. i hope that the success of policing will mean that arms, increasingly, are not required.
- i call question no 31 by mrs ulla margrethe sandbæk (h-0540/01) subject: access of the poor to medicinesin view of the growing testimony and concern of citizens about the negative impact of the wto patent rules on access of the poor to medicines, will the eu support and promote the proposals of the developing countries at the next trip councils and the wto ministerial meeting in qatar that wto members decide to reconsider the implications of the trip agreement on public health and development and adopt a moratorium on trade disputes with developing countries on the subject of development, pending the completion of this review, and to allow the developing countries to review the scope of the trip agreement for public health reasons, and to reduce the scope of the trip agreement for the duration of the agreement and to allow the developing countries to revise the scope of the agreement?
commission - the first of these three points concerns the interpretation of the trips agreement. we have our interpretation; we have put it on the table, but we will not stop there: we will insert it in the context of a discussion in the council of intellectual property which we have helped, with others, to demand. we are therefore among those who believe that this balance is correct in the text, but that its interpretation should be discussed among wto members, so that judges do not have to do so. so it is an expression of political will. the second point, which concerns transitional periods, has not, to my knowledge, been the subject of any requests. there is no dispute on this point either, since - as you probably know - this matter between brazil and the united states - in which, i should like to point out, the union was not involved - was settled amicably last week. the third and final point concerns the duration of protection. in this case, we consider that the current durations of protection strike, once again, the right balance between the need to protect intellectual property and the needs of public health. we have a position on this which i consider to be active. we are among those who are drawing attention to this factor of accessibility to medicines. there are certainly others in terms of public health systems, the availability of care regimes, etc. in this case, i think we are demonstrating the position we generally take, which is to build an acceptable and proactive bridge between the concerns of developing countries and those of a number of countries in the north who are concerned about the protection of intellectual property.
commission. - that is a very good question. in fact, between the strict protection of intellectual property, that is to say the patent system, and the exceptions to this system, exceptions of the compulsory licence type, there is an intermediate area which we have explored with the pharmaceutical industry and a number of the countries concerned, which is that of differentiated prices. this means that a pharmaceutical company, while retaining the ownership of its patent, can make in one country, for example in africa, reductions of the order of 10% on the prices it charges in our markets. this process is under way, at present on what we consider to be a modest scale, and will be the subject of an international initiative, which has already begun under the auspices of the secretary-general of the united nations. this is the idea of a common fund, which has already been provided by several countries, and which will be used for the wholesale purchase of low-priced medicines, thus solving - provided the necessary financing is there, and for the moment it remains very modest - that part of the accessibility problem linked to prices. i would remind you that the price of medicines is only part of a much larger problem which essentially covers the health care system, the distribution system and the ability of the populations concerned, particularly in the case of aids, to take medicines regularly, which involves a very complicated medical work. but in general, to answer your question, yes, the international community is moving in that direction and the union will follow it as it already has a number of funds for that purpose.
subject: cosmetic product testing on animals and the wto under wto rules, imported products must be treated in the same way as similar products of domestic origin. the settlement of past disputes is based on the final product and not the way the product is obtained. some have therefore argued that banning the marketing of cosmetic products if they have been tested on animals would cause a trade war, since the absence of animal testing would not be taken into account. in the light of parliament's decision of 3 april 2001 to move towards such a ban, what steps could the commission take to avoid a potential trade war and does it consider that wto rules should be interpreted in such a way as to take account of how a product is produced when deciding on its 'similarity'? questions to mr solbes
commission. - my job, mr purvis, is to deal with the commercial disputes we have. it's all the better because i try to avoid them. and so i consider it my duty, particularly in relation to the council and parliament, to be perfectly clear when a decision of the council or parliament puts us at risk of losing a case. i think you yourself have understood the risk. the evidence is that we are now wondering what the consequences of all this will be in terms of sanctions. i cannot say what the situation is because, for a sanction to be taken against the european union, there must be a panel, we must lose that panel and then the amount of the sanctions must be assessed. in general, the amount of the penalties is assessed by reference to the volume of trade affected. in this hypothetical case, that is to say, if this proposal were to become the union's proposal, which it is not yet, if it were to be attacked and if we were to lose, we would have to assess the volume of trade in question and then we would have an idea of the sanctions system. i would remind you, for your information, that in this case the sanctions are not necessarily, and usually are not, directed against the industries which are the cause of the problem. they target others, since the choice of sanctions is left to the party winning the wto litigation.
commission. - on the first point of your question, madam president, i am certainly responsible for implementing the policies which the union has decided, including those on external affairs. it is my duty, and i believe i am doing so openly, to explain that when a political decision of the union conflicts with our international obligations, which is the case, then those who take that decision must know the risk they are taking. if you want to take that risk, take it. i'll deal with him. i believe there are smarter, less risky ways of dealing with this problem. we could, for example, look for a middle ground between our proposal, which was a ban on testing, and your position, which is a ban on marketing, that of labelling requirements. from the point of view of international trade law, they are less risky than a marketing ban. if we could go in that direction, meet your point of view and ours, in my opinion, we would not be engaged in useless wars. secondly, we hope that a number of wto rules will be clarified to allow the union to go in the direction it wishes, for example in terms of production methods. we want to move in that direction: we are a little isolated at the moment. one reason for this is that we have a number of developing countries who consider that the use of these production methods can be seen as protectionist measures. so we need very good arguments to show that this is not a matter of protection, but a matter of collective preference, that we each have our own level of ethics. in the european union, animal welfare is part of our ethical standard, which is not necessarily the case elsewhere - and is conceived - in terms of differences in development. that is our position. we will do everything we can to get this on the round agenda so that it can move forward. i must say that this position is not shared by many other parts of the world at the moment.
commission - of course, mrs schierhuber, i am prepared for all of this because, again, part of the union's trade policy is to apply to its external trade the system of collective preferences that we give ourselves internally. well, from that perspective, it's pretty simple. it is sometimes a little more complicated, as was shown, for example, by the panel we lost on hormone beef: as we prohibit hormone beef within the union, we have banned it from importation, but in such conditions that this ban has not been considered to be in accordance with international law. in general, the principles that apply are the principles of non-discrimination, treatment and proportionality. these are the principles we want to see incorporated in our environmental agenda in the round, and in particular everything that revolves around the precautionary principle. we are not there yet. there are risks in what we do within the union - perhaps in a number of cases - in the light of existing legislation which is considered excessive. we must therefore, on the one hand, adjust our internal behaviour and, on the other hand, adjust international law to our own preferences, which is only possible if others than ourselves agree to change this international law, over which we have no control. as we are not particularly unilateral, it will have to be changed on a number of points or at least clarified on these issues. that's the situation now. we know your concerns in this area. we support them, particularly in the ethical field. i cannot conceal the fact that, as things stand, a number of your projects will pose serious problems from the point of view of the wto.
question no 33 by mr papayannakis (h-0565/01) subject: greek stability and development programme in view of the continuing deterioration in the forecasts for the economic situation of the member states of the european union, it is natural that they should review the objectives they had set out in the stability and development programmes. has the greek government provided data on its current estimates of the development of its economy and to what extent do these estimates differ from the particularly ambitious economic development targets of the order of 5 to 5.5%? the international monetary fund, for example, estimates that inflation will reach 3.4% in greece in 2001, but considers it unrealistic, in relation to the real possibilities of the economy, to estimate that growth will follow a pace of 5 to 5.5% this year. in addition, in accordance with commissioner solbes' statements, economic growth of around 3% can be considered very high in the euro area countries. what is the commission's view of the possible impact of the failure to achieve these objectives on employment and the balance of public finances in greece?
the commission - i'll try to answer that second point. as i said earlier - and the case of greece can be used for the other member states - stability pacts are based on the figures of the countries themselves. it is true that the commission's forecasts give figures higher than those in the stability pacts in some cases and lower than those in others. but leaving aside the statements in the stability pacts, which are nevertheless basic to the development of public finances, we can already say that our forecasts of 2.8% growth today represent an excessively optimistic position and that we believe that our current growth rates would be much closer to the union's growth potential, which is around 2.5%. however, even with that growth of around 2.5% - a little above or below - we believe that jobs will continue to be created in the union and so far we have not seen any substantial fall in the evolution of employment or an increase in unemployment. unemployment is still falling. we shall therefore remain relatively optimistic about developments in this field for the time being. as regards the issue of public finances, it is true that less favourable economic developments may have some impact. the commission, anticipating this situation, has already presented its position on public finances to the council, pointing out that, in our view, automatic stabilizers should be allowed to play their full role in those countries which have already achieved a position close to equilibrium in terms of public finances and in those others which have a public debt close to 60%. in that situation, the countries where automatic stabilizers should not be allowed to play their full role would have to be the four countries with deficits above 1% and the three with debt close to 100%. italy is included in both groups. the other countries are germany, france and portugal in the case of deficit, and greece and belgium in the case of debt.
question no 34 by mr bernd posselt (h-0578/01) subject: the euro in the former yugoslavia what is the commission's position on the introduction of the euro in bosnia-herzegovina, kosovo and montenegro, regions where the german mark is now the currency, and what is its assessment of this development?
- commission. - when there are people who hold large quantities of banknotes, especially from the euro area, and national currencies outside the euro area, two types of situations arise: the normal savings of these people and the search for protection against their exchange rate situation. in both cases, the holding of these securities is perfectly justified. and there is no problem in producing the exchange of those values into the new euro currency, through your commercial bank, or through the european banks that have subsidiaries and branches in the area. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european currency is not used in the same way as the national currencies. obviously, in my view, there should be no favourable treatment for this kind of situation. the same regime should apply as applies to exchanges in the european union, i.e. in cases where someone identifies himself as the owner of an amount, exchanges are carried out without any risk, even for amounts exceeding the minimums set out in the money laundering directive. when amounts are changed which do not reach the limits of the money laundering directive, the changes can occur without asking for the identification of the holder of the funds. but i think that when the quantities are large and exceed the limits, identification should be required. what you're asking me is a different problem. since this requirement will be maintained, it cannot be accepted that part of these assets should be converted into dollars. firstly, we do not have that impression, according to the figures for the banknotes in circulation at the various central banks; secondly, in the countries which have signed the obligations arising from the money laundering convention, the same criteria as those i have mentioned must be applied for the conversion of european currency into dollars. it is only in the case of some countries which have more lax legislation that allows today to change from one european currency to another, be it the dollar or any other, without being subject to the requirements i have mentioned, that the situation you have mentioned can occur.

- question no 35 by mr stenmarck (h-0535/01): subject: competition in 1996, a complaint was lodged with the commission, more specifically with the directorate-general for competition, alleging abuse of a dominant position by the port authorities of helsingborg. the complainants, a few companies using the port, claim that the port authorities' abuse of a dominant position leads them to levy too much tax. pending a decision, one of the complainant companies paid only half of the taxes due for the use of the port. the port authorities of helsingborg therefore demanded 240 million swedish kronor (approximately eur 26 million) from the company. today, almost five years after the complaint was lodged, the parties are still awaiting a decision from the directorate-general for competition. a response has been promised repeatedly but no decision has yet been taken. the result of this delay is that two small firms do not know in which financial framework they have to work. is it normal that the parties should have to wait almost five years for the commission to decide on the matter?
commission. – yes, it has been a long period. i agree with you about that. on the other hand, as i am sure you are aware, this case is very complex. from a factual point of view, the commission has to take into consideration the evolution of the port's activity over almost a ten-year period. the market itself, which is at the core of any competition analysis, is very difficult to determine. it depends on the type of traffic considered: foot passengers, cars, transportation of goods and so on. in addition, as i mentioned a moment ago, the situation has changed greatly with the opening of the øresund bridge last year. in addition, to make things more complex, there is no direct precedent. this explains why, as mr stenmarck underlines, this decision is eagerly awaited. the commission is in the process of analysing, in particular, the consequences of the opening of the bridge on the definition of the markets. all parties concerned will be asked to contribute all relevant information. the case is being given top priority and will be resolved as soon as possible. but i cannot, at this stage, indicate a time or possible outcome. that will depend on the facts.
- question no 36 by mr luis berenguer fuster (h-0537/01) subject: opening of an infringement procedure for state aid to the terra mítica theme park in benidorm (spain) the spanish media have reported the commission's intention to open an infringement case against spain for the granting of state aid to the terra mítica theme park in benidorm, although there is talk of delaying the date. does the commission intend to open this infringement case?
the commission - i can answer mr berenguer with a recent fact: at its meeting on 20 june 2001, the commission decided to partially initiate the procedure laid down in article 88 (2) of the ec treaty in respect of alleged aid granted by the public authorities to the 'mythical land' amusement park. this decision was the subject of a press release issued on 20 june. the text of the decision, excluding confidential information, shall be published in the spanish language in the official journal of the european communities.
- commissioner, the truth is that i wrote this question in may and when i heard that the case had been opened i thought of withdrawing it, but before i did, something happened that made me reconsider my decision. that something was a disproportionate attack on this member by the president of the region, mr zaplana, for the mere fact of asking this question. and that is not, commissioner. when, faced with innocent questions which merely seek to clarify matters which the government of the generalitat was concealing, it reacts violently, it is because something more is being concealed than i suspected, and that is why i invite you, mr commissioner, to have your services investigate firmly, away from the political pressures which they will undoubtedly receive, what is behind it: tax benefits, granting of guarantees or, what seems to me more serious, the construction of infrastructures financed with european funds in the exclusive interest of a private company. the truth is that the leaders of my autonomous community are such peculiar liberals that they advocate that hospitals and schools be privately owned, while the public sector is engaged in manufacturing caravans and amusement parks.
- thank you very much, mr. berenguer. i don't think you asked a question, but mr. monti can always answer it.
commission - i would like to answer the same question from mr berenguer to tell him that, as in all procedural cases, we are examining this one very carefully and very carefully. perhaps i could now provide mr berenguer with an additional element, namely the points on which the procedure is being opened, which are essentially: the financing of the infrastructure necessary for the operation of the park, the value of the assets and, in particular, the land and the brand 'tierra mítica' transferred to the private company managing the park, the conditions of a shareholder loan granted to the private company managing the park, worth eight billion pesetas, the reduction of municipal taxes in favour of the park by the city of benidorm and, finally, a possible contribution by the valencia tourism agency to the park worth six billion pesetas, the subject of mr berenguer's written question of 11 april 2001. i wanted to provide these factual elements out of the context of the more political remarks mr berenguer made a moment ago.

mr president, i would like to say that the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the rapporteur. in fact, the complainant continually brought new complaints as the park project developed. in this respect, the commission received 18 successive letters from the complainant. in addition, the case is complex and has also given rise to several exchanges of letters between the commission and the spanish authorities, which explains, among other things, the time that has elapsed since the initiation of the case. in reply to mr berenguer fuster, i referred to the point on which the commission has opened the procedure in order to give parliament a more complete framework. perhaps i should mention the other points, which concern in particular the allegations of the complainant concerning the cheap acquisition of the land on which the park is being built, the existence of expenditure on the park borne by the regional authorities, the non-compliance with the private investor principle, the syndicated loans in favour of the park, the capital injections in favour of the park and the existence of training aid and direct regional aid.
- mr commissioner, as the author of a report on the competition policy of the european union a few years ago, i know that public aid is one of the most complicated issues and that for years it has distorted the application of competition policy in the union. given the elements which the commissioner has mentioned in connection with the issue raised by mr berenguer, i would like to know - if it were indeed established that there has been an inappropriate use of public funds, in this case in the valencian community - what compensation mechanisms are in place to balance the competitiveness between similar structures existing in other tourist areas.
commission. - in the question by mr gasòliba i böhm there is a slightly more general reference to the logic of state aid control. in the present case, it is permissible to ask why the commission considers that aid to a park such as 'tierra mítica' may affect intra-community trade. in fact, the commission considers that large theme parks, such as 'tierra mítica', are destination parks, which affects - at least potentially - tourist flows. these parks also enhance the tourist offer of the regions in which they are established. in addition, the commission has already adopted several state aid decisions concerning amusement parks and other tourist investments such as hotels and marinas. finally, in the present case, the advertising of the park itself mentions how to get there from abroad. without wishing to prejudge the outcome of the procedure which has just been opened, i would point out, in a more direct answer to your question, that if the commission succeeds in establishing that unlawful aid has been granted, it will proceed with the recovery order. but this is in no way the time to prejudge the conclusion of the inquiry.
question no 37 by mr lennart sacrédeus (h-0551/01) subject: limitation of national subsidies to the film production of small countries according to the swedish press, the european union's competition authorities have asked that national public subsidies to the film industry be limited to 50%. the possible introduction of a ceiling was also interpreted as a precursor to a 30% limitation. the media have reported on this news as the commission reaffirms its commitment to guaranteeing equality and linguistic and cultural plurality in the union. european film production differs from american production in that the union has a large number of languages. so without any subsidies, it is very often impossible, for financial reasons, to produce films in small member states like my own, sweden. a film in a language not widely used is obviously at a great disadvantage compared to an english film. aid is therefore essential if we are to continue to guarantee national film production in countries with a small population. does the commission not consider that the introduction at european union level of a ceiling to limit national subsidies to the film industry is totally contrary to article 151 of the treaty, which provides that 'the community shall contribute to the flowering of the cultures of the member states, with due regard for their national and regional diversity ...', and is it therefore prepared to prevent the introduction of such a limitation?
commission. – mr president, in the meeting held in stockholm on 12 june 2001 with delegates from the national film institutes and the cultural departments of all the member states, the commission representatives made it clear that the commission does not intend to take a restrictive approach to aid for film production granted on cultural grounds, as suggested in mr sacrédeus' question. the 50% aid intensity limit was fixed by the commission, in its decision of 1998 on the french scheme of automatic aid to film production, with reference to the french situation. according to that decision this limit does not apply to difficult and low-budget films. it is up to each member state both to define the notion of "difficult" and "low-budget" films and to fix the aid intensity applicable to this category of work according to national criteria. furthermore, apart from this derogation for other member states with a comparatively limited cultural and linguistic influence, the commission has made it be known that it will study potential further derogations where they prove necessary to ensure the viability of films with great cultural content. in practice, the 50% aid intensity criterion constitutes a benchmark that can be exceeded on genuine cultural grounds.
commission. – i am happy to provide further information in response to mr sacrédeus' question. first, on cultural diversity – a key point in our community – the diversity of characteristics in the schemes operated by member states reflects the cultural diversity in the european union. accordingly, the commission does not wish to impose any particular model under the review. the commission does not want to harmonise the provisions of the different schemes but just to ensure their compliance with the four specific compatibility criteria that were set out in the french decision. on the issue of whether the 50% aid intensity threshold applies to smaller member states with limited cultural markets and could an exception be envisaged for them: well, the answer is that the 50% aid intensity threshold applies in principle across the board to all member states without distinction. it is to be noted that in the absence of territorialisation, the 50% aid intensity criterion becomes irrelevant. the commission might consider applying exceptions to the 50% aid criterion if such a limit would make cultural production impossible. the commission has already established an exception for difficult low-budget films. for certain smaller member states, in the case of territorialisation, the commission might consider authorising higher aid intensities on a case-by-case basis, if it is established that the 50% aid intensity level would not ensure cultural production because the cultural area and market diffusion were limited.
- question no 38 by mrs piia-noora kauppi (h-0557/01): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the victims of the floods in the united kingdom. the commission is currently examining the position to be taken on the intention of certain companies to share the infrastructure of third generation mobile telephony networks with competitors. at that stage, the commission indicated that telecommunications companies could infringe the community competition rules by choosing to share these infrastructures with their competitors. the european investment bank also indicated that it would take into account competition considerations on mobile telephony networks when deciding on the financing of third generation projects. when will the commission present its position on this very important matter? is the commission aware of the eib's intentions and does it consider that competitive considerations should be taken into account by the eib in its financing decisions?
commission. – thank you, ms kauppi, for this extremely interesting and timely question. it is true that currently, given the prevailing market conditions and, in particular, the decline in the market valuation of most technologies companies, network sharing has been seriously envisaged by certain third generation operators as a means to alleviate their debt burden and lower their network deployment costs. the commission has already indicated that, in principle, it considers network infrastructure sharing positively, due to the potential economic gains, always provided that competition rules and other relevant community laws are respected, in particular those of the licensing directive. this view has been expressed in the commission communication on the introduction of third generation mobile communications in the european union that was adopted on 20 march 2001. certain forms of networking infrastructure sharing, notably site and mast sharing, could greatly contribute to reducing the environmental impact of network deployment. so far, the commission has not been formally notified of any agreement between 3g operators, therefore, it is not yet clear how network sharing will take place and how it will be implemented. some operators may choose to engage in network infrastructure sharing within a limited geographical area, while others may opt for full geographical coverage. in the same vein, some operators may choose to share only sites and masts, whereas others may choose also to share antennas and what i would call 'active elements' of their networks, such as radio network controllers. from contacts with operators and manufacturers, it appears that the degree of cooperation among 3g license holders will be influenced by the availability of new technology which will enable operators to share even active elements of their networks, without having to exchange or share sensitive information among themselves or otherwise compromise their independence as competitors. the commission has already had some preliminary discussions with national regulators on the competition law issues raised by network-sharing. at this stage, the commission can only require parties to ensure that when they conclude network-sharing agreements, competition among themselves and with third parties is not restricted or affected. any restriction of competition could be tolerated only if it brought benefits to consumers and fulfilled all the other conditions set out in article 81(3) of the treaty. in any event, the freedom of contracting parties to disengage from their network-sharing cooperation and deploy their own networks in areas where they previously shared infrastructure should be preserved. given that the commission has not yet been formally notified of, or had occasion to examine, any case of network sharing, it is uncertain at this stage whether the commission might need to issue, in the future, any kind of specific guidelines on the competition law aspects of network sharing. finally, as regards the eib, the commission is aware of the bank's intention of taking account of competition considerations in assessing projects for loans. the commission clearly welcomes this intention as ensuring coherence between the bank's objectives in rolling out projects in accordance with its mandate, particularly following the lisbon european council and community policy in a liberalised environment.
commission. – as you underlined yourself, ms kauppi, the commission has an open attitude on this issue, provided that the competition rules are respected. as to the aspect of possible adoption of possible guidelines from the competition angle on network sharing, as i said in my previous response, the commission has not yet received any notification of a network sharing agreement. thus it is still too early to have a clear idea about possible anti-trust issues which may arise from such forms of cooperation among competing network operators and which may require the commission to publish some sort of guidelines in order to provide further needed clarification for the industry concerned. what needs to be made clear is that network sharing is subject to the same rules of competition law as other forms of cooperation or collaboration among competitors. it would be wrong if operators believed that network sharing deserves different treatment under competition law provisions.

the committee on petitions has already adopted a number of amendments. - mr president, the first thing i have to say is that i do not recognise myself in the opinion i myself am signing on this report. this is for one fundamental reason: at the time of the vote, two paragraphs which i thought were very important were deleted from this opinion of the committee on petitions, mainly because of the vote of my colleagues on the right. i would like to quote those two paragraphs which i found so important and which, by disappearing from the text, forced me to abstain in my own opinion. in one of them it was stated - in fact, it was the end of a paragraph - that 'economic, social and cultural rights are indispensable for the exercise of civil and political rights'. a person who is hungry, who has no job, who has no home is not in a position to enjoy civil rights. i thought that was an important sentence and it was deleted. the other - perhaps a little more controversial - stated that 'the charter of fundamental rights of the european union should be supplemented by binding rights as important as the right to work, housing, minimum income, the right to a healthy environment or the right to vote of third country nationals who have resided for five years in the union, as well as the extension of civil rights to immigrants who come to europe in search of a dignified life'. this paragraph was also deleted. i therefore had to abstain in my own opinion, mr president. however, i think that the committee on petitions makes a very clear contribution to the defence of the rights of european citizens. the proof is that more than 1400 citizens in europe send petitions to this committee every year, relating to the recognition of qualifications, free movement, the right of immigrants and the right to a healthy and healthy environment. mr president, i regret to have to remind you that in europe we have a scourge, terrorism, which seriously violates human rights of expression and the fundamental right to life. we would very much like - i repeat this from my modest position in recent times and i will continue to repeat it - that europe today be a distinguished continent in the defence of human rights within its own borders and of human rights abroad. i think we have that part to play. i think that, unfortunately, we are not doing that at the moment, but i hope that in the future we can.

- mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate mr wuori and mr cornillet on their reports and on the excellent work they have done. however, i am sorry that mr wuori's report makes no reference to the situation of one of the most violated and at the same time most neglected fundamental rights: the right to education, to acquire the basic training necessary to get out of the underdevelopment and poverty in which so many children and adults are condemned to live because they are not guaranteed the exercise of this fundamental right. according to unicef, 130 million children have never attended school and another 150 million have started primary school but have left before completing the literacy process. in sub-saharan africa, moreover, the number of out-of-school children is increasing rather than decreasing. this is despite the objectives set at the world conference on education for all in jomtien in 1990 and the world education forum in dakar in 2000. in the face of this reality, we cannot remain indifferent, nor can we ignore the lack of political will on the part of the european union and its member states to translate the rhetoric of grand declarations into budgetary appropriations. if we say that we are defending human rights, we must also defend the right to education with all its consequences. just as we defend the right to life or the right to non-discrimination or the right to freedom of expression. because let us not forget that human rights are indivisible, inalienable and universal.

- since their objects are related, i call questions 1 to 10 simultaneously. question no 1 by nelly maes (h-0516/01) subject: the commission's proposal to extend the scope of the directive subject: the laeken declaration the european council in nice in december 2000 approved a declaration on the future of the union. this declaration calls for a broad and thorough debate on the future of the european union. not only the member states but also the applicant countries, the national parliaments, the european parliament and public opinion must be involved in this debate. the european council has wrongly and in complete contradiction to the principle of subsidiarity ignored the democratic added value of constitutional regions. the belgian foreign minister, mr louis michel, recently stated that he intends to allow meps to be members of the belgian parliament. we are pleased to hear minister michel speak of greater involvement of parliamentarians, provided that he also means representatives of the communities and regions. will the council, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, involve the constitutional regions in shaping the future of europe? question no 2 by mr pere esteve (h-0518/01) subject: laeken declaration given the growing importance of sub-state levels, which are becoming more active in participating in the various eu decision-making processes, the broad debate on the future of the union which is being prepared in the run-up to the laeken summit should also provide institutional responses to the legislative and judicial participation of constitutional regions (sub-state entities with legislative powers, guaranteed by the constitution of the state to which they belong) in the development, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of eu policies. in this context, would the council not consider recommending a reform of the treaties (part v, section 4 of the ec treaty) to give these regions the right to bring an action directly before the court of justice when their prerogatives are threatened, in the same way as member states can do? question no 3 by mr gorka knörr borrás (h-0520/01) subject: the laeken declaration on the european union and the european union's relations with the countries of the former soviet union the belgian presidency is expected to adopt the laeken declaration on the future of the european union. some member states, such as germany, austria, belgium and the united kingdom, have established mechanisms for the participation of their regional or federal authorities in the council. given that the autonomous communities of the spanish state, the länder in germany and austria or the regions in belgium have a high degree of specific powers and that community decisions affect many of these powers, would the council be prepared to accept the establishment of direct representation of the regions before it? question no 4 by mr bart staes (h-0522/01) subject: the laeken declaration by presenting the laeken declaration on saturday 15 december, the belgian federation will be making its contribution to the debate on the future of the european union. in this connection, the positive initiative of the belgian prime minister, guy verhofstadt, who is the author of the community political declaration of seven constitutional regions, should be particularly welcomed. at the end of may, the latter received the ministers-president of the autonomous community of catalonia, the land of salzburg, scotland, the flemish region and the walloon region, as well as the ministers responsible for european federal affairs of the land of bavaria and north rhine-westphalia, all of whom insisted on strengthening the role of the constitutionally recognised regions within the european union. since the constitutional regions bring a democratic added value to the construction of europe, does the council support their wider and more conventional commitment to the european project? if not, can he explain why he is opposed to such a commitment by the constitutional regions to the project on the future of the european union? question no 5 by mr neil maccormick (h-0524/01) subject: the laeken declaration on the european union and the european union's role in the world annex iv to the treaty of nice contains a declaration calling for a broad and thorough debate on the future of the union. the igc also recognised the need to continuously improve and ensure the democratic legitimacy and transparency of the union and its institutions. this formula opens the way for the convening of a convention consisting of representatives of the national parliaments, the european parliament and the governments of the member states. contrary to the principle of subsidiarity, the constitutional regions were not mentioned. will the council, in accordance with the democratic principle of subsidiarity, involve all the parliaments of the constitutional regions when it opts for a convention? question no 6 by jillian evans (h-0525/01) subject: the laeken declaration on the future of the european union according to the declaration in annex iv to the treaty of nice, the debate on the future of the european union should focus on the following questions: how can a more precise delimitation of competences between the european union and its member states be established and maintained in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity? the current notion of subsidiarity, as it appears in the treaty, is usually interpreted as governing only relations between the union and the states. this interpretation needs to be extended, as the european parliament stressed in its resolution of 26 october 2000 on the commission's report to the council entitled 'better lawmaking'. will the laeken declaration propose to amend the treaties so that the political and legislative powers of the internal political units of the member states in their relations at the executive, legislative and judicial levels with the institutions of the union are recognised and respected? question no 7 by mr eurig wyn (h-0526/01) subject: laeken declaration annex iv to the treaty of nice contains a declaration calling for a broad and thorough debate on the future of the union. it also recognises the need to continuously improve and ensure the democratic legitimacy and transparency of the union and its institutions. in december 2001, the belgian presidency will conclude with a contribution to this debate, namely the laeken declaration. will the laeken declaration recognise that further democratisation of the european decision-making process requires a radical reform, dividing legislative power between two chambers, the european parliament and a reformed council, which would take over some of the powers of the current committee of the regions and significantly strengthen the role of the constitutional regions? question no 8 by mr carlos bautista ojeda (h-0560/01) subject: laeken declaration annex iv to the treaty of nice contains a declaration calling for a more in-depth and wider debate on the future of the european union. following a report to be submitted to it at its meeting in gothenburg in june 2001, the european council, meeting in laeken in december 2001, will take appropriate initiatives to continue this process. according to the declaration, this should include the following: how can a more precise delimitation of competences between the european union and the member states be established and subsequently maintained, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity? will the council, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, refrain from encroaching on the powers of the constitutional regions? how does it intend to establish and then maintain this respect for the constitutional regions' competences? question no 9 by mr josu ortuondo larrea (h-0531/01) subject: declaration no 54 on subsidiarity annexed to the treaty of amsterdam the declaration no 54 annexed to the treaty of amsterdam under the heading 'declarations taken note of by the conference' deals with subsidiarity. it states that 'the german, austrian and belgian governments take it for granted that the action of the european community, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, concerns not only the member states but also their entities in so far as they have legislative powers conferred on them by national constitutional law'. similarly, declaration no 23 (future of the union) annexed to the treaty of nice states in paragraph 3 that in 2001 the swedish and belgian presidencies, in cooperation with the commission and with the participation of the european parliament, will encourage a broad debate involving all interested parties (...)' and in paragraph 4 that 'the european council, at its meeting in laeken/brussels in december 2001, will adopt a declaration containing appropriate initiatives to continue this process'. how does the belgian presidency intend to deal with declaration no 54 of the treaty of amsterdam on the principle of subsidiarity and the entities with exclusive competence? how, in its view, should disputes arising from decisions which might be taken by the community institutions and which would encroach on the exclusive powers of the entities in question be settled? would it not be better to give the court of justice of the european communities jurisdiction to rule on possible appeals from constitutional entities and to confer on them, by treaty, a legitimacy which would enable them to defend their interests before the european courts? question no 11 by mr william francis newton dunn (h-0545/01) subject: public access to council documents now that the council has endorsed the commission's proposal, what timetable and procedure has the council foreseen for the public to begin to have access to its documents?
i need advice. - the answer to mr newton dunn's question is as follows. first of all: the council welcomed the progress made in the area of openness and transparency since the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, and in particular the adoption of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 regarding public access to european parliament, council and commission documents. the council would point out to the honourable member that regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 of the european parliament and of the council of 30 may 2001 regarding public access to european parliament, council and commission documents pursuant to article 19 will only apply from 3 december 2001. until that date, requests from the public for council documents will be dealt with as before on the basis of council decision 93/731/ec on public access to council documents. each of the three institutions concerned will therefore have to make preparations to ensure that the new regulation is actually applied from 3 december 2001. article 15 requires them to set up an interinstitutional committee to examine best practice, to deal with any disputes and to discuss future developments in public access to documents. as far as the council is concerned, the competent bodies are currently examining the measures to be taken to give full effect to the rights enjoyed by citizens under the new regulation. i would add, mr president, that it is the presidency's ambition to be able to conclude all the agreements before the entry into force of this regulation, if it can even manage to do so, but again, we cannot do this entirely on our own and i hope that we will find the necessary support.
council. – i am afraid i cannot guarantee that. i would be a fairy if i could. i can only tell you that we will do our utmost. we will take up where the work left off to see to it that the directive enters into force on the set date, 3 december 2001.
- question no 12 by mr lennart sacrédeus (h-0550/01): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the french company subject: equal treatment of turkey in the field of preaccession aid the european council in helsinki in december 1999 decided that turkey was a candidate country alongside the other 12 candidate countries. turkey has therefore been promised some help in the often long and difficult process of accession negotiations. current support for all candidate countries includes funds such as ispa and sapard. turkey does not benefit from this. the country was refused the aid promised in helsinki on the grounds that the union lacked financial means. is it not time for the council to ensure that the decisions taken at the helsinki summit, which put turkey on an equal footing with the other 12 candidate countries, are implemented and that the aid promised to turkey is paid, especially since the commission has just decided to reimburse €11.6 billion to the member states?
council. - having decided to grant turkey the status of candidate country for accession, the helsinki european council asked the commission to present a single framework for union financial assistance to that country for the pre-accession period. the commission presented its proposal to the council on 27 april. the main objective of this proposal for a single financial framework is to ensure that financial assistance is allocated according to the priorities set by the accession partnership and to bring together the existing instruments into a single instrument in order to maximise their effectiveness. the gothenburg european council, which made it clear that the accession partnership is the centrepiece of the pre-accession strategy, invited the council to adopt this single financial framework by the end of 2001. the council has started the procedure for consulting the european parliament and encourages it to deliver its opinion as soon as possible.

- question no 13 by mrs maría izquierdo rojo (h-0553/01) subject: the belgian presidency and afghan women considering the inhumane conditions faced by more than 11 million women in afghanistan, would the council be prepared to promote the creation of an international commission on afghanistan, in coordination with the united nations?
counsel. - mrs izquierdo rojo, we were colleagues on the committee on institutional affairs in the previous parliament. so it gives me great pleasure to be able to answer your very judicious question. as stated in previous replies to questions on the same subject, the council fully shares the concerns of the honourable member regarding the dire situation of large sections of the afghan population, and in particular the dire situation of women and children. given the humanitarian and political difficulties in afghanistan, in particular the negative attitude of the taliban towards both the un and women, the council is not entirely convinced that the establishment of an international commission on afghanistan, in coordination with the un, would be of a nature to really improve the situation of women on the ground. the council will nevertheless carefully consider the advantages and disadvantages which might result from the creation of such a committee, as soon as the matter is raised in the un framework and provided that the terms of such a proposal have been carefully studied. in the meantime, the council will continue the actions it has defined to help afghan women. in this connection, the council also refers the honourable member to the answers he has already given to earlier questions on the same subject. these are questions h-0032/01, h-0052/01, h-0170/01, h-0088/01 and, more recently, question h-0481/01.

- the next item is the report (a5-0218/2001) by mr callanan, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the member states relating to pleasure boats.
commission. – mr president, first of all i would like to thank mr callanan and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy for this comprehensive report. it is very well timed for european citizens, who are now preparing for their holidays and may experience the problem daily. engine noise, air and water pollution are becoming an increasingly common irritant in recreational activities. i recently read in the press that, in the past, no attention was paid to research and technology on noise pollution and that is the reason for the delays in development. while exhaust emissions from recreational craft are relatively small in comparison to the total amount of pollution in the environment, the effect of pollution is amplified by the way recreational craft are used. noise pollution has been targeted, because motor boats are often used in areas where people go to relax. recreational areas free of unpleasant noise are an important but scarce national resource that should be protected. this has led to the introduction of different emission requirements in the different member states. the proposed legislation therefore seeks to avoid fragmentation of the internal market and at the same time to ensure a high level of health, safety, and environmental consumer protection. the commission proposal is a good example of synergy between environment and industrial policies contributing to sustainable development. comparable legislation exists in the united states on exhaust emissions from recreational out-board engines. the environmental protection agency is currently preparing legislation to cover recreational in-board and stern drive engines. these cases are under discussion under the auspices of the transatlantic business dialogue, in which i am also participating. mr callanan and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy are to be congratulated for the amendments which aim to simplify the noise-testing procedures, produce the conformity assessment costs for smes and clarify requirements in the case of replacement engines. the commission can accept the amendments which aim to clarify and improve the wording of the initial text in relation to partly completed craft and weather conditions, as well as those concerning the simplification of the noise-testing procedures. the amendments concerning the distinction of stern drive engines, the formulas to be used for the noise-testing procedures and clarification of the coverage of replacement engines can be accepted in principle. while we have no problem with the general direction of the proposals, we need to analyse further the values and definitions proposed. as regards the institutional aspects, the proposal envisages, in conformity with the rules governing comitology, a regulatory committee to deal with a number of standard issues relating to the adaptation of technical provisions to technical progress, including measures concerning the evolution of exhaust and noise emission limits. a regulatory committee is thus essential for the efficient implementation and the regular update of a specific range of technical elements of the proposed directive. it would be contrary to the simplifying aims of the comitology decision to initiate a formal modification procedure in the case of non-essential provisions subject to regular review. consequently, the amendments requiring the rescission of this provision relating to comitology cannot be accepted by the commission, as they are contrary to its executive powers under article 202 of treaty. nevertheless, in order to meet concerns expressed by some members of parliament, like mr lange, as regards further steps in the case of emission limit values, it may be possible to arrive at an acceptable formula in the light of subsequent negotiations. the commission will consider the most appropriate ways to take into account the evolution of exhaust and noise emission limits. for example, the question of possible further reductions in emission limit values could be dealt with in the report to be presented to the european parliament and to the council under article 2 of the commission proposal. i am convinced that further work in close cooperation with the european parliament, the council and the commission, will lead to a balanced solution offering a clear benefit for the environment and the internal market, while minimising additional burdens to smes. in conclusion, the commission can accept amendments nos 1, 6, 14, 18, 19, 22, 27 to 29, 37, 39, 41 and 44. furthermore, the commission can accept in principle amendments nos 3, 5, 7, 8, 12, 13, 21, 23, 35 and 36. in addition, the commission can accept in part amendments nos 10, 43 and 45. on the contrary, the commission cannot accept amendments nos 2, 4, 9, 11, 15, 16, 17, 20, 24 to 26, 30 to 34, 38, 40, 42 and 46 to 50.

- mr president, i should like to begin by congratulating the two rapporteurs on the work they have done, which, although it is certainly not the culmination of the work of the experts, is nevertheless a major step forward in the development of what will in future be a genuine european joint stock company, and therefore one which is fully equipped to respond to this concept. max weber defined the enterprise as the organization which, by controlling them, has as its object the production of goods and services for a market. obviously, the ownership of the company can be held by both a natural person and a legal person, and it is a widespread practice, also derived from the will of the individual entrepreneur to limit his liability - require amendment to the staff regulations will then be decided by the commission and implemented immediately. i am pleased to report that the basic objective of our february proposals, of which we
