- mr president, we are talking here today about european citizenship and the rights of those european citizens. i think our rapporteur, mr perry, clearly supports a code of conduct which reflects the intention of those who drafted article 41 of the charter of fundamental rights, the right of citizens to good administration. that code clearly requires good administrative behaviour from everyone - institutions and officials - and also requires that it be applied uniformly in all the institutions. the code must be as widely disseminated, as transparent and as accessible to the public as possible. it must facilitate the closeness and credibility of the european institutions (i think we still have a long way to go in that respect) and it must be applied without any discrimination on grounds of sex, race, colour, ethnic origin, language or religion. i would remind you, mr president, that a german colleague of kurdish origin, very dark-haired and with black eyes, is asked for her card even in this house with more 'diligence' than the rest of the members, because she does not look like a member of parliament. if that happens here in this parliament, what can happen outside it? it is therefore very important that the code of conduct is applied without any discrimination. i think that the agencies which have already adopted the code of good conduct proposed by the ombudsman should be congratulated, and i take this opportunity to congratulate the ombudsman on his work. i believe that the ombudsman and the committee on petitions of the european parliament, to which i belong, know very well from the complaints of citizens that we are still a long way from the community institutions being credible and close to these citizens and that it is up to us to facilitate this rapprochement and this credibility.
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to congratulate the rapporteurs and mr söderman on the work they have done, which gives me the opportunity to discuss with them very important institutional issues for the proper functioning of the european union, and particularly with regard to the citizens, those citizens who must be able to keep as close as possible to the institutions of the union. i would start with the bösch report, the annual report on the activities of the european ombudsman for the year 2000. i would like to reiterate once again the commission's thanks and appreciation for the excellent work carried out by the institution of the european ombudsman and, of course, in particular, the figure of the ombudsman himself, mr söderman, who is undoubtedly leading the work and who is, to a large extent, the driving force and the explanation of the results and the good consequences that the reality of the ombudsman is having, which - let us say it clearly - is becoming more and more known to european citizens. the ombudsman's task is to focus on maladministration and the commission is obliged to improve its management and the quality of its services for the benefit of citizens. in this context, the commission shares the concerns expressed by the rapporteur and, in particular, the need to give the ombudsman and the committee on petitions the best possible reception and resources. one aspect of the bösch report which particularly concerns us is the follow-up to be given to critical comments. last year we set up a new procedure within the commission for systematically examining the conclusions to be drawn from cases dealt with by the ombudsman. i understand that we are clearly improving the analysis, the approval and therefore the collaboration with the ombudsman. to illustrate this follow-up, let me give two examples: first, as a result of the ombudsman's initiative, the commission has accepted, as from 1 july 2000, the candidates' access to the written evidence of their objections. we are not talking about empty words here, ladies and gentlemen, but about concrete facts. i would ask one of your honourable members to look a little closer at what is actually being done. the commission is being criticised in a very serious way. and it is very good that the commission is criticized when it does things that are not right; what happens is that generic criticism, criticizing the work of the commission because, in my opinion, it does not help anything, neither the commission itself nor the institutions as a whole nor the idea of europe in the citizens. you have to give criticism when you deserve it. we will try to improve in all cases and, of course, we will always study them, analyse them, evaluate them and take them into account. the other case i will mention is the freedom of expression of citizens and the abolition of the age limit for recruitment. the commission, for example, supports these guidelines politically, but these are matters which go beyond our own powers and concern the other institutions. they must be the subject of an interinstitutional agreement, for example to change the question of age in the recruitment of staff. we support it, we accept it and we are prepared to discuss it with the other institutions, but we have to see whether they agree to accept this approach of mr söderman, which we of course share. i shall now concentrate on mr perry's report on the code of good administrative behaviour. mr perry stresses the crucial role of these codes of good conduct in ensuring a high quality service for european citizens. they are important means of turning the right to good administration, enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, into an operational guide for the staff of the european institutions. the commission therefore welcomed the european ombudsman's inquiry into the existence of these codes. moreover, the commission cooperated closely with mr söderman in the preparation of his code of good administrative behaviour, which is here and which contains a large part - i will not say 100% but certainly many - of his suggestions and contributions. i would like to thank mr söderman again for his always positive attitude in trying to make proposals to improve things. we have taken full account of the provisions contained in the draft ombudsman's code among the various codes adopted by the european institutions and bodies. the commission's code is certainly the closest to the model proposed by the ombudsman, not only in terms of its content and legal nature, but also in that it is binding on our officials. there is one thing i would like to say to the honourable members: let us not confuse the elements. the white paper on good governance is much more than administrative reform. the administrative reform is under way, it is the responsibility of commissioner kinnock, and very important positive steps have already been taken in this area - and so far the honourable members have agreed with the commission in this assessment. we have to finish it. we're working on it. mr. kinnock is working very hard on it. but that's one thing, and good governance is another. the white paper on good governance is much more than administrative reform, it is an approach aimed at clarifying how to better collect, how to better approximate, how to better integrate different elements within the chain of responsibilities in our complex society. it is a problem that is not just a problem for the institutions of the european union, but for all our countries, for all the advanced democracies, a society that is becoming more and more complex, with increasingly real technological means that make information flow much better and open up new possibilities, and where, in addition, the forms of organisation of citizens are also becoming more and more complex. that is where the white paper is: how all this fits into the european institutional game. that's a lot more than administrative reform. we should not therefore confuse administrative reform with the white paper on good governance which the commission is preparing under the leadership of president prodi. like mr perry and mr söderman, the commission deplores - and i want to say this very clearly to mr perry - the existence of a great variety of codes of different legal nature. this does not contribute to legal coherence or clarity. however, before we take further steps, as we are asked to do in mr perry's report, we must bear in mind that we must look at what the codes of good conduct recently implemented or adopted - in the commission ten months ago, in the council last july, just before the summer - show, and therefore in our view it is still too early to draw conclusions about the reality of these new codes of good conduct. we will therefore be preparing a report at the end of the year, particularly on the commission's own code of conduct, which will have been in force for one year. but when we have enough information, the commission can then consider whether a legislative proposal for a horizontal regulation is really being prepared or not. we need more information to do this and therefore we are not taking a position on this now. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. however, i must be brief on this report, because article 195 of the treaty gives the commission only the power to deliver an opinion - which is not binding. but i think it's important that our opinion be heard. the first point is to congratulate mrs almeida garrett on her excellent work. i have also had the opportunity to speak on this matter in the committee on constitutional affairs and to stress that the current statute has worked well. the commission has opened investigations on the ombudsman's initiative - as i have just said - for example in the case of the code of good conduct, and in general the commission responds constructively and - i thank mr söderman for pointing this out - by respecting the deadlines for the ombudsman's requests for information. the committee on constitutional affairs proposes three amendments. as regards the removal of the exception on confidentiality for access to files, i have already had occasion to point out that the commission has never made use of this exception in the 20 requests for access submitted by the ombudsman. it is true that we might be tempted to adapt the law to the facts and accept the position adopted by the committee on constitutional affairs, but on the other hand, since everything has worked out well, we also have the right to ask ourselves whether it is really necessary to change this point. we must always be cautious on a sensitive issue, because of the role of the commission and the kind of issues it is dealing with at the moment, which, depending on the evolution of european construction, will be very varied and increasingly delicate. we could also have problems with the governments of the member states of the union. the structure of the european union, based on three pillars, means that the role of the commission, as well as the role of parliament itself, varies according to the pillar in question. the commission will therefore return to these questions in greater detail in the opinion which we are required to deliver and which we will shortly forward to parliament when it adopts a final position on the text adopted. as regards the abolition of the principle that officials' testimony is given on behalf of the administration to which they are attached, the commission is not dogmatic, but we consider it important that officials do not speak in a purely personal capacity but represent and present the facts and explanations of a matter for which they are responsible. they must otherwise comply with the obligations arising from their statutes. and i do want to point out that, as a former member of parliament, as well as a member of the commission, i fully share the position of the rapporteur, mrs almeida garrett, on the differences in political and administrative responsibilities and on the responsibility of the european parliament for what are political responsibilities, which are those that we have as commissioners and not just commissioners but as members of the other institutions. as regards access to documents from the member states, as i said a moment ago, it would be appropriate to be consistent with the new regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 on public access to documents. the principle of obtaining prior authorisation from the state is laid down in article 4 (5) of the regulation and in the framework agreement with parliament. declaration no 35 annexed to the final act of the treaty of amsterdam goes in the same direction. in conclusion, mr president, i would like to congratulate all the rapporteurs once again and to thank mr söderman for his very constructive work, which is very helpful to us, because criticism - and we should be very aware of this - is certainly a stimulus to improve every day and also provides solutions. we have already made progress on the code of good conduct, on infringement procedures, on the freedom of officials, and on other matters. in this connection, i would like to say to the honourable members that many things are objectionable, because nothing is perfect, but that when we go beyond that and criticise without foundation, criticism can even lose its own value or at least be weakened.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by saying that i am very pleased to be the rapporteur for this report, since i am convinced of the social significance of the committee on petitions of the european parliament. this is because the institution of citizens' petitions is really the most direct channel available to europeans to denounce both the gaps still existing in community legislation and the cases in which the obligations arising from directives and regulations, already adopted, are ignored, either because they are not applied or simply because they have not been transposed. the institution of the european ombudsman also plays a key role in this great task. i am also very pleased that there was a high degree of consensus among all the members of the committee in our debates and votes. the figures speak for themselves: the report contains 16 conclusions, all of which were adopted unanimously, as were the five amendments tabled after a few minor compromises. for all this i must express my gratitude to the whole committee and its secretariat. as the honourable members are familiar with the whole report, i shall confine myself to mentioning some of the aspects which i believe may be more novel, such as the extension of the right of petition of european citizens - in my view a fundamental right - also to natural or legal residents and to those who are registered in a member state; the recommendation that this right be given the importance it deserves in the planned debates, which will be incorporated into the potential convention on european integration; the clear need to give the committee on petitions of the european parliament the status it deserves, because of its social significance, derived from direct contact between individuals and the institution. this must be so because something must be done to break the knot of distance between the people and the very high european institutions which all the surveys highlight. and one solution is, of course, to increase the number of own-initiative reports, particularly on those subjects where there is a certain anxiety on the part of citizens to deepen their direct contact with the institutions. it also seems reasonable to try to open up channels through this institution to the legislative initiative that is incubated and born in the popular heart itself, a circumstance that usually highlights the existence of a serious deficiency. the commission's right to access all relevant interinstitutional documents, which are essential for the commission's important work, is once again being demonstrated. in this connection it is only right to remember and to thank the invaluable help which we have been constantly receiving from both the commission and the ombudsman. we cannot say the same of the council which continues to be missing. the institution of the petition requires at this stage - it is already very clear - an increase in the level of knowledge by citizens either through information and education or, more specifically, by computer. authentic guides are needed for expeditious and general use. this is a work in progress. all too often there is a certain apathy on the part of some public authorities - community, national, regional or local - which is common to all cases - in seeking just solutions to the problems raised. some reaction is necessary to this dire situation. at the very least, we must ask the presidency of this house to give publicity to this failure to solve the problems and the gross injustices suffered by certain sections of the european people. finally, i would like to remind you of the great importance of maximum personal contact between petitioners and the european parliament, through its committee on petitions, and of the excellent services of the european parliament's directorate-general for studies and stoa, for the effectiveness of the results of the work of this committee.

- mr president, mr commissioner, for reasons of time i shall refer only to the fruit juice directive. the commission proposal is good enough not to be amended. i should particularly like to applaud the introduction of the double definition of concentrated juices and fruit juices, because this helps to inform the consumer. that is why i must express my disagreement with amendment no 29, which deletes the commission's text, and support amendment no 30, which deals with the same subject in greater detail by referring to annex i. i must also express my total rejection of amendments nos 18, 19, 23 and 25. the first concerns the prohibition of the use of fungicides in post-harvest treatments. it should be noted that in europe fruit is collected in principle for the fresh market and only after selection on the basis of quality and size is it known which lots will go fresh and which lots will go for processing. the maximum residue limit for fresh fruit is already set in directive 97/41/ec, and that is based on rigorous studies that are deemed safe for the consumer. i think the same directive applies equally to juice, fresh fruit or home-made juice or packaged juice. in addition, post-harvest treatments are necessary to ensure optimal storage, transport and distribution conditions and - as i have already said here - the poison is the dose, not the substance itself. as regards the quality of water for adding to concentrates, we also have another directive, 98/93/ec, on the quality of water intended for human consumption, including the food industry. finally, amendment no 23 seeks to introduce a positive list of authorized substances and it is not logical to define more substances than those already authorized in directives 89/109/eec and 90/128/eec on materials and articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs, because this would prevent the juice industry from adapting quickly to technological progress.
- mr president, also for reasons of time i shall speak only of the juice proposal. as the speakers who have gone before me have said, we believe that the council proposal is a clear step forward in establishing that clear distinction between fresh fruit juice and concentrated juice. it is extremely positive because it adds complete information to the consumer about two products with clearly differentiated properties and production methods. in this sense, we cannot accept any amendment which would distort, in whole or in part, this distinction which is clearly set out in the council's text. we cannot accept the amendments which seek to eliminate the use of fresh fruit from the market, which would be the case if we allowed the prohibition of post-harvest treatment. the use of this fruit supposes and makes possible the production of a healthy product of high quality and food safety for the consumer, as well as the absorption of surplus agricultural raw materials, which avoids a great deterioration and environmental pollution. we shall therefore vote in favour of the council's proposal. we believe that most of the amendments tabled in committee with the aim of clarifying or improving the situation only add to the confusion.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this problem. two million girls are subjected to this terrible practice every year. today the european parliament must speak out for the plight of millions of women. we have tried to work in a consensus with all the political groups to draw up this report. we have consulted experts, experts, concerned governments and non-governmental organisations. our aim is to convince the communities that practice fgm of the need to eradicate this practice. the practice of total or partial female genital mutilation is rooted in a radically unfair conception of the role of women in a society that regards women as inferior citizens, whose control is in the hands of decision-makers, who in most cases are men. the defence of these traditions has a very clear limit for us. the limit is the defence of human rights. in the name of no tradition is it possible to accept that women are severely mutilated irreversibly for the rest of their lives. information, education and awareness are therefore essential to deal with the consequences that will be disastrous for women's lives, even if most of them do not know it. they're going to suffer an irreversible amputation, but they don't even know what the real consequences of this are. we have produced a report calling on the commission, the council and the member states to draw up a comprehensive strategy, not just of penalties but of all the areas affected by this issue: social, health, judicial, legal, political, etc. we have considered female genital mutilation as a serious attack on human rights, and on this basis we are calling for its logical consequence: the right of asylum for women who want to flee this situation, to take them in so that they can escape something that will be irreversible in their lives. according to the geneva convention and the refugee statute, persecution on grounds of sex must be grounds for granting asylum. there is no other persecution on the grounds of sex more clearly than this. one or the other could abdicate their political views. one or the other might abdicate his religious beliefs. but it's impossible to give up the sex you're born with. so if we are dealing with a brutal violation of fundamental rights, it is also essential that we give them the possibility of obtaining refugee status. i believe that the directive which the commission has just presented on the rules concerning the conditions to be met by persons residing in third countries who apply for refugee status is in this direction, and this will be very important. for us, this is a matter of principle and we cannot abandon this demand. the report also calls for the encouragement of external aid to those african countries which have adopted legislative and administrative measures prohibiting and sanctioning the practice. we also call on the european commission to work closely with the non-governmental organisations, which are making a huge effort on the ground, often with very few resources. we also call for the human rights clause to be used to make the fight against genital mutilation a priority action in relations with third countries, in particular with those countries which maintain a close relationship with the european union in the framework of the cotonou agreement. ladies and gentlemen, many women, thousands of african women, are waiting to hear what we have to say about this. it's not an african woman's problem. it is a problem for all of us, because it is a fundamental human rights problem. they are waiting and we must give them an urgent answer.

- madam president, this is the first of a series of directives which have to complete the first part of the timetable designed to introduce, in the longer term, a common asylum procedure and a uniform status for persons granted asylum. that is the spirit and the letter of the tampere agreements and the treaty of amsterdam, although the legal basis of the common asylum procedure and the statute would have to be discussed. i would like to point out very briefly to the commission some technical reservations which arise in connection with the proposal for a directive which we are considering. the first concerns the extension of the minimum standards for asylum procedures. i think that the proposal is too regulatory and that a common asylum procedure has nothing to do with a single procedure, the same procedure in all the member states. i am afraid that the commission may have gone beyond what was agreed in tampere. the second reservation concerns the commission's interest in regulating the time limits, because i wonder: is a long procedure a factor of rejection for applicants? that does not mean that we are in favour of a long procedure. but from a practical point of view, european countries with long terms - over two and three years - have high numbers of applicants, and countries such as spain, with much shorter terms, have much more modest statistics. the harmonization of deadlines is acceptable if it is due to a concern for the legal cleanliness of the procedure, but i fear that it may prove ineffective and cause fear for legal, material or political reasons. the third and final reservation is conceptual. i believe that the difficulties in making decisions uniformly are more in the definition of refugee than in the procedure for identifying him as such. concepts such as 'safe third country', 'persecution of third parties', 'persecution in case of conflict' or 'state or non-state persecution' are examples of some of these problems. perhaps, as i said before, we should deal with the definition rather than the procedure.

- mr president, noise pollution is a reality, and it is increasing in most countries of the european union. it is an attack not only on the ear but on the entire nervous system of citizens, and it often alters not only the character by means of irritability and insomnia, but also causes ailments of the auditory system. i come from a country in the south and the truth is that on countless occasions i have thought: 'who could shut up this lawn mower next to me! - mr. president, i think sometimes the perception of the world changes so much that reality itself becomes serious, ridiculous or irrelevant. i think this is what happens with noise. in fact, noise and the activities that cause noise - there is nothing more terrible than a machine opening a hole in the street, which does not let us live - are for the most part subsidiary, are the responsibility even of the local authorities, to the point that the most difficult thing is to agree on a time to close some cities and others, for example, bars, because they all want to compete. however, despite this, i believe that this directive is a failure to seek to homologate us all, which i believe is contrary even to cultural diversity. i have often said that in mediterranean time the day has 30 hours and in the nordic countries the day has 24. but in our time, a day has 30 hours, because time is elastic: the grandmother goes to bed at 10 and the grandson, the same day, goes to bed at 5 in the morning and the next day everything works because it's a miraculous time, a flexible time, as flexible as society wants it to be. so to try to reduce all that to a mathematical one is practically impossible. i would even say that it is a lack of authority on the part of the european union that people think that their private world is going to be subject to these directives. i would also remind you that we are facing a serious problem of land use planning. there's no point in playing music to appease the beasts. we have to deal with the problem head on and this is land use planning. i also disagree with some of the amendments, such as the one on competition. what does competition have to do with airport noise? the commission. mr president, i would like to thank you. i would like to begin by thanking mr lange and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection for a comprehensive and well-covered report. i would also like to thank you for the amendments that have been tabled. we have here a basis for reaching a swift and effective settlement. the emissions of air pollutants from normal motor vehicles have been regulated within the european union for more than three decades. as a result, emissions are now less than 10 percent of what they were before we put these limits in place. consequently, the relative importance of other emissions has increased. at the same time, we can say, as we do in the commission's auto-oil programme, that we see that the air quality problems in the community require further action. the proposal we are discussing today concerns emissions from engines used in lawn mowers, chainsaws, leaf blowers, pumps, generators and similar equipment. each year, some 25 million of these machines are produced worldwide. although the statistics are somewhat incomplete, it seems that these machines account for about 10 to 15% of total hydrocarbon emissions in the community. we have already heard this expressed in another way, namely that one hour of use of a chainsaw emits as much hydrocarbons as more than 2000 kilometres of driving with a modern passenger car. these emissions contribute to ozone formation, which is one of our hitherto unsolved air pollution problems. it is obvious that we must do something about the emissions from these types of machines. the type of products concerned by the proposal are sold for the most part on the world market. they are manufactured for more than 90% of the large companies operating on this market. the commission has found that the harmonisation of legislation has been an important element in facilitating the rapid introduction of legislation, provided, of course, that this can be achieved with a high level of environmental ambition. the only legislation in this area is that of the united states. we believe that it meets the environmental needs well and it has also had a major influence on the formulation of our proposal. at the same time, i must draw your attention to the fact that it is not only these large companies on the world market that exist, but that there are also companies that do not operate on that market. although these companies account for a small part of the total production, the products are often specialised for limited uses. companies are often small and therefore have limited resources to develop the technology necessary to meet the emission limits. we have therefore proposed certain special exemptions for these products and companies, and these are the same kinds of exemptions that exist in the american legislation. in my view, the commission's proposal is a great example of a 'win/win' situation in that we are meeting the needs of industry while, by not having to split up industry's resources on different legislation, we have achieved environmental gains that would not otherwise have been possible. the commission can accept amendments which allow member states to label products which pass stage 2 and to use economic instruments to stimulate production and sales of such products even before the mrls become mandatory. the commission also accepts in principle an earlier date of introduction for stage 2, but opposes an earlier date of introduction for stage 1, as it would create an unreasonable pressure on small producers who do not sell their products on the world market. the commission also opposes changes to the definition of small producers. as regards the so-called averaging and banking system, we can understand some of the questions that have been raised about how it should be used in practice. we do, however, consider it an important element in the attempt to achieve harmonization in this area. if it is removed, european legislation will differ from american legislation. the reason for introducing such a system is that for technical reasons it is difficult to pass the step 2 values for some products. what those products actually are varies from manufacturer to manufacturer. in order to achieve the necessary environmental impact, it is important not to exclude products that could actually meet the requirements. through averaging and banking, we have introduced a flexible system that puts the administrative burden on the producers who want to use it, a system that has a good environmental impact. on the other hand, if the possibility of exempting certain products is used, there is a risk of drastically reducing the environmental impact, since these exemptions are not compensated, as is the case with the averaging and banking system. we must also bear in mind that the exceptions we are talking about are exclusively those fitted with two-stroke engines, which are the most polluting engines. the commission therefore wishes to stress the importance of maintaining this instrument in the legislation and opposes the amendments concerned. at the same time, i would like to emphasize that the important thing is not the averaging and banking system as such, but the flexibility, the harmonization and the environmental benefits that the system brings. exemptions for certain types of equipment should therefore only be accepted after a careful analysis of the environmental and other consequences. for this reason, the commission is opposed to the introduction of an exemption at this stage, but can accept that the possibility is opened up by the use of a committee procedure in the future. we also oppose amendments which exclude the use of two-stroke engines for generators and snowploughs. the commission is prepared to study the need for further legislation in this area, especially with regard to particulate emissions from two-stroke engines, and would like to coordinate this with the corresponding request concerning particulate emissions from motorcycles and mopeds. the commission can accept, or in principle accept, amendments nos 1, 10, 11, 13, 14, 18 to 28 and amendment no 30. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12, 15 and 17, but is open to considering solutions that can achieve flexibility, harmonisation and environmental gains. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 4, 5, 9, 16 and 29.

commission. – first of all i thank parliament's responsible committees and their rapporteurs. these proposals are the final product of a long discussion process initiated by the commission ten years ago. the concept proposed by the commission is to revert the ecsc assets to the remaining communities upon expiry of the treaty and to use the resources produced from these assets for the sole purpose of funding research in the sectors related to the steel and coal industry. this concept has been discussed with industry, the social partners, the european parliament and the member states. eventually all stakeholders endorsed it. the member states have been very closely associated in this discussion, which is completely justified since together they are the owners of the ecsc assets. if there were no agreement on the member states' side these assets would simply revert to them, in line with the principles of international law. the european council has provided us with detailed guidance on the subject, firstly at the amsterdam european summit in 1997 and more recently at the nice intergovernmental conference last year. on this latter occasion the member states adopted a protocol attached to the nice treaty which details the arrangements regarding the expiry of this treaty. the commission is bound to respect the decisions taken in nice. it is in this context that the commission has to address your amendments. you have requested that all three decisions should be adopted through the codecision procedure. i regret to say that the commission cannot accept this request. in the case of the framework decision, the decisional procedure has already been agreed upon by the intergovernmental conference in nice. for the two decisions on the financial and research guidelines respectively, the commission has followed the same line as for other, similar proposals in research policy or regarding our financial regulation. for example, the specific programmes of the european union research and development framework programme are submitted to parliament for its opinion, as is the case for the financial regulation. if the commission departed from this line it would not be consistent. on the other hand, i would like to stress that parliament's involvement in the proposed arrangements is much stronger than it was under the ecsc treaty. as regards the budgetisation of the funds after the expiry of the treaty, the commission agrees that the resources and the expenditure will be incorporated into the general ec budget. however, they will consist of earmarked revenue which, according to our interinstitutional agreement, is not covered by the financial perspectives. therefore we could not go along with the proposal to simply incorporate the resources and the expenditure into chapter iii, internal policies of the budget, and to delete any reference to earmarked revenue. you also suggested that within two years, by 24 july 2004, the commission should make proposals to enlarge the post-ecsc research fund into a european research foundation covering all research sectors over and above steel and coal. indeed, i am aware that such a foundation has been suggested to us on several occasions. i have noticed that the corresponding amendment refers to the draft decision on the research guidelines only. from a legal point of view the research guidelines lay down the technical provisions related to the implementation of the research activities, but they cannot cope with an issue of an institutional nature like this one. more generally speaking, the proposal to set up a research foundation has already been made to the commission on several occasions, in particular in the course of the discussion in the council, but it was rejected. the first reason is that the management of the ecsc funds after 23 july 2002 will involve three aspects: firstly, the management of the ecsc commitments existing on that day until their expiry – and in some cases they will continue for 20 years or more; secondly, the financial management of the ecsc assets; and thirdly, the management of the research fund financed from the resources produced from this financial management. the three elements are therefore closely interlinked and it is not possible to isolate any one of them. furthermore it is clear that a majority of member states oppose the implementation of the research fund through a foundation. finally, the very small amount involved in the proposed research fund would not justify the creation of a foundation. therefore the most sensible solution is that the commission, which has managed all ecsc operations so far, should continue to manage them all. finally, i have taken note with particular interest of your request that environmental considerations should be given priority in the operations of this coal and steel research fund. i am pleased to say that current research projects financed under the ecsc treaty already put much emphasis on cleaner technologies, energy saving and the protection of the environment in both the coal and steel sectors. i can assure you that we will continue to attach great importance to these considerations, as well as the issue of safety at work, in the research guidelines which we are now proposing. to conclude, let me answer mr mombaur's question on the specific issue concerning the legal basis of the three-year commission proposals. as you know, they are based on a protocol annexed to the nice treaty and we will now have to reflect on how to deal with the uncertainty surrounding the entry into force of the treaty. the commission's services are currently exploring this issue and considering alternative scenarios. so the answer is that we will have to continue to look at that particular issue. thank you once again for the careful analysis of the commission proposals, your contributions to this debate and for your attention.

- mr president, i think mrs roth-behrendt has expressed parliament's concerns on her central point. parliament does not object to the commission setting up all the consultative bodies it wants, meeting with all the non-governmental organisations it wants, consulting everyone on the internet, talking to all the citizens in person. we're fine with it, and we should probably do the same. what concerns us is the second part of the white paper, namely the proposals for improving community rules. the treaties of the european union - as mrs roth-behrendt has pointed out - are based on the principle of the separation of powers. there is an article 6 of the treaty which refers to national constitutional principles. all national legislation is based on the principle of the separation of powers, whereby legislative powers are vested in bodies representing the people. the european institutions have two bodies of popular representation: the directly elected parliament and the council, which is made up of ministers who are responsible to the national parliaments. the role of the commission of the european communities is to be the community executive - and we in parliament support and reinforce the commission's claim to be a genuine community executive. but if the commission enters into the regulatory field and intends to assume powers or competences which have been or should be conferred on the european parliament by the treaties, in this area - as mr swoboda and mrs roth-behrendt have said - the commission must be in close contact with parliament. in particular, i find mr prodi's suggestion that the commission could submit proposals to the laeken european council on improving community rules without waiting for parliament's opinion to be given, dangerous. i hope that the commission, before submitting any proposal to the laeken european council on the improvement of community rules, will make close contact with parliament so that it can hear our views and thus convey to the laeken european council the concerns and interests of parliament on this matter.

- mr president, europe is experiencing a tension between a low demographic and a real demand for labour from its labour market on the one hand and a population wary of the phenomenon of immigration on the other. in the face of this situation, policy makers can react in two ways: by using citizens' fears to their own advantage, at least in the short term, or by trying to manage the different faces of immigration in the best possible way, courageously explaining the reasons for this phenomenon, the benefits it brings to our societies, its most difficult aspects and the necessary policies. first, we had some examples here this morning. the commission has fortunately been clearly in the latter category with both communications, and we can only congratulate the commissioner and congratulate ourselves on that. it has also done so - and i want to stress this here - in accordance with the agreements and mandates of the european council in tampere. i can agree with my colleague mr evans on asylum, but i want to focus on the few minutes i have on the communication on immigration and the report. you both define some clear line to follow. the communication and the report speak of the external and internal causes of immigration, of the need for policies of co-development and a new partnership with the countries of origin, of a common european legislative framework to organise entry - in a fair, transparent and clear way -, residence and integration - which for me means rights. and only then does he talk about tackling, once these rules are in place, illegal immigration, because we need legal channels to do that. it speaks, finally, and we'll discuss it in detail here when we see the legislative proposals, to establish the new immigration policies of the 21st century for a new society, for a new economy, which cannot be the reissue of the guest worker policies of the industrial societies of the 1960s. i hope that the council will also be among the politicians who want to tackle this matter clearly and courageously. i hope so, and i say so knowing that we speak with reason and also with heart on immigration - and i say so knowing that i am being listened to by citizens of birth and of reception, invited by my colleague pedro aparicio, who are here today and who have hope in this debate. parliament will try to rise to the occasion and, although it is sometimes difficult for us, we will try, as the ppe-de group has not done in relation to asylum, to give strong support to this commission communication and we hope, mr president, that the laeken european council will be able to restart a strong political dynamic which will lead us to tackle this necessary common immigration policy.
- mr president, for the first time in this parliament we are talking in differentiating terms about economic immigration and asylum, which can be considered as a good thing by the european commission in its respective communications, because it will help us to organize and clarify the debate. this was a requirement of parliament and it has been fulfilled. i would like to make two brief remarks on the issues which are the subject of this debate: firstly, the migratory movements which are taking place towards europe are the result of a mass flight of citizens who do not find in their countries the minimum conditions for survival and who are being tragically exploited by the organised mafias which traffic in them. it's been said here. the cases of dover and our andalusian coast are clear examples. but illegal immigration of this calibre is the breeding ground for social rejection of this immigrant population and for labour exploitation of it, in addition to the outbreaks of xenophobia and racism that are occurring in some parts of europe. this problem must be solved through close cooperation and collaboration with the countries of origin, or else any policy in this field is doomed to failure. community programmes such as phare, tacis or meda, or the immigration and asylum action plans themselves, are absolutely necessary. but at the same time, and i want to emphasize this, we must also demand, and demand it politically, that the countries of origin take advantage of their natural and human resources, and very especially that they guarantee political and social stability so that their citizens have confidence in their governments. it is therefore a shared responsibility and not just that of the member states or the european union itself. countries such as morocco, algeria and tunisia are examples of what i have just described. moreover, in connection with the communication on the common asylum procedure, the main problem facing the member states is that of asylum seekers with unfounded requests, and the commission and this parliament must endeavour to remove the major obstacles to homogeneous solutions between the member states. i therefore do not think it appropriate to speak of a single procedure, which is different from the mandate contained in the treaty of amsterdam, which speaks of a common asylum procedure. it's not the same thing. in addition, concepts such as 'persecution of third parties', 'persecution in the event of conflict' or 'persecution on the basis of gender' are not clarified in the communication or in the evans report, for example, because the difficulty sometimes lies more in defining the concept of refugee than in the procedure for identifying him. we are on the right track: cooperation, solidarity, legislative clarity and realism in the face of a phenomenon such as immigration and asylum, which concerns many of us, are the necessary prerequisites for tackling one of the great challenges facing the european union in this new century. - mr president, at this point the european institutions and especially this parliament are fully aware that, given the complexity and transcendence of the subject before us today, a legislative programme is needed which will only be effective within the framework of a common and coordinated european approach. there are broad overlaps between the commission's communication and the reports we are discussing today. we need to develop a more proactive policy, one that recognises that the migratory pressure is bound to continue and that orderly immigration can bring benefits to europe, to the migrants themselves and also to their countries of origin. we aim to improve the management of migration flows in close cooperation with countries of origin and transit, by strengthening the fight against illegal immigration and by combating the criminal sectors involved, while guaranteeing the rights of victims. a more open and flexible policy is needed which, together with greater coordination of policies to reduce migratory pressures and strengthen border controls, could lead to a reduction in illegal immigration, which would favour those who really need the protection afforded by refuge and asylum. we must maintain these levels of protection at all costs, as provided for in the geneva convention, because this is also a sign of european identity which we are all proud of. i encourage commissioner vitorino to continue his efforts and the timetable he has set and i encourage the council to rise to the occasion in laeken and to fulfil the commitments made in tampere. it is time to take concrete decisions and not to make ambiguous, balanced statements. european citizens expect and need it.

commission. – i should like to begin the commission's contribution myself and then at the end of the discussion ask commissioner nielson to say something about the humanitarian situation in which he has been actively involved because of his responsibility for echo. if i have to leave before the end of the discussion it is not for lack of appreciation of the importance of what we are discussing – i believe this issue is going to dominate the international agenda for the next few months – but because i have to attend an important meeting before the eu-russia summit with the deputy-premier of the russian federation to discuss the modalities for beginning discussions on a common european economic area. we will try to agree the terms of reference of our work this evening before our summit with president putin tomorrow. there will be other reports on the troika visit that i took part in last week with the foreign minister of belgium, which holds the presidency, and with the foreign minister of spain – the next presidency – which demonstrated our commitment to the issues we were discussing. with my friend and colleague mr solana we went to pakistan, iran, saudi arabia, egypt and syria, all in the space of four-and-a-half action-packed, sleep-free days and nights. i should just like to say two or three words about that visit and make two or three points about the political situation in afghanistan, leaving the humanitarian issues, which are of such compelling importance, to commissioner nielson. then i would like to say a word about a draft regulation which the commission has today adopted. the main purposes of the troika visit were three-fold. first of all, we wanted to make the point clearly to the islamic countries we were visiting that the campaign against terrorism is not a campaign of the west against islam. it is not a campaign of europe and north america against the poorer countries of the globe. it is a campaign of decent governments everywhere against those who would try to make their political point through murder and mayhem. it is a fight, in my judgment, between those who stand up in favour of civilisation, of a number of different religious bases and those who represent the forces which have always been opposed to civilised values. we made that point strongly in every country we went to. for me, it is very important to recognise that if we are to make the point around the world that human rights are universally valid, including the right not to be murdered by terrorists – if we are to make that point successfully around the world – it is very important for us not to give the impression that we have a monopoly of virtue, that we in europe are perfect when it comes to talking about these matters. it is also exceptionally important for us not to concede that human rights bear a different weight according to the continent you are in. it feels exactly the same to be tortured, whatever sort of country you are in. it is exactly the same if you are locked up as a journalist or an editor because you disagree with the government, whatever country you are in. those sort of rights are universally valid. it seems to me that we dilute the integrity of our argument if we give the impression that somehow different civilisations have fundamentally different approaches to human rights. the second point we were seeking to make is that out of the appalling events, out of the atrocities of 11 september, we must hope that it is possible for some good to come. adversity sometimes produces an opportunity to be constructive, positive and to build better for the future. one thing we said in pakistan, iran and elsewhere is that we have a chance now – taking account of the awful things that have happened – of opening some doors and windows which have been closed for too long. thirdly, we say that it is a cliché, a truism when people talk about 11 september to say – rather like the fall of the berlin wall – nothing will ever be the same again. but it is actually true. nothing will ever be quite the same again. one way in which we have to make sure that nothing is ever the same again is to try to ensure this time that multilateralism, that international cooperation, works a great deal more effectively in the wake of those awful events than it perhaps has since the 1940s. that is the challenge to us: to make sure that when we discuss conventions against terrorism in the un, everybody signs them and everybody implements them. those are the sort of practical challenges that we are going to face for weeks and months and years in the future when these events are no longer on the front pages of the newspapers. those were three points that we – the only four-person troika in the business – were making insistently at each of our stops. concerning the political situation in afghanistan, which we were able to discuss both in pakistan and in iran, there were of course different views of the situation. in iran, for example, there are very strong views about the taliban. that is not surprising given the number of iranian diplomats that were killed three or so years ago by the taliban in afghanistan. there is a general agreement that the political situation in afghanistan remains extremely fluid. there are reports from neighbouring countries that the taliban are in terminal decline. there are also reports that speak of some taliban military successes and of a return to what passes for a sort of grim normality in kabul. the taliban continue to show no real sign of being ready to give up osama bin laden or forcefully to encourage his voluntary departure from the country. the opposition northern alliance has declared itself ready and willing to assist the united states and international coalition efforts. following the death of commander masood on 8 september – and i know he made an important visit to parliament not long ago – there is greater uncertainty as to the cohesion of this alliance. what is certain is that no wholly military solution is possible in afghanistan. in both pakistan and iran, where as i said there are very different views of the situation in afghanistan, there was agreement that only a broad-based government made up of representatives of all factions and ethnic groups in the country, taking account of the security concerns of neighbouring countries, can begin the process of restoring afghanistan to normality and pave the way for reconstruction. the means of doing this may be through the loya jirga or grand assembly mechanism. it would be for the afghan people to decide what kind of loya jirga process they want and what role different political personages might play in such a development. i repeat that there is a shared perception of what the outcome should be: a broad-based government. how you get to that broad-based government is incomparably more difficult to work out, but there is also a shared perception that the world outside – even in the shape of the united nations – cannot impose a political settlement on afghanistan. we can and should aim to facilitate a political settlement, and having facilitated it not then walk away. we have to make sure that a better government, which will emerge from that sad, embittered country will be able to count on the long-term support of the international community to rebuild from the ruin of the medieval ferocity which has been unleashed on afghanistan for the last few years. i should like to make one other point. we have in the commission today adopted a draft regulation on specific measures directed against certain persons and entities with a view to combating international terrorism. the draft proposal includes all those individuals and organisations potentially related to the 11 september attack covered by the us executive order issued by president bush last week. but it takes the form of a framework regulation which could serve as the vehicle for a wider campaign against terrorist financing. there is a considerable urgency to this regulation, which is put forward on the basis of article 308, for reasons which i am sure i do not have to set out for parliament. in these circumstances we would be extremely grateful if parliament could consider an emergency procedure, if possible completing the consultation process during this week's part-session. we would then be able to put the draft regulation to the general affairs council next monday. i know that the president of the commission will be writing to you on these lines, madam president. we understand the difficulties. we do not want in any way to curtail examination of this important measure; but if it could be done very rapidly it would send the right signals. it would be an opportunity to demonstrate that in exceptional circumstances the community institutions can act with real despatch. not only would we thereby signal the strength of our determination to rise to the challenges presented by the 11 september attack, but we would show that the eu institutions are able to respond to crisis situations. i will finish my remarks with that point. so far, in the proposals brought forward by my friend and colleague, mr vitorino, a couple of weeks ago, we have demonstrated that though we are sometimes the butt of people's humour about the lack of speed of our reactions, when it really matters we are able to react very rapidly and comprehensively and we are able to demonstrate in practice what multilateralism should mean. if there is any institution in the world, if there is any group of countries in the world that can demonstrate the benefits of multilateralism, of arguing about fish quotas or budgets, rather than murdering one another, it is the european union. that seems to me to give us a particular responsibility to show leadership in the coming weeks and months and i hope we will be able to do so with this regulation this week. which are the ones who have to make the big investments in the end - or the regions to plan their major projects not in the national interest but in the interest of transeuropean interconnection and, therefore, with a cross-border vision. that is why i said that this effort of transeuropean networks is really the first rational proposal of its kind since the romans. this will be possible by providing co-financing, the ceiling of which is now 10%. it could be as high as 20% if the proposals made here for some particularly important and costly projects are approved, but also because being part of these transeuropean networks makes it easier for the european bank to finance them. finally, i would say to mr bouwman that in this new proposal we have incorporated not only the north-south axes, which were the ones that were mainly included in the other transeuropean networks, because they were the ones that were most needed, but also the east-west axes, especially the basic paris-stuttgart-vienna axis, which will eventually have to link up with budapest; we have also incorporated the danube and its better communication with the rhine, making it possible to create a south-east-north-west axis that would cross the whole of the union. but there is no doubt that the 2004 review, when the new countries of the union will also be integrated, will further emphasise this east-west component, without losing the north-south component, which must always be maintained, in any case.

question no 27 by mr manuel medina ortega (h-0700/01) subject: illegal immigration into the european union via morocco what measures will the commission propose to regulate illegal immigration via morocco and to prevent a repetition of the dramatic events that took place this summer in community waters?
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr medina ortega, cooperation with morocco on immigration is part of the action plan approved by the council at the end of 1999. we are the first to stress that this cooperation must be based on a broad and comprehensive approach which integrates not only the issues of justice and home affairs but also the relationship between foreign policy, development policy and economic assistance policy. in the context of relations between the european union and morocco, we have identified three key areas for debate: the area of economic and social cooperation, the area of management of migratory flows and the area of preventing and combating illegal immigration, including transit immigration from sub-saharan african countries. the agreement on these three priorities will now be developed at the meeting of the council of the association agreement between the european union and morocco scheduled for 9 october. we are counting on the new budget line created in 2001, line b-7-6-67, which has an allocation of eur 10 million for 2001, to develop concrete actions, and which was in fact largely earmarked for concrete cooperation actions with morocco. the question of relations with morocco must be seen in the broader context of the relaunch of the barcelona process. we recognize that progress in this process is very limited. we are fully aware that the international situation and our specific relationship with morocco require a relaunch of the barcelona process. this is also the intention of the future spanish presidency, which has already been announced. the commission believes that the relaunch of the barcelona process will require the adoption of a regional programme on justice and home affairs which will include immigration issues but which should also cover other issues such as, for example, strengthening the rule of law, good governance and judicial cooperation.
- i appreciate your explanations, but i would like to stress the urgency of the matter. this summer, as far as we know, 30 or 40 people have drowned as a result of the operation of these networks of illegal immigration. it is estimated that last year four or five thousand people drowned trying to cross the space that separates the moroccan territory from spain. i would therefore like to ask, commissioner, whether there is any possibility that, without waiting for the outcome of the barcelona process and the wider renegotiations on association, a very practical agreement can be reached on police and control matters so that the moroccan authorities can prevent this killing, which is already taking on a really dangerous character, from continuing.
commission. - mr president, i fully share the view of mr medina that we are facing a human tragedy, that we cannot wait for the ideal solution, that we must walk the path. but to make the road, both sides must agree on the mechanisms to be applied. this is something that has not yet reached a point that i consider acceptable. we therefore have high hopes that at the association council next week we will be able to make progress in identifying concrete mechanisms for cooperation, including police cooperation in border control. i would like to stress, however, that in 2001 a very substantial part of the budget line i have mentioned was devoted to cooperation measures with morocco, increasing the administrative capacity of that country in dealing with illegal immigration, which is not just a human problem: it is a political problem, especially for spain. but it is also a problem for morocco, because morocco is today a transit country where a large number of sub-saharan illegal immigrants are staying, with very damaging social consequences for moroccan society. i believe that from next week we can have better prospects for cooperation, as i hope will be the result of the association council meeting.

commission - mr president, my answer is as follows. the commission is considering the initiation of a procedure under article 226 of the treaty in respect of finland, which extends the procedure initiated in 1998. this matter will be discussed at a commission meeting in the near future. the new procedure is likely to also include problems of application of directive 83/183 on tax relief for the transfer of residence. at the same time, the commission has written to all member states to draw their attention to the court of justice judgment mentioned in mr vatanen's question, namely the gomez-valente judgment of 22 february 2001, and the commission shares the honourable member's view that this is a judgment with implications outside the context of the dispute and paving the way for a treatment of second-hand vehicles more in line with the requirements of the european internal market. the commission notes, however, that the procedure for enforcing the abovementioned judgment must remain independent of any other procedure it has initiated or intends to initiate.
commission. – first of all i should like to thank mr vatanen for his very kind remarks. i feel the weight of all those motorists in finland on my shoulders – a very heavy load indeed. one complicating factor is that this is an area which has not yet been harmonised in the european union. the commission's legal basis for its actions is article 90 of the treaty on the one hand, which prohibits tax discrimination, and on the other hand two directives adopted in 1983. article 90 gives the court of justice the opportunity for abundant jurisprudence. since interpretations of the judgments of the court are not always unanimous, it is time to create a synthesis of all the various interpretations in order to determine clearly our future action. that need for a synthesis is one of the reasons that led me to include in the commission's working programme for this year a communication on motor vehicle taxation. it is my intention that this communication, which i hope will appear around the end of this year or the beginning of next year, will cover all the problems in connection with vehicle taxation and vehicle pricing, so that we can take a broader approach to them and settle the problem in finland to which mr vatanen has referred. i hope that will be to his satisfaction.

- question no 48 by mrs luisa morgantini (h-0747/01) subject: mont blanc tunnel and railway construction we're announcing the reopening of the mont blanc tunnel in the next few months. meanwhile, road traffic places a heavy burden on communities in terms of health, economy and environment. these considerations apply particularly to mountain areas, where the pollution rate is three to six times higher than in other regions. what concrete measures have been taken to accurately assess the cost of road transport, taking into account socioeconomic and environmental aspects? what initiatives have been taken to adopt, following the example of switzerland and austria, specific taxes to finance the repair of the socio-environmental damage thus caused and to make rail transport, which remains rich in opportunities, economically competitive?
the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the alpine regions is a very good one. considerable work has been carried out through a number of commission studies and the 4th and 5th framework research programmes, examining transport expenditure in alpine and other regions, including projects on alpine transport information systems or european multimodal strategic modelling and the ongoing alp-net project. the problem was also addressed in the reports of the high-level group, which parliament endorsed by its resolution, contained in the costa report on infrastructure charging, to which i referred earlier. the new commission white paper on common policy not only provides current estimates of road transport costs but also considers it a priority to solve the transport problems in the alpine regions through a wide range of measures to which i have referred earlier. in this context, we are considering the possibility of creating a system which would allow pricing to be tested as soon as possible in sensitive mountain areas such as the alps. these initiatives should not only have a possible impact on the current volume of traffic, but should also encourage the use of less polluting vehicles and thus help to reduce the negative effects of traffic on human health and on the fauna and flora of the regions concerned, and should also allow for cross-financing, which i also mentioned a moment ago. we believe, mr president, as i have said on many occasions, that the modal rebalancing of transport in europe is a key element not only for the quality of life of our citizens, for the protection of the environment, but also for economic development, because without this modal rebalancing we will be faced with a situation of collapse of our road networks and of our transport axes.
