- the agenda calls for statements by the council and the commission on the conclusions of the united nations conference on racism. i call mr michel, president of the council.
mr president, the world conference against racism, in conjunction with the united nations-sponsored international decade of the world's indigenous people, has been a unique opportunity to consider the challenges and dangers faced by these peoples and all stateless nations. unfortunately, i cannot agree with the optimistic view expounded by mr michel, though i recognise willingly the very important role played by him. i was in durban on that special occasion, and so i can give evidence to this house of a very insidious threat to indigenous peoples running through the provisional agenda of the durban summit, paragraph 27 of which states: "the use of the term 'indigenous people' in the world conference against racism... cannot be construed as having any implications as to rights under international law". through that paragraph the united nations summit tried to exclude all these peoples from the right to self-determination recognised by the united nations itself and international covenants. in response to such inadmissible discrimination and intolerance, the ngo forum in durban denounced very strongly the new expression of neo-colonialists that will, in the long run, provoke the decimation of the cultures and civilisations of these vulnerable peoples. this insidious action was prepared at the conference against racism with a view to the future. it looks to the future, not to the past. as the ngo final declaration clearly suggests, structural racism in the past, current manifestations of neo-colonialism and the denial of the fundamental right to self-determination lie at the root of indigenous suffering.
- the united nations conference on racism is of particular relevance today in these turbulent times, when bloodshed is being spoken and acted upon in the name of a clash of civilizations. we are witnessing armed conflicts that have their origin and their sustenance in racial or ethnic clashes and we are hearing, in shock, unacceptable claims, both in their content and their origin, about the superiority of some civilizations over others. i would therefore like to congratulate in a very special way the president-in-office of the council of ministers, mr louis michel, for his decisive efforts in the final success of the durban conference, in which i participated on behalf of this parliament. his actions made clear to the world the european union's unwavering position against racism and xenophobic attitudes. without ignoring the social, political and economic problems which racial discrimination causes in europe, i would like to focus on one aspect - the development perspective - which has been somewhat forgotten in the wake of recent events and also during the conference, because of the conflict in the middle east and the seriousness of events there, as well as the recognition of the suffering caused by the historical experiences of europe and the perversity of slavery and the slave trade, the practice of which we now consider a crime against humanity. most ethnic conflicts, with thousands of victims and deplorable human conditions, take place in developing countries, mainly in africa. i therefore believe that the success of this conference will depend on whether we are able today to put into practice everything that was stated in the final declaration. we call on the commission in this resolution to provide financial support to the administrations of developing countries for the implementation of national action plans for the elimination of all forms of discrimination, as agreed there. forums are created, observatories are created, observatories in africa, provincial observatories, regional observatories. we also ask for support for the united nations, so that they can follow up the results of durban, so that the fight against racism remains on the international agenda until its eradication. i think it is important that we continue to work to bring about what this declaration is about. the united states should not have left the conference, but it was not the first time it had left, it had already left on other occasions, so it was not a major event. the important thing is that we are able to make the european parliament, with one voice, repeat its message in a key way, to journalists, to the media, against racism and in favour of equality and integration.
counsel. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to reply to the speakers quickly with a series of considerations and perhaps with a series of more precise information. first of all, i quite agree with what mr van hecke has said, i quite agree with him that when such a conference is organised, i think that it is necessary to ensure that it is thoroughly prepared. i think that we have indeed paid a heavy price to a certain extent for the fact that a number of shortcomings were felt in the run-up to this conference. i believe that, to use a term which you are familiar with, there were still far too many leftovers in durban, which obviously made the task extraordinarily difficult. so i think that this preparation is, of course, extremely important. the second point i want to make about this type of conference is that i am not sure that the desire to draw up a document which deals in detail with each particular situation is not a lack of effort, that it does not ultimately impoverish the final document in substance. i think that if we had had a more compact text, with a number of principles that could be applied in a generic way, we could probably have had a stronger text. and one might even ask whether the european union could not perhaps imagine at some point doing this exercise, that is to say, drawing from this work in durban the substantive backbone which would make it easier to decline in all our states the work which was done in durban. because, finally, i've heard several speakers ask the question: "okay, there was durban, what happened after that?" i must say, however, ladies and gentlemen, that the question of what happens afterwards depends first of all on the states. as mrs boumediene has said, i believe that if a state wants to apologize, to express remorse or regret, it is ultimately up to it to know how far it can go. secondly, i think that each state can very easily, on the basis of the work done in durban, develop a specific action programme for each state based on these principles and on what was agreed in durban to combat racism. i have heard the commissioner say quite explicitly that the commission is also considering very concrete things. i think the commission has been working on this for a very long time. so i think there is a follow-up, there will be a follow-up after durban if we want it. in fact, it is the usual question of political will. i would also like to take this opportunity of course to thank the speakers for the overly flattering assessment they have expressed of me. i believe i was surrounded by very competent people from the commission, the council and of course my own delegation. i also had the opportunity to count on all the representatives of the various european countries. we have done, i think, a job that it made sense for us to do. i think it was perfectly normal. i would perhaps like to respond to a number of comments on what is missing from the documents. yes, there are obviously a number of points missing, of course. for example, why was the caste system not mentioned in the documents adopted in durban? i know that this is a matter of particular importance for the european union and i share that concern. as you know, the european union is concerned about the persistent discrimination around the world, so it was only natural that we should also express this concern. we have therefore followed the development of this problem closely and have supported a paragraph introduced by switzerland, in particular, which deals with this problem, this text referring to discrimination based on ancestry and occupation, which describes precisely the discrimination suffered by the untouchables in several countries of the world. unfortunately, despite all the efforts of the european union and other countries, especially south america, it has not been possible to get india's agreement on such a paragraph. the basis of this conference is consensus, as you know, and so the text has been deleted, and i regret that. but there are also realities to consider. you can't have it all. someone spoke very rightly, because it is a concern that is very personal to me, about the problem of the death penalty. as you know, the abolition of the death penalty is one of the priorities of the european union. i think it is good that we are recalling this, and we are trying to use all the opportunities that arise at international level to advance the debate on this point. this was the case at this conference. the european union supported a paragraph in the action programme referring to racial discrimination in the application of the death penalty. but after the united states had strongly opposed it during the preparatory process, this paragraph was also rejected by several countries, especially asian ones, for lack of time to negotiate more in depth, and therefore in the absence of consensus, it was not possible to retain this paragraph here either. i am of course quoting these examples to convince you that your concerns were translated, were expressed there in durban, but unfortunately we could not get everything. perhaps a word about the behaviour of ngos throughout the conference. as was stressed in the documents adopted in durban, civil society, and therefore ngos, have an important role to play in the fight against racism. this is why the ngo forum held prior to the intergovernmental conference was of particular importance to the european union. this is why, i believe, the european commission funded a large number of participants in this forum. unfortunately, although it gave rise to interesting debates, including one in which i took part, which i found very interesting, the forum was conducted in a process which was sometimes dubious and sometimes not democratic at all. extremist organisations seem to have monopolized this discussion space, forcing states to ignore the conclusions of this forum. some ngos, such as amnesty international, human rights watch and fidh, have also dissociated themselves from these results. moreover, it must be said that the certain aggressiveness and the reprehensible verbal violence shown by certain ngos raise the question of the sometimes unconditional support that the european union, but also the member states - in my own country's case - give to these organisations. i think it will also be necessary to engage with them in a discussion of their accountability for their representativeness and the limits of their responsibilities. i have already had the opportunity to say that i have very good relations with most ngos, and i also recognize that they have a specific role to play. i have just heard mrs boumediene use a rather subversive term - with all due respect, madam - but we may differ fundamentally. i am not prepared, as a democratically elected politician, to give up my prerogative of assuming political responsibility to the citizen. i am elected, so the citizen can punish me, that is what i call responsibility, and i must also be accountable to the citizen: these are, in the end, my two duties. i am therefore not prepared to let this prerogative be taken away from me because the day this mechanism of political accountability no longer exists, it will mean that we are no longer in a democracy. and that i cannot accept. one of the subjects i wanted to raise - and i believe mr sylla has mentioned it - is that of discrimination based on sexual preference, which is one of the many forms of discrimination. the european union was in favour of highlighting the many forms of discrimination suffered by certain categories of people. this concept is well established in the texts. however, when it came to defining the possible sources of these multiple forms of discrimination, it was not possible to introduce concepts of importance to the european union such as discrimination based on sexual orientation. this idea has met with strong opposition in some countries, as you can imagine. the only acceptable elements for all were the sources of discrimination listed in the universal declaration of human rights, namely race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, wealth, birth or other status. what about a possible follow-up to the conference? i would like to conclude by saying that it was up to each state to monitor the conference, but it was nevertheless decided that the high commissioner for human rights would be primarily responsible for monitoring it. a number of actions will have to be implemented, including the creation of an 'anti-discrimination unit' within the high commission and the appointment of five leading independent experts to monitor the implementation of the provisions contained in the action programme and the political declaration. these experts shall be appointed by the secretary-general of the united nations. i would like to make this point, of course, firstly because i also wanted to welcome the relevance of the speeches by the members of parliament and to tell them that their strong conviction has been a remarkable motivation and support in defending the views we expressed on your behalf in durban.

- madam president, first of all i would like to congratulate mr mayer on the report he is presenting to us today. i know very well that this is not the report you would have liked to have approved and, if this is of any consolation to you, i would also like to say that i would have preferred that the report finally adopted by this parliament had been the one originally drafted by mr mayer. in the face of powerful interests concerned to prevent global trade in branded products, in the face of an unusual report by a consultancy firm which claims that consumers would not benefit immediately from purchasing goods at lower prices and in the face of the lukewarm stance of the commission which does not seem to be interested in finding a solution to a problem which is affecting european consumers very negatively, the rapporteur, mr mayer, has been able to put forward a report calling for the search to be continued for formulas which prevent manufacturers of branded products from maintaining abnormally high prices on european markets. when the court of justice delivered the judgment in silhouette in july 1998, it caused a great deal of commotion in countries which had recognised the principle of international exhaustion of the trade mark. whether by law, as was the case in sweden, for example, or by case law, as was the case in my country, spain. the judgment is legally unassailable from the moment it is stated that article 7 of the trade mark directive, by imposing the principle of community exhaustion, is indirectly imposing the prohibition of international exhaustion. but this is a legalistic interpretation which does not prevent us from recognising, as the judgment does, the harmful effects on consumers of the fact that trademark owners can prevent the importation of their own products if they come from third countries. the arguments used by those who advocate the prohibition of international exhaustion of the trademark - the fight against counterfeiting, the maintenance of the aura of prestige, the transfer of income from the manufacturer to the importer - clash with a reality which is reflected in the documents drawn up by the rapporteur. when parallel imports from third countries are allowed, the prices of branded products are lowered. the data on price increases in germany, when the reform of german law prevented international exhaustion, are conclusive. and although my experience has little scientific value, i must say that i have had the opportunity to see how in the united states a product which i buy in spain for 10 euros costs just 1.5 euros. for this reason, and despite the reluctance to reach consensus in favour of a more ambitious resolution, it is important that the commission takes the initiative in favour of consumers and puts forward proposals to strengthen the world market by facilitating the destruction of trade barriers, which are not only customs but are often anti-competitive practices by companies aimed at defending their own interests.

- mr president, at this stage of the debate i think we know three things. firstly, we know that the crisis affecting the european industrial sector today is more serious than the one it suffered during the financial crisis of 1998. secondly, we know that the crisis in the world economy today is much more serious than the one that occurred in 1993, after the gulf war, because it affects at the same time, for the first time in history since 1929, the three major economies: the american economy, the european economy and the japanese economy. thirdly, we all know, except mr abitbol, that the european economy is much better prepared today to deal with this crisis than it was before. we have, as has been said, a single currency which protects us from exchange rate crises; we have a policy which protects us from exorbitant price rises; and we have a stability pact which defends us from the wastefulness of public administrations. we do not know, but we do suspect, that this crisis is not a crisis of demand - like the post-war crisis - nor a crisis of supply - like the one that happened in the yom kippur war - but it is a crisis of confidence. and as a crisis of confidence, what differentiates the resolution we are presenting from the one the left is presenting is not that they want to grow and we do not. obviously, we all want to grow up. the thing is, there are recipes that move forward and recipes that move back. and we believe that ours move forward. why do i say this? because if it is a crisis of confidence, the first mistake would be to relax monetary policy and allow price increases which would be an attack on the consumer confidence line. secondly, because to revise the stability pact would be tantamount to sending a signal that we want to shift these burdens onto future generations, which does not help to increase confidence. and thirdly, because if we relax the budgetary policy that the stability pact embodies, we will prevent interest rates from being reduced, as the americans are doing. a ship is measured not by whether there is a storm or not, but by how it sails through the storm. and right now, in my opinion, it's true that we have to change the way we navigate. the european central bank may have to cut interest rates, but its ultimate objective is to maintain the dogma of price stability in order to maintain consumer confidence. it is likely that some governments, those which have done their homework, will be able to let the automatic stabilizers run without having to try to compensate for the tax cut by raising taxes or cutting spending. but those who have not, the prodigal sons, are not in this arrangement. and thirdly - the commissioner has said this and none of the speakers have said it - it is time for europe to take a step forward, to take a firm step towards launching the lisbon process for a modern, innovative and competitive society. the commissioner was much more convincing on the tobin tax in his interview with the digital vanguard, in which he said that it was a useless instrument, than in his speech today, in which he said that it was one more of the possible instruments. then you said it wasn't possible; today it's starting to be possible. i agree with your statement in the paper, not your statement here.

- mr president, the revision of the directive on television without frontiers is also very urgent for us. firstly, because the scenario in which the television market is developing today, as described, is so different from that which existed in the last revision of the directive that it does not seem possible to maintain it for two or three more years. we could estimate that the directive affects at most 50% of the problems facing the sector today. secondly, because we need to provide solutions that were not available then. television remains the primary means of information and entertainment for most europeans, and i believe that its major problems, apart from the poor quality of the content, are threefold: the excessive broadcasting of advertising, without regard for age, times or timing; the very limited broadcasting of european films, which is humiliating for european culture; and the growing business of coding programmes for viewing on payment. these problems were certainly present in 1996, but they have increased to serious limits, indicating that while the directive has been effective in the free movement of television services in the community, it has failed in other important respects. in the light of the commission's communication, we cannot assess the efforts made by the member states to remedy these situations over the three years under review. suffice it to say that three of them did not even transpose the directive into their own legislation. the results have certainly not been the same in the other cases, but the commission does not provide us with this comparative study. nor does it go into the situation in the candidate countries, which will have to be assessed very carefully in the new directive. for all these reasons, mrs hieronymi - and i think she has good sense - did not want to anticipate in her report a substantive debate, which will have to be held when the directive is revised, and what she is asking for is this revision. it also sets out some guidelines to be taken into account, including the mandatory introduction of new services based on new technologies, the need to stimulate and accelerate the transition to digital technology or the coordination of the new directive with the revision of the directive on electronic commerce. the socialist group will therefore vote in favour of the report and will table two amendments by mrs junker, including the requirement that events or shows of great interest to citizens be protected from being broadcast in code and be offered free of charge to all social groups by means of community legislation.

commission. - mr president, i should first of all like to thank mrs hieronymi very much for the quality of her report and, in general, for her commitment to television and cinema. this commitment shows that parliament understands the importance of the 'television without frontiers' directive and its application. i would like to make it clear to the honourable members that mrs hieronymi's report is not about the development of television in general, or cinema, but about the commission's report on the application of the 'television without frontiers' directive between 1997 and 2000. i fully agree with the members who have deplored the situation of european cinema, on our screens and in our economy, and i would draw their attention to the fact that last week the commission published its report on cinema. i am sure, mr president, that parliament will have the opportunity to engage in a wide-ranging debate on the development of cinema in europe, a wide-ranging debate which i wish to see. it should be noted that the logic is slightly different when it comes to television. i would simply draw attention to the fact that in the case of the promotion of the distribution and production of television programmes - which are the subject of articles 4 and 5 of the directive - we find that the weighted average of the transmission of european works by the major channels varies between 53% and 81%, except for one country. it should also be noted that most member states have introduced legislation which is more stringent than that provided for in the directive. the situation is therefore, fortunately, much better for television than for cinema. i therefore propose, mr president, that we should have a serious discussion of cinema in this house for once. such a debate is very important. several meps have raised the need for a review of the directive. that process is ongoing. it was launched this year with a very wide consultation of professionals. he's being sued next year. you know that we have launched three studies on different aspects of the audiovisual directive. we have insisted that these studies be carried out by independent commission consultants so that they are not commission studies but independent studies, benefiting from the input of the profession and allowing an objective view of the situation on the ground. the consultants organised workshops bringing together professionals from industry, administration and politics. parliamentarians were also invited to these workshops. other workshops are being prepared. the work of collecting the opinions of the interested parties is of course supplemented by reflection and drafting work which will lead to the preparation of reports which our consultants should send us at the end of the year or at the beginning of the next. the commission will then start its own consultation process with the publication of a working document, to which everyone will be invited to respond by summer 2002. mr president, parliament will therefore still have ample opportunity to review the main lines of the hieronymi report, but also to comment on future lines in particular, as the institutional debate on the directive will be opened later on, on the basis of the work and the results obtained, with, as far as necessary - and i share the opinion of the members on the need to reform the directive - the commission's proposals for a new directive by the end of 2002. this is to remind you of the complexity of the process we have embarked upon, a process in which parliament will be heard at every stage. by giving a large amount of space to this review process, mrs hieronymi's report also illustrates the complexity and importance of the debate. mr president, allow me to emphasize two points in the text of the report which has been tabled by parliament and to comment on recital (h) and article 1 (e). according to recital (h) the directive is obsolete and applies only to the type of general-purpose, free-access television for which it was originally established. well, that's just not accurate. the directive has a much wider scope. it applies to broadcasting in general, including pay-tv and thematic channels, but also to digital and analogue broadcasting. the remarks in recital (h) are therefore simply wrong and dangerously wrong for the following reason: the directive does not apply to the internet, because the internet did not exist when it was drawn up. the commission will therefore have to take appropriate measures when the directive is revised. it is dangerous to say that the directive is obsolete for the simple reason that it can give the national authorities who have not yet implemented it weapons. your rapporteur has emphasized this: why apply an obsolete directive? in that case, it will be inertia and there will be no more means of pressure and, in the end, parliament will get the opposite of what it actually wants. this could also cause problems with the applicant countries - which i will mention later - which are having great difficulty in introducing the acquis communautaire into their legislation. will they be forced to implement an acquis which parliament considers to be obsolete? in the interests of this dossier, mr president, it is therefore essential to amend this point in the text and to ensure that it does not send a negative signal either to the member states implementing the directive or to the candidate countries adopting the acquis, but on the contrary to remind them that the directive continues to provide legal certainty for operators in our european audiovisual area. some members have rightly stressed this point. point 1 (e) of the report deplores the fact that the commission has provided only insufficient information on the efforts made by the applicant countries to return to the acquis in the audiovisual sector and has not stressed the need for the latter to intensify their efforts. i would remind you that the report drawn up pursuant to article 26 of the directive concerns only the application of the directive in the member states of the european union. it does not concern the transposition of the acquis communautaire by the applicant countries. it is therefore understandable that it does not contain any details on the take-up of this acquis, much less recommendations for these countries. however, i have good news in this respect, because the situation regarding the recovery of the acquis has improved markedly since the end of 2000. for all the candidate countries, except romania, hungary and turkey, chapter 20 on audiovisual is provisionally closed, which shows that for a large part of the countries concerned, national legislation is in line with the acquis. mr president, i would like to thank parliament for its strong support in my efforts to make progress in the interests of our cultural industries, but also in the interests of our cultural diversity. i can tell this house that our work is only just beginning, because the revision of the 'television without frontiers' directive will be a very large and extremely complex task, for which i will need the resolute support of this house day after day. my experience tells me that i will get that support.

the commission mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr agag longo, and mr evans for their speeches. i am in awe of the quality of mr longo's report and i appreciate the many constructive comments that have been made. i am aware that the report also contains critical remarks and i can assure you that, although it is impossible to take a definitive position on all the comments made in it, i can nevertheless assure you that they will all be examined very carefully. i am also grateful to the other speakers at this sitting - mr konrad, mr berenguer fuster, mr riis-jørgensen - for their political and, i would say, cultural support for the european union's competition policy. the 30th annual report reviews developments in the year 2000: a quick glance at the competition sector shows that it continued to be very active, with a total of 1206 new practices, 564 state aid cases, 345 mergers and acquisitions and 297 antitrust cases. the legislative work has focused on the reform of our basic legislation. this activity led to the adoption of the new block exemption regulations for horizontal agreements. new guidelines on vertical restraints were adopted, as well as the new 1999 block exemption regulation. you know that these new settings give more weight to economic orientation. the fact that the number of antitrust cases has decreased can be attributed to these new vertical restraint rules, which have significantly reduced the obligation to notify this type of agreement, leaving more room for the services to focus on the most serious and difficult cases. there has been considerable progress on the reform of the antitrust procedure, which parliament gave decisive support to a month ago with such a large majority vote on mr evans' report. in the field of mergers, a notice on remedies and a simplified procedure for certain non-problematic categories of operations have been adopted, which now allows us to deal in this way with about 40% of merger cases. in the field of state aid control, the commission introduced for the first time three sets of exemption regulations on the application of the de minimis rule, on aid to small and medium-sized enterprises and on training aid. i take mr riis-jørgensen's point on the recovery of illegal state aid, because i too consider it of great importance for overall credibility. the general trend of declining aid levels is confirmed, but this does not mean that they will not remain very high. i would like to point out, mr president, that contrary to what paragraph 2 of your motion for a resolution suggests, the commission has already initiated proceedings against state aid in the form of tax relief, and on 11 july there were 15 such proceedings. we are also intensifying our efforts to recover unduly paid amounts of state aid. i should like to mention three areas to which we are paying special attention, not only in the last annual report but also in our daily work. the first and most important is the impact of competition policy on consumers. i know that parliament shares our view that the consumer must be the final recipient of competition policy. it is certainly necessary to make consumers more aware of the benefits of competition policy and to inform citizens about our activities and the effects it has on them. as you will have noticed, the report illustrates some decisions by example, showing the benefits to consumers. a good example is the decision against opel nederland to defend the right of consumers to buy a car without obstacles in a member state where prices are lower; other more recent examples are a similar decision against volkswagen or the opening of an inquiry into mobile telecommunications prices charged by roaming operators. as regards cars, i note the reference made by mr evans: the commission is working hard to formulate a proposal for the period after 30 september 2002, when the exemption regulation for the category of motor vehicle distribution agreements will expire. i intend to table a draft of the new regulation towards the end of the year and i am sure you will be happy to give your views on it, given the great interest shown by parliament so far in this matter. as regards consumer information, i would like to recall the initiative which was launched during the discussions in this parliament during the european competition days. after lisbon, paris and stockholm, the next meeting will be held with the belgian presidency in antwerp on 11 october and will focus on competition in the pharmaceutical sector. a second priority line of work which we are pursuing - and to which several people have referred this evening - is that of state aid, not only to make the controls more rigorous but also to make this matter more transparent with initiatives such as the register and the scoreboard, which is easily available on the internet. the third priority area of work is precisely that of globalisation, of how competition policy can, by seeking better coordination between the various parts of the world, make its contribution to the governance of globalisation. in this context - apart from, of course, the very close relations within the european union with the national competition authorities - outside the european union we have established close bilateral working relations and established a very happy and deep cooperation in particular with the antitrust authorities of the united states, and last week we had an intensive working session in washington, planning for the further development of this bilateral cooperation. i believe, however, that the bilateral dimension is not enough and we are proceeding, with the full weight of the conviction that the european union has in this matter, to the development of two modes of multilateral cooperation. one is the intention to have some basic binding rules on competition within the world trade organization; the other is the recent initiative to launch a global competition forum that provides a forum for global discussion among antitrust authorities. among the priorities for the near future is the work on the modernisation of the antitrust procedure, which is currently under way and which we are pursuing with even greater conviction after the european parliament's strongly favourable vote. we also intend to complete the review of the de minimis notice within the year, which, by defining which agreements between undertakings are not prohibited under article 81 (1), will make it possible to reduce the burden on undertakings, especially the smallest ones, to comply with the legislation. having already referred to the exemption regulation for motor vehicles, i would also like to point out, as regards the policy against cartels, which is a fundamental pillar of any competition authority, that by the end of this year we will be further developing and updating the leniency policy, based on the non-commitment or reduction of fines in cases of cooperation in the detection of cartels. this is another area of convergence between the american and european approaches. the commission's priority for 2001 in the area of merger control will be to continue the review of the merger regulation. in this connection, i intend to draw up a formal consultation document on this subject within the year. as regards the handling of new cases, our work is focusing in particular on the recently liberalised markets, referred to in particular by mr konrad, mr evans and others, such as energy, air transport, telecommunications and postal services, precisely in order to prevent the former monopolists from abusing the position of strength they traditionally enjoyed. i would like to thank all of you again for your support and encouragement of the commission in the competition field: i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this, but i am saying that it should be involved in the work of the european parliament.
- thank you very much, mr. monti. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.

commission. – the commission takes heart from the broad support for the commission's objectives in the field of e-commerce and financial services – support evidenced by the report of your economic and points which were also raised by various members in the debate. on the need for a road map setting out what needs to be done and when, in may the commission published a financial services policy group report to the ecofin council. that contains just such a road map and hopefully brings greater clarity about the way forward. amongst other things that road map sets out the concrete steps that must now be taken to enable the country-of-origin approach to apply across the board to cover those financial services currently derogated and to be applied to other traditional distance training modes. in broad terms, that would involve further convergence in national consumer protection rules, in particular by updating eu legislation which predates the e-commerce directive. on the commission's process of receiving the first replies from member states. i should like to assure parliament that it is not the commission's intention for the guidance to represent a de facto additional derogation redundant by the 2005 lisbon deadline for an integrated european market in financial services. in respect of this point i would particularly like to say to mr radwan that earlier this year the commission helped to put in place a network for the handling of cross-border complaints in financial services which ought to serve to raise still further the level of confidence of consumers who venture onto the internet. i hope that is to the liking of mr radwan. may i further welcome parliament's call for a single payments area in which it would be easy and cheap to transfer money across borders. i should like to recall that in july the commission adopted a proposal for a regulation to align the costs of cross-border payments with those made at national level. i can also inform parliament that with a view to making payments more secure, the commission in february adopted a communication on the prevention of fraud and counterfeiting of non-cash means of payment, which set out a three-year action plan. this point was also raised by mr harbour and i should like to add that the commission is looking into the possibility of refunds. i will inform mr harbour later of the progress in this respect. finally, i take note of parliament's interesting suggestions that the commission should seek to negotiate mutual recognition agreements with third countries, at least with those third countries that provide similar levels of prudential supervision and investor protection. the commission finds that a very valuable suggestion and we should like to consider it further. in conclusion, i very much welcome the draft report as its stands. i should like to thank the rapporteur, mr huhne, for his strong support for the country-of-origin principle. indeed all speakers this the past. that support was so manifest and so vital at the time of the adoption of the electronic commerce directive last year, when members voted unanimously in favour of the directive and the underlying country-of-origin approach. that is precisely the approach which the commission, with the support of parliament, would like to continue.

- the report (a5-0310/2001) by mrs berger, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the commission communication 'a strategy for the internal market in services' (com (2000) 888 - c5-0103/2001 - 2001/2052 (cos)).
commission. – mr president, firstly the commission would like to emphasise the economic and political importance of its communication on a new internal market strategy for services, which i hope, will henceforth enjoy the european parliament's full support. a functioning internal market in services, far from being a reality, remains an objective to be achieved. it is an objective which ought to be considered a priority if we really want the european economy to become the most competitive in the world by the end of this decade – the ambition we set ourselves in march 2000 in lisbon. just to quote a single fact, services account for two-thirds of the european economy and, therefore, any progress we make on that front will greatly benefit the citizens of this continent. achieving that goal is rendered all the important by the growing dynamic of the information society, with all its potential for cross-border trade, and by the imminent introduction of the euro, which will increase the transparency of costs and encourage businesses and consumers to look beyond national boundaries for the provision of services. unfortunately, at present there are still too many legal and administrative obstacles preventing our businesses and consumers from considering the whole of the european community as their true domestic market. that means that we are failing to realise the enormous potential for growth and establish a framework in which millions of new jobs can be created. at no other time in our recent history has it been more important to encourage entrepreneurship, innovation and opportunity. just as the 1992 campaign enabled us to focus on – and to a large extent achieve – an internal market in goods, it is now crucial for us to concentrate on dismantling the barriers to trade and services. this new strategy seeks, above all to enable two groups – namely small and medium-sized enterprises and consumers – to reap the full benefits of the internal market. in many instances, small and medium-sized enterprises – which mr harbour and mr beysen have mentioned also evening – will not have the means to establish themselves in all or several member states. if they try to do so, they will be faced with the need to expand their infrastructure and with extra financial and administrative burdens. therefore, they must be allowed to offer their services freely throughout the community from their establishment. as far as consumers are concerned, this strategy is designed above all for them. we shall not have succeeded until european consumers have greater access to and a wider choice of, safe and reliable services at more competitive prices, and that means there must be more competition between service providers. the strategy is the first attempt to apply, at community level, a horizontal approach to trade and services since the general programme for the removal of barriers to services of 1962 was introduced almost forty years ago. it calls for the cooperation and support of national authorities, the participation of all interested parties and the active engagement of the community institutions. the report by parliament's committee on legal affairs and the internal market has highlighted many of the difficult issues preventing an effective internal market in services from functioning. i am delighted that the committee on legal affairs and the internal market shares the commission's philosophy and supports its ambitious approach. i also hope to be able to count on the full support of the european parliament in implementing both the first and second phases of the strategy. the first phase is now being carried out. this means that existing restrictions to the freedom to provide services and the freedom of establishment are being identified and evaluated. in the second phase, legal and operational instruments for the elimination of barriers will be put in place and our approach will be based on harmonisation, assuring a high level of consumer protection combined with the principles of country of origin and mutual recognition enshrined in the treaty. accordingly, the commission would not welcome the newly tabled amendments. those amendments appear to run counter to the principles of mutual recognition and country of origin and, in the commission's view, would undermine the positive and well-balanced approach of the report, for which the commission is duly grateful. i should like to thank mrs berger on behalf of the commission for having drafted that report. the commission feels that the newly tabled amendments would significantly weaken the support of the european parliament for the proposed internal market approach. in conclusion, i refer to the earlier discussion between mrs berger, mr harbour and mr beysen on the various merits and demerits of harmonisation, mutual recognition and the country of origin. large-scale harmonisation may waste time, prove unnecessarily bureaucratic and divert political goodwill and attention away from the key issues that member states should agree on. it may also contravene the subsidiarity principle in the treaty. on the other hand, it must be admitted that harmonisation may be necessary where there is a need to establish a high level of protection, notably for consumers. mutual recognition, on the other hand, can be made to work more satisfactorily if it is implemented through secondary community legislation which clearly identifies the areas in which mutual recognition must be accepted. both principles have their merits and demerits, but by and large i am inclined to agree with mr harbour's view that the quickest way of achieving an adequate level of protection for the consumer is to adopt the country-of-origin principle. in conclusion, may i thank mr beysen for his kind remarks on the sales promotion directive adopted by the commission this week. lastly may i apologise to mrs berger for having omitted previously to thank her on the commission's behalf for having withdrawn almost all of the amendments tabled on the previous matter.

commission. – mr president, i should like to begin by saying that the commission is in a very comfortable position because it agrees entirely with the content of the resolution adopted almost unanimously on 28 august of this year by the committee on economic and monetary affairs. the voluntary code of conduct which underpins the commission's recommendation is the very first example of an agreement reached between banking and consumer associations on the standardisation of information which must be made available to consumers before a contract is concluded. its existence proves, as has rightly been pointed out in the resolution, that market participants are best placed to negotiate proper solutions and to ensure an appropriate balance of interests between contractual parties. but however well placed they might be, market participants need a neutral and indefatigable broker to accompany, and sometimes remotivate them, during the long and difficult negotiations of this code. tribute has been paid by the rapporteur to the commission's role and the commission is duly appreciative and grateful to the rapporteur for that acknowledgement. as agreed between and called for by all parties, the broker, that is, the commission, will now transform itself into a notary and, if need be, into a referee. as a notary, the commission will, in line with the resolution, keep a register of home-loan lenders who adhere to the code. that register will be kept up-to-date and made available online. i say this in particular to mr radwan who wanted this code to be on the internet and it will be. it will be made available online on the commission's website and appropriate transparency will therefore be ensured. during the negotiation phase the lack of appropriate transparency was deplored in the report. it is a point well taken by the commission, but at least when the register is on the net then that transparency will be restored. that is with the commission as a notary. as a referee the commission will monitor compliance with its recommendation and assess its effectiveness. the commission made it clear in its recommendation that it will consider presenting binding legislation should the terms of its recommendation not be fully complied with. parliament will, as is rightly called for in the resolution, be closely informed – that also is a point that was raised the rapporteur. - mr. president, i don't think you're going to use the five minutes. this is a third reading and it is a conciliation process that we have been following for some time. i would like to welcome the dialogue that has existed between the council, the commission and the european parliament, which has made things much easier. of course, the outcome of a compromise is never all right for some or all right for others. it's usually pretty good, but with a few flaws. i think that the other two institutions have taken up important amendments from the first amendments tabled by the european parliament at first reading. for example, taking into account the responsibility not only of producers but also of distributors for the safety of products; clear information on possible risks in the languages of the different states of the union; a faster exchange of information; greater cooperation between states to prevent dangerous products from reaching the market; and also the withdrawal of products that are considered dangerous, even if they are already on the market. an amendment was also included, although not as the uk colleagues wanted, which sought to include the specificity of certain charity shops in the uk. i think that a large part of the european parliament's proposals were taken up. however, not all of them were included, and at second reading we tabled only seven amendments which attempted to include what was not accepted by the other institutions. these amendments were about something very important to us: the inclusion of services in a proposal which the commission is working on and which it has committed itself to delivering in 2003. i think that is a very important proposal for us, because the safety of services must have the same status as the directive we are reviewing today. the precautionary principle must also be taken into account, that is, when there is a well-founded suspicion that a product is unsafe, the precautionary principle, which is so much talked about and which is little applied in practice, must be applied. and the possibility of an external certificate to complement the official certification. there is also an agreement on comitology, which is not what parliament wanted in this case either, but there is a proposal for continuous and regular information to the european parliament and the council. the final proposal also clearly addresses some of the issues that have been of concern to us. i would just like to emphasize an issue which was proposed by the commission itself at the outset, namely the prohibition of exports to third countries of products which are not considered safe in europe. that proposal did not pass the house by very few votes and is naturally not included in the final document. i have to say, as rapporteur, that this is perhaps what concerns me most. i think there is a real risk, as we see every day, of unscrupulous people exporting unsafe products to third world countries. this is a subject that concerns me enormously. we have the verbal assurance from the european commission that there will be very strict controls to ensure that this does not happen, but it would have been safer if it had been included in the proposal and there would have been no risk of exporting to third world countries products which we europeans consider to be dangerous. so, mr president, despite this thorn in the rapporteur's side because the directive does not include an express prohibition on the export of unsafe products to the third world, i think it is a proposal which, as i said at the beginning, is not the best for the council and the commission, perhaps it is not the best for parliament either, but it is the result of a conciliation process in which there has been, yes, a very fruitful dialogue between all the institutions and i am very pleased with it.

- mr president, in 1979 willy brandt presented his famous 'north-south report, a programme for survival', in which he warned of the risk that by the year 2000 a large part of the population would continue to live in poverty. shortly after that statement, shocking figures were published: every 24 hours 35,000 people die of hunger in the world. in two years, famine killed more people than both world wars combined. the year 2000 arrived, and the situation has only worsened. according to the world health organization, extreme poverty - misery - is the main cause of suffering in the world and also the one that takes more human lives every year while we continue to talk about poverty and how we are going to remedy it. a few months ago, before the summer, at our headquarters in brussels, the united nations, together with the eu, organized the third conference on the least developed countries, which was devoted specifically to analysing the causes, consequences and solutions of poverty. we have even set ourselves an ambitious target of halving poverty by the year 2005. some studies have shown, mr president, that what we are doing, the plans and projects we are trying to implement, and above all the resources we are allocating and those which are planned to be allocated, will not be able to achieve this objective. our concern now is to fight international terrorism fueled by enlightened fanatics. that is true, that is the problem now, but, ladies and gentlemen, that is not the root of the problem. the problem is poverty in a large part of the world. until we solve poverty and especially extreme poverty - misery - in which hundreds of millions, about 1.5 billion human beings live, and i am talking about conservative figures, we will continue to be exposed to situations like the ones we are living in now. some of us have been between september 13 and 19 visiting some of the poorest areas on the planet in the south of the african continent. mozambique has 19 million inhabitants today, but in 9 years only 13 million will be alive; the other 6 will have died of aids. today mr khanbhai in his report proposes a series of measures to combat aids, malaria and tuberculosis in the context of poverty reduction. i myself and my colleagues have seen, during a visit to a field hospital lost in the middle of the african savannah, how people die as victims of a cholera epidemic - believe me, right now - a spectacle as dante as it was lived in europe in the middle ages. this is also true of other centres that are not in the middle of the jungle. in mocuba, there is a provincial hospital where women stand next to patients with aids, with tuberculosis, with leprosy, with meningitis, with infectious diarrhea of all etiologies. for all these diseases that can be cured and eradicated today, there are drugs. it is a question of resources and, above all, it is a question of political will. mr khanbhai, i congratulate you and thank you for the important contribution you make to us in your report. but, my friend bashir, you know your native africa better than i do. let us not be mistaken, the problems of poverty in the world today are of such magnitude that these measures, with the current resources, are like a drop in the ocean. we'll figure it out one day. either we fight poverty with all our strength and resources until we have conquered it, or poverty with its many faces - now in the guise of terrorism - will conquer us.

commission. – the problem raised by the patents granted by the european patent office to myriad genetics does not appear to derive from the field of ethics. these patents highlight a technical question deriving from the field of patent law. the situation is thus completely different from that raised by the famous "edinburgh patent". the problem resides more in the extent of the protection to be granted to these patents. this question is highly complex since, as it applies to gene sequences, it undoubtedly involves a situation relating to competition and innovation, and in no way fundamental principles relating to the dignity or integrity of human beings. it should be noted that this patent is of undoubted interest for the scientific community. it should make it possible to improve the early detection of breast cancer in women. the commission considers there are no imperative reasons why the commission should raise any objections, as the contested patent does not infringe essential ethical rules and concerns the field of application which can be granted to a patent relating to a dna sequence. nevertheless, the commission will study the question of the field of protection for inventions relating to gene sequences in depth and will communicate its observations to the council and parliament in the reports provided for by directive 98/44.

the second report on the schengen information system, i believe that it is a key element in the functioning of the borderless area. the need to develop a second generation sis was already recognised several years ago. this is primarily due to the limitations of the current sis system. the system allows only 18 countries to be integrated. the prospect of enlargement of the union therefore requires the development of a second generation sis which will allow the full integration of new member states. without sis ii, the conditions for the abolition of internal border controls in the countries currently applying for membership of the european union will not be met. the two initiatives on which you are giving your opinion today confirm that the european parliament and the commission now have an increased role in relation to the development of sis ii, both in this initial phase of funding and in defining the future architecture of the system and its practical operation. these two initiatives are in line with the conclusions of the jha council at the end of may this year in favour of financing the development of sis ii from the community budget from 2002 onwards. under the two initiatives to set up a committee to assist the commission in the development of sis ii, the european parliament will be kept systematically informed of the work in progress, via the parliament's - mr president, i would like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur on her excellent work and, having said that, let me remind you that article 31 (1) of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union proclaims that every worker has the right to work in conditions which respect his health, his safety and his dignity. this is a broad statement, within the chapter on solidarity, which includes not only measures against obvious risks (a risk of falling, a risk from abrasive material) but also preventive measures against risks that may go unnoticed by most people who are not experts in this field. the risks to which workers in the mining, construction and transport sectors are exposed are as follows. in total, say the researchers, up to 24% of european workers, and this in its dual manifestation of vibration transmitted to the hand-arm system with the manifestation of soft fingers, decreased compressive force, etc., or vibration transmitted to the whole body (back pain, lumbar pain, hernias, etc.). it should be remembered, commissioner, that these measures must not be limited to physical agents in the case of vibrations, but must also cover noise, waves and electromagnetic fields, optical radiation, etc., all of which must be covered with the necessary transitional period for adaptation to the requirements arising from the adoption of these decisions. i am convinced that all employers and workers have the same objective: to improve working conditions and the working environment, to create a suitable working environment. a transitional period will be necessary to replace equipment, improve and adapt procedures, and differences in technological development and type of activity, for example agricultural, will have to be considered, in the belief that there is no such thing as zero risk and that the fight for safety is the responsibility of all those involved: workers (self-employed or employed), employers, local, regional and national administrations.

first time that we have agreed to finance operations in russia and the operation is of interest not only to russia but also to the countries bordering the union. the commission had proposed the guarantee normally provided for in this type of operation, namely 65%, which is the guarantee provided for in the general mandate of the european investment bank. however, it is known that the council, by a series of decisions linked precisely to the unique nature of this operation and the desire for greater transparency, raised the need for an extraordinary 100% community guarantee in this case. the urgency of using this year's resources has led the commission to accept this 100%. i do not know exactly the procedural problems which have caused the information to reach parliament excessively late, but according to my information the council itself informed parliament on 20 september of the proposed amendments, on 12 october the belgian presidency explained the changes in greater detail and on the same day the commission sent the committee on budgets information on the reasons why we accepted the council's amendments. with a unanimous decision of the council, with the acceptance of the commission, there was no need for a new proposal from the commission. we believe that it is urgent to adopt this decision in 2001 for the same reasons as those you have raised. a postponement to 2002 would clearly make it difficult for us to finance because of the limited room for manoeuvre we have for the next year. however, this decision will not affect other types of operations. in his report mr seppänen has made some references to other financing: the turkish case is the most obvious, with the appropriations for the year 2000. the 2000 and 2001 actions have already been funded and no problems of this nature arise. however, there is another problem in the longer term: how are we going to manage the financing capacity of the european investment bank in our lending mechanism? mr färm also asked what we intend to do as a commission. i would first of all like to say that the commission thanks parliament for raising this problem of the limited borrowing capacity we have within the guarantee fund mechanism. the commission has already raised this problem in the council and even here in parliament on a number of occasions, and we believe that if there are new initiatives in the context of 2002, the existing problems will be exacerbated and some decisions will have to be taken. the commission is currently considering a number of options and we intend to take an initiative in a relatively short time, in a communication to be sent to the council and parliament. i cannot answer mr färm by saying what option we are considering at the moment, but i would nevertheless remind him that we have already proposed in the past a reduction in the coverage rate from 65% to 60%. this could be one of the instruments, like any other, needed to give greater room for manoeuvre in future. these are the comments i can make to you at this time and i would like to thank you for your cooperation in the debate on this report.

- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are now in the second reading of an important directive on the application of the principle of equal treatment for men and women as regards access to employment, vocational training and promotion and working conditions. this directive has taken many hours of work, meetings and agreements between the various groups to get a text acceptable to the majority of this house, as well as to the council and the commission. it has not been easy, but the desire to have a legal text that would be a good instrument to facilitate women's access to the labour market on equal terms and to enable them to reconcile family and professional life, which still poses enormous problems for women and, in particular, young women, has prevailed. article 1 (2) which guarantees the retention of the job after maternity leave is of the utmost importance. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the right to vote is guaranteed to women in all member states. these problems are mainly women's problems, but the directive provides that when the father has paternity leave, he can obtain the same guarantees as the woman, even if this leave is after the specific leave for childbirth, which is specific and exclusive to women. positive measures to promote the presence of the under-represented sex in a particular workplace are also included, in order to allow greater equality between men and women. it is also important to note that a problem at work is being considered which unfortunately affects women more than men: sexual harassment, which will not only be prosecuted and punished, but also preventative measures will be taken in companies. although we are aware that small businesses may have problems in complying with this directive, we believe that it is an important achievement for equality between men and women. i hope that it will ultimately help women and not create additional problems for them.

the rapporteur. - mr president, the committee on regional policy welcomes the initiative to establish in a regulation the nomenclature of territorial statistical units, thus providing it with a legal basis. until now, and in the absence of this legal basis, the changes and updating have been carried out through gentlemen's agreements between member states and eurostat. i maintain that statistics are neither neutral nor politically innocent. i therefore believe that this proposal for a regulation has a wide political scope, not only because it is applied to determine the regions and regions to which the structural funds will devote their resources, but because it gives a certain vision of europe, of its territorial reality, of its regional and provincial organization and, consequently, of its disparities and imbalances. the proposal maintains the division of the territory of the states into statistical units organised hierarchically at three levels, while proposing criteria for the definition of these regions in the candidate countries, which it asks to continue to be determined on the basis of territorial organisations and within existing demographic thresholds. the committee on regional policy shares the objectives set out by the commission in its proposal for a regulation, but nevertheless considers that the breakdown obtained does not entirely conform to them, which translates into the perception by citizens of an artificial division of the european territory. in the annex, the commission merely sets out the administrative territorial units existing in each member state, mixing them with others which do not have this institutional character, which is a clear lack of homogeneity. the committee on regional policy believes that the proposal should include a european approach capable of transcending the framework of national borders. in this respect, the nuts 1 level should take account of large territorial units which transcend these borders and which are intended to serve as a basis for future european spatial planning. the nuts 1 level, ladies and gentlemen, is clearly lacking. only the regions of germany and belgium are considered as units, whereas in other member states, such as spain, france or italy, nuts 1 level corresponds to huge conglomerates of entirely artificial and, in most cases, arbitrary regions. at the opposite end of the spectrum, the proposal places the finnish island of åland as a nuts 1 unit, even though its 25 000 inhabitants fall far short of the 3 million minimum required in the demographic range. i still think that the commission's proposal should have been bolder, more coherent and perhaps, if i may say so, more european. the disparities are widening at level 3, where one member state, germany, has more units than the sum of eight member states: france, italy, the united kingdom, spain, the netherlands, denmark, ireland and luxembourg. the imbalance in the size of the territorial units is also evident, since the criterion which prevails in the proposal is that of population and not that of territorial extent. the committee on regional policy encourages the commission and the member states to work towards the establishment of nuts 4 and even nuts 5 levels, which would represent local authorities. the committee on regional policy has tabled eleven amendments to this proposal. i must say that this report was adopted in committee by 43 votes in favour and one abstention. as rapporteur, i am in favour of these amendments and against the others tabled in the plenary, which were already rejected in committee. i think that the report adopted by the committee on regional policy is acceptable to the council and to the commission. acceptance of it would save us the second reading and conciliation procedure and would allow it to enter into force on 1 january next. if so, then we should be pleased to have laid down in a legal text the basis for determining the territorial units needed for the collection of statistical data in this great europe before us. let us not fall into the trap of the famous phrase that statistics are the art of showing that two people eat well when, in fact, one of them has eaten two chickens and the other has eaten none.
- mr president, commissioner, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur. i think that the rapporteur has put forward a good draft report to the committee on a commission proposal with good intentions, with good lines, with - let us say - good accents, and that the result obtained by the committee, as the rapporteur has pointed out, is highly satisfactory. it would be good if the commission and then the council took up the proposals of the committee on regional policy of this parliament. europe is built on agreements and consensus. here is an example of what this has often been: gentlemen's agreements. but many of these agreements must now be reflected in the treaties, with a relevant legal basis. this is a very important subject, as the rapporteur has very well said. we are faced with what is the european territorial construction. clear, homogeneous and geographical criteria are required here. criteria which are based on - let me use the word redundancy - political-administrative criteria. we must not create fictitious units which, in the end, lead only to a lack of confidence in the european project on the part of the various states, the various regions and, in the end, the citizens. i therefore welcome the proposal from the committee. finally, i would like to mention an amendment which reflects the spirit of what we are talking about: mrs cerdeira's amendment on the division of the cities of ceuta and melilla, which are political and administrative units, each with its own statute. i would like to remind you, in this particular case, that mr hernández mollar of my group also fought for this recognition for a long time, and i believe that tomorrow, when the report presented by the committee on regional policy is adopted, a satisfactory result will have been achieved. that is the example and the reflection of what we want in terms of the division and structuring of europe.

streamlining the meetings in geneva and facilitating the participation of members who are not represented at the wto. if i take these two examples, to which we could add the efforts made to promote hormone-treated beef. contrary to what is stated in the report, the union has not been condemned for having banned hormones in beef farming. the wto explicitly recognised in this case the right of each member to set its own level of protection. the union was condemned because at the time it did not provide the necessary scientific basis to justify this ban. some other nuances, even minor differences, are related to your own assessments or suggestions. you mentioned the crisis of democratic legitimacy, and that was taken up by a few speakers. i do not subscribe to that criticism. the system can certainly be improved: it must be made more open and developing countries must be better integrated. this is a considerable challenge in reconciling our agenda - 'civil society' - with our agenda - 'development'. in fact, your report shows some of these difficulties, since on some of the subjects you propose both external transparency and basic social standards. we are well aware that our sensitivity to the positions of the developing countries on these two subjects forces us to moderate our ambitions in a particular way: we are therefore not always in a position that is free of all contradictions, and this is reflected in your report. however, to call the current situation a serious crisis of democratic legitimacy seems to me a bit exaggerated. as far as i know, the marrakesh agreement has not only been approved by the governments of the member states but also ratified by both the national parliaments and your assembly: the marrakesh agreement has been ratified by the european parliament. as for the claim that decision-making in the wto is the exclusive domain of the rich countries, i believe that if this were true, it is less and less so in an organisation of over 140 members in which small discussion groups are inevitable in the day-to-day work. we are trying to ensure that they bring together rich and poor countries and that they are representative both geographically and in terms of their stages of development. these informal groups may facilitate consensus formation, but they never make decisions, as we know. the last few weeks have been filled with preparatory meetings of this kind: the mini-ministerial meeting in mexico city at the end of august, the meeting between europeans and asians in hanoi in mid-september, the meeting between europeans and africans in nairobi in mid-october, the apec meeting last weekend. and i think that, from the standpoint of the method of preparation, the lesson of seattle has been that the stakeholders are more numerous, more informed in the sense that you suggest. as regards dispute settlement, which you have also dealt with, i would like to make three points. first, let us not forget that the main objective of the dispute settlement mechanism is the effective and disciplined enforcement of commitments that have been freely negotiated and accepted. this is what a wto member wants to achieve when it uses the dispute settlement procedure. we are, like you, opposed to immediate implementation and trade sanctions. there must be more room for trade compensation. i would be more reserved about your suggestion that sanctions be replaced by fines. i am afraid that monetary sanctions will not improve the imbalance between rich and poor countries, but will rather allow the rich countries to pay the price, in a way, for breaching their obligations. as regards the transparency of panels, we are in favour, as you are, of the opening to the public of hearings of panels of the appellate body. let us just remember - between us - that the developing countries have very strong positions on this point, which are not ours. as regards the relationship with other rules of international law, there is indeed a need to strengthen coherence and avoid conflicts between commercial and non-commercial standards. this must be done at the level of the very substance of the commitments in question. as for the question of the revision of the intellectual property agreement, which you consider necessary, i do not think that it should be thoroughly revised. the agreement provides for a wide range of measures to ensure that intellectual property rights are protected in accordance with the principles of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. it is up to wto members to interpret, to specify this flexibility, and we think it is better to do this through discussion or negotiation than to leave this task to the panels. that is the reason for our position in geneva, as i said in the previous debate. mrs auroi, the question of the compatibility of the intellectual property agreement with the convention on biological diversity is one of the
