the rapporteur. - mr president, i come to you to present and ask for your approval of a new fisheries protocol, in this case - as you have rightly said - with madagascar, with whom we have had relations since 1986. from the point of view of what has been called cost/benefit, it is an excellent protocol which clearly shows the profitability of this type of agreement for the european union. in this case, the community fleet, industry and market are ensuring the stable supply of a raw material such as tuna, of which we are highly deficient, through their own fleet, which allows a high rate of community employment to be maintained, not only in the extractive sector but also in the related activities. the protocol also demonstrates once again the high degree of exploitation of fishing opportunities under the southern agreements, which in this case amounted to 91% for purse seiners. the cost-effectiveness for madagascar is not much lower, for which, in addition to a financial compensation of eur 308 000 per year, another eur 517 000 is added in the form of development aid measures, mainly aimed at improving fisheries control in the area and training its fishermen. the number of malagasy crew members who must be on board is also increased from six under the current protocol to 40 under the protocol under consideration. a quantity leap, therefore, really important. the community's fishing activity does not interfere with the small-scale fleets, since our fleet has no access to the twelve-mile area. the presence of the european union itself provides an important component of control and guarantee of a greater sustainability of the resource. it should not be forgotten that the fleet carries all the community policy control regulations, which is a very important element in knowing details of catches and the state of the resource in the region, to a degree impossible to match by the rest of the various foreign fleets operating in these same malagasy waters. after this brief summary of the content of the protocol, and reminding you that, as an agreement of the south, shipowners contribute to its financing, i would like to dwell on two points. first of all, i would draw your attention to the fact that in this agreement, as in the southern agreements in general, the possibility is open for those member states concerned who would not have access to fishing opportunities by virtue of relative stability, as evidenced by the presence of italy and portugal, to obtain licences. it is therefore time to ask the commission to implement at once the 1997 guidelines of the council of fisheries ministers, which clearly call for the use of unused fishing opportunities by the fleets of the member states concerned in all european union agreements. secondly, i do not think it is necessary to recall the commitment of all of us to the development of third countries, and the lannoye report, which preceded the fisheries debate, is a good example of this. the fisheries sector has been one of the first to contribute to this development, since its presence in the waters of third countries has been the seed of many of the first industrial centres in their coastal areas, if not the definitive component of what is now the determined vocation of many nations as fishing states. but, having said that, i think that the matter is reaching a point where clarification is needed from several points of view. first of all, it must not be forgotten that, as the council of fisheries ministers also made clear, the fisheries agreements are essentially commercial in nature. however, fisheries agreements are increasingly being used as a complement to community development aid policy. in the case of this agreement, the part allocated to development cooperation measures already amounts to 62.6% of the total cost of the agreement from the community budget. this situation raises many questions. firstly, the fisheries budgets do not have to finance the budgets for development policy and, from the point of view of budgetary transparency, this situation should be clarified as soon as possible. secondly, this situation must also be clarified so that those who complain about the high budgetary cost of fisheries agreements are no longer heard, when in reality, as we have seen, well over half of this budget is purely for development policy.

- the next item is the report (a5-0346/2000) by mr carnero gonzález, on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on the amendment of the rules of procedure with regard to the constitution of interparliamentary delegations and joint parliamentary committees.
the rapporteur. - mr president, until this parliamentary term the standing committees, the interparliamentary delegations and the delegations to the joint parliamentary committees of this assembly were constituted by a uniform procedure: the plenary, on a proposal from the conference of presidents, appointed the members and the latter, at the constituent part-session, elected the bureau of each of these bodies. the reform of the rules of procedure introduced by a decision of the house at the end of the last parliamentary term changed this situation as regards interparliamentary delegations and delegations to joint parliamentary committees. from then on, both were elected and constituted differently from the standing committees: their tables were approved by this plenary, on a proposal from the conference of presidents, and the latter appointed the rest of its members. in doing so, at the beginning of this fifth parliamentary term, a contradiction in article 170 was noted. it said that the delegations in joint parliamentary committees would be constituted in the same way as the standing committees and at the same time it stated that it would be done in accordance with rule 168, which had already been amended in the sense i have mentioned above. as a result, there was a contradiction, undoubtedly the result of the error of this house, which had adopted by majority vote an oral amendment without removing from the text of the rules the reference to the previous procedures. to resolve this contradiction, the committee on constitutional affairs was requested by the conference of presidents. the report before us today is the result of the work of that committee. this report was adopted by the european parliament exactly one year ago, almost unanimously. i would stress that for a year this text has been "the dream of the just". the reasons for this escape me. in any event, it is clear that at that time the chairman of the committee on constitutional affairs, mr napolitano, and some of the coordinators, insisted that it be placed on the agenda of this house. here's the report. the important thing is that during that period there was time to reflect on the following: firstly, the contradiction in the regulation must be put to an end; it is absolutely necessary if we do not want the same doubts to be repeated next january as we had in july 1999. at the same time, the committee on constitutional affairs proposed in the report that a uniform procedure be re-introduced for standing committees, interparliamentary delegations and delegations to joint parliamentary committees. it seems that this period of "the dream of the just" for the report has served to make the parliamentary groups consider that, while it is absolutely necessary to amend the rules of procedure in order to put an end to the contradiction in article 170, there are nevertheless doubts about the need to return to the uniform procedures for the constitution of the three bodies of this parliament which i mentioned at the beginning of my speech. the rapporteur is clear on a number of points: when it comes to the reform of the regulation, two principles must prevail: first, consensus and, secondly, efficiency. and since we are talking about consensus, it is clear that the rapporteur understands the view of the political groups and therefore believes that we must proceed tomorrow to put an end to the contradiction in article 170 and to leave the procedure for the constitution of interparliamentary delegations and delegations to joint parliamentary committees as it stands at the moment. the second issue is efficiency. in january we will again be faced with a process of reconstitution of these organs, which must be rapid, so that they continue to function as well as they have so far. i would also like to personally congratulate these interparliamentary delegations and the delegations to the joint parliamentary committees on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs. i would like to ask the committee on constitutional affairs and its representatives for a third principle, which is consistency, which is also essential in any case. finally, mr president, i would like to recall a spanish saying: 'better a bird in the hand than a hundred in the air'. let's resolve the contradiction, which is the most important thing today.
- thank you very much, mr corbett. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.

the essential question about unsolicited e-mail. i would just like to point out that the commission cannot support amendments nos 16, 25 and 34 that were rejected by parliament on 6 september and are now resubmitted to the vote. the commission can support the new amendment no 43 on itemised bills. i will now focus on what has turned out to be the single most important topic in the debate on the proposed directive, namely unsolicited e-mail. this house has been discussing the question of opting in or opting out for several years now and the result of the vote on 6 september showed how difficult it still is to find a compromise solution that is acceptable to a broad majority. however we cannot hesitate for much longer, we need to decide. we have not hurried this decision. there has been huge public international debate with industry, with scientists, with lawyers. i have myself participated in intensive debates in the united states and in europe on this issue. i strongly disagree that asking a person whether they wish to opt in before you can bill them is a restriction on civil liberties. that is completely illogical. we can disagree on the details, but if people are asked to pay, they should have a choice beforehand, not afterwards. we should no longer be thinking mainly about messages arriving at a pc on our desk. we should be thinking about the future. technology is changing rapidly. the wireless internet will be different from the internet available only on desktops. the positive point about the proposal made by the committee on citizens’ freedoms in amendment no 33 is that it recognises that unsolicited commercial messages to mobile phones are a real problem which can only be addressed by a harmonised opt-in approach. i fully agree. however, the flaw in that proposal is that it is based on the assumption that a mobile terminal can only receive sms messages. unfortunately that is no longer true. you can already receive e-mail messages on mobile devices which are connected to the internet. if you want to test that i can give you good examples. and with convergence it is very clear that sms will certainly merge with other electronic messaging systems. the sender cannot know whether a message will be received on a mobile or fixed terminal because of the convergence. that is a technological fact. banning unsolicited commercial sms messages while allowing unsolicited electronic messages based on other technologies is therefore not a workable solution. another problem i have with amendment no 35 is the technologically biased approach in paragraph 4. this paragraph apparently tries to address the problem of cost for users but the solution proposed is not a good one. european isps tell us that the technology of viewing the subject line before downloading a message is not compatible with the majority of systems used in europe today. it would require substantial investment; it would be costly for the industry to introduce this feature and this does not seem justified when it is only a halfway solution. in short, apart from not being compatible with the single market, amendment no 35 does not meet the need for technology-neutral and future-proof legislation. amendment no 44, on the other hand represents a technology-neutral compromise solution and has the merit of being a fully harmonised eu approach to unsolicited commercial e-mail. in paragraph 2 of this amendment a rather substantial exemption from the opt-in principle is made for e-mail addresses obtained within existing customer relationships. here an opt-out approach would continue to be allowed, although this will mean an important concession as compared with the original commission proposal. the exception can be justified because in the context of an existing customer relationship, companies have a lot to lose and are more likely to use marketing instruments with consideration. we should look at the future challenges. it is interesting to see what is happening in japan today, where the wireless internet has already taken off successfully. nevertheless, the operator is facing a serious problem. it estimates that 85% of the 950 million messages sent daily to mobile devices are unsolicited commercial messages to mobile numbers chosen at random. this is causing a huge problem for network capacity, especially since most of these messages are addressed incorrectly and cannot be delivered. moreover, it greatly annoys users who have to work their way through great quantities of unwanted commercial messages. the cost of purging the system of junk mail is estimated to be more than usd 8.2 million. so if we want to create a positive environment for the development of electronic commerce and third generation mobile services, now is the time to make sure that the uptake of wireless internet services is not hampered by huge amounts of junk mail which the consumer is paying for against his will. valuable capacity within networks and in battery-dependent mobile terminals must be available for communications, messages and services that users really want to receive. amendment no 44 is most likely to achieve that purpose.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.

- report (a5-0347/2001) by mr maat, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the report from the commission to the council and the european parliament on the experience gained by the member states since the implementation of council directive 95/29/ec amending directive 91/628/eec on the protection of animals during transport.

legislation must lay down rules to ensure that they are so and the authorities must monitor that they are complied with. i would like to make two points: firstly, the conditions must be the same for long haulage as for short haulage. we must not demonize long-distance transport, because that would distort competition in the internal market. secondly, the conditions of transport must also be the same for all animals travelling, whether they are on their way to the slaughterhouse or whether they are travelling to be reared at a greater or lesser distance from their place of origin or to take part in a competition. these issues are not reflected in the report, and i would like to see them, commissioner, reflected in future commission proposals. i also welcome and thank the rapporteur for introducing an amendment on behalf of my group to remove the references to temperatures. because it doesn't make sense to talk about temperatures without matching them to the corresponding relative humidity. moreover, from lapland to the canary islands, europe is very large and very diverse in climate, population density and socioeconomic conditions. finally, i would like to draw attention to the importance of transport in the spread of epizootic diseases. this has nothing to do with the length of the journey, but we would have to be rigid about the rules and the control of their compliance. for example, the classic swine fever we had in spain in 1997 was caused by piglets that traveled from holland. this can and must be avoided.
commission. – mr president, i am pleased to outline to you the commission's position on mr maat’s excellent report. the subject matter of this report is animal welfare and animal transport in particular. we all know that this is a very sensitive issue. i made clear when i presented the original commission proposal that the views of the council and parliament would help shape the proposals which i intend to present early next year. the report under discussion here today shares most of the objectives of the commission. however, there is one key building block missing in the construction of the commission’s final proposals and that is the opinion of the scientific committee on animal health and animal welfare, which is expected shortly. this opinion will provide the commission with the necessary scientific advice on key issues such as travelling times and loading densities. on such issues, our actions must be guided by good scientific advice on animal transport conditions. let me nonetheless indicate some general impressions on some of the key issues raised in your report. first of all on travelling time, i was very glad to note that some of the more extreme suggestions, such as a four-hour limit on animal transport, have not been supported in mr maat’s report. the consistent advice to the commission is that the stress and risk to animals in transport arises primarily from three factors: travelling time, loading and unloading of animals and the conditions in which they are transported – ventilation, humidity, density and so on. the commission has already presented proposals for improvements in these areas or will be presenting them shortly. however there is too much emphasis in some quarters on travelling time. i consider that a reduction to four hours is simplistic and takes no account of the wider interests involved. we cannot ignore the interests of the farmers and the meat and livestock industry. such a reduction would be viewed as an attack on their livelihoods rather than a genuine contribution to animal welfare. if we wish to retain their support for improved animal welfare then we must also respect their interests. i wish to work with them rather than against them and hope that you share this view. i would now like to turn to the issue of resources. your report calls for the number of inspectors in the food and veterinary office engaged on animal welfare to be increased to fourteen, compared with the current figure of four. the reality is that such an increase could only be achieved at the expense of other priorities, including bse, foot-and-mouth disease, meat hygiene, residue levels and food safety generally, where the commission is already over-stretched. i have consistently refused to make promises on which i cannot deliver. it would be dishonest to do so, both to this house and to the european public. you stress the lack of enforcement of the current legislation in member states. i fully agree. member states must make the effort and provide the resources to ensure better implementation. it is a point which i have made repeatedly to the member states in the agriculture council. judging from the correspondence i receive from members of parliament, the best way to achieve better enforcement is through legal proceedings against the member states. however it should be pointed out that sometimes it is more effective to work with member states than against them, so proceedings should be the last resort. they are, after all, responsible for the on-the-ground implementation of community legislation. but let me be clear: where efforts to find solutions through dialogue do not succeed, the commission will initiate infringement proceedings against the member states concerned. in fact, proceedings are under way against several member states and are under consideration for several more. finally, in this respect, i would call on the house to assist the commission’s efforts in encouraging member states to take animal welfare more seriously. in particular i would call on members to remind your political colleagues in your own member states of the need to put more efforts and resources into ensuring that the community provisions on animal welfare are complied with. mr maat, ladies and gentlemen, i will be returning to you shortly with the commission’s formal proposals. this will provide you with the opportunity to shape the hard legislation on animal welfare. i can assure you that mr maat’s report will be a major influence on this legislation.

question no 29 by mrs nuala ahern (h-0849/01): does the commission intend to put in place the appropriate institutional instruments to prepare within six months a full analysis of the range of options for reducing the threats to nuclear installations from possible deliberately caused aircraft accidents and other malicious acts, including the potential benefits of dry storage of irradiated fuels in installations which can withstand acts of sabotage, the suspension of the removal of stocks of highly radioactive liquid waste until they are vitrified, or the use of vitrification in a programme to render plutonium excessively dense?
the commission's first task is to act within the limits of the treaties. i want to tell you that nuclear power stations are not designed to take the impact of a large commercial aircraft. it is true that not all nuclear power stations in the european union are the same; those with a second layer of protection, and in particular the latest ones built in germany, may have better resilience or safety in such situations than others. but i would like to stress that security, in its two aspects - security against terrorist attacks, external agents or sabotage, and security against possible accidents - is a national responsibility. the honourable member is right, however, and we are concerned about these issues, particularly in the light of enlargement and the achievement of safety standards in nuclear power stations in the countries which will join the european union in the future. we are analysing precisely how far we can go within the euratom treaty to incorporate and seek equivalent levels of safety within the nuclear installations of the countries that are part of the union, but, i repeat, within the margins set by the treaties. like the honourable member, i consider it necessary to ensure maximum security. finally, we must not only refer to nuclear power stations. the large petrochemical plants, the large chemical plants, the large reservoirs are other installations which present a major risk and which can unfortunately cause major catastrophes if a certain type of attack or sabotage occurs. this is something that various countries are working on, not just those in the european union.
the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been involved in the negotiations on the euratom treaty. however, at the moment the wenras, where all the regulators from the different member states of the european union meet, are working on finding equivalent safety standards which, in my opinion (which are shared by the services, although it is not an official position of the commission, so i am taking the appropriate distance), are necessary and beneficial for everyone: for the states which have taken the non-nuclear option, but also for the whole, because i think, like the honourable member, that if there is an accident at a nuclear power station the repercussions go beyond administrative borders and the problem is pan-european or even global. the vienna commission, which is under the united nations, must therefore be supported. it is therefore appropriate to establish such equivalent safety standards, with a degree of bindingness similar to that required in the community, which would offer a greater guarantee for everyone. we are making these analyses on the basis of the situation and, if it were necessary to make a proposal to amend the treaties, we would have to consider it.

- question no 38 by mr jonas sjöstedt (h-0821/01): subject: prohibition of cadmium in fertilisers marketed in sweden sweden is due to lift its ban on cadmium in marketed fertilisers on 1 january, when the eu's exemption expires and new regulations are not yet ready. when sweden joined the eu in 1995, it was granted the right to maintain stricter regulations than the eu on various chemicals and dangerous substances for a period of four years. as regards the strict regulations imposed in sweden on the use of cadmium in marketed fertilisers, the derogation has been extended for three years and will end on 1 january next, while no new regulations are yet ready. this temporary derogation was intended to allow the eu to strengthen its regulations on dangerous products in the meantime, which it did except for cadmium in fertilisers. pending a common regulation, which will not even be ready by 1 january next, it would be necessary to extend this derogation which concerns not only sweden but also finland and austria. the commission proposal is not yet ready, especially since it will have to be endorsed by the council and the european parliament. this will be followed by a period of time during which marketed fertilisers with a high cadmium content can be officially marketed in sweden. does the commission consider that sweden can, in the meantime, continue to apply its own rules?
commission. – on 14 september 2001 the commission proposed the regulation of the european parliament and of the council relating to fertilisers in which the derogation permitting austria, finland and sweden to maintain national limits on the level of cadmium in fertilisers is extended up to 31 december 2004. this proposal is now in the hands of the council and parliament for the codecision procedure. the issue of cadmium in fertilisers has been under study by the commission for a number of years, originally with the aim of introducing appropriate harmonising legislation before the derogation expires on 31 december 2001. however, due to the complexity of the scientific issues involved, and the delays in the risk assessments carried out by the member states, it was not possible to propose the required legislation at an earlier stage. for this reason, the commission decided to extend the derogation on cadmium in fertilisers for a further three years and it did so by including the appropriate provisions in a proposal for a regulation recasting the existing fertiliser directives. as the major part of the text of the proposed regulation is not new, it is hoped that this proposal will be adopted rapidly, possibly at first reading. the commission is doing everything possible to facilitate rapid adoption of the regulation. but if it turns out that it is not possible to have the proposed regulation in place before the end of the year, the member states concerned can ask for a derogation under article 95(4) of the treaty.

question no 43 by mrs maría izquierdo rojo (h-0794/01) subject: fundamentalist laws applied in the territory of the european union with reference to certain violations of women's rights, linked to fundamentalism, which are found on the territory of the european union, does the commission intend to take appropriate measures to avoid the application of regulations which are incompatible with human rights? does the commission accept that under the guise of religious beliefs, cultural practices or customary law, fundamental human rights can be violated? what measures does it intend to take in the short and long term?
commission. - the violations of women's rights to which the honourable member refers take different forms and would call for a differentiated analysis. however, the commission notes that, in accordance with article 6 of the treaty on european union, the european union is founded on the principles of liberty, democracy, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, and the rule of law, which are common to the member states. as was reaffirmed at the fourth world conference on women in beijing in 1995, the promotion and protection of women's rights is an integral part of universal human rights. the commission cannot accept that under the cover of religious beliefs, cultural practices or customary law, the fundamental rights of the individual may be infringed. this position is dictated by the charter of fundamental rights of the european union - articles 1, 4, 21, 23, 24 - and by other texts relating to fundamental rights, such as the universal declaration of human rights - articles 2 and 5 - or the european convention on human rights - articles 2, 3 and 14. the vienna declaration, adopted in june 1993 by the world conference on human rights, states in paragraph 18 that all forms of violence against women, based on cultural a priori, must be banned. apart from national protection of fundamental rights, and women's rights in particular, it should be noted that the community has been developing a policy for the promotion of gender equality since 1975. equal access to the labour market, to governing bodies and to social rights are important rights in this regard, as is the right to be protected from violence and sexual harassment. there is a body of community legislation, directives and even the case law of the court of justice, based on a specific legal basis, namely article 141 of the treaty establishing the european community. in addition, the treaty requires that gender equality concerns be mainstreamed into all union policies. this is article 3 of the treaty establishing the european community.
- thank you very much, commissioner, for this reply, which shows that the commission has understood the problem. as a supplementary question, i would like to know whether, in accordance with your answer, you envisage and support that immigrant women should be informed about their rights within the european union. could immigrant women have access to services to defend their rights? i would like to know what you think and if there are any plans to do so.
- i will be glad to answer. i would begin by saying that all the initiatives which the commission has put forward on the right of asylum and legal immigration have specific legal rules to deal with the very special situation of immigrant women or women seeking refuge and asylum in the countries of the european union. we have made provision for the granting of asylum requests to be subject to specific conditions in order to deal with the situation of women. for example, the possibility that a woman who has been a victim of sexual abuse can ask for the interrogator to be changed from a man to a woman, because she might feel more comfortable telling the story on which her asylum claim is based. the honourable member has raised a very important issue: the information of immigrants on their rights. the commission is certainly concerned that immigrants, as well as refugees and asylum seekers, should be given as complete information as possible about their rights. i think that if the honourable member examines the specific proposals which the commission has made to the council and parliament, both on immigration and asylum, she will see that the idea of rights information is present. it is the responsibility of the national authorities of the member states, as well as of the non-governmental organisations with which we work very closely in these areas, to provide complete and comprehensive information on the rights of immigrants seeking asylum in the european union.

i would like to congratulate the commissioner and the rapporteur on this report because the green paper on the security of energy supply is a magnificent document and has been accompanied by a great report. this document represents the first major step in europe's energy strategy; it offers a global perspective of the situation and puts all the relevant issues in this sector on the table, without complexities or conditions. it notes that our main problem is supply, characterised by a high degree of external dependence, which will be accentuated in the coming decades. but we must not forget the environmental issues, which are inseparable from the use of energy. in this respect, the adopted directive on renewable energy sources and the proposal on the promotion of biofuels will be a major step forward in diversifying the supply of clean energy, but they are not the solution in the short or medium term. we must not restrict any type of energy, especially if it produces no co2 emissions. the solutions, as the commission rightly points out, are to diversify sources of supply, especially clean sources - which do not produce greenhouse gases. we must insist on technological research into energy, energy savings and the liberalization of the gas sectors, if we are to have a genuine internal energy market. it would also be good if the treaties included a chapter on energy.

commission (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i want to thank the european parliament for the report on the commission's white paper on a future chemicals policy. i really do hope that it will be adopted tomorrow. it is incredibly important that we should take this step towards a new, better and more effective chemicals policy. i want to say a special thank-you to mrs schörling, who has put a great deal of work into her role as rapporteur. i also want to thank all those who have taken part in the debate, because it has been an important discussion in which important points of view have emerged. the white paper presents the commission's proposal for a new chemicals strategy. the modes of procedure presented in the white paper are well balanced, and i believe they involve a step forward in the direction of sustainable development. the debate in this house has perhaps shown that we have succeeded reasonably well in finding a balance between different views, even though there is scope for improvements. the background is as follows. chemical production has increased almost explosively, from 1 million tons in 1930 to 400 million tons per year today. we wish to maintain a high level of protection for the environment and human health, but we also need to try to make use of the advantages presented by chemicals. we all know that there are chemicals in practically all the products we encounter every day. it would be unrealistic to believe that, with a wave of the hand, we could get rid of all chemicals or that there could be a chemical-free modern society. however, we must balance these requirements. anyone who examined what is now the european union's 20 year-old system of supervision would see clearly that it is not effective enough by a long chalk. i would maintain that the system makes, for example, an artificial or arbitrary distinction between old and new chemicals. chemicals have many extremely important advantages for society. thanks to medicines and pharmaceutical products, it is possible to combat illnesses and suffering. it is probably the case that a majority of the products forming part of our modern lifestyle today are manufactured from plastic or contain chemicals of some kind. the chemicals industry is one of europe's largest manufacturing industries, employing 1.7 million people. between three and four million jobs depend upon it. ninety-six percent of all companies are small and medium-sized, and they account for approximately 23 percent of chemicals production. we are all of us exposed to chemicals on a daily basis. we have tried to look into whether this situation can be described in figures. calculated, for example, in tons, each and every one of us probably comes into contact with several tons of chemicals in our daily life. that should also mean that we are exposed to several tens of thousands of chemicals. more and more reports are coming in concerning health problems, allergies and asthma assumed to be connected with chemicals. as has already been mentioned, research results show that the human body can contain at least 350 synthetic chemicals which, in the natural course of things, ought not to be there. there are persistent and bioaccumulative chemicals, and these are now to be found in placentas, foetuses and new-born children, to which they are transferred. these chemicals are the first things a child ingests. chemicals are found in the depths of the sea and in the arctic, where they have never once been used. hormone-changing substances can affect our reproduction and our nervous systems. that's a fact. the procedures governing the present eu legislation have been rightly criticised for being too slow and unwieldy. even though we have made some progress within the eu when it comes to evaluating the risks and restricting and controlling the use of hazardous chemicals, there is still an incredible amount to do. at present, it is the authorities who have to demonstrate that a chemical is unsafe. that obviously has to change. as in the case of all other products, the responsibility for ensuring that products released onto the market are safe must lie with producers, manufacturers and users at later stages in the manufacturing chain. that, basically, is what eu legislation will amount to. can you think of any other product about whose content we don't even have basic information or for which responsibility is entirely assumed by the authorities? that is a basic error in the system. what we now have to do is find a suitable balance between, on the one hand, the advantages of chemicals and, on the other hand, the unacceptable risks they involve for human health and the environment. at the same time, we naturally want to ensure that the internal market is able to function and that the european chemical industry, which is the world's largest, can maintain its competitiveness. in order to better be able to assess the consequences of different ways of implementing the proposals in the white paper, we have set up an inquiry which will look more closely into the costs. the commission proposes that a 'reach system' be set up to cover both existing substances, many of which have been on the market for at least 20 years but have never been properly tested, and new substances released onto the market after 1981. the industry must be given incentives to gather data and, if need be, test the substances, preferably without using animal experiments. we must help each other ensure that animal experiments are restricted. an integrated policy is needed in order to do this. none of us, i trust, would happily see full-scale experiments carried out on living human beings, animals or the countryside involving chemicals whose contents we do not know enough about. there is, in actual fact, no denying that that is what happens at present, because we don't know enough about the chemicals that are released. pragmatic decisions are required in this area, together with a sensible application of the precautionary principle to chemicals policy. if there are reasons to suspect that a substance has harmful effects on health or the environment and if our scientific and technical knowledge is not sufficient to provide a clear appreciation of the risks, we must take no chances and restrict or prohibit the use of the substance until we know more. the absolute top priority is to fill the gaps in our knowledge of the risks involved in the 30 000 'existing substances' that are produced or imported in quantities greater than that of one tonne per manufacturer per year. the proposed new system includes a special arrangement for substances that give cause for special concern, or what are known as cmr substances. these are substances that are carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic to reproduction. they must be authorised before they are allowed to be used, and companies must show that they can be used safely on condition that risk management measures are taken. it should then be possible to authorise such safe use with reference to the cost and income analyses supplied by the companies. in this way, the burden of proof will be redistributed, and the risk assessment will be focused on those areas of use for which the companies have sought authorisation. in this way, approximately 1 500 substances, that is to say 5 per cent of all substances, will be covered by this authorisation procedure. the system will promote innovation, and that will lead to the most hazardous substances being replaced. i note that, in its draft report, the parliament proposes that several categories of substance be added to the authorisation procedure. i can appreciate its wanting to do that, but i believe that, as matters stand, it would be inappropriate to accord the system too much scope. we must be pragmatic to start with, so that we do not relapse into having an unmanageable system. if we overload the system, a large number of resources will be employed in managing a very small portion of all those substances that need to be investigated. we have limited resources, and we must establish priorities and decide how we are to use our resources in the most effective ways. the draft report also says that the proposed eu system must cover chemicals produced in quantities of less than one tonne in the form of substances or preparations that occur in products. on behalf of the commission, i would most definitely recommend a limit of one tonne so that it is possible to use the resources of the industry and of the authorities in the most effective way possible. if we want to get the proposal through, we must concentrate on what is most hazardous. there is no doubt a misunderstanding here. this limit does not apply to the most hazardous substances which, in each and every case, must go through the authorisation procedure. the very fact that the limit is set at one tonne does not mean that chemicals produced in smaller quantities escape monitoring. the industry is still obliged to carry out a risk assessment of the chemicals and to provide safety information to users in the form of marking and safety data sheets. it is the responsibility of the member states to ensure that these provisions are complied with. the industry must be able, upon request, to supply information to the authorities. the commission has now set up a number of technical working groups with experts from the member states, industry, non-governmental organisations and the commission. the outcome of their deliberations is expected in february 2002, and it will constitute one of the most important contributions to the draft legislation on the part of the commission. it is difficult to prophesy when the commission will be able to table its proposals. if everything goes smoothly, i believe that we can aim for april or may 2002, but the objective is, no matter what, to submit the proposals to parliament and the council before the summer of 2002. finally, i want to say a few words about the debate which i know is taking place and which is perhaps being conducted most eagerly in germany and the united kingdom. what matters is that the european chemical industry should remain competitive, but we are doing nothing that is not also being done in the united states, canada and japan within the framework of the oecd. roughly the same measures are also being taken by our competitor countries and in the world around us, where precisely the same problems are being experienced as in europe. if the desire is for the european chemicals industry to hold its own, sustainable development must be worked for. it must be possible to guarantee that what is produced is safe for use in terms of human health and the environment and that it corresponds to the requirements of consumers. we have tabled a balanced proposal which takes account of the needs of industry but which also states that what is most important is to bring about a high level of protection for human health and the environment. i think the best answer that can be given is to say that there's no need to be anxious. this proposal will lead to innovation in the chemicals sphere. we can defend our european chemicals industry through the safe use of chemicals in the future.

- mr president, free access to the market for port services and equal opportunities in this area are not only desirable but also a requirement of the union's treaties. in this connection, it is necessary to regulate and control the existence of state aid to ports, since this would undermine free competition between community ports. however, there are aspects which should not be regulated exclusively by the union. member states and their constitutional entities with competence in this area should retain the ability to include their specific rules for the award of contracts for the provision of port services and for the protection of the workers concerned. in addition, the dredging, mooring and handling of cargo, including stowage, stowage and transhipment, given their status as compulsory services, should not be included in the community directive liberalizing port services, but their regulation should be left to the states and their port authorities, for reasons of maritime safety. at an airport, chaos would result if there were more than one air traffic control service provider. in a port, for the same reason, there should only be one practice and one mooring service.

question no 4 by mr manuel medina ortega (h-0781/01) subject: landing of large numbers of illegal immigrants in the canary islands following recent reports of the use of mother ships to land large numbers of illegal immigrants from the african continent in the canary islands, what measures does the council intend to take to ensure the integrity of the community's maritime space in this region?
counsel. mr president, the council has already answered several times questions from members of the european parliament concerning illegal immigration by sea from the african continent. i would refer in particular to the answers to oral questions h-2701, h-0330/01, h-0699/01 on illegal immigration into the european union, and to the answers to written questions e-0085/01 and e-1045/01, which also dealt with these issues. the council has already taken several measures to combat illegal immigration. the development of action plans for countries and regions of origin of illegal immigrants and/or asylum seekers, within the framework of the high level group on asylum/migration, is a good example. another example is the early warning system developed within cirefi. measures to improve the effectiveness of member states' controls at maritime borders have been put in place in the framework of schengen cooperation. with the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, these measures now form part of the community acquis. the implementation of control measures is of course the responsibility of the member states, and the surveillance and control of the territorial sea is therefore their responsibility. the council also stressed that these preparatory bodies were currently examining the establishment of a set of good practices to better guide the member states in the implementation of these checks.

- question no 5 by mr camilo nogueira román, substituted by mr ortuondo larrea (h-0783/01): subject: references to nationalism in the conclusions of the european council of 21 september 2001 in the wake of the terrible terrorist attacks in the united states and the tragedy of 11 september, the people of this country reacted with great vigour, with clear expressions of nationalism or patriotism based on the democratic and moral values that underlie north american society. it is a similar democratic nationalism that gave birth to most of the current member states of the european union, in the face of absolutism. the fact that some european states have given in to violent imperialism, which has led to the tragic wars of european history, has nothing to do with the peaceful aspirations for freedom which characterize the democratic nationalism of the majority of our nations. it is therefore surprising that in the conclusions of the european council of 21 september 2001, motivated precisely by the attacks on cities in the united states, the term nationalism is repeatedly used indiscriminately on the same footing as the notions of racism and xenophobia, which objectively constitutes an offense to all europeans who feel themselves to be peaceful, democratic and supportive members of a nation and a national culture, as well as members of the european and international community. does the council not think that it is manifestly unfair to link the notion of nationalism in such a vague way with the notions of racism and xenophobia?
the council. - the council would point out that it is not for the council to comment on the conclusions of the european council. in this case, however, it should be noted that in its conclusions of 21 september 2001, the european council stressed the need to combat any nationalist, racist or xenophobic tendencies. and i insist, all nationalist drift, which is not the same as nationalism. the word "nationalism" does not appear in the text. only "abuses, misuse, in nationalist, racist or xenophobic terms" are shown. and in that sense, i do not think that the position taken by the council is really contradictory to the one you expressed in your question.

- question no 12 by mr sacrédeus (h-0797/01): subject: request for the death sentence of 16 afghans accused of conversion in kabul, afghanistan, a magistrate brought 16 afghans to trial and asked that they be sentenced to death. the main charge is their conversion from islam to christianity, for which the prosecutor is seeking the death penalty for all the accused, in accordance with the islamic law of the taliban regime. in a parallel trial in kabul, eight employees of the humanitarian organization shelter now international are being prosecuted for proselytism. in this case too, the magistrate demands the death penalty for all the accused under islamic law. germany, the united states and australia have taken diplomatic steps to defend the eight humanitarian workers and to ensure their legal security. in an earlier reply to me in plenary, the commission stated that the three countries had indicated that the eu did not need to deal with the matter. however, no diplomatic action was taken on behalf of the 16 afghan defendants, either by the eu or by individual member states. the eu is active internationally in the abolition of the death penalty and in the promotion of religious freedom on the basis of tolerance and respect for different beliefs. how has this position been expressed in the council's efforts in the case of the 16 afghan converts? how is the european union, through the council, following and acting in the context of the trial of the 16 afghans, and what concrete measures have been taken to ensure legal security, protection and the lives of the accused?
council. - the council shares your concern about afghan citizens and foreign aid workers who are accused by the taliban of religious conversion and proselytism and who therefore face a very serious threat of the death penalty. the council's position on the death penalty is well known. the promotion and respect for fundamental human rights, including freedom of religion or belief, are an essential element of the european union's policy towards third countries and are therefore enshrined in the common position of the european union on afghanistan. the main international legal instruments guarantee the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion. this right includes the freedom to change his religion or belief and the freedom to manifest his religion or belief, individually or in a group, in public or in private. the union has expressed its concern about the human rights situation in afghanistan in international forums, in particular before the third committee of the united nations general assembly, where all eu member states supported the italian draft resolution on human rights violations in afghanistan. since the eu member states do not recognise the taliban government, it is extremely difficult to communicate with them and to access the territories under their control. this was already the case before september 11, 2001. the bilateral diplomatic efforts to protect foreign collaborators, made by german, american and australian diplomats from islamabad, have so far produced no tangible results. since the beginning of military action in afghanistan on 7 october, it has obviously become even more difficult to follow closely the fate of the 16 afghans in question and to contribute to the political outcome of this matter. i regret that, but you will also understand that the situation is even more difficult to assess today than it was in the past.

the council. - once again, this house invites the council presidency to speak on relations between cuba and the european union. i would therefore like to take this opportunity to recall a few points and perhaps to clear up some misunderstandings about these relations. the european union's common position on cuba remains the basis of the european union's policy towards that country. as stated in the treaty on european union, common positions are one of the instruments of the european union's common foreign and security policy (see article 12), and decisions on the common foreign and security policy are taken unanimously (see article 23). the council, at the ninth review of the common position on cuba on 25 june, noted that it remained valid. the european union's objectives with regard to cuba remain to encourage a peaceful transition process towards democratic pluralism and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. at the same time, the council has consistently shown its readiness to maintain a frank and constructive dialogue on all matters of common interest. last june the council reaffirmed its intention to maintain this approach. it also expressed its support for the establishment of an open political dialogue and the search for a future framework cooperation agreement based on respect for democratic principles, human rights and the rule of law. it is in this spirit that on 23 and 24 august an exploratory mission of the european union troika, led by the deputy prime minister and minister for foreign affairs, mr louis michel, visited havana. on the other hand, at the occasion of the ninth evaluation of the common position, the council encouraged the european commission to strengthen its cooperation efforts, in particular with civil society and non-governmental organisations in cuba, so that a wider presence of eu actors on the ground would contribute more effectively to the achievement of the objectives of the common position. in addition, as you yourself have pointed out, cuba's main economic partners are the member states of the european union. however, it should not be forgotten that it was the cuban authorities who interrupted the dialogue between the european union and cuba when they cancelled, almost the day before, the mission of the eu troika at director-general level, which was scheduled for 27 and 28 april 2000. the cuban authorities also withdrew their application for accession to the cotonou agreement in may 2000. in addition, as the council had already noted at the ninth review of the common position, no significant therefore give any details of this second meeting.

- question no 16 by liam hyland (h-0810/01) subject: reversing the process of depopulation in rural areas has the council, under the belgian presidency of the eu and in consultation with the incoming spanish presidency, considered the need to implement a european union policy actively aimed at reversing the process of depopulation in rural areas of the member states, including ireland? is he prepared to make a statement on the issues that need to be considered, including the financial aspects, pilot projects, studies and the involvement of appropriate ngos? does it also intend to invite the commission to publish a communication on policies to reverse the process of depopulation in rural areas?
council. - i would first like to point out that, within the framework of european regional policy, and in particular in the current programming period 2000 to 2006, there is the possibility of supporting the economic and social conversion of objective 2 rural areas with a population density of less than 100 inhabitants per km2. the council would also draw your attention to the fact that, following the presentation by the commission of the second report on economic and social cohesion, representatives of the member states, the commission and the european parliament met last june, at the initiative of the swedish presidency of the council, in lycksele in northern sweden, to share their experiences and discuss the future of depopulated areas, including rural areas, a future for which the presidency, which we are assuming this semester, continues to work. the council considers that the main priority at this stage should be to seek to maximise the full potential of the current rules to combat depopulation and the impoverishment of certain rural areas. this is a task which falls mainly to the member states, in accordance with the criteria defined at community level. since the commission's proposals for the future programming period are not expected until 2004, the council considers that it is still premature to start a new debate on the implementation of a european union policy for depopulated or depopulated rural areas which would go beyond what is currently in force.
counsel. - i can only confirm what i have just said, namely that i think, and the council also, that the existing regulations must be used to the best of its potential. since this is a community framework, in which the member states must take concrete action, i am in favour of going further in the use of the present regulation, rather than prematurely embarking on a new debate on the implementation of a policy in favour of these areas. i believe that the existing framework can be better exploited, not only at community level but also and above all at the subsidiary level, that is to say at the level of the member states which must try to implement these policies within the framework of the criteria defined at community level.

this subject, in which it stated that the single market and the single currency should be accompanied by a common payment area. the commission was criticized in this parliament for being too passive. i remember that well. mrs peijs wondered when the commission would take action. the commission has listened to mrs peijs and acted, and no one can deny that. the commission has put forward a draft regulation based on a simple principle, namely that any payment in euro should cost the same, whether it is a domestic or a crossborder payment. this is of great importance to the citizens, as has been pointed out by many members of this parliament. today, the euro is a virtual currency, especially for citizens. but on 1 january 2002 the currency will take on a concrete form, as from that date 300 million europeans will use the same banknotes and coins. today, citizens in europe still accept that a crossborder payment costs more than a domestic one. the reason is that there are different currencies involved, but after 1 january this will no longer be the case. the citizens will then ask what is the use of the euro if crossborder payments are still as expensive as they are now. i would remind you that our latest study of the cost of crossborder transfers has produced astonishing results. it has been found that in 2001 the average cost of a crossborder transfer of eur 100 was eur 24. we had already carried out a similar study in 1993. we have unfortunately had to find that in eight years no progress has been made. the commission has therefore decided to use the instrument of a regulation. the market itself has not been able to find solutions to the problem and the legislator is trying to force the market operators to create the infrastructures that the market needs. as mrs peijs knows, i am a staunch liberal and i regret that i have been forced to propose such a forceful text for the banks. but it is the only way to encourage operators to make use of the new systems which are essential for the proper functioning of the internal market. i am therefore pleased to note that the first results are already being seen. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial system is in a position to meet the requirements of the single market. and that is proof that the proposal for a regulation is also realistic. the following is also true of the banking sector: where there's a will, there's a way. what surprised me, though, is the thinking of the banking industry: we, the banks, are committed to implementing the plan, so you, the commission, can withdraw your proposal for a regulation. firstly, it should not be forgotten that this plan can count on the support of only a part of the banking sector. there are three european banking associations and only one of them has written to me to propose this plan. that's an important fact. a payment system is a network, and a network develops at the pace of its slowest members. well, it's enough that a part of the members of a network refuse to evolve further, to block all the other members. that is one of the reasons why no progress has been made in the last ten years. secondly, the plan proposed is too late. it was announced in a press release two weeks before the proposal was to be debated in parliament. the commission has been asking for this matter to be dealt with for 11 years, but in all that time too little has been done, and for these reasons, mr president, the commission cannot respond positively to those members of parliament who have proposed that the banking sector should be given a certain degree of self-regulation. the banking sector has had enough time, now comes with its own proposal, at least part of the banking sector. it is too little, too late, and the commission must therefore propose a regulation. it is therefore not logical, mr president, to demand that the proposal be withdrawn before the first fruits are visible. the idea of suspending the regulation as proposed in amendment no 9 by mr maaten does not therefore seem acceptable to me. i repeat what i said about that: the proposals for self-regulation are too late. mr president, every call from the commission to the banking world is supported or has been supported by this parliament, and that is encouraging. i commend many members of this house in this connection, and especially the rapporteur, mrs peijs, who has worked with perseverance to reduce the cost of transfers. mrs peijs is expressing the opinion of the citizens and the great importance of this for business, not least small and mediumsized enterprises. the commission's proposal is a concrete expression of what is called the people's europe. i come now to another point of discussion, namely the date on which the present draft regulation should enter into force. some members of this parliament have referred to the opinion of the european central bank in this connection. it says that the ecb fully agrees with the objectives we are pursuing with our proposal but that we, the commission, would be going too fast and being too demanding. the key point in the ecb's argument is that banks need more time to set up the necessary infrastructure and logistical facilities. the european central bank therefore proposes 1 january 2005 as the date for the entry into force of the regulation. on the one hand, mr president, i do not deny that it will take time to create this infrastructure, but on the other hand i also believe that this problem should not be exaggerated. for years the banks have been telling us that crossborder transfers represent only 1% of total transfers. the entry into force of the regulation in 2003 will therefore not entail any insurmountable additional costs, and if our expectations are met and if it appears that the price reduction will result in increased use of this means of payment, then there is even more reason to speed up the work. mr president, mrs peijs' report contains 16 amendments, seven on the recitals and nine on the articles. there is only one amendment which is not acceptable, and that is amendment no 9 on the suspension of the regulation which i mentioned earlier. one amendment raises a legal problem, namely amendment no 4 on the increase in the cost of domestic payments. this is a political statement, which i fully support, but it does not fit into a legal text. i would also like to refer to the last speaker, mrs thyssen, who asked me what the situation was with banks recovering what they lose in international payments from domestic payments. as has been rightly pointed out, this proposed regulation is not a price measure: the prices of the transfers are not fixed, which means that the prices for domestic transfers could theoretically increase.
the commission - mr president, the commission has taken note of what mrs peijs has just said and will take a more detailed view of the matter. thank you very much, mr president.

- the next item is the report (a5-0395/2001) by mrs miguélez ramos, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the proposal for a council regulation to promote the conversion of vessels and fishermen who were, until 1999, dependent on the fisheries agreement with morocco (com (2001) 384 - c5-0407/2001 - 2001/0163 (cns)).
the rapporteur. - mr president, the european parliament gives the commission the opportunity to correct the proposal for a regulation which it once sent to parliament and the council. the report adopted by the committee on fisheries, which we are now discussing, is intended to correct the rigidities in the proposal which make it unable to solve the problems faced by those affected by the non-renewal of the ec-morocco fisheries agreement. from the moment it expired on 30 november 1999 until it became clear that a new one would not be concluded, owners of more than 400 vessels and some 4 300 fishermen were living in hope and fear as negotiations between the community and morocco dragged on. it was not until 26 march 2001 that commissioner fischler informed us that it had been impossible to conclude an agreement to our mutual benefit. the community has since set itself the objective of converting the fishing fleet concerned. by presenting this proposal for a regulation, the commission is in line with the guidelines set out by the nice european council of 7 december 2000. at this summit, the european council instructed the commission to propose a specific action programme for the restructuring of this community fleet. i must say clearly that this proposal for a regulation does not meet the needs of the sector concerned. once again the commission seems to be presenting proposals whose purpose is elusive to us, but which do not correspond to a determined action to support a fleet and regions in serious crisis. instead of helping to preserve the bulk of the fleet and its economic activity, the commission is putting forward a rigid proposal which, if the council approves it without the substantial changes approved by the committee on fisheries, will have the effect of scrapping a fleet for which shipowners and local authorities in these regions feel able to find alternatives. the proposal must therefore be amended in the sense approved by the committee on fisheries so that the measures envisaged can be effective for the benefit of the sector concerned. the committee on fisheries does not share the commission's scrapping vision. the commission could have focused on the opportunities in alternative sectors such as the processing industry, aquaculture and especially the promotion of fishery products. the proposal also excludes sectors directly affected by the non-renewal of the agreement, such as the non-extractive fishing industries. the shore-based companies, during the long negotiation process, have suffered a series of economic losses which have led to employment regulations and layoffs, causing them a significant volume of losses. today they face a future as uncertain as that of the fleet on which they depend. in view of this approach, which gives priority to scrapping, the sector concerned and the regional authorities have made verbal commitments to companies and shipowners in several maghreb countries to set up joint ventures, so that, according to estimates by the craft sector itself, a hundred ships could be relocated with the aid of this specific measure, if it were more flexible, reducing those destined for scrapping to 26. this would maintain a vital economic activity for certain regions and ensure the continuity of ship owners and fishermen who want to remain so. the amendments to the fisheries committee's report, in summary, amend the proposal for a regulation as follows:in addition to shipowners and fishermen, the shore-based fishing industry, whose activity was directly linked to the existence of this agreement, is included, provided that its loss volume exceeds 70%. the requirement that the persons concerned must have been subsidised for at least nine consecutive months for cessation of activity is abolished in order to benefit from this specific measure. this requirement would mean excluding those who, sometimes temporarily, found alternative employment while awaiting the conclusion of a new fisheries agreement with morocco. this is all the more serious when we consider that these shipowners and fishermen had not been warned that, if they found an activity, they would be penalized when they were converted. the committee on fisheries has also rejected the demand for repayment of the aid received for modernisation. it is not appropriate to apply a penalising criterion retroactively to aid which was not subject to such conditionality at the time it was granted. the commission proposal proposes to increase public aid per shipowner by 20% in the event of scrapping or transfer to a third country. the committee on fisheries believes that fishermen should also benefit from this 20% increase. we have also made another allocation in relation to the financial amount allocated to this specific measure, reducing the amount for scrapping to 30%, the creation of joint ventures to 35% and socioeconomic measures to 35% as well. this will allow for a better implementation of the specific measure. finally, a word on the budgetary aspect. in line with the conclusions of the nice european council, the commission proposes to allocate up to eur 197 million for this specific measure. it proposes to mobilise the flexibility instrument in 2002 and to allocate the appropriations corresponding to heading 2 of the financial perspective. the savings from the non-renewal of the agreement amounted to eur 500 million. it is only natural that the community should also share in the cost of converting this fleet.
- mr president, this house is perhaps hearing for the last time words relating to what we have known for 14 years as the fisheries agreement with morocco. tomorrow, with the vote on the report under discussion today, our institution will be writing the last page of a story that has been with us since august 1987, when the european union signed its first fisheries agreement with this country, but which for spain goes back almost 25 years. there are therefore community fishermen and shipowners whose lives have been exclusively linked to the existence of the moroccan fishing industry. our duty commission. – mr president, i wish to begin by thanking and congratulating mrs miguélez ramos, the vice-chairperson of the committee on fisheries, for her report on this extremely important regulation which aims at facilitating conversion for those thousands of fishermen and hundreds of vessels whose activity has been suddenly cancelled because it has not been possible to conclude a new fishery agreement with the kingdom of morocco. beyond the availability of existing instruments, the community has decided to make a special effort with a twofold initiative. firstly, the council regulation aiming at widening the scope of existing provisions and, secondly, additional credits for a specific action. while the proposal for additional credits is currently being discussed by the budgetary authority, today's debate focuses on the legislative proposal. the commission welcomes the fact that the emergency procedure should allow the adoption of the regulation by the end of november instead of the end of december. the report includes 18 amendments, which may be grouped in a few categories, which i shall review now. the first group consists of amendments nos 1, 2, 5, 10, 11 and 13. the commission does not believe that the land-based industries – that is to say, fish-processing factories, as well as services to vessels – ought to benefit from the new regulation, nor should the coastal regions themselves. indeed, regional development programmes already exist, and those industries in need of conversion or those coastal communities in need of diversification should benefit from the european regional development fund and the european social fund. aquaculture and the fish-processing industry should benefit from the financial instrument for fisheries guidance. the second group of amendments consists of amendments nos 3 and 4. the commission does not believe that all fishermen and vessel owners who have received indemnities in 2000-2001, irrespective of the actual duration of the cessation of activity, should benefit from the new regulation. therefore a minimum duration of compensation, as a simple criterion, has been proposed and a nine-month duration has been considered a reasonable minimum. moreover, until now, no evidence has been given that such a duration would penalise those who have tried to find alternative activities and are still in a difficult situation. the third group consists of amendments nos 6, 7 and 8. with respect to the age of vessels to be withdrawn, the commission has proposed to reduce the minimum age to five years in the case of the exporting of vessels. all other rules should be maintained. moreover, the commission has proposed that the accumulation of grants for construction should be prevented premiums for withdrawal. any alternative rule would be against the sound management of public money, and therefore the commission could not support those amendments. on amendments nos 9 and 12, the commission would stress that social premiums for fishermen are already available in the existing regulation. nonetheless, it may support increasing those premiums in the new regulation. however, spain and portugal should guarantee that such increased premiums do not create distortion in relation to equivalent social premiums that may be available for workers of other industries in the same member states. i turn to amendments nos 14 and 15. the additional credits are not structural funds. providing them allows the commission to set up some rules. those rules should be in line with today’s priorities, which amount to scrapping redundant vessels and also to social measures. no ‘adjustment’ or ‘variation’ should be allowed. then there is amendment no 16. from the commission’s perspective, granting a joint enterprise in the fisheries sector is quite a risky action. two legal provisions limit that risk: firstly a bank guarantee, and secondly, a partially delayed payment (that is, after two years of satisfactory operation). the budget rules for using additional credits imply the relaxation of the second provision, but the commission is willing to maintain its financial risk at the same level. therefore it has proposed to balance that loss by increasing the bank guarantee to 40% of the premium. but that is a purely mechanical calculation. then there is amendment no 17. if the budgetary authority decides to earmark all the commitment credits dedicated to the specific action in the budgetary year 2002, the wording of that article should remain unchanged. otherwise it should be adjusted accordingly. lastly, amendment no 18, which has no practical consequence. the wording of article 7 should remain consistent with the wording of the equivalent articles of regulation (ec) no 2792/1999. in conclusion, the commission has a favourable opinion of amendments nos 9 and 12, and my colleague, mr fischler, will propose to the fisheries council that it includes them in the new regulation. amendment no17 may be considered, depending upon the decision taken by the budgetary authority. i was speaking on behalf of my colleague, mr fischler, who, i am sure, will deal with any questions that i was unable to answer.

- madam president, madam commissioner, before i begin my speech i should like to say to mr bouwman that he was referring to the sintel company, which went bankrupt and left a large number of workers on the street, but it is quite some months since the spanish government took over the back wages of this company and relocated and looked for solutions for all the workers. that's to complete your information, mr. bouwman. i now turn to my comments on this report. the document we are discussing is a proposal to amend directive 80/987/eec on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer. mr bouwman has indeed given a very clear example of this situation. the amendment is intended to take account of the evolution of insolvency law in the member states and the need for consistency with other community directives on labour law which have already been adopted. all this is based on the political will to guarantee wage-earners a minimum of community protection in the event of the insolvency of their employer. the difficulties in achieving the objective of implementing the directive are, in my view, of three kinds: first, the concept of insolvency; second, the complexity of the measures introduced to limit the amount and the time to be calculated; and third, insolvency cases in transnational situations. in order to clarify matters, the group of the european people's party has reiterated two amendments: no 16, which covers situations of outsourcing or similar, subcontracting, false selfemployment, etc., which could conceal a real employment contract. we believe that the reality must be unveiled before protection can be enjoyed: the employed person is protected. the opposite would be to open a wide door that would soon exhaust the respective fund. amendment no 17 clarifies the remuneration that can be protected from the corresponding national fund and prevents fraud. this is all part of the statutory nature of labour law and is inspired by the desire to define clearly the concepts necessary for the fund to fulfil its purpose. conceptual clarity leading to legal certainty and harmonisation. unfortunately, this is a case which - as we have seen recently in another belgian company - is happening in large companies, because of the restructuring of these companies and the relationships that exist at the moment in the economic world.
