to be poor in nicaragua means having to live on a dollar a month. in macroeconomic terms, nicaragua has an external debt of $6.5 billion, exports less than a third of what it imports, and the country is in balance of payments and lives, in short, on international aid and remittances from emigrants, particularly to the united states and costa rica. as for the situation in cuba, on another visit by the delegation, i think we will all agree that the situation in the country is extraordinarily dire. cuba is currently living, firstly, on remittances from emigrants and, secondly, on tourism, which is more important than all cuban exports combined. the resolution therefore seeks first of all to show solidarity with the people affected and with the human victims of the hurricane. secondly, and i am speaking very specifically to the commissioner, i want to express the satisfaction of this parliament with the way the humanitarian aid office has acted. thirdly, i ask that in the case of honduras and nicaragua the damage being assessed be considered in the context of the reconstruction programme for central america. as we are talking about nicaragua, there is an amendment tabled by the socialist group, and i am addressing myself to the rapporteur, which says that, as there has been a diversion of funds - and it refers to european funds - this or that must be done. i have taken the trouble to call the commission delegation in nicaragua. i have a fax here which tells me that in no case has it been proved, nor has there been any investigation into these funds, so it cannot be said that there is any misappropriation. on the recent visit we found that these accusations had been made in the context of an election campaign, but that there is no judicial decision on the matter. i therefore find it extremely reckless to make statements on this subject. mr president, as far as cuba is concerned, the phrase we have added can be interpreted by the various political forces as they see fit. but when we say that we want a cooperation agreement to be concluded in accordance with european doctrine, we mean what the newens report said and what the common position said, we will go to a cooperation agreement when the cuban regime makes significant progress in improving respect for human rights and progresses towards a pluralist democracy. that is the doctrine of the union, which is implicitly contained in this resolution.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i think we are facing a very important european council, the one in laeken. we are facing one of those times axis, as karl jaspers called it. we find that the introduction of the euro will increase the feeling of belonging to europe. the enlargement negotiations will be the realization of a long-standing dream of many europeans. i believe that the terrorist attacks on washington and new york on 11 september have awakened the conscience of europeans, who are asking us for more europe and a better europe. the responsibility you have, mr president-in-office of the council, is therefore great. but let me say that i think you are doing a very good job, and i want to say publicly that this belgian presidency has had an exquisite attitude towards the european parliament, of collaboration, of participation, of listening and, in short, of doing things together. the commitment to the convention is a commitment which this parliament made a long time ago, even before nice. in the resolution of 17 november 1997, which i had the honour of presenting with mr dimitri tsatsos, on the treaty of amsterdam, we already said that the intergovernmental method for revising the treaties had come to an end and that another method had to be found. that method is the convention. and do not think that the european parliament was doing this out of a mania. i'm not sure. i did so because the convention brings europe closer to the citizens, because it is more open, more public, more transparent, more participatory; it allows, as the convention which drew up the charter demonstrated, citizens to be involved in the making of europe. that is why we have voted for the convention, and i am glad that the convention will become a reality in the laeken declaration. but we must not be deceived about the convention. the convention is an instrument. of another famous convention in history, the philadelphia convention, george washington said he could talk about anything, propose anything and decide anything. this one too. we want to help decision-making, bring europe closer to the citizens, to the people, and bring together the different legitimacies of the european union. therefore, ladies and gentlemen of the council, there is no need to fear the convention. we must not use a success tool and empty it of content. the convention must not be restrained. we must give the convention a chance to succeed. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. let me highlight some of them. firstly, what the european parliament is asking for is that, if we use the convention which drew up the charter of fundamental rights as a model, the four parts of it should be balanced. there were 16 meps and 62 members of the convention. in the proposal which you, mr president-in-office of the council, have sent to the capitals, there are still 16 european members, but there are 112 members of the convention. and i don't care if some of them are observers, because observers have exactly the same rights as everyone else, and that's how it should be, except for participation in the final consensus. final agreement. i want to say, despite what some previous speakers have said, that the commission has been involved, and very much so, and i want to commend the reflection notes of commissioner barnier, which have been very important. but perhaps there is a misunderstanding about consensus: consensus does not mean unanimity. it was not in the convention that drew up the charter. there were members of the convention who were against - here are some very notable ones - but there was a sufficient majority, a sufficient consensus. so we do not repeat that consensus means unanimity. no, it means a final endorsement of the resulting text. mr president-in-office of the council, there is a subject which you have said is still up in the air, and that is what is called cooling down. and when i have to explain that after the work of 112 people to reach a final result, governments want to cool it down, it is extremely complicated. what's that about cooling down? if the result is good, adopt it immediately, and let's go do something else. let's go set up the enlargement. in short, mr president, i think we must lose our fear of the convention. we must think that europe is demanding an identifying sign from us. what identifying mark? it's the intergovernmental conference. and i hope that at the end of that process, the identifying sign will be a constitution for the european union. the council. - madam president, i am indeed pleased to be here representing the presidency because the minister of justice is unfortunately unable to be here. i have been asked to speak on his behalf on this subject, and i am naturally very happy to do so.
commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to congratulate mrs gebhardt on her report on the creation of the eurojust unit. the ideas expressed by the commission in its communication of november 2000 and the recommendations adopted by the european parliament in may this year following a report by mrs gebhardt are largely taken up in the text currently under consideration by the council. i think i can therefore limit myself to two or three points in particular. firstly, as mrs gebhardt has said, the rules on the protection of personal data, in the version currently under consideration, have been developed and improved. the project takes a balanced approach that respects both the legitimate interests and fundamental rights of citizens and the need for effective coordination of investigations and prosecutions. there shall be a joint, independent data protection supervisory authority and, where necessary, legal remedies available for access to review by national courts. secondly, the role of the union institutions has been strengthened and the commission is fully associated with the work of eurojust in its various responsibilities. parliament will be fully informed on budgetary matters and i hope that the task of discharge will also be entrusted to it. the excellent report by mrs gebhardt also includes a list of supplementary amendments, most of which have the commission's approval. i will just mention as examples the composition of the joint supervisory authority for personal data, cooperation between the commission's anti-fraud agency, olaf and eurojust, budgetary discharge by parliament, the time limits for data storage or the law applicable in the event of damage resulting from incorrect data processing. i hope that the council will continue to take these suggestions into account. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, in relation to the two other initiatives under consideration, the events of 11 september 2001 have tragically confirmed the soundness of the recommendations adopted by the european parliament on 5 september 2001 following an own-initiative report by mr graham watson. as the commissioner responsible for justice and home affairs, i would like to congratulate and publicly pay tribute to the honourable member and chairman of the committee on civil liberties of this parliament, whose efforts and whose name will be associated with this far-reaching political initiative, the fight against terrorism and crime in the european union. the recommendations of the september watson report have been largely taken into account in the proposals which the commission presented on 19 september and which are currently being considered by the council. i would like to start with the proposal for a framework decision on the fight against terrorism. the council's discussions on this proposal have focused on the three most important and at the same time most problematic issues: the definition of a terrorist offence, the characterization of the rules of jurisdiction for the prosecution of terrorist acts and the framework of sanctions applicable to terrorist acts. as regards the definition, there was concern to ensure that legitimate action, such as in the context of the activity of trade unions or anti-globalisation movements, could not under any circumstances fall within the scope of the framework decision. the commission has from the outset subscribed to this interpretation and considers that the solution we are moving towards is one which, while respecting the essential structure of the commission's initial proposal, namely 'defining a terrorist offence on the basis of the identification of an objective element, a terrorist act, accompanied by the identification of a subjective element, the terrorist motive in the terms of the proposal' - this is the text currently under consideration by the council - allows the requirements to be met in order for the offence contained to be considered a terrorist offence to be identified in more detail in the legal rule itself. we therefore support the improvement of the definition contained in the text under consideration in the council. this provides an additional guarantee that no ordinary crime, not even violent acts committed incidentally in the margins of certain demonstrations, will be covered by the instrument for the suppression of terrorism. the council is now considering the possibility of introducing a declaration which would clarify that all those who have acted in the interests of preserving or restoring democratic values, as was particularly the case in some member states during the second world war, cannot be considered terrorists. this is in line with some of the amendments proposed by parliament to ensure that the fundamental rights and freedoms on which our countries are based will not be endangered by this framework decision. as regards the powers, the council's debate is moving towards a solution which is very close to that advocated by the amendments tabled by the european parliament. there is a consensus in the council for a balanced formula combining the commission's initial proposal and the more ambitious project suggested by some member states and parliament, namely that jurisdiction could be extended to the whole of the union. as a result, member states may, if they so wish, extend their jurisdiction if the offence was committed anywhere in the territory of the union. as regards the third question, that of sanctions, i believe that in this framework decision it remains the main problem given the lack of consensus on a common level of sanctions for individual terrorist offences. the commission is not yet satisfied with the approach currently used in relation to individual offences whereby sanctions for terrorist offences committed by individuals would not be harmonised but would instead apply sanctions that are heavier than those provided under national law for the same offences but committed without the special intent required for terrorist acts. i think that if we limit our ambitions in this way we are not fulfilling the mandate of article 31 (e) of the treaty, nor the recommendation contained in the watson report. it would also be inconsistent with the fact that in previous instruments we have been able to adopt common sanctions for counterfeiting the euro, for aiding illegal immigration or for trafficking in human beings, and it would be inexplicable if we were not able to achieve the same level of ambition when it comes to sanctioning terrorist acts. i hope that a solution can be found on the basis of the commission's proposal to establish a sanctions grid for the individual offences listed in articles 1 and 2 of the commission's proposal, with greater flexibility in adapting it to the scale of penalties in force in the national law of each member state. finally, this framework decision provides that member states are to take all possible measures to ensure appropriate assistance to the family of victims, applying, where possible, article 4 of the framework decision on the status of victims in criminal proceedings. this approach is fully consistent with parliament's view. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, as regards the second framework decision, the european arrest warrant, we believe that it should be based on the principle of mutual recognition of judicial decisions in criminal matters, thus corresponding to the conclusions of the tampere european council of october 1999 and the indication given to us by the heads of state and government at the european council in ghent on 19 october last. the text now under discussion, presented by the presidency, includes a positive list of offences for which the double-billing requirement should not be checked. as you know, the commission proposal under discussion today is aimed at eliminating double criminalization for all, with the exception of a negative list identified by the commission. since the european council in ghent it has become clear that this approach of the commission would not have majority support in the council. the presidency has therefore put forward a compromise proposal, which assumes that the execution of the european arrest warrant for offences included in the positive list does not require the verification of double criminality. the commission is prepared to support this proposal for a compromise by the presidency provided that the content of the offences included in this positive list is substantial and that it sends a clear and unequivocal message that we are strengthening the mechanisms of judicial cooperation to combat transnational forms of organised crime. for the positive control mechanism to function and be effective, it is necessary that the definition of positive list offences complies with the content of those offences in the legislation of the member state issuing the search and seizure warrant. this is an essential element. without this element, the double-entitlement condition would be reintroduced for these offences as well, which is exactly what is intended to be avoided. i think we are getting closer to an agreement on the content of the positive list. but at the moment, that agreement is not yet fully achieved and guaranteed. i hope that by the council meeting on 6 and 7 december we can reach unanimous agreement on a substantial positive list which meets the objective of an effective and easily implemented european search and seizure mechanism. the commission has incorporated into its proposal a set of rules which aim to reconcile the effectiveness of the fight against crime on the one hand and the protection of the fundamental rights and freedoms of citizens on the other. i hope that the council will resist the temptation to abolish protective provisions on the grounds that they are not necessary, since member states are obliged to respect legal guarantees in any case. it is true that one of the essential elements in the construction of this mechanism is the principle of mutual trust which results from the member states signing the european convention on human rights of the council of europe of 1950 and jointly proclaiming the charter of fundamental rights of the european union in december 2000. but i think it is important to stress some specific mechanisms to be introduced in this framework decision to guarantee and safeguard the fundamental rights of citizens. the commission also proposes to amend the wording of the ne bis in idem rule in article 29 of the commission proposal to reflect the wording of article 50 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, so as to provide that the arrest warrant must be accompanied by proof that the person concerned was effectively informed of the proceedings in time to prepare his defence in the event of his conviction in absentia. another good example of these rules is the deduction of the period of imprisonment from the penalty provided for in article 24 of the commission proposal, where the period of detention in the executing member state must be taken into account for the purpose of calculating compensation in the event that the person to be surrendered is not convicted. there should be a balance between the need for speed and efficiency in cooperation between judicial authorities and the interests of individuals, who should not be subject to additional or excessive constraints or have their defence possibilities restricted. the commission considers it desirable to develop these rules further in order to identify the rules and principles which guarantee fundamental rights in a european judicial area, and the commission is therefore aware of the desirability of continuing the work of approximating the criminal procedural laws of the member states. we must ensure at the same time that legal action is effective and that individual rights are safeguarded. it may therefore be necessary to address more convergently at union level the right to linguistic assistance, the proper handling of evidence or the issue of the legal regime of bail. the commission is considering the possibility of presenting a communication on these aspects which could cover a wide range of elements. these issues require a horizontal approach and we therefore propose to develop it further in a specific mechanism. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to conclude by referring to mr watson's oral amendment tabled in this house today. at the moment when we are debating the commission's position, we must continue our negotiating effort to reach an agreement with 15 members. not an agreement at any price, but one chairman of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market. - madam president, i think that our reflection today must start with the basics, the fortune and the responsibility of living in democratic states of law. in a democratic state governed by the rule of law, any political demand is admissible and respectable, and democratic confrontation of ideas is always welcome; that is our flag, our innermost essence, our sign of identity, in which the whole of the european construction plays a part. but the democratic rule of law also rejects those who reject their ideas in bloodshed. in the face of those who sow terror, death and destruction in our societies, there is only one possible dialogue, that of law enforcement. that's the bottom line. i have said that we are building a democratic europe of law on the basis and principles of our legal systems of a democratic state governed by law. we had a situation where there was an absolute asymmetry between the progress in the field of security and the progress in the field of freedom and justice. the three proposals under discussion respond - and it was high time - to a demand from the citizens and to a clear political impulse at the highest level from the heads of state and government, which, as mr watson has rightly pointed out, goes from vienna to tampere and is reinforced after 11 september at the extraordinary european council in brussels and ghent. these three measures are also in line with the principles on which europe was built. first, cooperation and coordination, that is eurojust, let us cooperate and coordinate to be more effective in justice. secondly, the mutual recognition on which the internal market is based, which is - as the commissioner has said - the corollary of trust between states, that is essentially the search and seizure order. finally, harmonisation where necessary and the need for harmonisation in relation to terrorism is evident as only six member states had legislation. madam president, i am confident - i am sure - that by voting overwhelmingly - tomorrow - in favour of these reports, parliament will, as it has always done, give the political signal which, as responsible representatives of the citizenry, we have an obligation to give in the construction of the democratic societies of law in which we are fortunate to live.

- madam president, the two provisions we are debating today are based on a conviction and a goal: our conviction that it is possible to defeat terrorism and our aim is to strengthen the rule of law by giving it all the instruments to achieve this. in a democracy, political ideas are submitted to the ballot box, never represented by terrorists. i am sure that all my colleagues share this view. i would like to stress in particular what will change about these two initiatives when they are adopted by the laeken european council: firstly, europe will no longer be 'in solidarity with' but will be 'responsible for'. the solidarity of europeans with the spanish democrats in their fight against eta will give way to the responsibility of all european democrats to defeat terrorism. secondly, as regards the arrest and surrender warrant, agreements between governments will be replaced by recognition and cooperation between the different judicial systems. a judicial injunction shall be enforced without delay, whether it is issued by a spanish or a french court or whether the person against whom the proceedings are brought is in one or the other of those territories. no more embarrassing shows like olano's, so that i'm understood. but beyond reflection on the future, i cannot help but think bitterly that these two provisions come too late, too late, for the victims. what a difference it would have made for them if we had done this earlier! - doc. a5-0415/2001 by mrs foster, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on the establishment of common rules in the field of civil aviation security (com (2001) 575 - c5-0481/2001 - 2001/0234 (cod)).
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. parliament, the council and the commission agree on the need to improve aviation safety. the discussions which have just begun on this subject have shown that we are in complete agreement on the basic tendency. the events of september 11 have, of course, also revealed additional gaps that must be considered in isolation from the structural problems that many airlines have already had. you can't mix the two. we believe that all areas of safety, that is, at airports, in advance, in baggage handling, also in the airplane, need to be improved. my group and i also believe that since safety is in the public interest, since safety must be guaranteed for every citizen who uses airlines, the public must also share in the costs of this increased safety. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the air transport sector is not left behind. we are, of course, aware that we have a problem. in general, this parliament always discusses liberalisation, so now we want to increase security in this liberalised sector with public funds. this means, of course, that we need to have a general discussion about what measures can and must be taken to intervene with public funds in liberalised markets.

- doc. a5-0390/2001 by mrs theato, on behalf of the committee on budgetary control, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the criminal protection of the community's financial interests (com (2001) 272 - c5-0225/2001 - 2001/0115 (cod)); - a5-0393/2001 by mr bösch, on behalf of the committee on budgetary control, on the commission's 2000 annual report on the protection of the communities' financial interests and the fight against fraud (com (2001) 255 - c5-0469/2001 - 2001/2186 (cos)) and on the commission communication on the protection of the communities' financial interests and the fight against fraud, commission action plan 2001-03 (com (2001) 254 - c5-0470/2001 - 2001/2186 (cos))
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. in 1995, the member states signed a convention to protect the community's financial interests and to make fraud against the community's finances a criminal offence. protocols were later signed which also designated corruption and money laundering as criminal offences. there is nothing really to be said against these conventions and protocols, except that they have not all been ratified yet, and therefore are not yet in force. i do not want to conceal the fact that in 2000 there were moves towards ratification. i have also repeated in all my meetings with the finance ministers, in a prayer-mill fashion, the demand that ratification be carried out, only the latter determines the speed. the protocol, which also criminalizes money laundering, has so far been ratified by only seven member states. that's how long it would take to complete this process. we won 't accept that . the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would like to thank you, mrs theato, and of course the whole committee, for joining us in saying that enough is enough, that we are now turning to community law and not relying on the convention, the instrument of the third pillar. the committee on budgetary control has tabled many amendments which have been voted on in committee. the commission shares the aim and the concern of many of these proposals. the commission has not yet adopted the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. i would therefore ask that the proposal for a directive not be seen as a tree on which many legitimate wishes, concerns and proposals can be hung. this is particularly true of the european prosecutor. mr bösch, i would like to reiterate the following: the commission is, of course, the guardian of the treaties. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we believe that the legal basis for the olaf monitoring committee is lacking, and we share this view. it would also not be possible to choose the instrument of regulation, because, for example, the proposal as it is now before you provides for the establishment of an investigating judge at the ecj. the tasks and judicial functions of the ecj are, however, defined in detail in the treaty. it is therefore not possible to institutionalize a new investigating judge by means of a regulation. that too requires a contract amendment. but we are going to be presenting the green paper in a few weeks' time - and mrs theato has mentioned this - and we have to be very careful about the way we present it. the green paper will of course open up a wide-ranging debate. i am quite sure that you, as the protagonist of this proposal, will carry this very debate, so to speak, into the professional circles and into the member states, so that we do not have to go through the same situation as we did in nice, where there were reservations but no agreement. we also believe that the legal basis for further amendments is lacking. the court held that the provisions on cooperation between national law enforcement authorities were incompatible with article 280 of the treaty, since they concern the application of the criminal law of the member states and the administration of justice in those states. the commission cannot support the proposal to convert the directive into a regulation because the community cannot at present create a law directly applicable in the member states. i understand your concern and, of course, in view of the present situation, i support the call for this concern to be implemented quickly, but we are far from the point where the european community can create a law that applies immediately. i am sure that this would not be accepted by the national parliaments. the commission can accept without reservation amendments nos 2 and 11. they reiterated the importance of the introduction of the new article 280 for the protection of financial interests. amendment no 27, which provides for custodial sentences which may lead to extradition, is essential for an effective fight against economic crime, and the commission would also like to support the first sentences of amendments nos 3 and 7, since they should be voted on separately tomorrow. i would also like to say explicitly that the proposals to extend the list of criminal offences for the protection of financial interests are very important and, in my view, very worthy of consideration, namely to include tender fraud and abuse of office. here it's really more a matter of the strategy you choose. the commission's proposed strategy is to adopt the text of the convention, as it were, tel quel, and thus to put the member states in a situation where they have already given their consent to this text and there is no reason to transform it into another instrument with a clear deadline for implementation. this is one of the legislative measures proposed by the commission to protect the community's financial interests. the commission has listed in the anti-fraud report the proposals we made in 2000, for example the proposal to amend the money laundering directive, the proposal to protect the euro against counterfeiting or the measures to combat product piracy. that is part of the fight against fraud. the commission's report also lists the measures taken by the member states in 1999 and 2000 to protect the community's finances, totalling 50 pages. this is the case, for example, with the extension of the customs administration's jurisdiction by belgium to a twelve-mile zone off the coast, the establishment of a central control information system in the customs and tax administration of denmark, and the increase in the number of staff in the general inspectorates for agricultural expenditure in the regions of spain. in the united kingdom, for example, a coordinating body for cross-cutting studies on the structural funds has been set up. the rapporteur has included, mr bösch, the very critical report by the court of auditors on the implementation of the regulation by the member states, which states that errors in the implementation of the structural funds must be reported. i can assure you that i share your criticism and that of the court of auditors. we are therefore working very hard with the member states to ensure that this reporting regulation is implemented more uniformly and, above all, more thoroughly. this is the first step towards success. i would like to say again that although we may differ on the interpretation, the implementation of the directive has been very hesitant in the years before. it took ages to report a bug, according to our findings. it's actually better now, but it also leads to more errors being reported. it's like police statistics. is it good or bad that the number of cases the police uncover is increasing or decreasing? i would therefore ask you not to discredit those member states which take their error reports seriously and actually report them frequently in accordance with the regulation, and not to say that they are the strongholds, so to speak, because it is a difficult instrument. we have a negative incentive, so to speak: the more errors are reported, the more information we have to make financial corrections. we just can't afford to let this go. i agree with the rapporteur, i agree with you too, mr bösch, we must make statistics more meaningful in order to determine what are new reports, what are reports which were already in the statistics before? first of all, we must examine what has actually been the result of the reports, what measures have been taken. olaf is working on it, dg budget, dg regions are working on it, but it is a difficult business. i am sure that next year we will not have the success we are seeking, but we will see that sector by sector we will be able to speak out more. it also depends on cooperation with the member states, where olaf works closely with the so-called cocolaf. i can however inform you that any suspicion of fraud - especially in the structural funds - is referred to olaf. the most frequent irregularities in the structural funds are, for example, cases where member states approve projects after the actual end of the funding period. the commission has also made a number of errors, in particular in the sense that other community policies have not been taken into account. a very common mistake is that projects have been approved without any environmental impact assessment. the damage, but perhaps it is environmental damage because the environmental impact assessment has not been done. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that case by case by 15 december. this is information that we don't have and won't have any time soon. the commission can assure you that we are now trying to get this information directly for the new error messages so that they are meaningful messages, in order to see exactly what the errors are that are associated with financial damage. how is the directive on the protection of financial interests likely to be dealt with in the council? unfortunately, some member states have already taken a clear position against this directive, for reasons of legal dogma. you mentioned it. the council then says, yes, of course, that we must do something in this area, but then it argues that no, that would be a matter for the third pillar and not the first. so, i would like to see these ministers of justice who argue like this, bring it up in a public debate. no human would understand. the people also do not accept that it is said that we cannot do anything here because this is the first pillar, the other is the third pillar, and only through the third pillar could there be joint action. it is quite clear that the protection of the community's interests also requires community instruments, and i am very glad and very grateful to you that the european parliament and the commission are working together on this!

president of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy. - mr president, we have come a long way since the lisbon european council in a relatively short space of time. the three institutions, the council, parliament and the commission, were aware that time is a vital factor in one of the most rapidly evolving technologies. the directive on electronic commerce has already been adopted, we have adopted the directive on the dismantling of the local loop - which, by the way, the member states have not yet fully implemented - but now the telecommunications business, which seemed to be a safe business, is becoming increasingly problematic, without the users benefiting from it either. a new framework is therefore necessary. and that is the reason for the package of directives before us. it's not about regulating anymore. it is a question of regulating what is necessary in a balance between operators and consumers. but above all, it is a question of regulating in the same way, of regulating in the same way, in order to avoid precisely what was happening: a fragmentation of the internal market. that is why the european parliament tried to solve this problem, why the council, in its common position, made a counter-offer, which i think was below the minimum, but now the presidency has got a package that is above the minimum. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
commission. – the four directives with you today, together with the spectrum decision, make up the new regulatory framework for electronic communications – a cornerstone of the eeurope strategy, the information society for all agreed at the lisbon european council. since lisbon, successive european councils have called on the commission, council and parliament to ensure that the new framework is in place by the end of this year. we still have two weeks to go. time is running short, but the eu still has the chance to meet this deadline. the package of compromise amendments before you today has a broad level of support in the council, as the presidency told us today. it is, of course, a compromise. nobody gets everything they want – neither parliament, the council nor the commission. but the commission nonetheless believes that it is a balanced compromise. my assessment is that neither institution is likely to get more from conciliation. agreement on this package will send an important, positive signal externally. we all know that the communications sector has had a rough ride over the last year or so. early agreement on this package will be a welcome boost. the package will have a positive impact on the sector in a number of different ways. the new framework will deregulate, requiring regulators progressively to remove regulation as it becomes unnecessary, so that they regulate only when there is market failure. in this way, the package provides a transition to the final objective we all share: reliance on competition law to control market power in the electronic communications sector. the new framework simplifies and deregulates national licensing regimes, removing prior regulatory control over market access for network and service provision, and focusing such controls only on frequency and numbering resources. it preserves and strengthens universal service, striking the right balance between the rights of users and the need not to impose disproportionate burdens on operators. in particular, it makes it clear that functional internet access is a key part of the bundle of services that must be affordable and available to all eu citizens. mr martin asked me about the impact of this solution for the digital divide and employment. it is very clear that universal service has a key impact on availability. but we also need policy measures which concentrate on the skills of all citizens and on content. we need availability at a low price; we need skills and content in everyone's own language to close the digital divide. finally – and crucially – the new framework, with the amendments contained in the compromise package, would include the necessary safeguards to ensure that regulators act consistently across the eu, so that companies can expect to be treated similarly in similar situations throughout the eu. here i particularly want to thank the european parliament for its strong support, without which we would not have been able to achieve this kind of compromise with the council. i will explain how the compromise package deals with the three fundamental issues that dominated discussion between the council and parliament during second reading: right of appeal (article 4), the transparency mechanism (article 6 of the framework directive), including matters related to radio spectrum, and finally interoperability of digital tv equipment – which has been raised by many colleagues tonight. on right of appeal, the compromise package takes parliament’s line by requiring member states to ensure that the merits of the case are duly taken into account. on the transparency mechanism, the compromise package goes a long way towards parliament and the commission’s position. the text gives the commission hard powers to require national regulatory authorities to withdraw draft measures in the key areas linked to the functioning of the single market: definition of markets and designation, or otherwise, of undertakings with significant market power (smp). commission decisions are subject to an advisory committee procedure. radio spectrum is covered by article 6, paragraph 2, whereby regulators are required to cooperate with each other to ensure consistent application of the regulatory framework. the compromise does not provide for hard powers of intervention by the commission on spectrum matters. nevertheless, the commission believes that this provision, together with the spectrum decision, will improve co-ordination of radio spectrum policy matters across the eu. with regard to the spectrum decision, the commission is very satisfied with the compromise proposal, as the major objectives pursued in the original commission proposal are met. the adoption of the spectrum decision in this form would constitute a major step forward. furthermore, it demonstrates how far positions in this important matter have evolved, given the failure not so long ago of legislative proposals along similar lines. the spectrum decision in its present form will set up a general and permanent framework for addressing radio spectrum policy and legal issues in the context of all relevant community policy areas. it thereby reflects the increasing importance of radio spectrum in the context of community policy objectives which depend on the availability and efficient management of frequencies as a vital resource for the provision of economically and socially important wireless usage in electronic communications, transport, broadcasting and so on. the spectrum decision makes it possible to take appropriate action to ensure efficient use of spectrum and spectrum management. it also provides for technical implementing measures to be adopted under the spectrum decision as a mechanism to ensure legal certainty. many members of the european parliament have raised the issue of digital television. we clearly have got the message from the european parliament. on digital tv interoperability, the compromise package goes towards parliament’s position, by taking over much of the european parliament text. a new article and corresponding recital would be inserted in the framework directive, dealing specifically with interoperability of digital interactive television services. it would impose an obligation on member states to encourage the use of open application programme interfaces by platform operators and equipment manufacturers. in addition, member states would also be required to encourage api owners to make available, on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms, all such information as is necessary to enable service providers to provide all services supported by the application programme interfaces. clearly an obligation to encourage does not go as far as an obligation to ensure. but – and i emphasise this – the provisions of article 16 on standardisation allow standards to be made mandatory one year after entry into force of the directive if interoperability cannot be ensured by the use of voluntary standards. the combination of these two provisions constitutes a step forward for the interoperability of digital television, which we all agree is a desirable outcome for european consumers. article 16 means that one year after entry into force of the directive, the commission must organise public consultation then propose the comitology procedure, followed by commission adoption. furthermore, as we have really understood the strong will of the european parliament to go forward with interoperability, the commission is ready to start actively to promote european standards for interoperability with all stakeholders concerned. mrs read and mr fitzsimons raised the issue of the disabled here today. firstly, on the amendments on the disabled, most of them have been accepted in the council position, except perhaps for two, which overlap with the council text. secondly, i am personally convinced that information technologies give us better chances than before to give equal possibilities to the disabled. when we make society better for the disabled, it is better for all of us. last week we had the information society technologies conference, in which mrs read also participated. we saw fantastic new applications which make life for the disabled better. we must absolutely encourage their use. the same was true with the e-government conference. we proceed along those lines. the accessibility guidelines recommendation from the commission a few weeks ago is another example here. as far as the link between the rtte directive and this package goes, we are ready to consider and study that issue. i will come back to that later. the compromise package is always a compromise. no institution gets everything it wants. but this compromise is a balanced one. it represents a proper balance between the views of the council and parliament. as such the commission would recommend that the house accept it. the commission will transmit to the sessional services of the european parliament the detailed position on the amendments, including those not covered by the council compromise. finally, i thank the european parliament and the presidency for their particularly close and substantial cooperation on this file. my particular thanks go to the rapporteurs, mrs niebler, mr paasilinna, mr harbour and mr brunetta, the rapporteurs for the five telecom directives, as well as the chairman of the committee, mr westendorp y cabeza. but i do not want to forget the shadow rapporteurs and those other members of the european parliament who have participated so actively in the discussion of the telecoms package. it has been an excellent example of how community method at its best can work. it has been an extremely complicated legal package. everybody had a role to play. we worked towards the same compromise solution and – if it goes through this week – very rapidly. the outcome of this would be that europe would have the most modern, technology-neutral legislation for the future. i am sure it would be good for jobs, good for growth, good for equal access for all. i hope that this package will be accepted this week in parliament.

i need advice. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a pleasure to meet you again to explain the main points of the second reading of the draft general budget of the european union, as it was drawn up on 22 november. it is one of the last but also one of the most important stages in the sometimes complicated process of drawing up the community budget. i am very pleased to be able to make this statement to the members of the european parliament, who are here in plenary as representatives of european democracy. this second reading by the council was preceded, in accordance with the rules of the interinstitutional agreement, by a consultation meeting of the european parliament, the council and the commission on 21 november. i think i can speak for all those who took part in that long meeting, which ended only in the early hours of the morning, when i say that it was a success not only in budgetary terms, because the general budget for 2002 will soon be adopted, but also in political terms, because we were able to agree on the treatment of a number of new elements that have emerged since our first reading, as well as on a number of priorities. i would like to thank the 'external policy' for possible future needs in these areas. this margin is also in line with the agreement reached with the european parliament on maintaining a minimum margin of eur 70 million for possible needs in afghanistan and surrounding countries. i would also remind you that it was also agreed to set aside a minimum of eur 35 million in the emergency aid reserve under heading 6 to cover fishing fleets following the absence of a fisheries agreement with morocco. the council entered in the draft budget an amount of eur 170 million in commitment appropriations under heading 2 and specific allocation of eur 30 million in commitment appropriations under heading 2 for the regions bordering the applicant countries and the use of the flexibility instrument for the corresponding amount. in the framework of the agreement with the european parliament on the amount of eur 20 million in commitment appropriations under heading 3 for these border areas, the council approved the pilot project: "effects of enlargement in the border regions". this agreement was certainly one of the key points of the 2002 budgetary procedure. to make this a permanent feature, the european parliament, the council and the commission decided to include in the 2003 budget, within the limits set in berlin, the 27 million euro not included in the 2002 budget, which is part of the 197 million euro proposed by the commission in the financial memorandum on the programme for the conversion of the fleet, and 15 million euro for the border regions. as regards the priorities, i would remind you that in march this year the council adopted for the first time formal conclusions on the budgetary guidelines for the forthcoming budgetary procedure. the council thus set out its budgetary priorities for 2002, as the european parliament and the commission already do. the council has constantly referred to these principles and priorities during the negotiations and has adhered to them. i think this is a good method because it gives more clarity about what is at stake and what the objective is, and it increases transparency. i therefore believe that it is in the interests of all of us that the council should continue to do so. let us begin with the priorities which are close to the heart of the european parliament. i am pleased that agreement has been reached in the framework of the joint declaration on the control of the amounts still to be paid (the rals) and the elimination in the medium term of what has come to be known as abnormal rals. i would point out that abnormal rals, which we have defined as dormant commitments for which no payment has been made in the last two years and old commitments which have been in the budget for at least five years, can be reduced not only by increasing payment appropriations but also by cancelling a large proportion of commitments. i believe that the measures announced by the commission will lead to a satisfactory solution of this matter in the long run. we also agreed on a statement on the implementation profile for the 2002 budget. this declaration implies that the implementation of the budget is spread over the year as evenly as possible. the so-called december fever must be prevented. to this end, the commission has envisaged the following measures. it shall endeavour to implement the 2002 budget in line with the implementation of the 2001 budget and to improve it where necessary. the budgetary authority will be informed if the implementation profile differs substantially from the proposed one. in addition, an implementation plan for the 2002 budget per heading of the financial perspective will be sent when the preliminary draft budget for 2003 is presented. i am convinced that these measures are in line with the horizontal amendments adopted by the european parliament at first reading, so that we can look forward to the adoption of the budget with confidence in its implementation. the council also paid particular attention to the priorities set by the european parliament at first reading, including by agreeing to the additional appropriations for e-learning and immigration. i am naturally pleased with the post-ecsc arrangements and the commitment of the spanish presidency to the revision of the financial regulation. i would like to conclude this last list of priorities by mentioning one of the council's essential priorities, namely the controlled increase in payment appropriations. i'll get back to that later. the second reading of the budget took account of the agreements reached during the consultations. we have tried to adopt a budget which, on the one hand, covers all the priorities of the european union and, on the other hand, takes account of the points raised after the first reading without losing sight of the real needs and the possibility of spending the appropriations. i should like to briefly review the other results with you, by heading. the agricultural expenditure is as follows: the amendment note no 2 is accepted in its entirety. the council also restored the amounts proposed in the preliminary draft budget for the budget lines which were reduced at first reading and which are not covered by the amending note. an additional amount of eur 4.5 million was entered as agreed at the meeting of 21 november, taking account of parliament's comments. in a joint declaration with the european parliament, special attention was paid to the protection of animals during transport. i am also pleased that our institutions have been able to reach agreement on the points in this note of amendment relating to rural development expenditure, fisheries agreements and the budgeting of the available surplus of the previous financial year of eur 1.2 billion. i think i have already outlined the main results of the structural measures, namely the inclusion of eur 170 million in commitment appropriations and eur 39 million in payment appropriations for the conversion of the spanish and portuguese fishing fleets, and the amount of eur 30 million for the areas bordering the applicant countries, both using the flexibility instrument. the council also adopted a number of important amendments tabled by parliament, including the inclusion of e-learning with eur 5 million and the increase of the european refugee fund by eur 5 million. the rapporteur has tried to convince us and has succeeded, but i think the council's willingness to cooperate should also be emphasized here. it is under this heading that a significant proportion of the measures for the areas bordering the applicant countries will be financed. as regards external policy, the council not only increased the budget lines for asia and tacis by eur 66 million compared with the draft budget, but also accepted amending note 2 on international fisheries agreements. the commission has also adopted a communication on the implementation of the european union strategy for the mediterranean, which is to be published in the official journal of the european union. as regards administrative expenditure, the three institutions agreed to discuss in depth the report of the secretaries-general on the multiannual trend at an informal trialogue next year. i think there are still a lot of possibilities here. as regards the budget of the european parliament, the council adopted draft supplementary and amending budget no 5 for 2001, which anticipates expenditure on buildings in the 2003 budget, with the commitment to reduce expenditure in 2003 by an equal amount. for some years now, the council has been reading the budget in a comprehensive way, i.e. the draft budget is mainly based on the priorities set and the size of the category of expenditure. this approach has enabled the council to remain below the existing annual ceilings for expenditure set in the financial perspective in the interinstitutional agreement of 6 may 1999. it has also been able to ensure, in accordance with the interinstitutional agreement, that margins remain available within the limits of the financial perspective, thus allowing priority to be given to various community measures and policies. in drawing up the second reading, the council has observed budgetary discipline so that the budget increases in line with the increase in national budgets. the total increase in payment appropriations will therefore be limited to 2.0%. as you know, an agreement was reached on 21 november in the context of this general agreement, with the support of the commission. the council expects the european parliament to continue this trend during its second reading so that the rate of increase does not exceed the agreed ceilings. before you discuss the budget definitively, i would like to emphasize that the council has endeavoured to respect certain budgetary rules and basic provisions concerning the entry of appropriations in the reserve, the classification of expenditure, legal bases, preparatory actions and pilot projects. the council therefore reiterates its opposition to the use by parliament of conditional reserves, which is contrary to the financial regulation. the council also reiterated the outcome of the first reading of the draft budget for title b7-1 concerning the european development fund, since the inclusion of any financing or even of any budgetary item lacks the necessary legal basis and is therefore not possible. it should be remembered that this is in fact compulsory expenditure. i should like to conclude this brief review of the second reading by the council by stressing that the budgetary procedure has proceeded in a good spirit. as in the past, the discussions have sometimes been violent. each has made his point clearly, briefly, sometimes long, but forcefully. the aim of the consultation procedure is nevertheless to: the commission's proposal is to bring the two arms of the budgetary authority into line with one another so that we can adopt a budget which will enable the european union to meet its challenges, taking the best possible account of the situation and developments which are to be expected in the course of the financial year and in the 2002 programme. i would like to thank in particular, on my own behalf and on behalf of the council, mr terence wynn, chairman of the committee on budgets, and the two the rapporteur. - mr president, first of all i should like to apologize to the house for my absence, as i have some duties due to my vice-president position in a few minutes and will therefore not be able to attend the whole debate. the report i have the honour to present is an important contribution to the community's budgetary and programming system. we had an agreement, based on the joint declaration of 20 july 2000, in which we established a system for programming and monitoring the commission's activities in relation to the financial perspective. the purpose of this was to guide the decisions of the budgetary authority, to provide an overview of the margins available under each heading, taking account of the appropriations approved for programmes already under co-decision, and to facilitate the application of the new evaluation procedure resulting from the abovementioned joint declaration. we are now in the midst of an important exercise and, for the first time - and we thank the commission for this - we have the opportunity to see the programming of headings 3 and 4 in relation to our activities. there is a question of interest to us, a very methodological question, as to how to programme programmes already in progress for the future, and there is only one point of concern to us: for some programmes, for some budget lines, future inflation is included, by means of what the commission calls a budgetary deflator, and which, in our opinion, would rather be a budgetary inflator. there we have a technical contradiction. the financial perspective is expressed in constant euros, while the programming is in current euros for each year. the result: we do not really know, when we reach an agreement, what the value may be for the last financial year because it will depend on real inflation. anyone who has been a trade unionist knows that statistics can be manipulated in many ways and this is one of them: mixing current prices with constant prices; and therefore i will not insist. i will give you an example: by hiding future inflation in the framework programme, the commission comes to the conclusion that, with its figures, between 2002 and 2006, we will have an increase in annual appropriations of 14.3%. inflation is hiding from us that, in the end, we really only have an increase of 4.9%. this is the actual increase. the other thing, the difference up to 14%, is inflation. this is what we don't like. the commission said the other day in the committee on budgets that inflation is dead with the euro. praise the lord! i accept, but i'm from the school of st. thomas and i prefer, in these things, to play to believe. when i have seen that inflation has disappeared, i will agree to abolish this kind of differentiation between constant and current prices and that is the crux of our point of view. the rest, that is to say, all the rest of the commission's work, we find excellent. our concern is really to avoid the situation that, with his technique, the higher the real inflation, the greater the margin available. it is a contradiction, and therefore our request, contained in the motion for a resolution, is very simple: if the commission is to continue working, for whatever reason, in terms of current euros, then let it do so, but the data it offers to parliament should also be expressed in constant euros. this would be the main point of our report. i would also like to congratulate the commission on the effort it has made to provide us with this data for the first time.

- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in order to achieve the objectives set out in the treaty on european union and, more specifically, in the treaty on economic and monetary union, the community needs high-quality statistical instruments which provide all the institutions, governments and economic and social operators with a set of harmonised and reliable statistics on which to base their decisions. in this regard, it is necessary to amend the regulation to allow the use of esa-95. in our view, the new esa-95 is a major improvement on the previous version, which dates from 1979. progress has been made in the harmonisation of methodology and in the precision and accuracy of the concepts, definitions, classifications and accounting standards to be applied in order to obtain a quantitative description of the economies of the member states. it is clear that, in implementing the changeover to the new system, member states have made further improvements in the quality of their national accounts, as a result of a complete review of their sources and methods used in the compilation of the accounts. of all the various uses of national accounts data in the ess in the budgetary - question time to the commission (b5-0536/2001): the agenda is closed. we shall now consider the questions put to the commission. part one
- question no 39 by mr william francis newton dunn (h-0878/01): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the united kingdom for the construction of the railway line between london and london. the aim of the project is to secure the external borders of an enlarged union. there are some 370 border crossing points between slovenia and neighbouring croatia. the slovenian government is currently only able to finance guard posts for about 90 of them. some 270 border crossings are now largely open. in view of terrorism, organised crime and illegal immigration, what does the commission intend to do to ensure the security of the enlarged union's borders?
commission. – mr president, one of the future external borders of the european union is expected to run along the border between slovenia and croatia. there are 36 crossing points along this border where it is legally possible to cross. the figures quoted by the honourable member refer to places where crossing the border between croatia and slovenia is physically possible but legally prohibited – for instance, footpaths, roads and bridges. i agree with the honourable member that it is the reality on the ground – literally speaking – that deserves attention. the commission recalls that slovenia must achieve a high level of external border control upon accession. the commission is paying close attention to slovenia's progress in the framework of the negotiations under the justice and home affairs chapter, as well as in the pre-accession process. slovenia is required to demonstrate its capability systematically to check all persons crossing external borders and to ensure effective border surveillance between authorised border crossing points. in this regard, slovenia has prepared a detailed action plan for the implementation of the schengen acquis, as requested by the european union. in its action plan, slovenia has shown that it is taking the necessary steps to ensure that the appropriate infrastructure and equipment are allocated to the border with croatia. in addition, slovenia is taking measures to ensure greater coordination between its authorities involved in border controls. the commission wishes also to underline that slovenia is already engaged in intensive bilateral cooperation for control of the common border with croatia. this should be further expanded by the conclusion of the agreement on simplified border checks on road and rail traffic and an agreement on cross-border police cooperation. the latter agreement will also encompass joint border patrols for the surveillance of the green border, that is between the authorised border crossing points. in addition to the very substantial financial assistance granted to slovenia for upgrading its border controls – this is financial assistance within the framework of the pre-accession process – the commission is encouraging and directly supporting the bilateral cooperation between slovenia and croatia. this is funded under our assistance programme to croatia for integrated border management, which will also cover border crossings with slovenia. slovenia and croatia have recently reached agreement on the demarcation of the common border. while, in the past, the lack of demarcation did not affect in practice the quality of the border controls and of the surveillance of the green and blue border, this agreement, once ratified, is additional proof of the good cooperation between the two countries.

partners reach agreement. in parallel we are working on the rules of origin to see how the partners can be brought into the pan-european system. in order to lay the basis for a euro-med internal infrastructure needs from a regional or subregional perspective and, where appropriate, to draw up strategies for interconnection and for linkage with the trans-european networks to ensure that priority projects are funded and implemented. together with our partners we are developing a new regional meda programme on justice and home affairs and are engaged in discussions on these issues bilaterally in relation to the provisions of the association agreements and in meda programming. concerning new instruments and mechanisms, in recognition that cooperation between europe and the euro-mediterranean partnership, in particular to provide for more frequent political dialogue on regional and international issues. the commission will launch a policy dialogue with the mediterranean partners on employment policy, sharing eu experience on ways of combating unemployment and of creating new jobs. it will work to improve the available information and statistics as part of ongoing efforts to channel legal migration and to combat illegal migration. finally, the commission will consider ways to stimulate investment and joint development projects in the mediterranean, for example by studying the need for, and feasibility of, a new bank or other financing mechanism, building on the european investment bank. let me add some information concerning the performance this other budget lines benefiting the mediterranean partners. as far as payments are concerned, they are expected to represent over 56% of commitments this year to reach nearly half a billion euro, in fact the best ever result achieved in the region. this year is also the first year of the implementation of the revised meda regulation which puts in place mechanisms for more coherent programming of the aid, better coordination both with partners and with the other major donors, and more streamlined approval procedures inside the eu. consultations have already taken place with the partners and with the other donors on the country and regional strategy papers covering 2002 to 2006 and on the more detailed national and regional indicative programmes for 2002 to 2004. all these documents should be approved by the end of the year. i am reporting these details because i do not want to miss this opportunity to inform parliament about the meda programme which has been quite problematic in the past. we are now seeing some light at the end of the tunnel.

- thank you very much, commissioner. questions to mr lamy question no 42 by mr jonas sjöstedt (h-0895/01) subject: contacts between the commission and the tabd the transatlantic business dialogue (tabd) was launched in 1995 on the joint initiative of the commission (represented at the time by commissioners brittan and bangemann) and the us department of commerce. is it true that the commission and the tabd are in constant contact and exchange information and proposals? has the commission financed and participated in the annual conferences of the tabd?
commission. - this question concerns the transatlantic trade dialogue, which is one of a series of dialogue structures established in 1995 at the madrid summit. the objectives of this dialogue, as well as others, and i shall come back to them, are to build bridges across the atlantic, in particular by involving a number of non-governmental, private actors on the one hand, and policy-makers in the union and the us administration on the other. the dialogue structure which was established at the time certainly includes the transatlantic trade dialogue, but also a transatlantic consumer dialogue, a transatlantic labour dialogue and a transatlantic environmental dialogue, and so the commercial side is one of the pillars of this dialogue, which includes three others. the purpose of this panoply of dialogues is to draw up public recommendations for the commission and the us government and, in fact, on a rotating basis, they present their recommendations to political leaders at the eu-us summits. the commission attaches equal importance to all these dialogues, and we emphasize this importance because the result has been valuable in a number of developments, but in any case for the strengthening of balanced and solid transatlantic relations, participation in these various dialogues is open. it is open to all parties concerned in the various fields, and the result is obviously largely a part of the investment made by the various participants. we in the commission are involved at various levels in the events that are organized in the transatlantic trade dialogue, including an annual conference that brings together the ceos of the various companies and which is, let us say, the annual highlight of this dialogue. the recommendations are published and publicly available on the transatlantic trade dialogue website and on the commission's websites, since our reactions to these recommendations are also public domain, and a number of honourable members of this house follow the bilateral trade relations between the united states and europe closely and are regularly invited to participate in the annual conference of the transatlantic trade dialogue. when the first dialogue was established, this was the case in seville, and the costs of this event were shared by both sides. in 1998, at another summit between the union and the americans, we both committed ourselves to supporting all the dialogues and, moreover, in the same year, your assembly, the european parliament, created a specific budget line to support these dialogues. since 1998, and to answer your question precisely on financing, the commission has contributed to the financing of the trade dialogue, as it has also contributed to the financing of the other dialogues by means of annual contributions. in the case of the trade dialogue, part of the commission's contribution was to cover the costs of organising annual conferences, although the majority of the costs of these events are now covered by trade sponsorship, which is why the commission's financial support for the trade dialogue is substantially lower than the financial contribution it offers in support of the consumer dialogue, the labour dialogue and the environment dialogue.
commission - on the first point, i would like to say that, like the dialogue on consumers, the environment or labour, the transatlantic trade dialogue is designed to make wishes, recommendations and views which help to feed our own work. so it's a contribution that is far from exclusive. as is the case with a number of business circles, trade union circles and non-governmental organisations, we have a whole range of bodies which contribute to trade policy, including the transatlantic trade dialogue. and this dialogue is important because the european and american business circles are putting considerable effort into it, which is also in line with the scale of our trade relations with the americans. in this context, wishes, desires, recommendations and observations are expressed and discussed, as we do with a number of partners in the commercial field. as regards participation in the summit, as i said earlier, the parties involved in these dialogues - on business, consumers, the environment, work - are invited to come in turn and present their recommendations to the leaders of the two parties, that is to say, essentially to the american president on the one hand, to the council presidency and to the commission on the other. this is done in the margins of the official summit meetings, the official summit meetings, as is right, bring together only the political authorities on both sides who are duly responsible, this is done in the margins of these events.
