- we're going to change the order of the questions because mr. lund has to leave the room urgently. question no 49 by mr torben lund (h-0908/01) subject: authorization of excessive amounts of several heavy metals in fish according to the danish newspaper politiken of 15 november 2001, the european union intends to raise the limit values for heavy metals in fish, which could therefore contain higher amounts of these metals, even though a committee of experts within the union has specifically recommended stricter constraints. mercury, lead, and cadmium, which are found in shells that are in high demand, among other things, can weaken the nervous system and cause other very serious human diseases. i see absolutely no reason to raise these limit values. could the commission therefore state the reasons for raising these limit values and the studies which may have led to such a measure and those which go the other way? in this connection, i would draw the commission's attention to the fact that denmark has long tried to encourage the population to eat more fish, for reasons of public health. unfortunately, it seems that these efforts are being frustrated by the fact that the european union intends to raise, at the same time, the ceilings that limit the presence of harmful heavy metals in this type of food.
commission. – in respect of mercury the general maximum level is 0.5 mg/kg for fishery products. that remains unchanged as previously set under veterinary legislation, in particular commission decision 93/351. the only proposed change is that two additional species have been added to the list of fish species for the maximum level of 1 mg/kg. these are the grenadier fish and the emperor fish which are minor contributors to diet, but data showed the lower level was unachievable. you then asked me about shellfish. the proposals will not increase the safety level of eating shellfish for either children or adults. the only proposed change for limits in shellfish as bivalve molluscs is for lead. a slight increase from 1 mg/kg to 1.5 mg/kg is proposed, because data shows that the lower level for lead is not reasonably achievable. exposure to lead in the diet is well within safe limits. otherwise, there is no change for provisions on cadmium or mercury.
- question no 48 by mrs marit paulsen (h-0889/01): subject: consumer information in the form of 'smilies' in the food sector on 1 october 2001, the danish food inspection authority launched its campaign to display evaluation reports to the approximately 40 000 establishments in the country producing or offering for sale food or drinks, with the aim that at least one report will be in place in all these establishments within a year, in the form of four types of 'smilies' that will clearly reflect the findings of the inspection carried out by the authorities. a big smile means that the last inspection did not result in any comments on the controlled flow, while a decidedly sullen face indicates that the establishment has been fined, reported to the police or had its operating licence withdrawn. it would be difficult to devise such clear consumer information. is the commission aware of this new system put in place by the danish authorities? if so, would it be prepared to propose that other member states follow this good example? if not, does the commission not think that the system is at least worth examining in the light of future provisions in this area?
commission. – i agree with the honourable member that it is important to raise consumer awareness. the commission is favourable to any initiative protecting the consumer. however, the commission considers that the task of developing food quality and information to consumers on the results of official controls, surveillance and other monitoring activities in the food sector should be left to member states. member states are responsible for carrying out the official control of foodstuffs at all stages of production and distribution. it is for them to decide how best to inform the consumer about these activities. this is in line with the principle of subsidiarity. while the commission is not aware of this particular initiative by the danish authorities, it can encourage such steps or the voluntary implementation of such initiatives by other member states, but it is unlikely to make a similar proposal at community level. i stress that these points are made in relation to the outlets that you particularly refer to in your question.

- madam president, i too regard the results of the doha ministerial conference as positive and therefore i would like to join in congratulating commissioner lamy, commissioner fischler and the council on their undeniable contribution to this success. it is true that the final declaration does not say all that it should say and - i would say - sometimes even more than it should say, but all negotiation involves reaching compromises and all compromise involves concessions. what we really need to appreciate from doha is that the divergent - and sometimes even contradictory - interests of the wto member countries have been brought together and an agreement has been reached to launch a new round, to set an agenda, a timetable and a work programme, and secondly that the development dimension has been fully integrated into all the negotiations and that the least developed countries and the developing countries have spoken strongly and their voices have been heard and their concerns taken into account. the wto train, as you very well said, commissioner lamy, is back on track and has already left the station. i would add that the means have also been put in place to ensure that their destination is sustainable growth which also benefits the poorest countries. however, in order for this train to reach the station, the necessary means must be adopted, the texts, which are full of constructive ambiguities, must be interpreted correctly, and reciprocity in the opening up of markets and full respect for the rules governing multilateral trade must be guaranteed. in order to help overcome the poverty barrier once and for all, it is necessary to take the necessary measures to facilitate access, especially for the least developed countries, because these countries may suffer because of the multilateral trading system from the advantages we give to developing countries.

- mr president, more than two years ago, at the initiative of the government of josé maría aznar, a new stage in the construction of europe was opened in tampere: making a new common european area politically and legally viable, making freedom and security of citizens - and this is the great political debate - compatible with access to and the effective functioning of justice in that area. the events of the past two years, such as the tragic deaths of moroccan and sub-saharan citizens in the strait of gibraltar and on the andalusian coast, the deaths of immigrants in dover, the recent events in ireland, the disgusting trafficking and corruption of children and prostitution, together with the terrible murders by eta and the tragedy of 11 september, have convulsed the debate and have accelerated the measures to deal with such a dangerous and worrying situation. the balance sheet of the work done by the council, the commission and parliament in this field can be described as a mixture of light and shade. the fight against terrorism should be highlighted, and it is also right to highlight the important role played in this battle by our president, nicole fontaine, and commissioner vitorino. the euro-order and the definition of terrorism are the culmination of a hard-fought battle against terrorism which began in this house before 11 september. i would also like to stress the good work that has been done in separating for the first time the debates on economic immigration and asylum, which has helped us to clarify ideas, debates and even approaches. but, from my point of view, there is still a long way to go. there are too many shadows, and the most worrying of them seems to me to be the mess we are in because of the haste and lack of agreement in the council on matters such as the family reunification of immigrants, minimum standards for the asylum procedure, or reception conditions - to give a few examples - where our work is sometimes ineffective because we have to weave and untie what the council does, which shows that the working method is flawed and must be revised.
- mr president, as this is a multi-purpose debate, i would first like to say that i agree with every word mr watson has said in relation to his report. it seems to me that parliament is going to make a good contribution today to tackling a situation of violence in the streets of europe which concerns us all. on the progress made in the area of justice, freedom and security, i would first of all like to congratulate the commission on the achievements made yesterday, especially with regard to the arrest warrant, and the council on something very special: i would like to congratulate it on the sincerity of the belgian presidency's report on the progress made. i would like to express my concern, as the council does in this report, about the lack of progress on the common asylum policy, but above all on the common immigration policy. not only is there no european policy, but we have seen in recent times that many governments have developed new national policies and, what is more, in some cases, justified these decisions by appealing to europe. i hope that at laeken we can make at least some progress and acquire a new commitment in the sense defined by the commission in its two communications on asylum and on immigration. i think, on the contrary, that the agreement reached on the mutual recognition of judicial decisions, the so-called euro-order, is very important. i think that this is a giant step forward, of course, in the fight against terrorism, but also in the fight against money laundering, in the fight against corruption, in the fight against trafficking in human beings - including women for sexual exploitation - and in the fight against organised crime. i think it is important, but i think it should also make us reflect, and that is what i would like to ask the council for in the third place: i think that at laeken you should see not only the progress made on the agenda but also how it has been made and what problems need to be tackled. it seems to me that unanimity and the lack of real power in this parliament are not helping. we live in a world of paradoxes. we said a few days ago, in quotes, that bin laden had given a boost to the anti-terrorism measures that the commission had planned and that parliament had long since called for. paradoxically, it has also been the spectacle offered by mr berlusconi's government that has brought the debate on the euro order to the front page of the newspapers. i would have preferred, frankly, that this debate had been generated in parliament, that it had been a citizen debate and that you could have picked it up. i would like to say, mr president-in-office of the council, that i am glad that you appreciate the institutional loyalty of this parliament. i would just like you to be able, in return, to show a little more institutional loyalty in analysing our texts, in including some of our positive ideas in your documents and i think this would help to close the positive circle of commission/parliament/council work.
the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i shall be relatively brief. i have only four concerns: one about the past, one about yesterday, so to speak, one about tomorrow, although i mean the day after tomorrow, and one about the future. allow me to go back in time. i think the idea of creating a european area of freedom, security and justice was born about 25 years ago. i think we have taken some essential steps in the right direction without being able to claim victory, without having achieved all the results we want to achieve. we have to do this, mr president, and i want to say this here in the european parliament, without having to organise a witch hunt and without having to use gestapo methods. on the contrary, anyone who has read the watson report, anyone who has read the opinions of the european parliament and anyone who knows the position of the ministers of justice and home affairs and of the commission knows that we do not use such methods. yesterday, and i am thinking back to tampere in 1999, when we decided to draw up a series of recommendations for the ministers of justice and home affairs, i was forced to conclude that we have since then made the right use of the three paths outlined there to achieve this area, namely harmonization, mutual cooperation and the creation of actors. tomorrow, and by tomorrow i mean the day after tomorrow, i hope that at the laeken summit we will give fresh impetus to the decisions of amsterdam and the recommendations of tampere which have not yet been implemented. i say this with all the more conviction because, in my view, there are two areas which absolutely deserve attention: the fight against human trafficking and the sexual and economic exploitation of minors. the future, mr president. i have often heard it said that one should choose between freedom and security, but i do not think that is necessary. justice and security are two instruments which are necessary to guarantee freedoms. a correct comment that i often hear and that we cannot ignore is that we will have to ask ourselves about institutional decisionmaking and more specifically whether or not unanimity should be maintained in the third pillar. these are some of the concerns i wanted to put to the european parliament at the end of this debate.
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, very briefly to tell you, in reply to a question that was raised during the debate, that the american president wrote a letter to the belgian prime minister and the president of the european commission, and that letter indicated a number of areas in which the united states of america considered that there should be a need to deepen cooperation with the european union in the fight against terrorism. this letter was replied to by prime minister verhofstadt and president prodi on 28 november. that is the first point i would like to clarify. there is no private or special correspondence between the president of the european commission and the president of the united states. there is an exchange of correspondence between the american president and the european union, represented by both the president of the council and the president of the commission. as regards the substance of the questions, the truth is that we had already, i must tell you quite frankly, taken decisions in most cases on the projects which president bush mentioned at the justice and home affairs council meeting on 20 september, and which were also supported by the heads of state and government at the european council in brussels on 21 september. as far as the future is concerned, i think there are areas in cooperation with the united states which are difficult areas, we must not hide this. i have always said so, and i said so in particular at the justice and home affairs council meeting last week before the us secretary of state, mr colin powell. we have of course supported and we support the agreement that has been signed between europol and the us police agencies to cooperate in the fight against terrorism. this agreement does not include the possibility of exchanging personal data, because we recognize that this is a sensitive area in which there are differing standards between europeans and americans, and this area will have to be addressed separately in specific work which, moreover, will be undertaken as soon as possible. secondly, there is a rather important area of cooperation: that is legal aid and, once we have eurojust as a definitive unit, we will have an important tool for mutual legal aid with third countries. but here too the rules for the exchange of personal data in the context of mutual legal assistance involving third countries will have to be clarified. thirdly, on extradition, i agree with mr watson's assessment of the internal imbalance in the usa patriot act as regards the legal status of us citizens vis-à-vis other citizens, including europeans. and this is probably an area which we will have to discuss with our american friends. i also had the opportunity to say that there are no exceptional measures in europe in the fight against terrorism. we have not waived the charter of fundamental rights, we have not introduced any exceptional measures in the fight against terrorism and therefore i do not think it is right to criticise europe for adopting measures which it does not adopt. all the measures that are being implemented to combat terrorism and are in force are those that already stem from the existing legislative framework, or else they are measures such as the european arrest warrant or the framework decision on terrorism, which was in preparation well before 11 september and, moreover, in the case of the european arrest warrant there is no ambiguity, it was asked of us by the heads of state and government in october 1999 to replace extradition. all those who insist on trying to make these measures emergency measures are wrong: no, europe has not responded to the terrorist threat by derogating from fundamental principles or by taking emergency measures. we have responded by taking measures which may have been taken in an exceptional atmosphere, but which were demanded of us and had been planned for a long time. moreover, on the question of extradition, i repeat here in the european parliament that the commission has always said that we have never changed our position on the question of the death penalty, and that we have said with the utmost clarity that our position in this dialogue does not allow for any possibility of extradition to member states which apply the death penalty. that being said, i will of course read very carefully the resolution which the european parliament is about to adopt, to reflect carefully on the implications of your recommendation. i do not share mr di lello's view that if there are guarantees that the death penalty will not be applied, that is enough to ensure that fundamental values are respected. and that needs to be said very clearly. finally, mr president, i would like to say that i hope that the laeken european council will enable us to give fresh impetus to this major task of creating an area of freedom, security and justice, both in the field of asylum and immigration and in that of police and judicial cooperation, by accepting the gradual, pragmatic approach that we are pursuing. but i'm not under any illusions. when it comes to making europe an area of freedom, security and justice, we are touching the very heart of european political integration, and we know from our experience of 50 years that this political integration is never easy. we will, however, persevere, because i believe that our citizens expect us to give a political answer to the needs of european integration. that is why i am delighted to be able to participate with you in this project for an area of freedom, security and justice. counsel. - mr president, i think it is important to say something in response to the remarks that have just been made. on the one hand, there is the cultural, linguistic and other diversity which is one of the great assets of the european union and of europe in general; i know that in the current version of the text the richness of these diversities is presented as one of the most important assets of the european union. that's not a problem. on the other hand, the question arises whether we should break with what has been the practice in the european union up to now: the institutions of the european union do not interfere in judging constitutional changes made by the member states, provided, of course, that these changes remain compatible with fundamental principles such as human rights, the protection of minorities, etc. it's a consistent policy. i think that respect for diversity should not be confused with breaking away: in fact, this would be breaking away from this long tradition which seems to me to be wise, even if it is a personal judgment.

- mr president, i would first of all like to congratulate the rapporteur on his excellent report on conflict prevention, a subject on which this parliament has always been very clear. there is no doubt that the best way to win a war is to avoid it, and to avoid it there is no better weapon than to prevent it. that is, to go to the causes that cause it and work to solve them. for this, it is essential to have not only a horizontal approach - the approach proposed by the rapporteur, and rightly so - covering all the common policies of the european union, but also a global approach, involving the whole of society. hence the importance of non-structural measures to promote reconciliation, especially in areas emerging from violent conflict. without these measures, all the peacemaking efforts of the international community, or of the local communities themselves that the conflict has created, may come to nothing, as any slightest dispute may rekindle the flames of hatred that had provoked or created the conflict. it is necessary - and i ask the commission to do so in a very special way - to devote not only more attention but above all more resources to education for peace, in line with the work carried out by mayor zaragoza when he was head of unesco and which, a few days ago, kofi annan reminded us of. on the other hand, if control of the arms trade is important, so is that of the trade in diamonds and raw materials. in this connection, i also ask the commission to tell us what measures it intends to take to improve and make more effective the code of conduct on the control of diamond trafficking, especially since, as the european institutions and the united nations itself have denounced, the struggle for raw materials is often behind many of the conflicts that plague the world, especially the african continent.
commission. – mr president, i would like to thank mr lagendijk for another excellent report. i would also like to welcome his challenging remarks today about, for example, the civil peace corps which i suspect will continue to be a subject of lively debate. above all i would like to thank him for what he said about the external aspects of sustainable development. that is a subject on which we should all focus our attention in the run-up to the johannesburg conference next year. i hope in particular that parliament will take a special interest in some of the issues he raised, which are of fundamental importance if we are to be credible on sustainable development. this is a topical debate. mr wiersma suggested it was a dutch hobby. i am bound to say that, if it is, it is an extremely good dutch hobby and i recommend it to every one of the member states. there is a growing appreciation of the need to reinforce our efforts to tackle the factors that make conflict and violence arise in the first place. in the last century, conflict tended to be between states; i do not argue that sort conflict is over and done with. but in today’s world we face a new type of danger – the failed state, the state that is a danger to its own people and a menace to the rest of the world. let me be crystal clear. nothing excuses or mitigates terrorism. but in rooting out terrorism, we have to work to make sure that the world is hostile terrain – not fertile ground – for terrorists and those who back them. that can mean taking tough military action, as we do from time to time. but it also means exporting and entrenching democracy, the rule of law and good government; it means liberalising world trade, and using that and our development assistance to shrink the gap between the richest and the poorest, in a world in which the planet's three richest men own the equivalent of the gdp of the 48 poorest countries. earlier this year, the commission published the communication setting out our new strategy of conflict prevention. it is based on four main objectives. first, we want to make a more systematic and coordinated use of the european union's instruments to address the root causes of conflict. simply put, we want to get better leverage from our position as the world’s largest donor and as the top trading bloc. we are starting by integrating conflict prevention into our strategies towards partner countries, taking account of conflict indicators, for example, in our country strategy papers. the second objective of our communication is to raise the effectiveness of our actions in tackling 'cross-cutting issues' such as trafficking in drugs or arms, the trading of illicit goods, environmental degradation and so on. on all these fronts, the challenge is immense. let me just take, for example, the issue raised by mrs ferrer. the commission has played, over the last few months, an active role in the kimberley process, dealing with conflict diamonds. that is aimed at establishing an international control regime for the import and export of rough diamonds. after the political agreement reached at gaborone, two weeks ago, between the participants in this process, the commission is now launching the preparatory work for the full implementation by the community of the control regime in the course of next year. the third objective is to develop our ability to respond rapidly to emerging crises. concrete recommendations have been put forward, notably to improve the cfsp instruments, such as political dialogue or the use of special representatives. i can only agree with mr lagendijk that 'conflict prevention implies stronger commitment and political direction on the part of the member states, as the community instruments alone are not enough to resolve all possible sources of conflict'. what is required is a bit more of that old-fashioned commodity – political will. at community level, we have set up, at my initiative, a special rapid reaction mechanism to equip us to respond with the speed that events in the real world demand, but which the commission’s procedures are not always brilliantly designed to cope with. it is now fully operational, and is proving invaluable in current crises, for example in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia and in afghanistan where i hope to use the mechanism first of all to provide support for ambassador brahimi's team, secondly to provide support for the interim administration and, thirdly, to begin the work of demining. the fourth message is to promote international cooperation with governments, international organisations and civil society. the honourable member raised this. mr sacrédeus raised this as well. the un is a key partner here. we have a new framework, agreed by the general affairs council in june, for eu-un enhanced cooperation on conflict prevention and crisis management. as recommended by mr lagendijk, i am ready to work together with the council on an enhanced framework for cooperation with the osce. let me finish by giving you one example of what we have we done and what we are doing concretely in a key zone of conflict. i am just back from the great lakes region where we had a useful troika mission. last month, we committed funds under the rapid reaction mechanism to support the inter-congolese dialogue, to launch preparatory actions for the reintegration of child soldiers and to support independent media or other confidence-building initiatives.in november, we also committed money under the cfsp budget to finance the south african guard support unit for the protection of the recently returned political leaders in burundi. i was pleased to be able to meet them and have a briefing from them. in the region, we continue to carry out rehabilitation, to deliver humanitarian aid and to contribute to poverty alleviation. we stand ready to finance demilitarisation and demobilisation programmes as soon as they get started. so we are, i hope and believe, raising our game. we were starting to do so before the horrific events of three months ago which the honourable member referred to. but we know now how much is at stake; we know how preventing conflict abroad is vital to our own security here at home. we know that we cannot slacken our efforts, but rather, as mr lagendijk has argued, we need to redouble those efforts. that is the very least we should be doing in response to the atrocities of 11 september.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 10 a.m.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of ships is not compromised by the fact that the safety of ships is not guaranteed by the safety of the ships. the commission has responded quickly to these demands by presenting the three proposals known as the 'erika i package', which we are still debating two years after that disaster, although we have finally reached two agreements with the council, which are final for the first two. in the case of the amendment of the directive on common rules and standards for organisations which classify, inspect and examine ships on behalf of maritime administrations, parliament's amendments to the commission's original proposal focused from the outset on the practical aspects of the application of the classification system, on improving transparency of information on the quality of inspections, on the periodic audit of such organisations and on the withdrawal of their community recognition in the event of serious accidents, and on the financial liability of such organisations for damage and accidents where there is evidence of negligence in inspections. after the council adopted its common position, parliament moved on to the second reading, where we insisted on issues relating to the management of conflicts of interest which may arise between classification societies or organisations and ship owners and/or charterers, and on financial liability in cases of negligence or omission in the examination of the ship. after the council had indicated that it could not accept all the parliament's amendments, the conciliation phase was started between the representatives of the two community institutions. the discussion focused first on the issue of conflict of interest, where finally the council accepted that a classification organisation should not be controlled by owners or shipbuilders or by other persons or entities that are commercially engaged in the construction, equipment, repair or operation of ships; and also that, at the time of applying for recognition, classification societies and their inspectors should individually undertake in writing not to accept regulatory tasks where there is a risk of conflict of interest and in particular where such societies are themselves the owners or shipowners of the ship to be inspected, or have commercial, personal or family links with the owners or shipowners. the parliamentary delegation, while considering that a large part of the work carried out by inspectors is the responsibility of the maritime administration and that this should be a subsidiary responsibility, accepted that it was not obligatory for the member states to set a ceiling on the financial liability of classification societies in the event of damage caused by their slight negligence in inspections, although, if they - the member states - wished to set such a ceiling, it could not be less than eur 2 and eur 4 million respectively, depending on whether the damage affected only objects or also persons. however, the delegations of the two institutions considered that this issue should be examined in the context of the evaluation report to be submitted by the commission within three years on the economic impact of the liability regime and, in particular, on its consequences for the financial balance of the recognised organisations. if necessary, the commission will, in the light of this evaluation, submit a proposal for amendment of this directive, which will, in particular, address the principle of responsibility and the maximum limitation of the financial contribution. in conclusion, i believe that the european parliament can consider the final result of the conciliation satisfactory, since most of our amendments have been incorporated, either in full, in a revised form or in their spirit, into the joint text, and we therefore propose that the latter text be adopted in plenary at third reading. finally, i would draw the attention of the competent judicial authorities to the fact that certain victims of the erika accident have still not received any compensation for the damage suffered, despite the fact that two years have passed since this sadly remembered event.

- doc. a5-0417/2001 by mr pérez royo, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on financial guarantee contracts (com (2001) 168 - c5-0131/2001 - 2001/0086 (cod)).
the rapporteur. - mr president, the commission proposal on financial guarantee agreements establishes the european legislative framework for such agreements and is an essential proposal for the functioning of the financial market at european level. this is an essential element of the package of legislative proposals designed to achieve this. the main objectives of the proposal are - very briefly - to ensure that there are effective and reasonably simple arrangements for the conclusion of agreements, both for security and for security with transfer of title or 'repos'. this requires certain amendments to the legal systems of the various member states, particularly in the area of the regulation of mortgages and also in the area of bankruptcy and insolvency proceedings. the aim is to create a sound and effective system to limit credit risk and thus ensure a reduction in its cost and, at the same time, improve the functioning and stability of european financial markets. from the european parliament's point of view, the main problem raised by the proposal was that of the subjective scope of the directive. the initial proposal was basically to restrict the scope of the directive to financial institutions and to non-financial companies which are really large, i.e. large commercial, industrial or service companies, which reach eur 100 million in share capital or eur 1 billion in gross assets. this proposal had two drawbacks from the point of view of the european parliament, or at least from the point of view of the rapporteur. firstly, the removal from the scope of the directive, and consequently from its benefits, of most non-financial enterprises, not only small and mediumsized ones, but also large enterprises which do not reach the very high quantitative limits to which i have referred. secondly, the very setting of quantitative thresholds raises the problem of their revision and updating. the proposal for a directive solved this problem by the technique of delegating this update to the commission, assisted by the securities supervisory committee, the so-called 'lamfalussy committee'. this is a legislative delegation, a delegation of powers which is inadmissible for parliament, or at least for part of it, as is well known, because this is not the first time that we have dealt with the lamfalussy committee, in this and other areas, with commissioner bolkestein himself. the amendment which parliament intends to introduce in this area essentially consists of the following: to remove the reference to quantitative limits and, instead, to establish the requirement that, in these cases of agreements with commercial or industrial undertakings, the other party to the agreement, normally the person taking the guarantee of the creditor, be a financial institution. this solution has the advantage of solving both the problems i have mentioned, namely the problem of the exclusion of small firms and the problem of delegation of powers - or the lamfalussy committee, to be precise. apart from this amendment, which is itself divided into several, there are others concerning the formalisation of contracts and the means of proving the provision of guarantees, the regulation of the right of use in cases of security by mortgage and other matters on which i shall not go into detail. in conclusion, mr president, i should like to point out - and this is very important - that from the outset i have tried to work closely with the commission and the belgian presidency, whose help i very sincerely thank at this time. the aim was to reach a consensus which would make it possible to adopt the proposal for a directive at first reading or at least to reduce the second reading to a mere procedure. we were basing ourselves on this claim, since most of the actors, both member states and industry actors, shared the importance and a basic consensus, except on a few points, around this proposal. this objective seemed to have been achieved, since it appeared that an agreement had been reached in the council working party which also satisfied the essential demands of parliament. at the last moment the initial agreement in the council working party has been broken and tomorrow a different agreement may be adopted in the ecofin, including other points which have not been able to be considered in detail by parliament. i am afraid that the purpose, to which i referred earlier, of avoiding the second reading, or at least reducing it to a procedure, will not be possible, and we will have to continue working on this directive from next month. in this case, for tomorrow's vote, i ask for the amendments which were adopted in the committee on economic and monetary affairs of this parliament to be voted on with a slight modification and i ask for the vote against an amendment which was tabled in parliament at the last moment, since the lack of consensus in the council, that is to say, the lack of consensus among the states, has also had the effect of breaking the consensus which had been expressed in the committee on economic affairs of this parliament.
commission. – mr president, i should like to begin by thanking very much your rapporteur, mr pérez royo, and the members of the committee on economic and monetary affairs for the excellent work and very constructive approach on the collateral proposal. this proposal, as was emphasised by mr karas just now, is a priority dossier in the financial services action plan and it is a crucial element for the timely delivery of the fsap by 2003 for an integrated european union securities market, and the year 2005 for the fsap overall. given that the value of outstanding contracts on the european repo market alone exceeds eur 1.8 billion, the expected benefits are extremely large. these contracts will, when the directive is implemented in the member states, be governed by one legal regime, instead of 15 different ones. such a uniform pan-eu legal framework for the use of collateral will contribute to the greater integration and cost-efficiency of european financial markets, by encouraging cross-border business and creating a more competitive european financial market. now i come to the tabled amendments. the commission generally supports all the amendments except for amendment nos 16 and 21 which deal with extended protection of top-up collateral and the restriction of the scope respectively. we fully support amendments nos 1, 2, 18 and19 as they stand. in addition, and subject to some rewording, which we do not expect will cause any difficulties for parliament, we can also accept in principle amendment nos 3 to 15, 17 and 20. but we may need some flexibility in finding a final agreement. by supporting amendment no 1, we are not abolishing protection of credit-related top-up collateral. but the commission cannot accept amendment no 16 which protects credit risk top-up collateral under the directive, and nor, we believe, can the council. nonetheless, as provided by amendment no 1, it would be possible under national law to protect that kind of collateral. to be more precise, amendment no 16 is not acceptable to the commission because it could strongly conflict with insolvency law policy which generally discourages improvement of a creditor’s position as a result of an insolvency-related event or at least in a context of deteriorating credit-worthiness. amendment no 21 is not acceptable to the commission because the commission would like to see as many non-financial companies as possible benefiting from this directive. those companies are already using these techniques in the market. in conclusion, i should like once again to thank members of parliament for their sterling cooperation. i have also been apprised of what has occurred today in coreper, as the rapporteur, mr pérez royo, mentioned. tomorrow, as he said, there will be an ecofin meeting at which i myself will be present. i do not know what the discussion will lead to tomorrow. i regret the need for a second reading for obvious reasons, but i cannot help that. the commission is in the hands of council on the one hand and parliament on the other. lastly, i should like to say to mr lehne that i quite agree with him on the timing of this debate. it is an commission. – mr president, article 96 consultations will not be easy but we should give them a chance. zimbabwe confirmed its participation, but the original date of 19 december for the start of these consultations was yesterday postponed. we do not have an indication of another date. the idea is to hold them next month. it has been indicated that sadc, acp and the oau will be invited to and included in these consultations. this is good because it broadens out the scope by anchoring in africa the kind of discussion we have to go through with zimbabwe. the consultations will focus on the issues which matter to us – human rights, democracy, the rule of law, good governance and the escalation of violence. the consultations will provide an opportunity to seek the government's views and their firm commitment in the following areas: politically motivated violence, elections, freedom of the media, the judiciary and illegal occupation of properties. i would like to reassure parliament that these consultations cover practically the totality of the issues raised in their draft resolutions. i would like to stress that there will also be a clear eu position on the points zimbabwe is bound to raise, such as land reform, interference in its internal affairs, alleged support for the opposition and the imposition of what they call "white values". finally, not pre-judging the outcome of the consultations and handling them in the spirit of the cotonou agreement is not only necessary to address the situation with zimbabwe, it is also necessary to maintain mutual trust and confidence between the eu and acp countries. but respecting the rules and the spirit of these consultations is not the same as carrying them out in a vague and weak manner. this is not how the piano is going to be played! as regards electoral monitoring, the commission is getting prepared for this. the government of zimbabwe has announced that it will not accept monitors; it will only invite friends to observe the presidential elections. the auguries for an eu presence are not too good, but we will be able to mount an eu mission should this be feasible. we are maintaining flexibility to react to developments and possibilities. a key requirement will be that no international observation mission – whether multilateral or bilateral – is manipulated by mugabe into sending short-term observers only for polling day. we have to keep in mind that last year polling day itself was relatively calm. it is clear that the campaigning period in the run-up to the poll is crucial for determining the fairness of the electoral process itself. the commission considers that a minimum length of observation time – that is, one month – is necessary and we are discouraging others from sending short-term observers only. the commission has suggested that the eu focus its approach on the sadc parliamentary forum's norms and standards, which comply with the un standards and have been endorsed by zimbabwe's ruling zanu-pf party. there are indications that other international partners, such as the commonwealth and the united states, will agree to use those standards, which would then allow the international community to judge the openness and fairness of the elections. in parallel, the sadc electoral forum and the electoral commissions forum of sadc countries are being encouraged to open a dialogue with the zimbabwe authorities and the political parties, on the preparations for the presidential election. we see close collaboration with sadc in this election-related activity as a way of creating some sort of base-line case so that we will be able to do something if we cannot participate directly. but this is the preferred option, and zimbabwe should welcome the eu observers. the commission has remained engaged in the country in order, on the one hand, not to pre-judge the outcome of the consultations and at the same time to up the stakes for zimbabwe of an eventual failure – thus increasing the pressure on them to cooperate. this is the rationale of what we are doing at this moment. we have therefore taken the following actions: the commission has currently a mission on the ground to assess humanitarian needs and food security issues. this we will do in any case, whatever the political outcome. preliminary results show that, remarkably, the deterioration of the situation is much slower than could have been expected. the commission has also participated in the undp land mission. successful or not, it is worth exerting a positive pressure on zimbabwe by doing anything possible to move forward the dossier of land reform. the commission has maintained, as i mentioned before, its offer to support the electoral process. we continue preparing our cooperation under the new five-year funding cycle, not least to demonstrate to the government of zimbabwe what it has to lose. we will not take any decisions on whether or not to proceed with signing and implementing the country strategy for zimbabwe until after the consultations have been concluded. to sign or not to sign is a very important question in many cases and here it is quite clear that we want the consultations concluded before we move on. but not to prepare would also imply lack of respect of the whole process of planning in the cotonou framework. the regional dimension is important. it appears that zimbabwe's neighbours are becoming increasingly concerned with the deterioration of the situation and the potentially very dramatic consequences for the country and the whole region. this is why we have taken the initiative to maintain close contact with sadc and nigeria in view of article 96 consultations. it is, in fact, the first time ever that the opening of these consultations has included a reference to the use of our partners in the region. the general affairs council accepted this approach, ensuring close coordination and complementarity with sadc and the abuja process. the commission and presidency have proceeded with a series of informal exchanges with sadc and nigeria against this background. we note that these african partners are already exerting effective peer pressure on mugabe so that a solution to the crisis may be found. the emerging african ownership approach has to be welcomed, particularly in view of the negative effect that the continuing crisis in zimbabwe is having on its neighbours. i must confess that the outlook is not optimistic. things look very bad as we move into these consultations.

commission. – the commission shares parliament’s concern about the humanitarian, economic and social problems caused by a variety of unexploded ordnance such as cluster bombs and the particular difficulties of clearing contaminated areas. a number of studies on cluster bombs show that no less than 10% of delivered cluster bomblets fail to explode on impact and that the remaining unexploded ones tend to have effects similar to anti-personnel landmines. they also are victim-activated and provoke fatal or disabling injuries as serious as those caused by landmines. the commission has taken due note of the proposal submitted by the international committee of the red cross to address the problems caused by cluster bombs and other 'explosive remnants of war' at the review conference of the un convention on the prohibition or restriction on the use of certain conventional weapons. this approach is broadly shared by the eu. at the review conference, which is being held in geneva from 11 to 21 december 2001, the eu will present a common position on the issue of the unexploded remnants of war, requesting concrete steps to address this issue under the ccw framework. with this in mind, we have carried out diplomatic démarches to prepare the ground for a successful outcome of the geneva meeting. parliament's initiative is therefore particularly timely and welcome. the commission will closely follow developments at the ccw review conference. on an operational level, the commission is already providing an indirect but tangible contribution to the reduction of the threat posed by cluster bombs and other unexploded ordnance through the legal and budgetary instrument of the anti-personnel landmines regulation. mine clearance carried out under this regulation encompasses de facto clearance of other unexploded ordnance. we are already engaged in such broader clearance activities in countries such as laos and the federal republic of yugoslavia and kosovo, where the anti-personnel landmine problem is very clearly connected to unexploded ordnance pollution. mine clearance is also supported as part of echo-funded humanitarian aid in many countries and as part of development activities when we are carrying out echo-financed reconstruction work or building roads, etc. in a number of countries. a week ago, in kabul, i saw de-mining activities funded by echo. through two organisations we have employed something like 1 500 to 2 000 local afghan staff who are continually working on de-mining. we walked on marked paths in areas where i counted 30 to 40 recent non-exploded cluster bombs. they do not necessarily stay on the surface of the ground. if a neighbouring cluster bomblet explodes it may bury a few others and functionally they become anti-personnel landmines. they have three functions: armour penetration capability, spraying shards of shrapnel from the casing, and starting a fire. it was a very morbid experience but it gives me real satisfaction that we are funding this kind of activity on a large scale. certainly this is a main priority in the present situation where we are working to make it possible for the refugees to return home safely.
